 Nup153p, a 58 kDa nucleoporin, is a component of the nuclear pore complex and plays an important role in the transport of large molecules into and out of the nucleus [2, 3]. Nup153p contains two important domains: (i) a 20 amino acid long nuclear localization signal (NLS) domain and (ii) a 45 amino acid long domain that is homologous to a nuclear export signal (NES) . The NLS domain is thought to function as a signal for nuclear localization while the NES domain is believed to function as a signal for nuclear export. The NLS domain of Nup153p interacts with Nup107/160, a member of the nucleoporin complex .
 The nuclear export of Nup153p is thought to be regulated by the NES domain. This is supported by the results of various studies [6, 7]. In the present study, we have tested whether the NLS domain of Nup153p is sufficient for its nuclear localization in a cell-free system. The NLS domain contains 20 amino acid residues, which is the minimal domain required for nuclear localization. Using a cell-free system, we have isolated the NLS domain of Nup153p and expressed the purified protein in the cytoplasm of HeLa cells. The protein was found to be translocated to the nucleus. In addition, we have identified a 56 amino acid long region of Nup153p which is sufficient for its interaction with the nucleoporin complex and its transport function.

rtant ) , they turned mathematics into a science .
The two men who did this were , respectively , Gottlob Frege and Bertrand Russell . They had both studied the writings of the German mathematician Georg Cantor , whose work on set theory had been published in 1891 . Cantor had shown by logical means that there were infinitely many different sizes of numbers; this was a ground-breaking result in the new discipline of mathematics , and Cantor was convinced that there were thousands more astonishing discoveries waiting to be made .
But when Cantor himself attempted to prove that there were in fact _no_ sets that were the same size as themselves , his argument proved to be invalid . It is a classic mathematical problem : Cantor gave the example of the real numbers, a set of infinitely many numbers that are all different from one another . He said that there were infinite sets that were _not_ equal to themselves: for example , the set of real numbers between zero and one , or the set of real numbers between zero and two . But Frege and Russell proved that Cantor's argument was invalid : _any_ set of numbers is equal to itself . In other words , there is no set that is _not_ equal to itself .
Cantor's paradox is the first in a series of devastating blows that mathematical logic will deliver to the mathematical enterprise. It shows that the arguments of mathematical logic are not strong enough to provide the foundations of mathematics. More damagingly , it shows that the assumptions that underlie the arguments of mathematical logic are not valid .
The implication of this is that the foundations of mathematics cannot be guaranteed by logical arguments . Mathematics is therefore not a science.
Let me explain what I mean.
Mathematics is a science because its theories are established by proofs that stand up to logical scrutiny . The most important step in establishing a mathematical theory is to prove that it is true . This step is what we normally mean by a mathematical proof .
A mathematical proof is simply a logical argument that demonstrates there is no other possibility but that the theory is true . For example , the proof that there are infinitely many real numbers between zero and one, say, is a logical argument that there is no other possibility but that there are infinitely many real numbers between zero and one .
A mathematical theory is a body of mathematical statements that are all true . We say that a mathematical theory is _consistent_ if it is possible to prove that all its statements are true , and _inconsistent_ if it is not.
This is how we recognize a mathematical theory: by its consistency .
So mathematics is a science because it is based on proofs that are logically sound .
But what if mathematical arguments fail to be logically sound? What if a mathematical theory is neither consistent nor inconsistent?
This is the situation that Frege and Russell discovered in Cantor's paradox. The argument that attempts to prove that there are no sets that are equal to themselves is clearly invalid: there _is_ a set that is equal to itself, namely the set of all sets that are equal to themselves. But no logical argument can disprove that there are no other such sets; there is no way of showing that the set of all sets that are equal to themselves is not equal to itself.
Cantor's paradox therefore shows that mathematics is not a science because its foundations cannot be guaranteed by logical arguments. Mathematics is therefore not a science.
#  **1.2 Mathematics as a science**
The fact that mathematics cannot be established by logical arguments is a disaster. It means that mathematical theories are not established by proofs , that mathematics is not a science.
To make matters worse, mathematical logic is the only known way of _defining_ mathematical theories. Scientific theories are defined by logical arguments: the theory of relativity, for example, is defined by the logical arguments that prove that the theory is true. Mathematical theories must therefore be defined by logical arguments too .
But if the logical arguments that define mathematical theories are invalid, then mathematical theories are not defined and are therefore meaningless .
Mathematics, then, is _not_ a science .
Why did Frege and Russell think that mathematics was a science?
The answer is that they believed that mathematical theories were the truths that simple logical arguments could prove .
But this belief is false. Mathematical theories are not the truths that simple logical arguments can prove .

He did not see the second plane hit.
He did not see the third plane hit.
But he saw the towers fall.

Dylan had seen the first plane hit, and he saw the smoke.
But he did not see the planes hit the towers.
But he saw the towers fall.

The 2004 Friends Provident Trophy was a one-day cricket competition, held in England in 2004. It was the 45th edition of the competition since its establishment in 1963. The tournament was won by Gloucestershire County Cricket Club, who beat Somerset County Cricket Club by 12 runs in the final at the Rose Bowl in Southampton, Hampshire. Gloucestershire won the title for the first time, having been beaten finalists on three occasions.
Middlesex and Surrey were the defending champions, having won the 2003 Friends Provident Trophy. However, they were both knocked out of the competition in the quarter-finals.
The tournament consisted of 32 teams, including the 16 first-class counties, the 16 teams in the second tier of the domestic one-day cricket structure, and Sussex, who were given a bye into the second round. The 32 teams were divided into eight groups of four, with each group having one team from Division One, one team from Division Two and two teams who had been given a bye into the second round. The top two teams in each group progressed to the quarter-finals, where the four Division One teams were joined by the four second-tier winners.
Gloucestershire won the competition, defeating Somerset by 12 runs in the final at the Rose Bowl. Gloucestershire's Chris Taylor was named Player of the Tournament.

Waterfall Gully is part of the state electoral district of Bragg , which has been held since 2002 by Liberal MP Vickie Chapman

and has been a Liberal seat since 1959.
The seat covers a large chunk of the Adelaide Hills and the foothills east of Adelaide in the Mount Lofty Ranges.
In the 2004 federal election, Bragg recorded a 4.9% swing against the Liberals, which was the biggest swing in South Australia.
The seat was first contested at the 1959 election when it was won by Liberal candidate John Cock who held the seat until his retirement at the 1972 election.
The seat was won by Liberal candidate John James at the 1972 election and held until his retirement at the 1983 election.
The seat was retained by Liberal candidate Peter Duncan at the 1983 election and held until his retirement at the 1990 election.
The seat was won by Liberal candidate Michael Johnson at the 1990 election and held until his retirement at the 1993 election.
The seat was won by Liberal candidate Vickie Chapman at the 1993 election and has been held by her ever since.

In chess tournaments and matches , the frequency with which each player receives white and black is an important consideration

for players.  Spectators who are unfamiliar with the game may also have an interest in knowing which player is to move first in a given game.
 There are many different methods of determining who should receive white.  One of the oldest is to flip a coin.  This method works well for some players, but some players have a losing record when playing with white.  Whether this is due to superstition or to an unconscious belief that it is somehow more advantageous to play with black, they may not want to use it in important games.
 Another method is called the "flip of the coin" . In this method, the players take turns flipping a coin.  If it is not decided by the coin toss, then the players flip again.  This method is easier to determine than the standard coin toss, but is less accurate because it is not based on a random process.

With the ever-increasing number of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in the world, it's not surprising that condoms are widely recommended for the prevention of STIs. They have been shown to be effective in preventing all STIs except HIV infection, and they are more effective when used correctly than when used incorrectly.
The widespread use of condoms for the prevention of STIs is based on a series of experiments on condom effectiveness. One of the earliest of these, the Waterhouse study of 1972, was a prospective study of 100 couples. These couples were asked to have sexual intercourse at least twice each week with the use of a condom. The women were examined for STIs at least once every three months. The results of the study showed that the condom was 98% effective in preventing STIs.
Subsequent studies have shown that the effectiveness of condoms in preventing STIs depends on a number of factors:
  * The type of condom – latex is more effective than natural rubber
  * The way the condom is handled by the user – it is estimated that incorrect use of condoms (for example, failure to use water-based lubricants) causes 15% of condom failures
  * The method of application – a study by the US National Institute of Child Health and Human Development showed that the effectiveness of condoms in preventing STIs was better when applied by a health worker than when applied by the user.
The subject of this chapter is the use of condoms for the prevention of STIs. Sexually transmitted infections can be thought of as being spread by three mechanisms:
  * direct transmission, in which the infection is passed from an infected person to a susceptible person
  * indirect transmission, in which the infection is passed from one person to another (for example, from an infected mother to her child or from an infected person to a sexual contact)
  * mechanically, in which the infection is transmitted by a reusable object, such as an injection or blood transfusion needle

The effectiveness of condoms depends on the type of infection and the number of sexual contacts.
**Direct transmission:** The effectiveness of condoms in preventing direct transmission of STIs is usually very high. For example, the effectiveness of condoms in preventing gonorrhoea is 98% (Waterhouse study, 1972); in preventing syphilis it is 97% (Waterhouse study, 1972); in preventing herpes it is 85% (US National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, 1989); and in preventing HIV infection it is 96% (CDC, 2001).
**Indirect transmission:** The effectiveness of condoms in preventing indirect transmission of STIs is lower than in preventing direct transmission. This is because most STIs are spread by the direct transmission of infection from person to person, but a few are spread by indirect transmission. For example, in preventing hepatitis B infection it is 94% (Kramer et al., 1995); in preventing hepatitis C infection it is 82% (Ward et al., 1996).

Condoms are most effective when they are used correctly.

Like all streams in Lycoming and Sullivan Counties , Plunketts Creek served as an area for settlers to establish homesteads , m

ined for coal and timbered. Laurel Lake, a reservoir built to provide hydroelectric power, dammed Plunketts Creek. The stream was also dammed to provide water for the nearby town of Potters Mills, and was the source for the town's drinking water until 1981, when it was replaced with water from the nearby Mill Creek.
The drainage basin of Plunketts Creek is 21.7 miles (34.9 km) long and covers 29 square miles (75 km2). For most of its length, the creek flows through the townships of Springville and Plunketts Creek in Lycoming County and the townships of Forks and Lake in Sullivan County. The streams headwaters are in Springville Township in Lycoming County, and the stream flows east for 3.1 miles (5.0 km) through Springville Township before crossing into Plunketts Creek Township. The creek flows southeast for 1.2 miles (1.9 km), then turns east for another 1.2 miles (1.9 km). After leaving Plunketts Creek Township, the stream crosses into Forks Township where it flows south for 0.8 miles (1.3 km). The creek then turns southeast for 0.9 miles (1.4 km) before crossing into Lake Township. The stream flows 1.5 miles (2.4 km) through Lake Township, then turns southeast for 1.2 miles (1.9 km) before crossing back into Plunketts Creek Township. The creek then flows southeast for 1.3 miles (2.1 km) before turning east for 0.4 miles (0.64 km) through Plunketts Creek Township. The creek then flows east for 0.8 miles (1.3 km) before turning southeast for 0.8 miles (1.3 km) and then turning east for 0.7 miles (1.1 km) before ending at Laurel Lake.
The watershed of Plunketts Creek contains two tributaries, both which are less than a mile in length. The first of these tributaries is called Lantz Hollow Creek, which flows into the creek in Plunketts Creek Township. Lantz Hollow Creek drains an area of 0.4 square miles (1.0 km2). The second tributary of Plunketts Creek is called Cutler Creek, which drains an area of 0.5 square miles (1.3 km2). Cutler Creek flows into Plunketts Creek in Lake Township.
The streams flowing into Plunketts Creek are mostly minor streams. The biggest tributary draining into the creek is called Mill Creek. Mill Creek flows into Plunketts Creek in Plunketts Creek Township. Mill Creek drains an area of 4.6 square miles (12 km2) and has an average discharge of 1.3 cubic feet per second (0.037 m3/s). The next largest tributary is called Cutler Hollow Creek, which drains an area of 2.6 square miles (6.7 km2) and has an average discharge of 0.6 cubic feet per second (0.017 m3/s). The next largest tributary is called Lantz Hollow Creek, which drains an area of 1.6 square miles (4.1 km2) and has an average discharge of 0.4 cubic feet per second (0.011 m3/s).
The United States Census Bureau determined the elevation of Plunketts Creek at 1,000 feet (300 m) above sea level.
Plunketts Creek flows through two major communities in its watershed. The first of these communities is called Potters Mills, which is located in Sullivan County. The second of these communities is called Springville, which is located in Lycoming County.
The watershed of Plunketts Creek is in the outer Ridge and Valley Province of the Northeastern United States. The Appalachian Mountains form a barrier that divides watersheds of the east coast from those of the central United States. The Ridge and Valley Province is located between the Blue Ridge Mountains and the Allegheny Plateau.

After McDougal 's June 1914 commissioning , she sailed off the east coast and in the Caribbean . She was one of the U.S. destro

ys that participated in the destruction of the German merchant raider SMS Dresden during the World War I . On 19 August 1914, McDougal under Commander J. A. Welch, was ordered to patrol the Strait of Dover . She intercepted the German merchant freighter SMS Dantzig and escorted her to the French port of Cherbourg. On 17 September 1914, while searching for the German submarine SM U-1, McDougal was struck by a torpedo fired by SM U-13. Despite efforts by McDougal's crew to escape, McDougal sank.
Reconstructed at the Philadelphia Navy Yard , McDougal was commissioned on 26 August 1915. Originally, McDougal was ordered to report to the Pacific Fleet , however, she was ordered to repossess the American destroyer USS Stewart , which had been seized by the Japanese government. After repossessing the Stewart, McDougal arrived in the Atlantic Fleet on 19 December 1915.
 McDougal spent most of her time training at the torpedo testing station in Newport, Rhode Island until being assigned to the Pacific Fleet as a unit of Squadron 3, Destroyer Division 21. Arriving in Hawaii on 27 January 1917, McDougal remained there until the United States entered World War I .
 McDougal sailed for the East Coast and arrived in Norfolk on 16 April 1917, where she was assigned to the Atlantic Fleet. On 25 June 1917, McDougal was involved in a collision with the battleship USS Wyoming , which led to McDougal's decommissioning and subsequent repairs in Philadelphia. During the collision, McDougal suffered significant damage, including a broken propeller shaft, and her boiler room flooded.
 McDougal was recommissioned on 11 May 1918, and sailed for the Atlantic Fleet. She arrived in Norfolk on 23 June 1918, and was assigned to Destroyer Squadron 4. In September, she sailed for France and arrived at Brest on 10 October 1918. During the voyage, she was the first American destroyer to cross the Atlantic Ocean east of the Azores.
 McDougal took part in bombardments of German shore installations in July 1918, and was at Brest on 11 November 1918, when the Armistice was signed. She was decommissioned on 28 November 1918, and was placed in reserve at Philadelphia.
McDougal was recommissioned on 17 January 1920, and was assigned to the Atlantic Fleet. She was assigned to training duties in the Caribbean , and in the spring of 1921 sailed to the Mediterranean Sea.
 McDougal returned to the Caribbean in 1922, and was decommissioned on 16 January 1923. She was struck from the Navy List on 1 March 1923, and was sold to Seattle Iron and Metal Company on 15 March 1923.

Track and field athletes are banned from ingesting or using certain substances by governing bodies for the sport [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_associations], from the national level to the international. The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_anti-doping_agency] has established a list of substances that are prohibited in-competition in order to prevent doping. Certain over-the-counter medications are also banned, as they may cause a false positive. In addition to the prohibited substances list, a list of therapeutic use exemptions (TUEs) is established to allow athletes with specific medical conditions to use the prohibited substances without facing sanctions.

The 2011 World Anti-Doping Code [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_anti-doping_code] has established a series of sanctions for athletes that are found to have violated the anti-doping regulations, ranging from a reprimand to a lifetime ban from the sport. In addition, many national and international sports federations have established additional sanctions for athletes that are found to have committed doping offences, such as fines, suspensions, injunctions, and ineligibility for certain competitions.

## History

The modern movement against doping in sports began in the 1950s in response to the use of anabolic steroids by athletes. In 1966, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_olympic_committee] established an anti-doping committee, which was later expanded to include other international sports organizations. The first international anti-doping organization was established in 1968, and by 1975, there were over 120 organizations in the anti-doping movement.

In 1989, the IOC established the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_anti-doping_agency], which was given the responsibility of coordinating and monitoring the anti-doping activities of the international sports organizations and national anti-doping organizations. WADA also established the World Anti-Doping Code [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_anti-doping_code], which is the basis for the anti-doping activities of the sports organizations.

Since the establishment of WADA, the number of national anti-doping organizations has grown from 120 to over 1000. The number of athletes tested has also increased significantly, from around 10,000 in 1999 to over 350,000 in 2009.

## International organizations

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_olympic_committee] is the international governing body for the Olympic Games and other multi-sports events. The IOC is also responsible for the development of the Olympic Charter [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_charter], which establishes the rules and regulations for the Olympic Movement, including the anti-doping rules.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_anti-doping_agency] is responsible for coordinating and monitoring the anti-doping activities of the international sports organizations and national anti-doping organizations. WADA also establishes the World Anti-Doping Code [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_anti-doping_code], which is the basis for the anti-doping activities of the sports organizations.

The World Association of Sports Federations (WADA) [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_association_of_sports_federations] is the international governing body for the sports industry. ## Plot

The USS Enterprise (NCC-1701-D) takes a shuttlecraft to Enterprise Station, a Starfleet outpost near the Klingon border, to deliver a diplomatic message. They are attacked by a Klingon bird-of-prey, and Captain Picard is injured. The Enterprise heads to the station for repairs. Picard, in a coma, is transported to the hospital. The crew of the Enterprise, on the station, discover a Klingon ship has been in the Enterprise engine room. They also discover a Klingon spy has been on the station.

A Klingon ship suddenly appears and, using the station's computers, takes over all Federation and Klingon ships in the area. Picard awakes and, with the help of Dr. Crusher, leaves the hospital to return to the Enterprise. The Enterprise arrives at the station and they discover that the station has been taken over. They are attacked by a Klingon Bird of Prey and a pair of Romulan Warbirds. The Enterprise, under the command of Worf, escapes to the nearby planet, Khitomer, where the Klingon and Federation governments signed a peace treaty.

The Enterprise is attacked by the Klingon ship and the crew is captured. Worf is killed. However, Picard is able to contact Starfleet and has Enterprise sent to the station. They discover that the Bird of Prey is under the control of the Borg. Picard and Dr. Crusher are transported to the Borg's central control facility. While there, they discover that the Borg have been manipulating the Federation and the Klingon Empire, which they are now using as pawns to contact the Q Continuum.

The Borg attempt to assimilate the Enterprise, but Jean-Luc Picard reprograms the Borg's central computer. The Borg attack the Enterprise and the Klingon and Federation ships. The Borg's first attempt to attack the Enterprise fails, and the Borg, under the control of the Continuum, remove their inhibitor chips. A Borg ship is destroyed by the Enterprise.

The Borg ships surround the Enterprise. Data and Troi, in the Enterprise, are taken over by the Borg. Crusher and Picard escape from the Borg control facility and are taken to the Enterprise, where they are needed to help reprogram the Borg's computers. Meanwhile, the Borg attack the Enterprise. The Borg begin to assimilate the Enterprise. The Borg begin to assimilate Picard.

Meanwhile, the Borg's control structure begins to fail and the Borg attack the Enterprise. The Borg's control matrix is destroyed and Picard is able to reprogram the Borg's computers to reverse the process of assimilation. The Borg ships begin to destroy themselves.

The Enterprise escapes the Borg attack and all Borg ships self-destruct. The Enterprise takes the Klingon and Federation ships to Khitomer, where they give the message they were sent to deliver. The Enterprise and the other ships continue on their way.

on the name "Kaw" or "Kansas" , a name accepted for the entire river. The Kaw was the western boundary of the Osage lands, and at the mouth of the Marais des Cygnes River was the western boundary of the Shawnee nation.
The Kansas River was named for the Kansa ("people of the south wind") , an Iowa-Otoe-Missouria-Ponca tribe who originally lived near the mouth of the Kansas River. The Kansa were among the first tribes encountered by the French explorers, and the name was applied to the river.
The name of the river is derived from the Kansa (Kaw), a tribe of Native American Indians who lived near the mouth of the river. It is the westernmost of the rivers of the Mississippi River system and flows southward for most of its course through Kansas .
The Kansas River , also called the Kaw River, is a major tributary of the Missouri River . It is formed by the confluence of the Republican River and the Smoky Hill River in what is now western Kansas .

Dylan had been in an accident on July 29 , 1966 at 11:30 P.M. on a country road in Woodstock , New York . Dylan had ridden his motorcycle in the same area of Woodstock , New York at least 10 times before the accident. In 1965 , he had spent time in Woodstock after a gig in the Catskills . He had also vacationed there with Suzie Rotolo . They had been visiting with a friend of theirs who lived in Woodstock. They had gone for a ride and stopped for dinner at a diner in Saugerties . Dylan was familiar with the country road where he had the accident. He had driven it many times before the accident .

Dylan was still recovering from the accident when his parents came to visit him. After his parents left, Dylan and Rotolo reconciled. They were back together by March, 1966 .

Hoover Dam , once known as Boulder Dam , is a concrete arch @-@ gravity dam in the Black Canyon of the Colorado River , on the

border  between the US  states of  Nevada and Arizona . Construction of the dam was approved by Congress in 1928; the resulting  Boulder Canyon Project was the first large-scale  federal water storage project and provided for  power production by the  Bureau of Reclamation ...
.[1]  The  dam  is located 30 miles (48 km) east of  Las Vegas , Nevada , 62 miles (100 km) southeast of  Los Angeles , and 221 miles (356 km) southwest of Salt Lake City . It is named for Herbert Hoover , who was President of the United States from 1929 to 1933.
Hoover Dam is visible from  Death Valley , California , and the  Las Vegas Strip . It is a tourist attraction and  National Historic Landmark. The dam is 1,244 ft (379 m) long with a crest elevation of 726.4 ft (221.4 m) . It is one of the 25 largest  dams in the  United States  by  volume  capacity; 126,000 acre-feet (155,000,000 m3) .
The dam was constructed between 1931 and 1936 during the  Great Depression by the  U.S. Bureau of Reclamation and has a generating capacity of 2,080 megawatts (2,800,000 hp). It is likely to be surpassed in size by the nearby  Glen Canyon Dam , which was built in the 1960s.
The dam is a 30-story  monolith  measuring 726.4 ft (221.4 m) tall. The dam's  concrete  volume is 4,380,000 cu yd (3,300,000 m3) . It has a crest length of 1,244 ft (379 m) and a spillway length of 1,168 ft (356 m) . The reservoir formed by the dam, Lake Mead , is the largest reservoir in the United States in terms of water capacity.
The dam is located on the border  between  Nevada and Arizona The Nevada side is administered by the  Bureau of Reclamation through the  U.S. Department of the Interior and the Arizona side is managed by the  U.S. Bureau of Reclamation through the  U.S. Department of the Interior's  Bureau of Indian Affairs.
The dam provides water and  hydroelectric power for public and private land in Arizona , Nevada , and California . It is 30 miles (48 km)  northeast of  Las Vegas and 25 miles (40 km)  southeast of  Boulder City .
Construction of the dam was approved by Congress in 1928. The resulting Boulder Canyon Project was the first large-scale federal water storage project and provided for power production by the Bureau of Reclamation. The project was authorized by the  Boulder Canyon Project Act of 1928, which was signed into law by President  Calvin Coolidge on 21 December 1928. The dam was constructed between 1931 and 1936, during the Great Depression, by the  Bureau of Reclamation. The project was designed to control floods, regulate water  levels, and provide  hydroelectricity for public and private lands in Nevada, Arizona, and California.
The dam was named for Herbert Hoover, the 31st President of the United States, who commissioned the dam and served as Secretary of Commerce at the dam's dedication.
Hoover Dam, originally Boulder Dam, has been known by its current name since 1947.
Hoover Dam has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1981.

Banksia violacea , commonly known as violet banksia , is a species of shrub or tree in the plant genus Banksia ( family Proteac

aeae ).
The leaves are elliptical to obovate, 25–75 millimetres ( 0.98–2.95 in ) long, 6–22 millimetres ( 0.24–0.87 in ) wide and have a serrated margin. The flowers are pale violet to pale purple and occur in large spikes on the ends of branches and new growth. The fruit is a woody follicle 25–95 millimetres (0.98–3.74 in) long, 7–15 millimetres (0.28–0.59 in) wide, with a single seed.
This banksia is found in south-eastern Western Australia and South Australia in the Eyre Peninsula, the Mt Lofty Ranges, the Adelaide Hills, and along the coast of the Fleurieu Peninsula . It grows in heath and woodland on sandy soils.
It was first formally described by the botanist Carl Meissner in Fragmenta phytographiae Australiae in 1845. The specific epithet ( violacea ) means "purple" referring to the flowers.
The foliage is dark green, elliptical to obovate, with a saw-toothed margin and a point. The flowers are pale violet to pale purple and occur in large spikes on the ends of branches and new growth.
The fruit is a woody follicle 25–95 millimetres (0.98–3.74 in) long, 7–15 millimetres (0.28–0.59 in) wide, with a single seed.
The species is relatively common in the far south-west of Western Australia . It is often found as a scattered shrub in heath, woodland and scrub.
The species is sensitive to fire, and is only found in areas that have been severely burnt at least once.

In the 1830s a group of squatters , mostly Métis from the ill @-@ fated Red River Colony , established a camp near the fort . B

ands of Cree , Assiniboine , and Saulteaux from the north began to arrive in the area . A village was established and by 1842 had a population of about 500 . It was named St . Joseph and became the residence of the North West Company and later of the Hudson's Bay Company .
Hudson's Bay Company chief factor and post-captain William Mactavish purchased from the North West Company 22,300 acres of land near the village of St . Joseph . He then planned an agricultural colony agricultural colony near the fort . The next year he began to sell parcels of his land to settlers .
McTavish recruited 700 settlers from the eastern Canadian colonies to begin farming in the area . The settlers were mostly Scottish farmers and their families . They were brought over in groups of 50 to 200 at a time . These "Home Landers " were paid for their passage and given a parcel of land , tools , and seed . They had to build their own homes and clear the land of trees and brush . In return , the settlers were expected to take up farming and sustain themselves .
The first group of settlers arrived from the eastern Canadian colonies in 1848. The next year, a second group arrived, followed by a third in 1850. The colony was known as the Assiniboia Settlement .
In 1851, the North West Company and the Hudson's Bay Company merged , and the Hudson's Bay Company became the sole fur trading company in the area .
The agricultural colony did not survive for long . The first two years were a disaster . In the spring of 1849 , heavy rains caused the settlement to be flooded . Diseases such as malaria , typhoid fever , and dysentery plagued the settlers . In the winter of 1849 , the settlers were struck by a severe cold snap . Disease and the cold killed a great number of settlers . In addition , the settlers had difficulty clearing the land to make farms . They continually had to fight trees and brush , and the rich prairie soil was difficult to break up .
In 1853 , the Hudson's Bay Company decided that the settlement was not profitable , and the Company dissolved the colony . The settlers were given two months to leave . Many returned to the Canadian colonies , while others stayed in the area and became farmers .
The Hudson's Bay Company sent a detachment of the Royal Newfoundland Regiment to St . Joseph in 1853 to take control of the settlement . The regiment established a military post at St . Joseph . The area was referred to as H. B. C . Settlement .
In 1855 , the Hudson's Bay Company moved the post to a different location . The town was moved to its present location .
In 1870 , the Hudson's Bay Company moved the post to Winnipeg .
There is a plaque commemorating the settlement in St . Joseph .

Direct studies on sentence spacing include those by Loh , Branch , Shewanown , and Ali ( 2002 ) ; Clinton , Branch , Holschuh ,

But he did little to protect the rights of the barons.
The concluding chapter of _The History of the Kings of England_ , completed in 1225, shows the author's awareness of the work of the newer chroniclers but also the degree to which the history had been revised in light of the original sources. The author had gone to considerable lengths to reconstruct the events of the period, and his account of Henry's reign is much fuller than his earlier narrative of the conquest of England. There is a new emphasis on the personalities of the kings and their ministers, an emphasis that earlier chroniclers had avoided. But the narrative is marred by a number of inaccuracies, including the king's death, the date of which is given as 1135.
The _History_ was compiled from the writings of Eadmer of Canterbury, William of Malmesbury, and the chronicler of St. Alban's, along with a number of other sources, some of them anonymous. The _History_ is an example of the way chroniclers strove to present a reliable, accurate account of past events.

The noisy miner is found primarily in open eucalypt woodlands and forests. It is also found in parks and gardens in the suburbs of cities and towns. It is able to adapt to a wide range of environments, and is commonly found in urban parks and gardens.

## Behavior

The noisy miner is a social bird. It is found in flocks of up to 70 individuals. It is highly aggressive towards other species , particularly the superb fairy-wren ( Malurus cyaneus).

About 250 Pictish stones survive and have been assigned by scholars to three classes . Class I stones are those thought to date

to the 6th and 7th centuries and are thus the oldest. Class II stones were erected from the 8th to the 11th centuries, and Class III stones were erected in the 19th and 20th centuries, to commemorate the discovery of a Class I stone.

The stone was discovered in 1814 and rescued from a pile of stones in Glenbervie by the landowner's gamekeeper. It was then taken to the gardens at Glenbervie House, where it remained until the 1960s. It was moved to the Clackmannanshire County Museum in 1965.

The church was constructed in 1838 to serve as a nondenominational " union church " . As many of the Mill Creek valley 's earli

er settlers were from the German states ( most of whom were Lutheran ), the church was built in a German Gothic style. The church was built by the local German-American community to serve their religious needs. The church was known as the German Evangelical and Reformed Church .
The church building, a simple one-story structure with a gabled roof , is constructed of local sandstone. The church was built in the German Gothic Revival style. The church is oriented north - south. The front facade of the church is divided into two sections, the church building proper and a small vestibule. The church building proper is a gabled structure with a steeply pitched roof. The building has an arched doorway and three stained-glass windows. A low stone wall separates the church building proper from the smaller vestibule. The vestibule is a one-story structure with a hipped roof. The vestibule has a recessed doorway and a window on each side. The church is a contributing structure to the Mill Creek Historic District and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Important theoretical work on the physical structure of stars occurred during the first decades of the twentieth century . In 1

911, the physicist Ernest Rutherford, who was studying the nuclear structure of atoms, suggested that the Sun is built around a gigantic nuclear "atom." For the rest of the century, the Sun's nuclear structure was a central pillar in models of stellar structure. The idea that stars are nuclear furnaces held by a shell of gases was the last piece of the puzzle.
 In the 1920s, the Danish physicist Niels Bohr and the German physicist Werner Heisenberg developed quantum mechanics, a new conceptual framework for physics. Quantum mechanics was an attempt to reconcile the laws of classical physics, which describe the behavior of macroscopic objects such as the planets, with the laws of quantum mechanics, which describe the behavior of microscopic objects such as electrons. The new quantum mechanical laws were inconsistent with classical physics in some cases. For example, the quantum mechanical laws predict that an object with mass can disappear and reappear in another location. This so-called quantum tunneling was not predicted by classical physics.
In 1929, the German physicist Max Born and the Austrian physicist Werner Heisenberg published a paper that explained how the quantum mechanical laws apply to light. They showed that the laws of quantum mechanics are obeyed by the photons that make up light.
The new laws of quantum mechanics did not immediately explain the origin of the Sun. But they did open the door for a new set of physical experiments.
In the 1940s, the German physicist Otto Stern and the American physicist Lester Germer were doing experiments to measure the size of an atom's nucleus. They had a brilliant idea. Instead of measuring the size of the nucleus with a microscope, they would measure the size of the nucleus by seeing how far light bounces off the nucleus without hitting it. They called this method the _Stern–Gerlach experiment_.
The light would bounce off the nucleus and form what is called a _Bragg reflection_. The Bragg reflection would be like a shadow cast by the nucleus. The distance between the center of the nucleus and the shadow would be the size of the nucleus.
In 1945, Stern and Germer performed the Stern–Gerlach experiment on a large sample of sodium, an alkali metal. The experiment revealed that the atoms in the sample were made up of protons and neutrons, as predicted by the quantum mechanical laws. The Stern–Gerlach experiment also revealed that the protons are much smaller than the neutrons. The protons are much smaller than the atoms themselves. This was the first direct evidence that atoms contain tiny, massive particles, called protons and neutrons.
In 1947, the American physicist Willis Lamb and his graduate student Robert Retherford performed the Stern–Gerlach experiment on hydrogen. They revealed that the protons are much smaller than the electrons. They also revealed that the electrons and the protons are smaller than the atom itself. In 1949, the American physicists Robert Marshak and Isidor Rabi performed a Stern–Gerlach experiment on a sample of rubidium. They revealed that the protons and the electrons are even smaller than the atom itself.
These series of experiments revealed that the structure of atoms is made up of tiny particles. The particles were called _nucleons_ because they are found in the nucleus. Protons and neutrons are called _nucleons_ , and electrons are called _leptons_.
The Stern–Gerlach experiments revealed that the nucleons are smaller than the atoms themselves. This was an important clue to the structure of the atom. State Route 516 ( SR 516 ) is a 16 @.@ 49 @-@ mile @-@ long ( 26 @.@ 54 km ) state highway in the U.S. state of Washington , se

@.@ @.@ ft @@ @ @@ @, 26 @.@ 49 km) in the northern part of the state. The route begins in the Everett area near the Puget Sound and ends in Mountlake Terrace on the south edge of Woodinville . It overlaps with Interstate 5 ( I-5 ) for its entire length.
SR 516 is the main north-south route through the Port of Everett and the Everett metropolitan area. The road is mostly rural but passes through Everett, Mukilteo , and Edmonds .
Until 1952, the current SR 516 was the northern end of US 99 . After that year, US 99 was moved north to a freeway and renamed I-5 . SR 516 then became the south end of I-5.
The route was originally designated as SR 516 in 1964. Previously, it was named County Road 21 and WA 11 .
Constructed between 1942 and 1949, the original SR 516 was a 9.41 mile (15.14 km) long state highway connecting Mukilteo with Everett. In 1964, the highway was elevated to the status of a state route and extended to the new I-5 freeway north of Mukilteo. The freeway was completed in 1970.
In 1972, the northern section of SR 516 was truncated to one mile south of I-5, moving the northern terminus to the Mountlake Terrace area. It was extended south to its current terminus in 1975.

The tawny nurse shark grows to a maximum length of 3 @.@ 2 m ( 10 ft ) . It has a robust , cylindrical body with a broadly rounded snout . Its colour is light grey to brown above with white below. The upper surface of the body is duller than the lower surface . It has a greyish brown head with a large black blotch at the base of the caudal fin and a greyish brown tail with a black tip . It has small , rounded teeth .
It is endemic to the coastal waters of New South Wales and Queensland in Australia .
The tawny nurse shark is a bottom-dwelling shark that uses ambush technique to catch prey. It feeds on fish , squid and crabs . It has an affinity for estuaries .
It is ovoviviparous . The young are born live after an 8-10 month gestation period . Females are believed to give birth to 3-5 young .
The tawny nurse shark is threatened by habitat loss , commercial fishing and recreational fishing. It is caught as bycatch by commercial fisheries . It is also caught in fishing nets . It is hunted for its meat and fins .
It is fished for food by aboriginal people .
The International Union for Conservation of Nature has rated the tawny nurse shark as Near Threatened .
The tawny nurse shark is also known as the tawny nurse shark , small-eyed nurse shark and brown-eyed nurse shark .

The extent to which his work was studied at an academic level was demonstrated on Dylan 's 70th birthday on May 24 , 2011 , when two volumes of Dylan studies appeared within a fortnight of each other. 1960s Dylan: A Decade of Revolution published by Continuum and edited by John N. Tamny and Michael Schumacher, included essays by such academic figures as Greil Marcus and Andrew Frisardi. There was also a collection of essays entitled Joyce and the Voice of the People: Dylan and the Art of Literary Allusion , edited by John Wenke and published by the University of Missouri Press. The latter was the first book-length work to examine Dylan 's use of allusion, and the contributors included such authorities as the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations editor F. N. Robinson, R. S. White and the editor of the Oxford University Press edition of James Joyce 's Ulysses , Jeri Johnson.
Dylan's work has been studied and written about by a number of authors, including Allen Ginsberg, Greil Marcus, Peter Petre, Michael Gray, Robert Shelton, Howard Sounes, Robert Christgau, and Sean Wilentz.
In 2004, the work of Dylan was the subject of the first ever "song-by-song" analysis in the journal Popular Music, a special issue of Popular Music Studies edited by Daniel C. Groenewegen and Mike Murphy, with commentaries by scholars such as Greil Marcus, Suzanne Boorse, and Mike Marqusee. An analysis of rock and pop music was also covered in the 2007 edition of the journal Popular Music Studies by Cynthia Cohen. A collection of essays, Dylan's Visions of Sin , edited by Kenneth Womack, was published in 2007 by the University of Mississippi Press. In it, contributors including Eric Lott, Aaron Fox and Elijah Wald explore the ways in which Dylan's work has been used by other artists, touched upon in scholarly articles, or transformed by the culture that has absorbed it.
In 2010, the University of Minnesota Press published a book entitled Bob Dylan in America by Elijah Wald, which examines the "roots of Dylan's imagery and themes." In 2011, the University of Chicago Press published a book entitled The Cambridge Companion to Bob Dylan , edited by Paolo Dilonardo and Jeff Burger. Among the contributors were Greil Marcus, Elijah Wald, Michael Gray, and Robert Shelton.
Dylan's literary work has also been detailed by scholars and literary critics, including the London Review author Richard Ford, and the New Yorker author Philip Weiss. In 2011, the University of Mississippi Press published a book entitled Bob Dylan's Shadow Kingdom: The Songs of the 1960s , by Howard Sounes. It is a comprehensive study of Dylan's work during the decade of the 1960s.
In 2012, the University of Minnesota Press published a book entitled How Does a Poem Mean? Bob Dylan, Theory, and Knowledge by Christopher Ricks. In it, Ricks argues that Dylan's work has been neglected by literary critics. The book was favorably reviewed by Robert Christgau, whose review was published in The New Yorker.
In 2014, the University of Minnesota Press published a book entitled The Cambridge Companion to Bob Dylan , edited by Paolo Dilonardo and Jeff Burger. It is a collection of essays, which examines Dylan's work in the context of literature, and includes essays by Michael Gray, Robert Christgau, Greil Marcus, and Peter Petre. In 2015, the University of Chicago Press published a book entitled Dylan's Visions of Sin: Rock Music, Religion, and Morality , edited by Kenneth Womack. It is a collection of essays, which examines the ways in which Dylan's work has been used by other artists, touched upon in scholarly articles, or transformed by the culture that has absorbed it.

Barbarian II : The Dungeon of Drax is an action video game released in 1988 for various personal computer platforms , such as C

64 , Amiga , Atari ST , DOS and ZX Spectrum . It was the first game in the Barbarian series .
The game is a direct sequel to Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior . Like the previous game , Barbarian II is a side-scrolling beat 'em up , which takes place in a medieval world.
Unlike the original game , in which the player controls the warrior , the player controls an unnamed adventurer in a dark dungeon in Barbarian II . The player must fight against various enemies such as skeletons , orcs , goblins , wizards and demons to eventually reach the final boss, Drax. The player is rewarded with a certain number of gold coins for each enemy killed.
The game was ported to the Amstrad CPC , Amiga and Atari ST .
A sequel titled Barbarian: The Dungeon of Drax II was released in 1990 for the Amiga and Atari ST .
In 1998, the game was re-released for the Game Boy Advance .
The game was re-released for the Xbox Live Arcade on July 25, 2007 as part of the Midway Arcade Treasures compilation.
In 2014, the game was re-released digitally on Xbox One and PlayStation 4 .
In 2015, the game was re-released on steam for PC .
The game was re-released for Nintendo Switch in 2019.
Barbarian II was critically acclaimed and became a commercial success .
The game received favorable reviews from critics who praised the game's graphics and sound, and its gameplay.
The game was considered the best game of 1987 by many magazines such as Commodore Magazine 64 or Zzap!64 .
It also won the 1988 Golden Joystick Awards Best Graphics award .
Years later, the game was included in the book 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die , edited by Tony Mott .

Religious worship among the Qedar , as was the case for most of the inhabitants of Arabia until the 7th century CE , was center

-less. It was the family or the tribe that provided the setting for prayers and occasional feasts, and it was the tribe that offered protection from the desert and from its nomadic neighbors. The Qedar , like the other Arab tribes, were nomadic tribes that venerated the goddesses al-Uzza and Manat, as well as the tribal _shaykh_ (leader) and the _shaykh's_ sons.
According to the Qur'an, the Qedar worshiped the sun, moon, planets, and stars at certain times and in certain places:
They worship the sun, the moon, the stars, and the like, rather than Allah; as if they are brands of fire, which are taken for light. Allah does not intend to make them lose their property, nor does Allah desire injustice for them. They worship things instead of Allah, that they might be guided. And those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We will surely give them a life of ours, and we will surely test them with suffering and hardship. (21: 2-6)
In the Qur'anic account, the Qedar are also linked to the progeny of Ad, who, like the Qedar , are accused of worshiping the sun and moon. They were also known as "the people of al-Hijr," which is the name of the place where the Qedar dwelled. The word _hijr_ is derived from the same root as the Arabic word _hajar_ , a rock or stone. The Qur'an calls the stone the _hijr_ a sanctuary:

Allah said, "What prevented you from prostrating, Iblis?" Iblis said, "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay." Allah said, "Get down from this, it is not for you to be arrogant here. Get out, for you are of the expelled." Iblis said, "Allow me respite till the Day of Resurrection." Allah said, "You are of those allowed respite." Iblis said, "Because You have sent me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them on your straight path. Then I will come to them from before them and behind them, from their right and left; and You will not find most of them grateful." Allah said, "Get out of Paradise, reproached and expelled. Whoever of them follows you, I will surely fill Hell with you all." ( _Q_ 2: 32-38)

On songs such as " Jump Street " and " Love Words " , Ellerbee incorporated distortion into his guitar playing , which gave the

songs a punk rock feel .

In 1996, Ellerbee was hired as bassist for punk rock band Hop Along , recording and touring with the band for six years. In 2002, Ellerbee was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma , which he successfully treated with chemotherapy.

After Hop Along's breakup in 2007, Ellerbee formed a band called The Shakes , releasing an album in 2009 . The band's second album, Daze So Long, was released in February 2012. After the release of the album, Ellerbee returned to Hop Along as bassist, touring with the band in support of Daze So Long throughout 2012 and 2013.

In 2010, Ellerbee married artist and musician Rachel Goodrich; the couple have two children together.

Battle of Taranto (1940)
The Battle of Taranto was the first naval battle in history to be fought by airplanes and the first action of the Royal Italian Navy in World War II . The battle took place on 11–12 November 1940 off the port city of Taranto, Italy , when the Italian fleet, made up of 2 battleships , 2 heavy cruisers , 1 light cruiser , and 3 destroyers , was attacked by British Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairey Swordfish biplane torpedo bombers . The attack took place during Operation Judgment , the RAF's continued attacks on Italian vessels that violated the Armistice of Cassibile . The attack on Taranto was also the first time that a large ship was sunk by airplanes.

Work began in 1882 on Fort Glanville 's northern sister Fort Largs — then known as the Port Adelaide battery — to the same spec

as the new South Australian battery, with five 12-inch guns. Fort Largs was completed in 1884, and was manned by the 1st South Australian Battery.
In 1886 the Governor of South Australia, Sir William Jervois, returned the two forts to the control of the Royal Artillery, with two companies of the Royal Garrison Artillery.
 Fort Largs was extended in 1890, with two more 9.2 inch guns installed, and two more in 1896.
The fort was decommissioned in 1901 and sold to the Port Adelaide Corporation in 1904.
In 1917, the Port Adelaide Council sold the fort to the State Government for £5000.
Fort Largs was declared a State Heritage Place on 27 November 1998 under the Heritage Places Act 1993.
Fort Largs is a fort on the St Vincent's Gulf foreshore, adjacent to the Port Adelaide Historic Precinct.  The fort is a rectangular structure with a corrugated iron roof and sandstone walls, constructed in the 1880s. It has three main rooms, a kitchen, a canteen and a guard room, which were used by the Royal Artillery from 1886 to 1901.
The fort was decommissioned in 1901, and sold to the Port Adelaide Corporation in 1904.

As the Belgian army clashed with the invading Germans in May 1940 , Hergé and his wife fled by car to France along with tens of

thousands of other Belgians. The Germans quickly overran France and then advanced further into southern Europe, reaching the outskirts of Madrid in the spring of 1941 . As the war dragged on, the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 made the situation in Europe even more precarious.
In August 1941 Hergé, his wife and daughter, and their maid took a cheap train from Bordeaux to Lisbon, the Portuguese capital. They travelled as refugees and were barred from travelling on to the United States. Hergé had left his wife and daughter in Lisbon while he went to Morocco in search of work, but the authorities refused him a visa. He had to return to Lisbon, where he spent six months waiting and plotting his next move.
In the spring of 1942 Hergé decided to move on, this time to Casablanca. On 11 April he arrived at the Hotel Transatlantique, which was run by his brother Paul. The following day he and his wife moved into the small apartment on the ground floor of the hotel, which they would occupy for the next three years.
Hergé's apartment was just around the corner from the American legation, which he visited on 16 April. As a result, he was granted an audience with the American consul, who offered him a visa to travel to the United States. However, the war was still raging and Hergé preferred to wait until it was over. The consul told him that he could apply for a visa again when the conflict was over.
Hergé was not alone in Casablanca. The Belgian Consul, Baron de Lambroek, had made his base there in January 1941 after leaving his post in Cairo, where he had spent the war years in exile. A number of Belgian businessmen also lived in the city, particularly in the hotel and café district around the old Medina. The Belgian Consul's office was situated in the Rue Descartes, just a few streets away from the Hotel Transatlantique.
On 1 June 1942, a number of important events took place in Casablanca, marking the beginning of the end of the war. The day before, the Americans had taken the city of Tunis from the Vichy forces, and the following day the Allies took Sétif in Algeria. In Casablanca itself, the French resistance movement had launched an uprising against the Vichy government. The Vichy authorities did not give in easily. The uprising was brutally crushed by the French police on 6 June, with 128 protesters being shot and a number of others being tortured and sent to prison.
The day after the riots, Hergé and his wife went for a walk in the Medina, where they saw a number of French police officers chasing after a young man. The man was caught and taken away. They stayed in the Medina for a while, taking a look at the Arab market, where the wares on sale included some exotic birds. Hergé then went back to his apartment.
His wife later told him that she had seen a young man being taken away by the police in the Medina. The boy was tied up with his eyes covered. She had tried to help him, but she had been unable to find the key to the handcuffs. She had then hurried back to their apartment to tell Hergé what had happened.
The next day, Hergé went to the Consul. He had heard that a young man had been shot by the police the previous day. The Consul told him that their man was still alive. He had been shot in the foot, but he was still alive and had been taken to hospital. Hergé said that he would like to go and see the boy.
The Consul said he would arrange it. He also told Hergé that the young man was called Jean-Pierre, and that he was a Belgian.

Under the British Mandate , Haifa became an industrial port city . The Bahá 'í Faith in 1918 and today has its administrative a

national gathering in Haifa , the Bahá'í World Centre . The city's economy was initially based on the import of cotton , which had been introduced in 1870. Banks and the port characterized the business life of the city , which was further expanded with the establishment of the American Colony in 1900 . In 1927, Haifa became a municipality , and in 1941 the port was expanded , which also brought the city with it . Since 1961, the city is a socialist municipality .
The Jewish community of Haifa is divided into two main groups: the Jewish religious and secular . The religious group is divided into the left-wing and the right-wing . The right-wing has its center in the neighborhood of Kiryat Shmuel . The left-wing is represented by the neighborhood of Kiryat Haim . The secular group is divided into the left-wing and the right-wing , which can be assigned to the entire city of Haifa .
The most important institution is the Bahá'í World Center . It serves as a spiritual center for all Bahá'ís . The center is located on Mount Carmel and consists of the Shrine of the Báb , the Bahá'í Gardens and the Arc of Triumph . The Shrine of the Báb houses the tomb of the Prophet of the Bahá'í faith, the Báb . The Bahá'í Gardens were laid out between 1987 and 2001 and are the most important place of pilgrimage for all Bahá'ís . In 1992, the Arc of Triumph was inaugurated . It is the world's largest triumphal arch and is located in the city center. The building, which has the same shape as the Arc of Triumph in Paris , was built by the Bahá'ís of Haifa in 1992. The Bahá'í World Centre in Haifa and the Shrine of the Báb are UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 2008 . The Bahá'í World Center has the status of a free zone , which includes the Shrine of the Báb and the Bahá'í Gardens.

The monument originally consisted of a sarsen stone chamber , covered by a low earthen mound , which was bounded by prostrate s

arsens forming a circular bank. The chamber contained no burials.
The site is located 1.5 miles (2.4 km) north of Avebury , 2.6 miles (4.2 km) south east of Beckhampton and 3 miles (4.8 km) north east of the village of West Kennet , grid reference SU088989.
It is a Scheduled Monument , and a Grade I listed building .
The horse-headed stone (sarsen
or netherhornton stone) is situated at the northernmost point of the stone circle – a large sarsen stone 16 ft 5 in (5.0 m) tall, which is 20 ft 7 in (6.3 m) long, and 12 ft (3.7 m) wide, weighing up to 40 tons. It was erected in 1847 by William Stukeley (1687–1765) in memory of the Reverend John Aubrey (1626–1697), and is inscribed with the date, 1680, on its front face.
In 1875, George Brougham authored an account of the monument in The Folk-Lore Journal . In it, he describes the stone as having a "very distinct resemblance to a horse's head". A local man was quoted as saying that "it is called Old Nick's head, because it is a representation of his head, and he is supposed to have ridden round the stones on a black horse."
Almost certainly, therefore, the stone is a natural formation.
The monument was probably erected by the Neolithic people who built the great circle around 3000 BC. The stone may have been a boundary marker.
The site is in the care of English Heritage .
William Stukeley , who excavated the monument in 1721, uncovered "a small stone cist containing the bones of a person, apparently a woman, placed in a wooden coffin".
The sarsen stone chamber was excavated by J. H. Evans in 1866, and he found the remains of a cremation burial, which had been placed in a simple wooden coffin.
Aubrey's Hole is an entrance to an underground passage beneath the barrow. It was originally covered by a capstone, which collapsed in 1849. It was "discovered" by William Stukeley in 1721, who believed it was the burial chamber of the Aubrey family.
It was excavated by J. H. Evans in 1866, who found a flint flake, 16 pieces of bone, and a piece of antler. Evans believed that the "chamber" was a natural cave, and that the passage was an artesian well. The underground passage was excavated by W. G. Coventry in 1869, and he discovered that it was man-made.
The site is now considered to be a pilgrimage centre, because of the manner in which it was discovered.
Aubrey's Hole was dedicated on 21 July 1996, by the Druid Order , as a place of worship.

The monument was restored in the 19th century by the Society of Antiquaries of London, who cleaned the stones and replaced missing stones.
The monument was restored in 1982 by the Avebury Trust, who reconstructed the earthen bank and prostrate sarsens.

Sully had three propeller shafts , each powered by one vertical triple @-@ expansion steam engine , which were rated at a total

of 19,500 shp (14,500 kW). The engines were grouped in two five-unit banks on each side of the ship, one engine in each bank being a spare. In addition, four auxiliary diesel engines were installed in the ship for use as generators.
The ship had four propellers, each powered by one of the four steam engines. The propellers were powered by steam supplied by the steam engines at high pressures. The propellers and the stern were protected by a bulbous stern.
The total displacement of the ship was 8,200 long tons (8,300 t) as designed. The full load displacement was 12,000 long tons (12,000 t).
Sully had a complement of 1,029 officers and men.
Sully had a maximum speed of 20.6 knots (38.3 km/h; 23.8 mph) and a cruising speed of 16.0 knots (30.0 km/h; 18.0 mph). The ship carried a maximum of 2,450 long tons (2,490 t) of fuel oil which gave her a range of 10,000 nautical miles (19,000 km; 12,000 mi) at 15 knots (28 km/h; 17 mph).
Sully was armed with a main battery of four 16 in (406 mm)/50 caliber Mark 7 guns in twin gun turrets fore and aft, one turret forward and one turret aft. These guns had a rate of fire of one round per minute. The guns could depress to −4 degrees and elevate to a maximum of +15 degrees. For anti-aircraft defense, the ship had sixteen 40 mm/60 caliber Bofors guns in twin mounts and fourteen 20 mm/70 caliber Oerlikon cannon in single mounts. The guns could elevate to +80 degrees.
Sully had a waterline length of 694 ft (211.6 m) and a beam of 78 ft (23.8 m). The ship's draft was 27 ft 9 in (8.5 m) forward and 30 ft 6 in (9.3 m) aft.
Sully was launched on 27 September 1934 by Mare Island Navy Yard; sponsored by Mrs. Mae H. McCormick, wife of the senator from California; and commissioned on 16 May 1935, Captain Harold M. Mayo in command.
After commissioning, Sully joined the Pacific Fleet and conducted routine training exercises along the west coast. The ship departed San Francisco on 29 May 1936 for her first overseas cruise, via the Panama Canal Zone and the ports of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and Buenos Aires, Argentina. She returned to San Diego on 19 August. During 1937 and 1938, Sully made two more overseas cruises, to the Far East and Australia, respectively. The ship took part in Operation Catapult, the large-scale fleet maneuvers off Hawaii and in the Hawaiian Islands in 1940.
With the outbreak of war in Europe, Sully, with a cargo of oil, departed San Pedro, California, on 31 August 1940 for the Panama Canal Zone. In the Canal Zone, the ship loaded aviation fuel and departed Balboa, Panama, on 9 September for Trinidad, British West Indies. From Trinidad, Sully sailed for Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, where she arrived on 21 September. After taking on aviation fuel, the ship sailed for Recife, Brazil, where she arrived on 27 September. The ship spent the next four days loading a cargo of high test gasoline and then sailed for Norfolk, Virginia, United States, where she arrived on 11 October. After refueling and replenishment at Baltimore, Maryland, Sully sailed for Florida and arrived at Key West, Florida, on 14 October. The ship departed Key West on 17 October for the Panama Canal Zone.

 Hurricane Ingrid was one of two tropical cyclones, along with Hurricane Manuel, to strike Mexico within a 24‑hour period, becoming the first time two hurricanes struck the country in the same day since 1958.
The first named storm of the 2013 Pacific hurricane season, Ingrid formed from a tropical wave on September 11, 2013. The storm gradually strengthened as it moved across the Bay of Campeche , and made landfall in the state of Veracruz as a Category 1 hurricane on September 15. Ingrid rapidly weakened as it moved inland, and it became a tropical storm on September 16.
Ingrid caused major flooding and landslides in Veracruz and Tamaulipas. It also caused major damage in Mexico City , resulting in the deaths of 15 people. Additionally, Ingrid killed 34 people in Guatemala.
The name Ingrid was retired by the WMO's RSMC/TCS Typhoon Committee and replaced with Isidro for the 2019 season.

For his work in films , Olivier received four Academy Awards : an honorary award for Henry V ( 1947 ) , a Best Actor award and

Best Actor in a Leading Role for Hamlet ( 1948 ) , and a Best Supporting Actor award for The Elephant Man ( 1980 ). He also won six Golden Globe Awards , three BAFTA Awards and a Tony Award . For his work on stage, Olivier received four Tony Awards , two Emmy Awards , four Golden Globes , and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the American Film Institute . He was awarded the CBE in 1944, knighted in 1947, and was made a Life Peer ( KBE ) by Queen Elizabeth II for his services to the arts in 1970. He received the Praemium Imperiale in 1982, the U.S. National Medal of Arts in 1984, the Order of Merit in 1988, and the Order of the Companions of Honour in 1994. He was honored with the AFI Life Achievement Award in 1979.
In 1979, the British government honored Olivier with the Companion of Honour for his services to the arts, and he was knighted by Elizabeth II in 1947. In 1981, he was appointed as the first chancellor of the University of Dundee .
In 1983, he was the subject of This Is Your Life , when he was surprised by Eamonn Andrews at the London Palladium .
Olivier was created a life peer by Queen Elizabeth II in 1970 and became Lord Olivier, of Brighton in the County of East Sussex. He served as the inaugural Chancellor of Exeter University (1955–1968), the University of Dundee (1971–1980), and the University of Plymouth (1972–1977). He also served as a patron of the Royal National Theatre (1963–1973) and the Royal Shakespeare Company (1961–1979).
Olivier's first marriage was to actress Jill Esmond in 1930. They had one child, a daughter, Camilla, born in 1931. The couple divorced in 1940, after Olivier had an affair with actress Vivien Leigh. Olivier and Leigh had two children, a son, Tarquin (born 1943), and a daughter, Julie (born 1945). The children took their father's surname and were known as Tarquin and Julie Olivier. Tarquin is an actor and a musician , and Julie is a writer.
Olivier and Leigh married in 1940, and remained married until Leigh's death in 1967. He later married actress Joan Plowright in 1961. They had two children, a son, Richard (born 1962), and a daughter, Julie-Kate (born 1966). They remained married until Olivier's death in 1989.
In 1975, Laurence Olivier was diagnosed with prostate cancer. As a result, he retired from acting in 1980. He died of complications from a stroke on 11 July 1989 at the age of 82. He was survived by his wife Joan, his four children (Richard, Julie-Kate, Tarquin, and Julie), and his grandchildren. His wife Joan Olivier survived him by 35 years, living until 2020.
Olivier's ashes are interred in the chancel of St. Margaret's Church , Westminster Abbey in London .
Olivier was a member of the Elmbridge Drama Club in Surrey .

Due to his own compositional talent and his genius for improvisation at the piano, he was able to earn a living from music. Alkan was a deeply introverted man, and a loner. He was five feet tall and suffered from dyspepsia for much of his life. He was very dedicated to the piano, and one of the most important things in his life was the study of counterpoint, which he taught himself from the score of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier. The fieldfare is a migratory species with a palearctic distribution . It breeds in northern Norway , northern Sweden , Finland

and Russia . During the winter it migrates to the United Kingdom and Ireland and overwinters in western France . The fieldfare has been recorded as a vagrant in the Channel Islands .

## Description

The fieldfare is 19–20.5 cm (7.5–8.1 in) long and weighs 55–63 g (1.9–2.2 oz). The males are the smaller of the two sexes.

### Adult

The fieldfare has brown upper parts with a white throat and breast. The flight feathers of the wings are black with a white inner edge. They have black legs. The summer male has brown upperparts with buff underparts. In autumn, the head and neck change to a darker chestnut, and the breast turns blackish. The female is duller and has a buff supercilium.

### Juvenile

The young fieldfares have spotted breast and belly, dark-streaked heads, and a white or pink bill.

## Distribution and habitat

The fieldfare breeds in northern Norway, northern Sweden, Finland and Russia. It migrates to the United Kingdom and Ireland in autumn, and overwinters in western France. A few reach the Channel Islands in winter.

## Behaviour and ecology

The fieldfare is an omnivorous species, eating berries, fruit, seeds, leaves, and insects. It is a colonial breeding species, nesting in trees and bushes.

### Feeding

The fieldfare is a generalist feeder, eating the seeds of many different plant species. It also eats berries, fruit, young leaves, and insects. It is not a purely granivorous species and will also eat seeds of the following plants: Arctium lappa, Cirsium arvense, Cirsium vulgare, Cytisus scoparius, Eupatorium cannabinum, Galium verum, Hippophae rhamnoides, Hypericum perforatum, Lonicera sp., Noccaea caerulescens, Papaver sp., Rubus chamaemorus, Rubus idaeus, Sanguisorba minor, Sanguisorba officinalis, Sanguisorba minor, Solidago canadensis, Solidago gigantea, Solidago virgaurea, Taraxacum, Taraxacum officinale, Tamarix ssp., Urtica dioica and Vaccinium uliginosum.

### Breeding

Fieldfares are colonial breeders, nesting in trees and bushes. The nest is a domed structure built by the female on the ground and lined with grass, hair, and feathers. It is built of weeds, grasses, moss, leaves, and stems. The nests are lined with grass, leaves, hair and feathers.

### Predators

The fieldfares main predators are foxes, stoats, weasels and crows.

## Status and conservation

The fieldfare is a species of Least Concern, although it is in decline.

### Behavioural adaptations

The fieldfares have developed a number of adaptations to conserve body heat during their winter migration. The fieldfares have a unique blood plasma that changes its composition in response to cold weather. The fieldfares also have a higher level of fat in their bodies in the winter.

### Migration

The fieldfares migrate in a V-shaped formation. They travel in flocks and their migration is guided by the sun.

### Migration routes

The fieldfares' migration route takes them through Spain, Portugal, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Poland. They also cross the English Channel.

On August 27 , 2013 , Columbia Records released Volume 10 of Dylan 's Bootleg Series , Another Self Portrait ( 1969 – 1971 ) .

The two-CD set collects previously unreleased outtakes and alternate versions of songs from the era of Dylan 's _New Morning_ , _Self Portrait_ and _Dylan_ albums.  The set was preceded by the single "Duquesne Whistle" released on August 6 , 2013 .
On November 19 , 2013 , Dylan was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom , the highest civilian award in the United States, by President Barack Obama at a ceremony in the White House . Obama praised Dylan 's ''poetical force,'' saying, ''There is not a bigger gift you can give to the world.'' Dylan was presented with the medal by George W. Bush , who had awarded him the Medal of Freedom in 2007.
On January 28 , 2012 , Dylan was awarded the Pulitzer Prize Special Citation , which the committee said was ''for his profound impact on popular music and American culture, marked by lyrical compositions of extraordinary poetic power.'' Dylan was the first songwriter to receive a Pulitzer Prize.
On December 6 , 2016 , Dylan received the Nobel Prize in Literature ''for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition .'' The 17-member Swedish Academy , which awards the prize, praised Dylan 's ''huge cultural importance'' and cited him as an ''epic bard who can be regarded as the great inspiring poet of the late 20th century.'' Dylan became the first musician to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, which had previously been awarded to such authors as Svetlana Alexievich , Doris Lessing , Harold Pinter , Seamus Heaney , Samuel Beckett , Toni Morrison and William Faulkner .
The Nobel Prize committee later announced that Dylan would not attend the award ceremony in Stockholm, saying that the musician was unable to make the trip, even though the prize would be picked up by a representative. Dylan 's publicist said that the singer had ''other commitments'' on that date. The ceremony took place on December 10 , without Dylan.
Dylan is the subject of the 2005 film _No Direction Home: Bob Dylan_ by Martin Scorsese . The film documents Dylan 's career through interviews, archival footage, and previously unreleased music. The film won a Grammy Award for _Best Long Form Music Video_ in 2006.
Dylan has published four books of drawings and paintings: _The Beaten Path_ (1975), _A Tangled_ _Web_ (1978), _Dumbarton Oaks_ (1994), and _The Drawn Blank_ _Series_ (2010).
Dylan has been married three times, most recently to his backup singer, Carolyn Dennis, whom he married in 1986. He has six children: four with his first wife, Sara, one with his second wife, Carolyn Dennis, and one adopted from China.
Beyond music, Dylan has also worked in movies and television. He acted in Renaldo and Clara , the 1978 film by Joan Baez and Dylan, who also directed. Dylan also wrote the screenplays and starred in Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid (1973) and Ride the Pink Horse (1947). In 1994, Dylan starred in and wrote the screenplay for the film _Godless_ .
Dylan has also appeared as himself in many films, including _Peter Bogdanovich 's_ _Mask_ (1985), _Hearts of Fire_ (1987), _Masked and Anonymous_ (2003), _Wonder Boys_ (2000), _Mighty Aphrodite_ (1995), and _The Door_ (1991).
Dylan starred in the television series _Trouble No More_ , which aired on Showtime in 1987. He also played himself in the television series _Seinfeld_ in 1994. In 1990, he appeared in a Chevrolet television commercial where he sang and played the harmonica to ''The Times They Are A-Changin''.

In early 1943 , Japan was still believed to be capable of invading , or at least bombing , the Torres Strait islands , and NEA

9 had been moved there to meet this possibility .
 
Main article: Japanese invasion of Port Moresby

## Raid on Tulagi

In March 1943 , NEA 8 , now based at Nouméa , was ordered to take part in a larger raid on Tulagi in the Solomon Islands , code-named Operation Mo . The task of the raid was to destroy defensive positions on Tulagi before the main Japanese force could land there. During the night of 3–4 May 1943 , NEA 8 attacked Tulagi as part of the larger force , planting explosives on the island and destroying defensive positions . The raid also destroyed a Japanese submarine and damaged several others .

## Battle of Kolombangara

Main article: Battle of Kolombangara

The following month , NEA 8 was ordered to join a larger force of Australian and American warships in a battle against Japanese naval forces in the Solomon Islands . At 07:00 on 13 June 1943 , NEA 8 set out from Nouméa with HMAS Australia as its mother ship . On 14 June , the force was spotted by a Japanese reconnaissance plane , and was attacked by Japanese aircraft and warships . NEA 8 was hit by a Japanese bomb which killed 11 of the 25 men on board . The remaining 14 were taken off the raft by the warships , and NEA 8 was scuttled with explosives .

The Galactic Federation is planning to evacuate a large number of colonists from the planet Tau Cygna V. The Federation has already sent a survey team to the planet, which has located 900,000 potential settlers, but the team was not able to contact them. A thunderstorm broke out at the same time the team arrived, which destroyed the communication equipment.
After the team was rescued, Federation envoy Keevan reports to the Federation Council on the incident. The Council demands that all communication equipment of the Federation be destroyed, since the team could have been captured by the Shedai . Keevan also warns that the Shedai are preparing for war, and that the Federation will need to fight.
Odo is assigned to the task force, which is to search for the colonists. The task force is led by Captain Benjamin Sisko and Commander William T. Riker.
