Originally described in 1822 as Agaricus indigo by American mycologist Lewis David de Schweinitz , the species was later transf

used onto Agaricus in 1838 by French botanist Henri François Anne de Raphèle-Van Etten. The fungus is found in the eastern United States and southeastern Canada , the species name is derived from the Latin for "black", and the specific epithet refers to the color of the fruiting bodies. The name is also used in the popular vernacular for Agaricus brunneus , the type species of the genus Agaricus .
Agaricus indigo is a saprobic species, it grows in clusters on the ground, and in the fall it fruits on the ground. Fruit bodies are medium-sized, convex, or flat, 4-12 cm in diameter, clavate, and have an odor and taste. The stem is 3-8 cm long and 5-8 mm thick, and is smooth or finely matted. The spore-bearing flesh is white or cream-colored, and the spores are elliptical, smooth, and measure about 5.5 by 3.5 μm. The species is considered edible, though it is not commercially cultivated .

The main goal of this project is to create a fixed-wing flying robot that is more like a bird or a plane, while having the same aerodynamic advantages as a helicopter. In addition, it should be able to fly in the same way as a single rotor helicopter, i.e. with forward flight and hovering.
At the same time, I want to showcase that this can be done without any electric motors or sensors, and that it is possible to build a flying robot that is simple, robust, and safe enough to carry people or cargo.
This project started in 2009. In its current design the robot is controlled by a joystick.
The first prototype was built in 2012 and has flown twice in the wind tunnel (see below).
A second prototype was designed in 2013, and is being built in 2014. It will be able to fly autonomously, and will be designed to be as light as possible. The goal is to build a robot that weighs 50 grams or less.
The third prototype is currently being designed. It will be a gondola-type flying robot with two wings. This gondola will also be the platform for a camera or a small payload.
In addition to the flying robot, a paper will be published that describes the flight characteristics of the current prototype in detail.
The reason why I am looking for crowd funding is because this project is too big for me to do on my own. I would like to hire an aerodynamicist to help me optimize the design of the flying robot, as well as a machinist to make all the parts.
So far, the project has cost me ~$5000, and I have spent ~200 hours working on it. I have not yet done any fundraising, and I have not yet recruited any volunteers.
I am willing to do a discounted rate for the work of the machinist, and I will be able to offer advice for free to the aerodynamicist.
If I manage to get crowd funding, there is a good chance that the aerodynamicist will be able to help me optimize the design of the flying robot for free.

Cresswell rejoined his first club York City , playing in League Two , on a one @-@ month loan on 19 March 2013 . He marked his

26th birthday date 30 March 2013 by scoring his first senior goal for York City in a 1–1 draw with Gillingham . He made four @-@ appearances for York City before returning to Bradford City at the end of March 2013.
Cresswell signed for Bradford City on 1 August 2013 on a free transfer. He made his debut on 10 August 2013 in the 1–1 draw with Leeds United . His first goal came in a 2–0 win against Doncaster Rovers on 28 September 2013.
Cresswell’s contract was extended for a further season on 10 April 2014, having played 37 times in all competitions in his first season. He scored his second goal for the club in a 1–1 draw with Notts County on 18 October 2014. He continued to establish himself in the Bradford side and was voted the club’s Player of the Year for the 2014–15 season.
Cresswell left Bradford City for Bolton Wanderers on a three-year deal on 1 July 2015 for a fee believed to be in the region of £500,000 (although he would not be eligible to play until the 2015–16 season). He made his debut in a 2–0 defeat to Bristol City . He scored his first goal for Bolton in a 3–2 win against Rotherham United on 28 September 2015.
Cresswell played in the 2016 EFL Trophy Final , where Bolton lost 2–1 to Oxford United . He scored his first league goal of the 2016–17 season in a 1–1 draw with Queens Park Rangers on 11 December 2016. He scored his second goal of the 2016–17 season on 15 April 2017 in a 1–1 draw with Brighton & Hove Albion .
Cresswell signed for Wigan Athletic on 26 July 2017, agreeing a three-year deal.
In his first season, Cresswell made 40 appearances for the club, scoring three goals. One of these came in the 2017–18 EFL Cup , where Wigan beat Leicester City 3–1. He also scored his first goals in the EFL Championship , scoring in the 5–1 win against Bolton Wanderers and the 2–1 loss against Nottingham Forest .
An injury crisis saw Cresswell make his first league appearance of the 2018–19 campaign on 4 November 2018 in a 3–0 win against Birmingham City . He scored in the 1–0 win against Bristol City on 12 January 2019.
Cresswell was named in the EFL Championship Team of the Year for the 2018–19 season.
Cresswell has represented England at under-17, under-18 and under-19 levels.

Tropical Storm Brenda was the second named storm of the 1960 Atlantic hurricane season . It developed in the northeastern Gulf

18 May. Tropical Storm Brenda made landfall in Florida and then weakened over land. Brenda was the first tropical cyclone to affect the United States in 1960.
The storm formed on 18 May south of Apalachicola, Florida, on the same day as Tropical Storm Alice. Brenda was a large storm, with its center located 35 miles (55 km) south of Apalachicola. The storm moved to the north of the state and began to curve westward about 100 miles (160 km) south of Tallahassee. A reconnaissance aircraft found that the storm had intensified into a tropical storm about 100 miles (160 km) north of Tampa. Tropical Storm Brenda then slowly turned northwest, and by 21 May the storm was centered 100 miles (160 km) north of Tampa.
On 21 May the storm made landfall near Cedar Key, Florida with 60 mph (95 km/h) sustained winds. The storm then moved west over the Florida Panhandle, and by 22 May the storm was centered 25 miles (40 km) west of Pensacola, Florida. The storm then turned northwest, making landfall near Fort Walton Beach, Florida with 55 mph (89 km/h) winds on 22 May. The storm then moved over land and weakened. The storm dissipated over Alabama on 23 May.
Due to the storm's proximity to Florida, a hurricane warning was issued for the coast of Florida. In Florida, 150 homes were damaged and 3,000 people were left homeless. In the United States, no casualties were reported.

On Mahashivaratri ( February ) , a procession of Shiva proceeds from the Mahamrityunjaya Temple to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple

( the "Golden Temple " ). The procession is in the form of a Naga, a snake, the sacred symbol of Shiva. The Nagas were used as a vehicle by the great Sage Kapila , who later became one of the seven great sages . The Nagas are also associated with the river Ganga  and Shiva's consort, Parvati . In Kashmir, a Shiva temple is called a Nagara Temple and the temples of Kashmir are famous for their Nagara style architecture . There are various festivals and rituals, such as the Maha Shivaratri ("Great Night of Shiva") observed in honor of Shiva, Shivaratri is a very important festival for Shiva devotees.
Mahashivratri, the great night of Shiva, is celebrated every year. The day is marked by devotees of Shiva keeping vigil and fasting all night in honor of Lord Shiva. On this day, devotees also perform special prayers and rituals to propitiate Lord Shiva. Lord Shiva is hailed as the destroyer of evil and darkness.

Flying schools are commercial businesses engaged in the training of pilots , both for recreational purposes and for those intending to work in the aviation industry. The training is generally conducted in small aircraft , such as the Piper PA-28 or Cessna 150 . The training is conducted under the supervision of the Civil Aviation Authority .
The first step in the process is gaining a private pilot's licence by passing the exams required and flying with a flight instructor . This requires having a small amount of flying experience and a log book of relevant flight experience. The log book is used to record the flying experience of the pilot .
Once the pilot has gained their licence they can progress to the next level, the commercial pilot's licence. This is normally gained by having the minimum amount of flight experience and by the passing of the commercial pilot's exams. Once this is gained the pilot can apply for their instrument rating.
There are a number of flying schools in the UK, each one offering the necessary courses for each level of pilot qualification. There are also a number of flying clubs that allow members to train as pilots.
The main flying school in the UK is the Air League . There are also a number of international schools that offer courses to pilots from around the world. These include the British Airways * Flight Training School , the Air Training International *, and the Airways Aviation *.

In a 1929 article appearing in the Lowell Sun newspaper , physician Morris Fishbein speculated that for Ali 's nut feat , the o

xygen-rich blood in his body was "pumped into his limbs by a ventilator under his form-fitting trunks."  Fishbein's comment illustrates the peculiarity of the time period, as the idea of ventilators and pumping blood into the limbs was not conventional. In fact, the idea of using anything other than normal breathing to supply oxygen to the body was extremely novel, and would not become conventional until the 1940s.
In the early 1940s, doctors began to experiment with the use of artificial ventilation as a means of improving the quality of life for patients suffering from neuromuscular diseases such as spinal muscular atrophy , muscular dystrophy , and polio . By the 1950s, artificial ventilation was also being used as a means of providing increased oxygen to patients suffering from lung diseases such as emphysema , especially in patients who were suffering from asthma attacks and had difficulty breathing.
In 1948, physician John H. Emerson published a book entitled "The Pneumatic Pillow and Other Treatments of Respiratory Distress." In the book, Emerson described an experiment in which he used a ventilator to keep a patient with myasthenia gravis alive. In an interview with the Milwaukee Journal , Emerson is quoted as saying that the ventilator was used to "oxygenate the blood and to make it possible to remove the carbon dioxide from the body."  However, at the time Emerson's experiment was being performed, doctors were not yet aware that the lungs were the primary organ for removing carbon dioxide from the body, and so the use of a ventilator to remove carbon dioxide from the body would not become commonplace until the 1950s.
In the 1950s, the concept of using artificial ventilation for the treatment of lung diseases and other conditions became more widespread. In 1951, Arthur D. Little and his colleagues at the MIT Research Laboratory of Electronics developed the first commercially available ventilator, dubbed the "Baby Browder." The Baby Browder ventilator used a face mask to administer oxygen at a regulated concentration. Around the same time, doctors began using ventilators to provide increased oxygen to patients with emphysema, especially in patients who were suffering from asthma attacks and had difficulty breathing.
There is some evidence to suggest that artificial ventilation was used in the treatment of polio patients during the 1950s. In an interview with the Milwaukee Journal , physician John H. Emerson recalled that in the 1950s, he and his colleagues at the University of Wisconsin-Madison used a ventilator to "oxygenate the blood and to make it possible to remove the carbon dioxide from the body."  Though Emerson did not specifically recall if the ventilator was used to treat polio patients, Emerson's recollection is consistent with reports from the time period that artificial ventilation was used to treat polio patients, which is discussed later in this article.
The use of artificial ventilation for the treatment of neuromuscular diseases became more widespread in the 1950s. In 1957, the first artificial respirator designed for home use, the Stryker-Bunnell Model 500, was introduced.  The Stryker-Bunnell Model 500 was a breathing machine that used a face mask to administer oxygen at a regulated concentration.  The Stryker-Bunnell Model 500 was relatively expensive, costing $1,200 in 1957, which was equivalent to about $11,000 in 2017.  The Model 500 was designed to provide a continuous flow of oxygen, which meant that patients were required to wear the mask 24 hours a day, every day.

There was always a certain amount of trouble [ being the son of Sir Oswald ] until I came into motor racing . And in one of the

most difficult years I ever had in my life – 1973 – I had a fight on my hands with the British Racing Drivers' Club – the two eldest sons of Sir Oswald and Sir John Whitmore. And that was because I was the only driver in the field who had a non-British car.
The fights were tough . I think the club was very good to me on the whole, but there were always a few people around who were always trying to get me out of racing. They were trying to get me out of Formula One – that was the thing that was so difficult. I remember the year before, 1972, we had this big controversy with the BRDC over the fact that I was using a non-British engine. I had an eight-cylinder BMW engine, and I was the only one who had an eight-cylinder BMW engine. The rest were all six-cylinder Cosworths, so I was a bit of a renegade, and the BRDC were not too keen on that. They stopped me from getting a driving test, but I managed to get a test anyway.
I was always good friends with John Cooper . John's son John Cooper-Williams was my best friend. John was a very, very good friend of mine. When I was getting my driving test in the Lotus, I had 40 laps to do and I had to do them in forty minutes. John was there with me and he said, 'You know, I think we'll have a little word with the officials at the club here, and they'll let you do an extra lap to make it forty-one.' And I said, 'Do you think they'll do that?' He said, 'I'll arrange it for you.' And he did. He made a phone call and they said, 'Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.'
And then I had to go out and drive the last lap. And I hadn't driven the car very much since the last time I'd driven it, and it was raining. And I had to do it in forty-one minutes. And I did it, and they gave me the test. And that was good. I was delighted.
As the years went on, though, that was always a problem, because people were trying all the time to get me out of Formula One. I was the only non-British driver in Formula One. I had to work very hard to keep my seat. And I think I did do that, because I started to become a good driver, and I think I'm still one of the best drivers that's ever lived, even though I'm not in Formula One. But that was a very difficult time for me.
 And I remember once I was doing the Indy 500. I had my own team with my brother, and we had a team of three cars. And it was a very big, strong team. We had a big budget. We had a lot of sponsorship. And I had a real good chance to win the race. I had a 1-2-3. The way it was going, I was going to win the race. And then the day of the race, something happened. It was a distraction. And I was in fourth place, and I had to pit. And when I was on the track again, I couldn't get back up to the pace. I think I was three or four laps down when the race was over. And I couldn't get back up to that pace. And I lost the 1-2-3. I lost the race, and I lost the team. Because I lost the team and I lost the sponsorship. And that was one of the toughest things I've ever had to do.
 The problem with the team was that, at one point, one of the mechanics, he had been working in England with me in the team, and he had come to work for me in the United States. And he was a very clever guy, and I think he must have been working for the other team. He was giving the other team information about me. And that was very, very tough.
 That was a very difficult year, and it nearly finished my career. But I had a good friend of mine, a guy called Tom Sneva. He was the 1983 Indy 500 winner, and he was a good friend of mine, and he was helping me out. He was helping me to get a sponsor, and he was helping me to get a team back together. I managed to get a team back together, and I won the race in 1983.

The oribi is diurnal ( active mainly during the day ) , though some activity may also be observed at night . The animal rests i

n dense cover during the day and emerges to graze at sunset . The oribi is a precocious breeder, and females raise their young alone. The oribi is a ruminant, feeding in a manner similar to antelope. The diet consists mainly of grasses, but some forbs and shrubs may be taken.
The oribi is a social animal. In South Africa it is common for the oribi to be seen in pairs or small groups, mainly consisting of females with their young (usually between 1 and 3 young per litter). Males and females form permanent pairs only during the breeding season.
The oribi breeds all year round, though peaks in numbers of young occur during the rainy season (spring). The gestation period is 200 days and the average litter size is between 1 and 2 young. The young are weaned at 4 to 5 months of age.
The oribi is a medium-sized antelope with a compact and robust body. It is brown or reddish-brown in colour, and has white in-between the ears and on the throat. The tail is black below and white above and is longer than the body. The oribi has a small, compact head with large, prominent eyes. The hooves are black with white rings on the soles.
The oribi is found in the Cape, Free State, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo and North West provinces of South Africa.
The oribi occurs in a variety of habitats, including dense bush, grassy plains, scrub and open woodland. It is found at elevations up to 3 000 m.
The oribi is listed as Vulnerable (VU) on the Red List of Mammals of South Africa. It is also listed on Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).
The main threats to oribi are habitat loss and degradation, as well as persecution by farmers and stock farmers.

" Moment of Surrender " made its live debut on the opening night of the U2 360 ° Tour in Barcelona , Spain during the encore ,

13 years after its initial release. It is also the first song that the band has performed live without playing the full version. The song was first played in its entirety during the second show of the tour in Berlin , Germany, and has since been played in a shortened form, often with different lyrics added in.

## Live performances

" Moment of Surrender " was first performed on the opening night of the U2 330 ° Tour in Barcelona, Spain on 30 June 2009. It was the first performance of any of the new songs from the album No Line on the Horizon. This was the first time that a song that was previously unavailable in any form had been performed in its entirety. It was also the first time " Moment of Surrender " has been performed since its release 13 years earlier. " Moment of Surrender " was the final song of the encore for the first six shows of the tour, and the first encore song of the second half of the tour.

After performing it on 18 July 2009, Bono dedicated the song to "the memory of the 58 who died in the holocaust in Poland" and invited the audience to sing a prayer in Polish in response. The song was played in a shortened form on the opening nights of the second half of the tour, and in a longer version on the second night in Berlin, Germany.

" Moment of Surrender " was played in a shortened form at the first three shows of the U2 360° Tour on 18 July 2010 in Barcelona, Spain, 8 July 2011 in Toronto , Canada, and 13 July 2011 in East Rutherford , New Jersey on the first night of the second leg of the tour. It was played in its entirety on the first night of each leg of the tour, with Bono adding lyrics in the final verse. " Moment of Surrender " was not played at all on the second night of the tour.

A live performance of the song is available on the U2 360° At The Rose Bowl DVD.

Both sides in the battle realised the importance of the railway as a supply line. The first to recognise its importance was the Australian 3rd Brigade under Brigadier General Arthur Allen, which was based around the Romani area. It controlled the railway, and from 12 December instigated daily patrols along the track. While this was effective for controlling the railway, it did not allow the brigade to exploit the railway to its full potential. By 15 January, Allen was ordered by the Anzac Mounted Division to halt all movements on the railway, after an attack by a Turkish force near Tel-el-Kebir. However, a few days later, Allen received orders for the brigade to set up a railway camp, and extend the railhead to Tel-el-Kebir. The camp was created on 1 February, with strong patrols set up around it.
With the arrival of the New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade on 15 December, the Anzac Mounted Division was split into two brigades, with each brigade taking responsibility for a section of the railway. The Australian 3rd Brigade controlled the section from Tel-el-Kebir to Romani, while the New Zealand 1st Brigade controlled the section from Romani to the El Arish. The first patrols along the railway were carried out by the 2nd Light Horse, 3rd Light Horse, and the 12th Light Horse. Each of these were composed of two companies, and covered the railway for a distance of 20 miles (32 km).
After the formation of the Anzac Mounted Division, General Allen was promoted to major general, and given command of the division. He was replaced as commander of the 3rd Brigade by Brigadier General C. E. G. Ryrie. Under Ryrie's command, the 3rd Brigade made use of the railway as a supply line, in conjunction with its patrols to control the railway. The 3rd Brigade was also responsible for a section of the Suez Canal that was held by the Anzac Mounted Division.
By 15 February, the 3rd Brigade had a limited railway camp at Tel-el-Kebir, and was establishing a camp at Romani. This was to allow the brigade to extensively use the railway. On 20 March, Allen was promoted to major general and given command of the Anzac Mounted Division. He was replaced as commander of the 3rd Brigade by Brigadier General C. E. G. Ryrie.

This was done by conducting patrols along the line, and also by constructing sidings at Berbuge and El Arish. In the autumn of 1841 , after the birth of his brother Otto , Busch 's education was entrusted to the 35 @-@ year @-@ old clerg

yman Johann Georg Rietz , who had a great influence on Busch 's life. Busch was at that time a quiet and obedient student. After a year, however, his "strong will" became apparent, which was partly the result of his bourgeois background. He also had a tendency to "behave like a gentleman" and was often stubborn.
In the autumn of 1844 Busch applied to the gymnasium in the nearby town of Büdingen . He was regarded as a gifted student and was admitted to the grammar school. The 18 year old Busch was quickly noticed for his maturity. He was very interested in literature and philosophy and achieved high grades. He was also a member of the literary society "Blüthenbund". In addition to the German literature, he was interested in French literature and became friends with the poet Adolf Strodtmann .
In the autumn of 1846 Busch passed the final exams . He then studied law at the University of Marburg and the University of Göttingen . During his time as a student, he was not only interested in the law, but also in politics, history and philosophy. He was a member of the "Göttinger Burschenschaft" and of the N.S.V. Phi-Beta-Kappa. In May 1848 he took the first state examination.
Busch started his career as a lawyer in 1848 in Büdingen , where he worked for two years. In 1851 he moved to the town of Obernburg ) near Mainz . There he wrote the essay "Friedrich von Schiller as a Poet" and made the acquaintance of the poet and writer Eduard Mörike . He also met the painter Karl Ferdinand Sohn and the writer Karl Gutzkow . In 1852 he was called to the district court in Gießen .
In 1855 Busch married Wilhelmine Ramdohr (1833–1917), the daughter of a merchant from Eschwege . The couple had three children: a daughter, Helene (1857–1938), and two sons, Ernst (1859–1948) and Hugo (1860–1923).

In 1856 Busch was appointed as a judge at the district court in Hanau . He was appointed to the district court in Gießen in 1859, where he was promoted to the rank of senior district court judge in 1863. From 1867 to 1880 he was the presiding judge of the district court in Gießen.
August von Busch died in 1880 in Gießen at the age of 60 .

Nobody knows for sure where the phrase comes from, although it has been suggested that it is a reference to children's games.
A number of versions of the story exist. In one, children from neighboring villages would play a game with two pails of water at a brook. One child would climb up the bank and empty the pail into the brook, and the other would use a pail to try to "retrieve" the water. In this game, the child who climbs up the bank is said to be "Jack," and the child who uses the pail is said to be "Jill."
In another version of the story, Jack and Jill are playmates from neighboring villages. Jack comes to Jill's village and asks her to fetch a pail of water from the spring for him. Jill tells Jack that the path is too steep for her and that he should go himself. Jack responds to Jill by saying, "Nay, not I, for I am Jack, and I'll not fetch, but I'll throw it."
In a third version of the story, Jack and Jill are lovers who have climbed to the top of a cliff and are throwing a pail of water. Jill says to Jack, "There will be no more of this foolishness, Jack; I'm not going to climb back down this cliff more than once." Jack replies, "Not I, for I'm Jack, and I'll not climb down, but I'll jump down." Jack jumps down, and Jill follows him.

ours and one to boost the safety of the air tour community. These were to increase staffing at airports to make sure that the airport was not overloaded, to ensure that air tour operators had regular access to rest facilities, and to launch a campaign to increase the safety awareness of the air tour community.
 The second step of the NTSB investigation was to hold a short hearing in order to collect further evidence and ask specific questions of experts and witnesses. This hearing took place in Washington D.C. on June 20 and 21, 2007. The NTSB received statements from experts on fatigue, air tours, and the use of night vision goggles. The NTSB also heard from five witnesses who were pilots or passengers on flights with the same air tour operator that had crashed the previous year.
 The NTSB considered the evidence from witnesses and experts and concluded that the crash was due to fatigue. They made 14 recommendations as a result.
 The third step of the NTSB investigation was the on-site investigation. This began on November 19, 2007 and lasted for two and a half weeks. The NTSB were able to examine the wreckage and the surrounding terrain and to speak to witnesses.
 The NTSB examined the flight-data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder that were recovered from the wreckage. These record what the pilots were saying and doing up to the moment of the impact. They also record the performance of the engines and other aircraft systems. They show that the airplane was flying relatively smoothly until a few minutes before it crashed, and that the pilots' conversations were routine and unremarkable.
 The NTSB found that the crash was caused by the fatigue of the pilots, which caused them to make errors in their decision-making and flying of the aircraft.

Weather hampered the wing 's activities in January 1945 . No. 1 Squadron was withdrawn to Queensland to re @-@ equip with Mosqu

On 19 February the squadron conducted a raid on the Japanese airfield at Balikpapan, but it was not until 1 March that the squadron was involved in a bombing raid on the Japanese aircraft industry.
 On 21 February, 1945, two Mosquito Mk.VI aircraft from No. 30 Squadron (also in the Philippines) and two Mosquito Mk.VI aircraft from No. 21 Squadron (in Morotai) attacked the Hikari aircraft factory at Arima, Japan. Two Mosquito Mk.XVIs of No. 30 Squadron bombed Hikari on 28 February. On 1 March, the same squadron attacked the Hikari aircraft factory again.
 No. 487 Squadron (RAAF) was formed in the Philippines on 15 January 1945, with 12 Mosquito Mk.XIX aircraft. The squadron was equipped with the Mosquito Mk.XVIs from 24 February. The squadron moved to Morotai in March.
 The Mosquito Mk.XVIs of No. 487 Squadron were involved in bombing raids over Japan during March and April 1945.
 No. 487 Squadron was disbanded on 25 June 1945, and was reformed on 17 October 1945, as a flying training unit in Australia.
RAAF squadrons were not the only Mosquito units on active service in the Pacific. On 24 November 1943, the VLM's 212 Squadron was formed in Australia with 12 Mosquito Mk.II aircraft.
 On 22 January 1944, 212 Squadron was disbanded, and the aircraft were transferred to Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) units.

Howard ran for the Democratic nomination for Virginia Attorney General in 2009. He competed in the Democratic primary against fellow state senator Mark Herring , who was supported by Governor Tim Kaine . Herring defeated Howard in the June 9 primary by a margin of 69.1-30.9%.

### 2013 gubernatorial campaign

Main article: 2013 Virginia gubernatorial election

Howard ran for the Democratic nomination for Virginia Governor in 2013. He was the first African-American to run for Governor of Virginia. He lost the nomination to Terry McAuliffe by a margin of 54.7-41.9%.

the Georgian script, the Unicode Consortium first considered making use of the Unicode block for Cyrillic scripts and made some preliminary proposals based on that model. The Georgian script was the first script to have its own block as a standalone script, although the Armenian script has also been treated as a standalone script in Unicode since version 2.
 The Unicode Consortium does not have a position on which languages use which scripts. This position is left to the community.  But the Consortium does have a position on how to deal with a situation where two scripts are used for the same language. It is the opinion of the Unicode Consortium that separate blocks for distinct scripts must be used to support two scripts for a given language.  Therefore, the Consortium takes the position that Unicode should support the use of two scripts for the Georgian language.  There is no reason to believe that the use of two scripts is a temporary phenomenon. In fact, the use of two scripts was an important aspect of the Unicode proposal for Georgian. For example, the Unicode Consortium proposed to treat the Georgian script as a standalone script, not as a variant of the Cyrillic script.  This position has been the position of the Consortium since 1991.
 The Unicode Consortium also takes the position that the two scripts should be treated the same in Unicode.  That is, text in either script should be treated as text in Georgian, not as text in Georgian written in the Georgian script or text in Georgian written in the Cyrillic script.

present-day script. We must remember that the oldest of the Georgian manuscripts, the Kutaisi Gospel, was written in the eleventh
century, and that it contains the same letters as many Old East -Slavic manuscripts of the time. The Byzantine letters have a number of
distinctive features, among them the addition of a dot to the meta-like character to distinguish it from the simple meta. The Georgian
script has borrowed this feature, and it is found in the same character in the Old East-Slavic script. Since we know that a Byzantine
manuscript was used in Georgia in the tenth century, we can assume that this is the source of these additional features. The Georgian
script has also borrowed the use of lower-case letters and the shape of the slanting letters and the vowels.
The Georgian script is, however, quite different from the Old East-Slavic script. The Georgians have borrowed the use of the
digraphs, but have greatly simplified them, and have reduced the number of characters to 33, the same as in French. The Georgian
script is, then, essentially the same as the Old French script. (All the bizarre shapes of the Georgian letters are due to the fact that the
early scribes were using Byzantine models, and in the early days of the Georgian script they tried to reproduce the Byzantine shapes ).
The Georgian script has also borrowed four letters from the Greek script, namely, the letters delta ( ), theta ( ), pi ( ), and
rho ( ).
The Georgian script is quite easy to learn, because its letter-forms are simple and geometric, and it uses only one diacritical sign
(the dot), which is placed on any letter when it appears at the end of a word.
The Georgian script, as we have seen, has been greatly simplified from the original Byzantine forms. It has become so simple,
indeed, that it can be used by anyone, even those who have no previous knowledge of writing.

Corn crakes were first described by Linnaeus in his Systema Naturae in 1758 as Rallus crex , but was subsequently moved to the

genus Capellinus and then to the genus Galerida in 1952.

The corncrake is up to 20 cm in length with a wingspan of up to 47 cm. It is a large member of the rail family with a long down-curved bill. The back is brown with a blackish patch behind the eye. The underparts are white and the wings are brown-black.

Corncrakes breed in marshes, grasslands and arable fields and are most often found in damp grasslands and wet meadows with abundant vegetation and wet areas. They are usually found along watercourses, in or near marshes, or in grassy areas. They are found in the northwest of Europe.

This species is not migratory, but does move between breeding and wintering grounds. It is mainly solitary and nocturnal.

## Feeding

Corncrakes eat insects, spiders, snails, slugs, seeds and berries.

## Breeding

Corncrakes breed from June to early July. The nest is a shallow scrape on the ground, lined with leaves and grass. It is located in a patch of long grass, often in a hedgerow or rough grassland. It lays three to five eggs.

## Status

The corn crake is on the European Red List as a species of least concern, and the IUCN Red List as a species of "least concern".

According to 13th @-@ century Arab historian Ibn Shaddad , the Mirdasid emir of Aleppo , Shibl ad @-@ Dawla , established a set

of Byzantine -style laws, one of which was the introduction of a regular army .  The emir is said to have also built the city's first mosque .  The Mirdasids subsequently lost control of Aleppo and a new dynasty, the Zengid , seized power .  The Zengid ruler, Imad ad-Din Zengi , further established the city as an important military base and expanded the existing fortresses.  Zengi also began the construction of an impressive citadel , which was completed by his son Nur al-Din .  The latter strengthened the city's fortifications , and improved its water supply and sewage system .  Nur al-Din established Aleppo as his primary residence .  After his death in 1174, the city came under the control of his brother, Sultan Shahanshah .  During his reign, the citadel was expanded and a wall was built around the city .  He also had a number of large public buildings constructed .
 In 1183, the city was seized by Saladin .  In 1190, Saladin's son al-Adil I , the new ruler of Aleppo, established a regular army and an administration that was modelled after that of the Ayyubid dynasty .  Under al-Adil's rule, the city flourished and became a centre for trade and scholarship .  The city grew so much in size that by the 13th century, it was the largest city in the Muslim world .
 After al-Adil's death in 1218, the city was captured by the Khwarizmian Empire .  In 1236 , the city was recaptured by the Ayyubids and, under the rule of the Sultanate of Rum , it became the capital of a large emirate that stretched from the Mediterranean Sea to the Iranian border .  Aleppo flourished during this period and its population grew to approximately 200,000 by the end of the 13th century .  The city's religious institutions grew and it became an important centre of learning.  Its scholars established the Dar al-'Ilm, the first public school in the city .  The city was also home to the largest library in the Muslim world .  During this period, Aleppo became known as the "City of Scholars" .  The city's prosperity declined during the 14th century due to Mongol raids and the Black Death .  The Mongols captured the city in 1250 and 1260 , before the Mamluks under Baibars recaptured it in 1260 .  In 1315 , the city was again captured by the Mongols .  The Ilkhanate restored order and the city began to recover.  In 1342, the city was sacked by the Black Death , which killed 60,000 people .  The city was captured by the Egyptian Mamluk sultan An-Nasir Hasan in 1362 .  In 1400, it was conquered by Timur and then regained by the Mamluks in 1401 .
 During the 15th century, the city's population declined and the city became much less prosperous .  In 1442, the city was captured by the Ottomans under Sultan Murad II .  The city was retaken by the Mamluks in 1448 .  The Ottomans recaptured Aleppo in 1471 .  The city was an important trading centre in the Ottoman Empire .  It was also known for its silk weaving industry .  In 1670, the city was captured by the Arabs and the Ottomans reconquered it in 1673 .  The city's population fell from 150,000 to 50,000 during this period .
 1875 , the Ottomans built a new citadel on a hill to the south of the old citadel .  The new citadel was used as a prison and housed a military garrison .  The city's population grew from 50,000 in 1850 to 150,000 in 1900 .  During the First World War , the city was captured by the Entente powers, but was recaptured by the Ottomans in 1918 . The vitamin B12 deficiency test is done to see if you have a deficiency of vitamin B12. This is done by injecting a small amount of the vitamin under the skin and then looking for a reaction. Vitamin B12 is important for healthy blood and nerves. Blood cells (red blood cells and platelets) are made in the bone marrow. Bone marrow needs vitamin B12 to make red blood cells. Platelets need vitamin B12 to work properly. If you do not have enough vitamin B12, your blood cells and platelets may not work properly. This may cause anemia (low red blood cells). Vitamin B12 deficiency can also cause problems with the nerves. Without enough vitamin B12, the nerves cannot function properly, and this can lead to numbness, tingling, and weakness. In some cases, a severe vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to nerve damage and paralysis.
The B vitamins are important for proper functioning of the nervous system and formation of red blood cells. B12 is found in animal products such as meat, fish, poultry, milk, eggs, and dairy products. Some people do not get enough vitamin B12 from their diet. Vegans (people who do not eat any food from animals) may have this problem. This is a blood test to measure the level of vitamin B12 in your blood.
This procedure is done by a phlebotomist, a person who takes blood samples. A phlebotomist may work in a doctor's office, a clinic, a laboratory, or a blood bank.
The health care provider will tell you how to prepare for this test. You may be asked to stop taking some medicines before the test.
If you are a vegan, your health care provider may order a vitamin B12 test to make sure you are getting enough vitamin B12 in your diet.

A smooth tongue

The following steps can help prevent a vitamin B12 deficiency:
Take vitamin B12 supplements.

Arguably the most successful of the Missouri Company expeditions was that of James MacKay and John Evans . The two set out along the River Missouri, Canada, in 1805, and followed its course to the Saskatchewan River. They then travelled to Fort Dauphin, at the headwaters of the Saskatchewan, before returning to the Missouri River and exploring the Canadian side of Lake Winnipeg, the Souris River, and the Red River Valley to the headwaters of the Red River. They travelled over 2,500 kilometres (1,550 miles) in all, and were the first Europeans to enter the region.
MacKay's name appears on the list of the expedition's members, but his role is not clear. He was most likely one of the two men who were sent to the headwaters of the Saskatchewan River to find a route to the Pacific. A man named MacKay was listed in the expedition's pay book, but nothing further is known about him.
MacKay and Evans were accompanied by three voyageurs, and by two half-breed guides, Louis Chaboillez and Francois-Gabriel Dumont, both of whom had been with Radisson and La Vérendrye. The trip was not without danger, and on one occasion the party killed a grizzly bear.

Sholay was the first movie in Hindi cinema to use a promotional jingle . This was sung by Lata Mangeshkar.
Sholay released on 15 August 1975 and was one of the most successful films of all time, making a profit of ₹14.1 crore (US$24 million) at the box office.
The 2014 re-release made ₹1.2 crore (US$200,000) at the box office.
Sholay's success led to it being dubbed into other Indian languages and being remade in other Indian languages.
In 1981, it was remade in Telugu as Sholay Mrugam (lit. "The same fire ", "The same flames ").
 Sholay is one of the most popular films in India. It is considered to be one of the most influential films in Indian cinema.
The film has been dubbed into over 18 languages.
Image:SholayPoster.jpg|right|thumb|250px|Poster for SholaySholay was the first Indian film to be shot in the then newly released 70 mm film format. It is also the first Indian film to be shown in 70 mm.
 In a 2005 poll conducted by the channel STAR World, Sholay was voted as the "Film of the Millennium" by the Indian public.
In 2010, Sholay was ranked number 2 on Empire 's list of "The 30 Greatest Indian Films of All Time".
 Sholay was among the top fifty worldwide grossing films of 1975, according to the Variety Insight database.
Sholay was the first Indian film to be shown on European television.
It was first shown in an Indian Television channel Star Plus in 2000.
The film has been released on DVD, VCD, and LaserDisc.
Sholay was re-released in India on 28 August 2013 to commemorate its 40th anniversary. On its first day of release, the film grossed ₹1.3 crore (US$200,000).
The film was dubbed into Malayalam as Sholayirile Smaranam (lit. "A memory of Sholay ").
The film was remade in Telugu as Sholay Mrugam (lit. "The same fire ", "The same flames ").
 Sholay is credited for the establishment of the Dharmendra as an action hero.
The film also marked the breakthrough of Hema Malini as a lead actress, and she was later on dubbed as "Dreamgirl".

## The assassination

### Assassination

On the night of 9 May 1977 António Baptista Leite, António Ramalho Eanes and Estrela de Carvalho, all members of the Communist Party of Portugal (PCP) and ministers in the Fourth Government of the Portuguese Republic, decided to assassinate Balbino dos Santos, a member of the opposition, in revenge for the murder of the communist party leader, Álvaro Cunhal.

### Aftermath

The Communist Party of Portugal (PCP) declared that the assassination of Balbino dos Santos was a “criminal act” and that the government should “investigate the case with the utmost rigor”.

on 12 June 1944. The attacks went ahead despite the evacuation of 150 wounded back from the front line.
The 5th Brigade had one Australian and two New Zealand battalions:
**5th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (5th RAR).** The 5th RAR had been in France since October 1943, and had fought in the invasion of Italy in March 1944.
**2nd/14th Battalion, Royal New Zealand Infantry Regiment (2/14 RNZIR).** The 2/14 RNZIR had been in France since April 1944 and had fought in the invasion of Italy in May 1944.
**23rd Battalion, Royal New Zealand Infantry Regiment (23 RNZIR).** The 23 RNZIR had been in France since May 1944, and had fought in the invasion of Italy in June 1944.
There were two brigade support units:
**2nd Field Company, Royal New Zealand Engineers (2 Fd Coy RNZE).** The 2 Fd Coy RNZE had been in France since March 1944.
**4th Field Park Company, Royal New Zealand Engineers (4 Fd Park Coy RNZE).** The 4 Fd Park Coy RNZE had been in France since April 1944.
The brigade had one armoured regiment:
**2nd/6th Armoured Regiment, Royal Australian Armoured Corps (2/6 AR).** The 2/6 AR had been in France since May 1944.
There were two regiments of artillery:
**13th Field Regiment, Royal New Zealand Artillery (13 Fd Regt RNZA).** The 13 Fd Regt RNZA had been in France since April 1944.
**26th Field Regiment, Royal New Zealand Artillery (26 Fd Regt RNZA).** The 26 Fd Regt RNZA had been in France since May 1944.
The 5th Brigade was part of the 7th Armoured Division.
The 7th Armoured Division was commanded by Major-General Sir Sydney Rowell, who had been in command of the 7th Armoured Division during Operation _TORCH_ , the invasion of North Africa, in November 1942.

The romantic Vasanta and the nihilist Vasugupta have both been labeled the " Father of Tantra ". It is easy to understand why, since both Vasanta and Vasugupta wrote Tantric treatises, and both were associated with the Śaiva Tantras. However, the two men deserve to be remembered separately, because they had very different lives and viewed Tantra in entirely different ways.
The life of Vasanta (c. 700–750 CE) is recorded in the Sanskrit literary work _Hari-bhakti-vilāsa_ , which means " The Way of Devotion to Hari ". This is a treatise on devotion to Vishnu, but it also includes a brief account of Vasanta's life. Vasanta was a prince of the Nanda Dynasty, and he was the son of a king called Śiṅgha. It is not clear whether the kingdom of Śiṅgha was actually Kannauj, the center of what is now Uttar Pradesh, India, in the time of Vasanta's life, or whether it was an independent state.
When Vasanta was young, he was married to a girl called Kamalāvatī, but he fell in love with a courtesan called Vasundhara. Vasundhara was very beautiful, and she was not averse to helping Vasanta to get his way with his beautiful wife. Kamalāvatī was deeply unhappy with her husband's behavior, and she eventually told her father. This was a terrible mistake, because the prince was angry with her. Kamalāvatī was given a choice: she could either return to her husband or be stripped and left outside the palace gates. No one in the palace would talk to her or give her food. She chose the latter option.
Vasanta was deeply upset by the way his wife had been treated, and he decided to leave the palace. He stayed in a forest for some time, living as an ascetic. He was not a real ascetic, however, because he still ate food and had sexual relations with Vasundhara. One day he saw a _yogin_ (meditating holy man) practicing tapas (austerities). The _yogin_ was named Madan, and Vasanta was so moved by the _yogin_ 's tapas that he decided to renounce his wife for the sake of austerity.
Vasanta now stripped himself and began to live in the forest. He was very powerful, and he often had bouts of anger. Vasundhara was terrified of him, and she was afraid that he would kill her if she came to see him. She therefore decided to leave the forest and seek refuge with a well-known Tantric teacher called Nārada. Nārada was pleased with Vasundhara, and he gave her a _yantra_ (a magic formula or diagram) to wear around her neck. She was also given a necklace of _akṣaras_ ( _liṅgas_ ), and a _siddhi_ (power) called _nidrā_ was placed on the necklace. _Nidrā_ was a Tantric power that allowed one to become invisible.
Vasundhara was now able to visit Vasanta in the forest, and she spent a great deal of time with the prince. Vasundhara was able to keep her Tantric powers secret from Vasanta, and he eventually forgot all about his wife through the power of _nidrā_. Vasundhara was happy with this arrangement, and she spent much of her time with Vasanta and Vasanta's spiritual teacher Madan.

The Coldrum Stones are named after a nearby farm , Coldrum Lodge , which has since been demolished . The monument lies in a " r

idgeway " that leads from the point where the River Tay leaves the Highlands and crosses the valley of the River Earn, past the hill fort of Ardoch, and out into the lowlands of Perthshire . In the 1990s, the ridgeway was rediscovered and excavations found signs of habitation dating from the first millennium BC, as well as more recent pits for extracting iron ore. The Coldrum Stones are the remains of two pillars that formed part of a stone circle .
The pillars once stood around 12 feet apart, with the bottom of each pillar being around 3 feet wide, narrowing to 12 inches at the top. They were each around 12 feet tall and the top of each pillar was square. The pillars were formed of a kind of greywacke , which is a sandstone with large chunks of quartz. The stones were originally surrounded by a circular ditch and mound, with the original entrance to the circle on the east side.
A large stone that was originally situated beside the pillars is now missing. It may have fallen down or been removed for use elsewhere. The Coldrum Stones are located in a field that is private property but which is sometimes open to the public. It remains unclear whether the field is still privately owned or whether it is now owned by the state.
The Coldrum Stones are on the left of the road.
This monument is categorised as a Scheduled Ancient Monument by Historic Scotland. It is also a Scheduled Ancient Monument in care of the Secretary of State for Scotland.
In 2007 the monument and the surrounding area was designated the Ardoch and Coldrum Ridgeway Scheduled Monument, which includes a number of sites around the area. These include an Iron Age Hill Fort at Ardoch , Coldrum Lodge, a Blair Stone and a Bronze Age Cairn. The sites are all considered to be of national importance.
This monument is of national importance for its potential to enhance our knowledge of prehistoric ritual and funerary practices. The monument forms an important element within the wider context of the ritual landscape and is of particular importance for the study of prehistoric burial practices. The monument is of regional importance because it is an important prehistoric funerary site and because it has the potential to enhance our knowledge of the wider landscape in which it is situated. The monument is of local importance as the site of an important funerary monument, and because it forms part of the wider Coldrum ridgeway.

Tobacco smoking is the most important single source of cadmium exposure in the general population . An estimated 10 % of the ca

. 2000 kg of cadmium consumed each year by the general population in the EU is due to tobacco smoking. However, 10 % of the total cadmium exposure is due to the use of cadmium-containing pigments in several consumer products such as paints, plastics, and cosmetics.
No specific target levels for cadmium exposure have been set. The overall goal of the EU legislation on cadmium is to minimize the risk of adverse health effects, particularly for workers and consumers exposed to cadmium and cadmium compounds.
Generally, the risk of adverse health effects increases with increasing exposure to cadmium. There are no data on the specific effects on health of exposure to very low doses of cadmium. However, based on epidemiological studies, the following adverse effects of cadmium exposure are known to occur in humans:
•  lung cancer,
•  kidney disease (including glomerular damage, tubular necrosis, tubular renal dysfunction, and interstitial nephritis),
•  bone disease (including osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and osteitis deformans),
•  renal tubular acidosis,
•  congenital renal tubular acidosis.
•  reproductive problems in both men and women,
•  decreased immunity.
These effects occur primarily in people exposed to cadmium dust in the workplace, such as smelter workers, battery workers, and foundry workers. In recent years, the health effects of exposure to cadmium among the general population have been the subject of scientific debate. There is no clear evidence to suggest that exposure to low-level cadmium is associated with an increased risk of any negative health effects. However, there is evidence that higher exposure to cadmium may increase the risk of renal tubular acidosis in children and renal damage in adults.
There is no evidence that exposure to cadmium from the use of cadmium-containing pigments in consumer products is associated with an increased risk of adverse health effects.
In the 1990s, the Council of the European Union set a maximum level of 0.005% for cadmium in the paint of children's toys (Commission Directive 92/13/EEC). This Directive was adopted in response to the risk of adverse health effects among children exposed to cadmium through the use of cadmium-containing pigments in toys. The Directive was amended in 2007 to include a limit of 0.002% for cadmium (Commission Directive 2007/45/EC).
In 2012, the current legislation in the EU was reviewed and it was concluded that there is no need to revise the existing cadmium regulations for paints, plastics, and cosmetics.
In 2009, the total annual exposure to cadmium from all sources in the EU was estimated at 1.2 mg/kg bw. This estimate includes 0.13 mg/kg bw from tobacco smoke and 0.97 mg/kg bw from the use of cadmium-containing pigments in consumer products. The estimate of total exposure to cadmium from all sources also includes exposure from food (0.03 mg/kg bw) and from the environment (0.01 mg/kg bw). The total annual exposure to cadmium from tobacco smoking is thus estimated at 0.4 % of the total cadmium exposure in the EU.

 Sclerodermatineae was circumscribed in 2002 by Manfred Binder and Andreas Bresinsky. The family Suillaceae was transferred from the suborder Suillineae into the suborder Sclerodermatineae. A similar willingness was also expressed by John Fleming , who was head of the ASIO office in Canberra during the 1970s .
Fleming was involved in the investigation and prosecution of the attempted assassinations of the Queen and Australian prime minister in 1970 , and the 1978 trial of the men who planted bombs in the Sydney Hilton Hotel.
In 1977 , Fleming was promoted to national secretary of ASIO , a position he held until 1983 . He resigned to become a public affairs consultant.
 Fleming said the 1970s era of 'dirty tricks' and 'fairy tales' was 'a blip' .
He said that at the time , ASIO was trying to protect the government from 'the perceived threat of terrorism' and that the then prime minister's office , under Gough Whitlam , was 'not overly supportive of ASIO's operations against alleged terrorists' .
As a result , Fleming said , ASIO was 'compelled to resort to covert activities and to use some unorthodox methods . . . to try and achieve the aims of protecting the nation against terrorism' .
However , he said the spying on journalist Paul Wilson was 'nothing to do with terrorism or security of the nation or any other reason' .
 Fleming said Wilson was spied on because he was 'a perceived threat to the government of the day' . 'It was over the Whitlam dismissal , it was over the alleged abuse of the intelligence services at the time , it was over a whole range of things and Paul Wilson was just a convenient target,' he said.
 Fleming said he knew Wilson's phone was tapped , but said he did not know about the bugging of his home.
 Fleming said he had 'no idea' who Wilson's informant was .
 In the 1970s , Fleming said , the public affairs office of the ASIO director general , which was responsible for 'vigilante activities' , was 'reclusive' .
It was not until 1986 , he said , that he realised his office had been involved in the bugging of Wilson's home. 'I was very surprised that ASIO had been doing that,' he said. 'I didn't know about it. I was never briefed about it. I had no idea it was going on.'
 'I can't quite believe it's true,' he said.
 'I think the best way to put it is that I am appalled by the whole episode and I'm very sorry that it happened,' he said.
 Fleming said he was not surprised that ASIO had spied on Wilson. 'It was just the way things were done in those days,' he said.
Fleming said he was not a 'sycophant' of the Whitlam government , but was 'an employee of the ASIO director general at the time and I did what was asked of me' .
 'Like many people in the government service at the time, I was just doing what was asked of you,' he said.

Sarnia 's population experienced a continual growth from 1961 to 1991 , with a 1991 population of 74 @,@ 376 . In 2001 the popu

- lation had increased to 76 ,974 . This increase helped to make Sarnia the 15th largest municipality in Ontario, and the second largest city in the Lambton County. The increase in population was due mainly to the growth of the population in the 30-39 age group.
Sarnia 's economy is based on the manufacture of chemicals and petroleum products. The city is the largest concentration of petrochemical industry in Canada. It is a major centre for production of polymers and plastics, with a large proportion of the Canadian production of polyethylene. Sarnia is also home to a large number of other major firms, primarily in the chemical industry.
Sarnia is also an important port on Lake Huron, which has been an important part of the city's economy for more than 160 years. Agriculture is also a major part of Sarnia's economy.
Sarnia is home to Lambton College, a well known community college.
Sarnia is the hometown of hockey legend Gordie Howe.
The history of Sarnia is as diverse as its economy. Sarnia 's original name was Clearwater. It was changed in 1823 to Sarnia, after Sarni, one of the five towns in the Austrian-Hungarian Empire. The name was chosen by Colonel Thomas Talbot.
The first permanent settler in the area was Moses Smith, an American Revolutionary War veteran. After the War, he settled near the mouth of the Sydenham River, and began to clear the land. The first white settler in what is now Sarnia was a Loyalist from Connecticut, Jeremiah Rix. He settled near the mouth of the Sarnia River, and cleared 100 acres of land.
In 1804, the first native settler, a native name unknown, settled at the mouth of the Sarnia River. He was later joined by his brother, and a third settler, William Foster. The three men built a cabin, which they called Fort Sarnia. The name was mispronounced by early settlers, and became known as Sarnia.
In 1807, Colonel Talbot arrived in the area to survey land for settlement. He chose Sarnia as the site for his new village, with the intention of making it the capital of Upper Canada.
Sarnia was incorporated as a village in 1853, and as a city in 1855. In 1914, the city of Sarnia was amalgamated with the villages of Point Edward and Port Huron.
The city is located on the shores of Lake Huron, a few miles from the St. Clair River, which forms the border with the state of Michigan. The city is also about 20 miles from the city of Chatham.
The city's climate is humid continental, with cold, snowy winters and warm, humid summers.

During the Bush War , the Rhodesian Army augmented its ranks with foreign volunteers , who were accepted into regular regiments

and deployed with the same pay and benefits as the regular soldiers. After the war , many Rhodesian citizens emigrated to South Africa , where they were welcomed by the South African authorities. Many Rhodesian Air Force pilots and other professional and technical personnel emigrated to the United Kingdom , Australia , Canada and the United States.
 After the Lancaster House Agreement , the new government of Zimbabwe effectively expelled white Rhodesian citizens from the country. The expulsion was largely voluntary, as those who stayed risked their lives in a campaign by government-sponsored militant groups known as "terror gangs" , who were often armed with automatic weapons and hand grenades. The government of Zimbabwe also continued to restrict the movement of former Rhodesian citizens into Zimbabwe. In 2007, former Rhodesian and Southern Rhodesian MPs were given permission to return to Zimbabwe to take part in a parliamentary election.

The last two chapters feature Peshkin 's commentary on the school in society , its tradeoffs and comparison with other total in

centive systems. The idea of the school's tradeoffs, and the possibility of a system that is better than the school in every respect, is a central theme that runs through the book. The final two chapters conclude with Peshkin 's views on the future.
#  **THE SCHOOL AND THE SOCIETY**
The school is viewed by most economists, if not by all, as a highly effective incentive system. But the school is not a system that has been designed to maximize the welfare of the society. Instead, it has been designed to maximize the utility of the participants, and it has succeeded in this goal. This is not necessarily a bad thing. The school maximizes the utility of the participants; the society, however, may not be maximizing its utility.
In the first chapter I argue that the utility of the society is the greatest when the incentives in the society are as good as possible. To accomplish this, we should design such a system. I argue that the school does not provide the best incentives. In the second chapter I argue, to the contrary, that the school does provide the best incentives. The military penetration of southern Florida offered the opportunity to map a poorly understood part of the country . As late a

1850, only fifty-one of 36,000 square miles of Florida had been mapped by the U.S. Coast Survey. In 1845, American troops occupied Florida and, after the Civil War, the military mapmakers produced topographic maps of the state. The Florida Topographical Department was created in 1866 and its personnel produced maps to accompany the official census of Florida in 1867. Another war interfered with the work and the Florida Topographical Department ceased operations in 1870.
This map is the product of the Florida Topographical Department. It is based on the work of the U.S. Coast Survey, which began to chart the state in 1845. The map shows the state of Florida in the late 1860s and includes the counties of Alachua, Bay, Brevard, Citrus, Dixie, Duval, Escambia, Flagler, Gadsden, Gulf, Hillsborough, Levy, Marion, Orange, Pasco, Pinellas, Putnam, Santa Rosa, St. Johns, St. Lucie, Sumter, Suwannee, Taylor, Walton, Washington, and Wakulla.
The map clearly shows the military penetration of the state in the mid-nineteenth century. The map shows the main forts and military outposts, including Fort Pickens, Fort Taylor, Fort Jefferson, Fort Barrancas, and Fort Matanzas.
The map also shows the railroads in the state, as well as counties, the larger towns, and the rivers.
The map is oriented with north to the right. The scale is 400 feet to the inch.
This is a fine map of Florida issued by the U.S. Coast Survey. It is dated 1866.

'I was keen to seek advice from other officers who had been in the job. I wanted to know how to get on with my generals and my government, and how to undertake the job of building up the army.'
Eden's first billet had been a room at the Carlton Hotel , which his predecessor, General Sir John Harding , had used for his office. It was in the basement, and Eden found it stuffy and unsuitable. He was looking for somewhere more convenient when he met Major-General Herbert 'Blubber' Patterson, the GSO1 of IV Corps, who had been given the job of finding Eden's new accommodation.
Patterson was not keen on the job. He was a strait-laced career soldier who had served through the Second World War and Korea. He was not, by nature, an opportunist, but he had no hesitation in approaching Major-General Sir Robert Thompson , then the Director of the British Military Mission in Saigon, and offering to 'take it out of him' if he could have the job.
Thompson was an officer of a very different type. A veteran of two world wars and an expert on Vietnamese affairs, he had been in Saigon since 1954 and had been appointed Commander of the British Mission in 1963. He was a walking encyclopaedia on the country. He was also a man with a wicked sense of humour who believed in making life as difficult as possible for officers trying to set up their own staff.
Patterson got the job, and set about persuading Eden to turn the basement of the Carlton into an office. Eden was not convinced, but he thought it would be a good idea to 'get rid of the general'.
Thompson, however, had other ideas. He was not prepared to allow the British commander in Saigon to have his office in the basement of a hotel.
Patterson was one of the most senior officers in Saigon, and Thompson believed that he should have a proper office, not a cupboard. Thompson told Eden that Patterson would be miserable in the basement, and that he should not permit it. Eden agreed, and the job of finding Patterson a new office fell to Thompson. He began calling around the various senior officers with an empty office in their headquarters, but no one would allow him to use it.
Finally, he went to General Le Cao, then the Deputy Chief of the Army General Staff. Le Cao was a young man, recently promoted to the rank of major-general, and he was not keen on taking on a responsibility that he felt would interfere with his other duties. However, Thompson was not to be deterred.
'I don't want to move in with you,' he said, 'but I want to see if you will think about it.'
Le Cao agreed to think about it. He told Thompson that he would go home and have a good night's sleep, and that he would call the following morning.
Thompson was delighted. He had finally found an office for Patterson, and he was sure that Le Cao would let him have it. He went to bed with the problem solved.
The next morning, however, Le Cao was true to his word. He woke up, had a good breakfast, and told Thompson that he had decided not to move in with him.
Thompson was furious. He called in Patterson and told him that he had failed.
Patterson was not that surprised. He had been in Saigon for a few months, and he knew that Thompson was a formidable opponent.
'You can't stop me,' he said.
Thompson was not convinced. 'You can't force me to have you in here,' he replied.
Patterson was unfazed. 'I'm coming in,' he said.
He was as good as his word, and Thompson was forced to move out. It was not, he told me, the only time he had been kicked out of an office.

Because acute promyelocytic leukemia ( APL ) has the highest curability and requires a unique form of treatment , it is importa

nt for oncologists to understand the mechanism of this disease.
 Although the genetic lesion was discovered in 1991, the pathogenic mechanism of APL is still not completely understood. Genetic lesions in the retinoic acid receptor-α ( RAR-α ) gene are present in almost all cases of APL . This mutation leads to a shortened form of RAR-α that is unable to bind to retinoic acid ( RA ). The most common mutation involves the fusion of the RAR-α gene to one of the retinoic acid receptor-β ( RAR-β ) genes, but other mutations can occur.
 The absence of RA receptor activity results in a state of hypersensitivity to RA , which can be detected with the addition of phorbol esters ( which mimic the effects of RA ) to cultured leukemic cells.
 RA is a vitamin A derivative that acts as a hormone through the RAR and RAR-β receptors. It is the ligand for these receptors, which bind RA and bind to DNA. This leads to gene transcription and the regulation of the cell cycle.
 APL is characterized by a blockage in the cell cycle at the prometaphase-metaphase transition, necessitating the therapy of those patients with all-trans retinoic acid ( ATRA ) and arsenic trioxide ( ATO ).
 ATRA binds to RAR-α and RAR-β with high affinity, resulting in transcription of the gene that codes for the protein pML ( promyelocytic leukemia ).
 ATRA-induced differentiation of promyelocytic cells is associated with the production of apoptosis-inducing factor ( AIF ) and cytochrome C .

The Local Government Act 1888 created elected county councils to administer services throughout England and Wales . Where a mun

cipal borough had a population exceeding 10,000, it could choose whether to become a county borough, with no interference from the county council, or to join its neighbouring county boroughs and become a county borough. These were then termed county boroughs. In 1965, under the County Boroughs (Reorganisation) Act 1965 , county boroughs were abolished (except Liverpool) and all boroughs with populations over 10,000 were known as metropolitan boroughs.

From the Rocky Mountains of Montana and Wyoming , three streams rise to form the headwaters of the Missouri River . The longest

of these streams is 520 miles in length, the shortest 320 miles, both of them running through a region whose beauty, grandeur and solitude are unequalled anywhere in the West. The streams and their headwaters are the Missouri of Lewis and Clark fame and the Yellowstone, whose name was given it by the famous explorer named after the French monarch. The third is the Bighorn, a name as beautiful as the river itself, the name of which was given it by the Indians.
To the left of the Yellowstone River, and bordering the main road which runs from Miles City to the Bighorn Mountains, are the acres of Tony's ranch. To the right of the Yellowstone is the road which runs from Miles City to the Missouri River. This road is the route of the Old Yellowstone Trail, and it is on this road that you may find Tony's ranch.
In the early days, when the white men first came, the Indians called the Yellowstone "the river of the Big Horns." The whites named it the Yellowstone, and the Indians, being rather slow to adopt new names, let it stand. As the years went by, and the railroads pushed westward, the Indians lost more and more of their ancient domain, and now there are few left who still speak their native tongue. But the old name of the Yellowstone still remains, and with it an old tradition, handed down from generation to generation, which has to do with a beautiful young Indian maiden who was captured by the Sioux and held for ransom.
The Indians had learned that the Sioux were at war with the whites, and that they were in search of a beautiful young Indian maiden. The Indians had learned that the Sioux were camped near the headwaters of the Yellowstone, and that they were on the lookout for such a maiden. The Indians sent a party into the Sioux country, and brought back a young Indian girl, whose name was Mary Lone Eagle.
The Sioux, at war with the whites, demanded the ransom of the young girl, and the Indians prepared to pay this ransom. But on the very day that the white men were to meet the Sioux, Mary Lone Eagle was stolen away. The Sioux, in their eagerness to ransom the girl, had followed her, and, in the joy of their reunion, had left their camp unguarded.
The whites were outraged by this treachery, and, taking the names of those Sioux who had captured the girl, they rode after them, leaving the ransom behind. The Sioux, who had been following the trail of the girl, rode after the whites, and the two parties met in a narrow valley between the Rocky Mountains and the Bighorn Ranges. There was a swift stream running through the valley, a small stream, but very swift, and in the center of this stream, just as the two parties met, was a mass of driftwood, and on the driftwood was a corpse.
The Sioux were thirty in number, the whites thirty-five. As the two parties rode into the valley, they met sudden death. Seventeen Sioux were killed, the rest were wounded. The whites, fighting hand to hand, cut down seventeen of their foes, and only the remaining three escaped.
The battle had been short, and for a few minutes after it was over, only the bodies of the dead lay in the valley. Then a shriek was heard, and, as the smoke of the battle cleared away, a form was seen standing in the center of the stream, upon the driftwood. The body was that of the young maiden, Mary Lone Eagle, and in her hand she held a copper tomahawk, the tomahawk which had been given her by the Sioux chief.
The Sioux, in their haste to ransom the girl, had left their camp unprotected, and the young maiden, knowing that the Sioux, with their great numbers, could not be defeated, made her way back to the Sioux camp, where she had been captured. The warriors, startled by the sudden shriek, rushed to the scene, and found the body of Mary Lone Eagle, with the copper tomahawk in her hand.

The mycorrhizal associations of several Sclerodermatineae genera have been established . Studies have demonstrated that Astraeu

opanthera, Bletia, Neobrookleya and Sclerodermatium species are mycorrhizal with fungi in the genus Mycena . The mycorrhizal status of Cyrtandra and Pleurothallis was also established by the presence of hyphal structures in the roots . However, the mycorrhizal relationships of these two genera are still unknown.
Previous research has revealed that Pleurothallis has an ectomycorrhizal relationship with a Nidulispora sp.  and that Cyrtandra roots are infected by an AFB1 (Actinomycetales) . In this study, we investigated the mycorrhizal status of these two genera, and the mycorrhizal fungi associated with them.

He had written _The Princess_ , his first long narrative poem , in a desperate burst of inspiration in June, and wanted to publish it as soon as possible in order to relieve the financial pressure on the family. He had seen that _Poems_ was doing well in the bookshops, but he had only published the volume in 1831 and had not yet seen any money from its sale. He was living on an annuity of £200 a year from his father, and the only money he had from the sale of the book was £100, which he received in July. He was only thirty-two years old, with no money of his own and no job, and it was entirely up to him to provide for the family.
Soon after Hallam's death, Tennyson had begun to write a poem on the subject of death, but he had not thought to publish it. In a letter to Hallam's widow, he wrote: 'I have written a poem which I will send to you... in manuscript for the present. It is a kind of lyric or meditation on death, and I thought it might please you, for it was written in the very time of your affliction. It is cold and measured, but I think it is not inelegant.' He sent the poem to Hallam's wife, but she did not like it, and it was not published until 1842, in _Poems_ , when it was called 'The Palace of Art'.
The poem is a series of meditations on death, ranging from a brief, vivid picture of a witches' sabbath to a long and austere consideration of the eternal fate of mankind. It does not address the particular death of Hallam, and it is not in any way a poem of mourning. In the years that followed, Tennyson would sometimes say that he had written the poem in order to take his mind off his grief. But he later wrote: 'I had no grief, no sorrow, to deaden the brain, or to intensify the fancy. I had no real grief. What I had was this – a sense that I was going to be a poet, and that I had been called upon to compose something in memory of my friend.'
The poem was not written in one sitting. Tennyson wrote it in three separate parts, one in the middle of the night, one in the early morning, and another later in the day. The first part was written in the middle of the night, when he was wakened from a dream by the death of his friend. He was able to write it down quickly, and it was completed in the early morning. The second part was written later in the day, when he was still thinking about death. The third part was written later that night, after midnight, and it was in this part that he spoke of the soul of Hallam 'being in its element when earthly passion is extinct'. ## Plot

The film begins with Verma showing a montage of his mother and himself as a child. After her death, he is raised by his father, an alcoholic. After 17 years, he returns to his hometown to work at his father's business. He stays at his father's house, right next door to his childhood sweetheart, Anju, the daughter of the police chief.

Verma is shown to be an unconventional man who does not follow traditions. He wears blue jeans in a society where people wear western clothes on special occasions only. He does not believe in arranged marriages, but chooses his own wife. He does not believe in ghosts, but is scared by a ghost in his house and hires a pandit to exorcise the house.

Anju is a conservative woman, who grows up into a beautiful young woman. She is given a proposal by her father and her childhood friend, and Verma's cousin, Hemant. But she does not accept, saying that she will only marry Verma.

Verma falls in love with a prostitute named Hukumtan. Hukumtan rejects Verma, who is heartbroken. Verma sees Anju at her wedding and leaves. However, he returns to Anju's house and, as he stands in the rain, she comes out and embraces him.

The pandit sees Verma and Anju together and tells his father, who is a police chief. The police chief tells his wife and son, who tell the police. The police come to arrest Verma, who is now arrested and taken to the police station. Anju is informed of this and runs to the police station. She forces the police chief to release Verma.

Verma is now thought to have killed his father. Anju goes to Verma's house and her father fires his son. Verma follows Anju to her house, where he is beaten by her father's men. Verma's cousin, Hemant, finds Verma in the hospital and tries to kill him. Hemant is beaten by Verma's father.

Verma is now in a coma. The pandit tells Anju that Verma will be all right if she marries Hemant, but she refuses. Verma's father is hospitalised, suffering from a stroke. Verma, in the coma, hears Anju chanting. Verma wakes up and asks Anju to marry him. She agrees and the two are married.

In Mexico , the diamond stingray is one of the most important components of Pacific artisanal shark and ray fisheries , comprising 25% of total landings. Its meat and eggs are imported to the United States , Europe , and other markets. We conducted a reproductive biology study to investigate the life history of this species and, to the best of our knowledge, it is the first comprehensive data set on its reproduction. We found that the diamond stingray migrates to depths of at least 1,300 m to spawn. It is oviparous, with a continuous spawning period from January to September. Spawning occurs year-round, with the highest density of reproductive females occurring from May to August. Trematode parasites were recovered from the digestive tracts of 45% of the specimens and from 100% of eggs. These results will be used to improve management of the fishery and to improve design of future conservation and management measures.
