Thomas Lawton was born on 6 October 1919 to Elizabeth Riley and Thomas Lawton senior in Farnworth , Lancashire . His father was

a working-class weaver and his mother was a domestic servant . From the age of twelve, Thomas had to work down the pit, despite the fact that he had an auditory defect that made him unable to hear above 100 decibels. He left school at the age of fourteen to work in the pits. He married Alice Owens in 1940 and they had two children, a boy and a girl.
During the Second World War, Lawton joined the home guard and was a Territorial Army (TA) soldier. In 1944, he was transferred to the Royal Engineers and served in the Far East.
After the war, Lawton attended the London School of Economics and qualified as a teacher. He worked in the teaching profession for twenty-five years and during this period he became the secretary of the Lancashire and Cheshire branch of the National Union of Teachers.
Lawton's early experiences as a child made him an early supporter of the rights of the working class. He became a Communist Party member in the 1950s and was elected to the London School of Economics Labour Club. He was also a member of the National Union of Teachers' executive committee.
In 1992, Lawton moved to Spain. He died on 5 December 2015 in Barcelona .

**Lawson, Jemima** (1806–1872)
Jemima Lawson was born on 27 August 1806 in Scotland . She married Henry Lawson, a Methodist minister, on 26 June 1827 and they had five children. She was a leading figure in the Independent Labour Party (ILP) and the Socialist League. She wrote for the _People's Paper_ , the _Labourer_ , the _Toiler_ , the _International Review_ and the _Workman's Advocate_.
In 1847, she was a delegate to the National Anti-Corn Law League conference in Manchester . She had been a member of the General Council of the British Association for the Advancement of the Science of Eugenics since 1929.
In 1913, she was one of the founders of the ILP. In 1919, she became secretary of the London branch of the ILP. She also became a member of the editorial board of the _Labour Leader_ and the _Labour Chronicle_ , and a member of the Women's Labour League. During the 1920s, she was chair of the Women's Advisory Committee of the National Union of Women Workers. She was also a member of the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom and a member of the editorial board of the _International Review_.
She died on 24 October 1872 in London.
See also: _New York Times_ 26 October 1872, 'Death of Mrs Lawson'; _The Guardian_ 25 October 1972, 'Mrs Lawson'.
**Lawson, Linda** (1950–)
Linda Lawson was born on 21 January 1950 in the USA . She is a professor of urban and environmental policy in the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County.
In 1998, she was the only woman to serve on the president's council on sustainable development. In 2001, she became the first African-American woman to chair the board of the American Geophysical Union. In 2002, she was appointed as the chair of the US President's Council on Sustainable Development.
Lawson has written many books. These include _Global Climate Change: Policy and Politics_ (2002), _A Handbook for Women's Environmental Leadership_ (2004), _The Climate Crisis: The Story of Denial_ (2009) and _The Climate Crisis: What Everyone Needs to Know_ (2010).

The forest is located in the southern Cascade Range , approximately 60 kilometres (37 mi) south of Vancouver , British Columbia , and 50 kilometres (31 mi) south of the U.S. border. The forest covers an area of 2,771 square kilometres (1,070 sq mi), of which 2,266 square kilometres (875 sq mi) is federal land and 405 square kilometres (156 sq mi) is provincial land. The forest is located on the western slopes of the Cascade Range , and is bounded on the north by the Fraser River and the Cheam and Manning River drainages. The southern boundary is in the vicinity of the communities of Hope and Boston Bar, and the eastern boundary is approximately 20 kilometres (12 mi) east of Agassiz. The forest receives an average of 1,100 millimetres (43 in) of precipitation annually.
The forest has a diverse topography, consisting of mountains, river valleys, plateaus and river terraces, as well as wetlands and lakes. The forest is divided into four distinct vegetation types: coastal western hemlock , western hemlock , western redcedar , and interior spruce . The forest's wetlands and cool temperate rainforests are a significant portion of the forest, and are also one of the largest in the world. The forest's elevation ranges from sea level to a maximum of 916 metres (3,005 ft) in the Tum Tum Range. The forest is home to several active volcanoes, many of which are located near the northwestern boundary.

Dylan made two important career moves in August 1962 : he legally changed his name to Robert Dylan , and he signed a management

contract with Albert Grossman . Grossman, a former boxer and carpenter who by 1962 had become a successful promoter of folk and blues acts in the Catskills and New York clubs, was looking for a way to break into the national market. He had been approached by the fathers of two of Dylan's friends, whose sons were part of the folk revival scene in Hibbing. He had also established a relationship with Murray Krugman, the manager of the Gerde's Folk City club in Greenwich Village. Krugman was trying to book Dylan for a New York appearance, and Grossman was looking for a way to promote him in the Catskills and nationally.
Krugman's first encounter with Dylan was on July 29, when Dylan, together with Bobby Vee and his band, the Shadows, appeared at Gerde's. The club had been booked for a folk concert, but the absence of the top names on the bill—Pete Seeger, Joan Baez, and Burl Ives—left Dylan as the star of the evening. Krugman, who would become Dylan's main manager for the next decade, later recalled that Dylan's performance was "one of the most unforgettable things I've ever seen." The next day, Dylan was at Columbia Records, where he cut two demo tapes, one of which was later released as _Bob Dylan_. Krugman had arranged for Dylan to meet the head of Columbia, Goddard Lieberson, and another executive, Bob Shad, to discuss his career.
Shad, who had been responsible for signing Seeger and many other folk musicians, turned down Dylan for two reasons. First, he didn't think "a Jewish kid from Hibbing" would have any appeal. Second, he thought that Dylan's voice wasn't strong enough to compete with the other folk singers. After all, he'd been turned down by Lieberson too.
Dylan had been quoted in _Billboard_ as saying that he intended to emulate Woody Guthrie and that he was a "sort of protest singer." Lieberson later recalled that Dylan "wasn't a protest singer at all. He was a folksinger. He was Woody Guthrie without the politics. He was a folk singer, and they didn't get much on the radio."
Dylan's signing with Grossman was a different story. Grossman was looking for a way to break into the New York scene, and he thought that Dylan could be his ticket. The plan was for Dylan to appear at the Gate of Horn, a club in Chicago, in September. Grossman, who would become Dylan's manager for the next decade, was also looking for an investor, and he found it in John Hammond, the legendary Columbia A&R man. Like many others, Hammond had been impressed by Dylan's Gerde's Folk City performance.
Hammond believed that Dylan had the potential to become the next big star. He persuaded his label to put up $5,000 to cover Dylan's living expenses in New York. It was the first time that Columbia had taken such a risk with an unknown folk singer. Grossman and Hammond's backing gave Dylan the confidence to believe in himself. They also gave him the opportunity to make a name for himself in the clubs of Greenwich Village.
Dylan's first gig in New York was at the Bitter End, a Greenwich Village nightclub owned by Cantor Fitzgerald. His performance was a success, and he was invited to play the Gaslight Café, another Village club. His performance there was also well received, and he was invited back to play other New York clubs, including the Village Vanguard. Dylan's first big break came in October when he was invited to perform at the Newport Folk Festival.
Dylan's early years in New York were not easy. He struggled to make ends meet, and he often had to borrow money from friends. But he was determined to make it in the music business, and he worked hard to improve his stagecraft and songwriting skills. He also began to develop a distinctive style that combined folk and blues influences. Dylan's early songs were often political in nature, and he became known for his sharp lyrics and distinctive voice.

The goal of the induction phase is to reach a complete remission . Complete remission does not mean the disease has been cured

or that it will not recur. The goal of cancer treatment is for patients to live longer than if they did not undergo treatment.
 The length of time that a patient stays in the induction phase depends on the type of blood cancer. For patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, the induction phase can last from 2 weeks to 12 months. Patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) usually stay in the induction phase for a longer period than patients with other types of lymphoma. Some patients with CLL or SLL do not reach complete remission and are switched to other treatments.
 The length of time that a patient stays in the induction phase also depends on the patient's response to treatment. If treatment is working well, the patient can be switched to consolidation therapy to continue treatment until the cancer is in complete remission. If the cancer does not respond well to treatment, the patient can undergo additional induction therapy.
 The patient's doctor monitors the patient's response to treatment with physical exams and blood tests.
 The goal of the consolidation phase is to maintain complete remission. This phase usually lasts from 6 months to 18 months, but it can range from 3 months to 3 years.
 The length of time that a patient stays in the consolidation phase also depends on the type of blood cancer. Patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) usually stay in the consolidation phase for a longer period than patients with other types of lymphoma.
 The patient's doctor monitors the patient's response to treatment with physical exams and blood tests.
 The goal of the maintenance phase is to prevent the cancer from returning.
 The length of time that a patient stays in the maintenance phase depends on the type of blood cancer. For patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), the maintenance phase can last from 2 years to 10 years or more. Patients with other types of lymphoma usually stay in the maintenance phase for 2 years.
 The length of time that a patient stays in the maintenance phase also depends on the patient's response to treatment. If the cancer does not respond well to treatment, the patient can undergo additional treatment.
 The patient's doctor monitors the patient's response to treatment with physical exams and blood tests.

Chemotherapy kills cancer cells by stopping them from growing and dividing. The drugs in chemotherapy can also damage healthy cells. This can cause side effects.
Combination chemotherapy means that a patient receives more than one drug. There are several ways to give combination chemotherapy.
Continuous infusion . With continuous infusion, the drugs are given through a needle in a vein (intravenous, or IV). The drugs are infused over a period of a few days or weeks.
Injection . With injection, a drug is given by injection into a vein, muscle, or under the skin.
Drinking the drug . With drinking the drug, the drug is given in pill form.

The Water of Life ( Das Quellwasser ) is a novella written by the German author and artist Carl Spitzweg . It is considered one of his best works and was first published in 1888.
The story was translated into English by William Furness in 1891.
In the story, the narrator is a poet who lives with his wife and works as a schoolmaster. He is a severe critic of the contemporary trend to naturalism in literature that was then gaining in influence. He is also an admirer of the poet Balduin Bählamm and his poetry. One day, Balduin Bählamm visits the narrator and tells him of his unhappy love and of his literary work. The narrator is moved by Balduin's story and becomes his friend. Balduin is looking for a new source of inspiration and is looking for a place where he can work undisturbed. He has heard of the narrator's spring and asks the poet to bring him to this place. Balduin spends the night in the house of the narrator's family but does not become friends with his wife, who is unfriendly to him. The next day, he stays in a cemetery and in the evening, the narrator brings him to the spring. The next day, Balduin visits the narrator again. He tells the poet that he has found the right source of inspiration and is now able to write again.
The Water of Life ( Das Quellwasser ) was published in 1888 by the publisher Hoffmann & Campe , Hamburg.

Arikamedu is a coastal fishing village , under the Ariankuppam Panchayat , on the southeastern coast of India , 4 kilometres (

2.5 miles ) from Pondicherry and 2 kilometres ( 1.2 mi ) from the Bay of Bengal . 

## Mythology

Arikamedu is a place of great historical significance. The site has been inhabited since the Sangam era (200 BC to AD 200). The 10th-century Tamil poet, Kambar, in his work Ramavataram, mentions that Arikamedu was a colony of the Pandya kingdom and that the colony was visited by King Ramayana (Rama) with his wife, Sita. 

Ramayana (Rama) and Sita, the main characters of the Ramayana, as depicted in the Rama and Sita temple at Arikamedu

The Pandya Dynasty (296–1343) was one of the principal kingdoms of the Tamil country. They came from the Pandya Desa, the homeland of the Pandya people.

## Discovery

The site is known to have been inhabited since the Sangam era (200 BC to AD 200). Upon excavation, many artefacts were found that indicate the settlement was inhabited by a Roman trading colony. 

The site was first explored in 1947 by the French archaeologist, André Mandouze, who uncovered a number of Roman artefacts.

In 1999, the Indian government declared Arikamedu a protected monument. The excavation and exploration of the site continues.

## Excavations

The remains of a Roman bathhouse, with six stone pillars and mosaic flooring, have been found. Another Roman bathhouse is still under excavation. The excavation has revealed that the site was inhabited by people from the Indo-Roman trade. The excavation has also revealed that the site was inhabited by people from the Tamil country. The excavation has revealed a temple dedicated to Rama and Sita. The temple was built by the Pandya rulers, and the temple was used to worship the deities of the Pandya kingdom. The temple is one of the few Tamil temples that have survived to the present day.

Soon after the Bechtlers began to strike their private issues , Secretary of the Treasury Levi Woodbury became an advocate of h

iring private mints to strike silver dollars with the same weight and fineness as the regular issue. The government would retain control over the composition of the metal, but the coinage would be contracted out to private parties. The contracts would be awarded to the "lowest responsible bidder." The government would pay for the metal used, and the coins would be delivered to the Treasury at a rate of $500,000 per month. The private mints would also be subject to audit and inspection.
Congress was not inclined to approve such a radical departure from the established system of government-owned mints that turned out coinage. The House of Representatives voted against it on March 3, 1836, but the Senate approved the plan on May 12. In the meantime, Woodbury had been replaced as secretary of the Treasury by the secretary of the navy, Roger B. Taney, who shared Woodbury's views. Taney persuaded President Martin Van Buren to issue the Specie Circular on May 18, 1836. The circular stated that the Treasury would accept gold and silver bullion at its face value, but that specie would have to be delivered to the Treasury in exchange for government-issued currency.
Within months, it became clear that the Circular was a failure. Only a small percentage of the specie that had been put into circulation during the 1830s was turned in—in fact, less than 300,000 of the $4.1 million in specie that had been issued. But the government was still required to accept specie at its face value. The Treasury had no choice but to accept the specie.
The Treasury was not the only one that had to find a way to deal with the new situation. Commercial banks that were required to keep a portion of their assets in specie faced a similar dilemma. If they took in large amounts of specie, they would have to turn it over to the Treasury at the government-mandated value. But if they kept the specie, they would be exposed to the risk that the government would later repudiate the Specie Circular and demand far less than the face value of the specie.
A group of New York banks met to discuss the problem. They came up with an ingenious solution: The banks would distribute certificates to depositors that were backed by gold and silver coin that the banks themselves had purchased from the Treasury. The certificates would be in the form of "notes" and "bonds," with each note representing a certain amount of gold and each bond representing a certain amount of silver. The banks would be able to use the notes and bonds to back their deposits.
The result was a new type of financial instrument that came to be known as "certificates of deposit." In 1837, the New York banks issued $1 million in certificates of deposit, and the following year, they issued another $3.5 million. In 1839, the banks issued an additional $6 million in certificates of deposit. From that point on, the amount of certificates of deposit issued by the banks increased every year as the number of commercial banks nationwide grew. By 1842, the banks had issued $62 million in certificates of deposit.
The banks issued the certificates as a way of dealing with the dilemma created by the Specie Circular, but they also issued them because they had a need for the money. As the amount of gold and silver coin put into circulation increased, the supply of gold and silver coin in the country grew. The need for gold and silver coin to be used in payments was decreasing, and the banks needed a way to deal with the excess supply of gold and silver coin. The certificates of deposit offered a good solution. The banks issued the certificates in a non-interest-bearing form for use in payments. The banks later created interest-bearing bonds that allowed the banks to earn a return on their excess reserves.
It was not until 1863 that a law was passed that allowed the government to issue its own certificates of deposit. The law was part of the National Banking Act of 1863, and the government issued its first certificates of deposit on April 22, 1863. The certificates were issued in $1, $2, and $5 denominations and were sold to the banks in exchange for the banknotes that the banks had issued as part of the process of redeeming the greenbacks. Innis attended the one @-@ room schoolhouse in Otterville and the community 's high school . He travelled 20 miles ( 32 km ) by

train to take courses at Michigan State College ( now Michigan State University ) in 1909 and 1910. Innis earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1914, and a Ph.D. in political science in 1916. Innis also attended the University of Chicago for two years ( 1916–18 ). He taught at the University of Toronto for 20 years, and was appointed to the Ontario Legislative Council in 1925. His most important contribution was his 1916 book The Bias of Communication, which is considered to be the first book on the history of communication.
 Innis studied the conquest of the Americas and the resulting conflicts of communication between Europe and the Americas. His research was based on the concept of "The Bias of Communication" which is the tendency to view the world from one's own perspective. He wrote that "India is eternally the other world, and to the starving man in England, the riches of India are as the stars in the sky." Innis demonstrated how misunderstandings between peoples and how they viewed their worlds could influence a wide variety of topics.
 Innis's work was criticized by early communication theorists such as Harold Innis, Marshall McLuhan, and Eric Havelock. According to McLuhan, Innis was "the first to see the bias of communication as an overwhelming force in history." McLuhan regarded Innis's ideas as a foundation for his own theories, and he credited Innis with the discovery of "the fundamental distinction between oral and printed culture." Innis also had a significant impact on McLuhan's ideas on the role of technology in the cause of social change. Innis's theories also influenced the Canadian historian and political scientist Donald Creighton.
 Innis was also profoundly influenced by Walter Benjamin.
 Innis was a prolific writer, publishing 30 books and over 300 articles and essays. He wrote on a wide range of topics, including economics, history, sociology, and philosophy. His books include The Foundations of Western Civilization ( 1926 ), The Canadian Commonwealth ( 1940 ), and Empire and Communications ( 1950 ). Innis's work has been translated into several languages, and he has been described as "one of the key figures in the development of Canadian studies."

Bond also learns that the attack was orchestrated by Raoul Silva (Javier Bardem), a former MI6 agent who had infiltrated the Chinese government. M and Silva are contacted by Patrice, an IT specialist who reveals that a terrorist group called "Patriots of the Silent Majority" (PSM) had hacked the "Silk Road" station and is using it to send out a warning: that the station's owner, Silk Industries, will be attacked.
Patrice warns Silva that he will be killed if he does not stop the attacks. Meanwhile, Bond, who is recuperating at a safe house, is visited by Eve. Bond begins to suspect that Eve is an MI6 double agent. M and Silva are attacked by a team led by Gareth Mallory (Ralph Fiennes), a new MI6 chief, who has been appointed after the death of the previous chief, M. Bond escapes and is later told by M that she has been reassigned. She also reveals that Silva will be killed in an upcoming assassination attempt. Mathis is killed during the meeting, and Bond and Eve follow Patrice to a server farm in Shanghai, where they are captured by Silva, who orders Bond and Eve to be tortured in a modified version of the "waterboarding" technique that Bond has used in the past. Silva kills the other agents in the room and frees Bond and Eve.

ATV ) programme of the Indian Navy.  The Arihant class submarines are indigenously designed and designed by the Indian Navy's Directorate of Naval Design ( DND ) and built by the Mazagon Dock Limited ( MDL ), Mumbai.  The first of class, INS Arihant , was commissioned into the Indian Navy on 26 May 2016,  with the second submarine, INS Arighat undergoing sea trials and the third submarine, INS Aridhaman under construction.  All three submarines are equipped with B-05 Sagar Missile System, consisting of 12 ballistic missiles.
The Arihant class is a continuation of the SSBN Akula-I class, being a licensed copy.  The first of the Akula class, K-152 ( Amur-1650 ) was commissioned on 29 October 1998.  The second Akula class submarine, K-158 ( Borey-A ) was commissioned on 28 April 2004.  The third submarine, K-159 ( Borey-A ), was commissioned on 11 April 2007.  The fourth submarine, K-160 ( Borey-A ) was commissioned on 22 December 2010.  The fifth submarine, B-05 Sagar ( Borey-A ), was commissioned on 28 December 2011.  The sixth submarine, B-06 Varshavyanka ( Borey-A ) was commissioned on 15 March 2013.  The seventh submarine B-07 Pskov ( Borey-A ) was commissioned on 23 May 2015.
The Indian Navy has bought 3 Akula class submarines from Russia and has two more on order.  Russia is building a second series of the Akula class submarines for its own navy.  The Indian Navy has plans for a third series of the Arihant class submarines.
The Arihant class submarines are based on the Akula class submarines. The Arihant class submarines are slightly larger than the Akula class submarines. The Arihant class submarines have a length of 110.4 m ( 362 ft ), a beam of 10.8 m ( 35 ft ) and a displacement of 6,000 tonnes.  The Arihant class submarines are nuclear powered and propelled by a pressurized water reactor supplied by the Atomic Energy of Canada Limited ( AECL ).  The submarines are equipped with a 90 MW nuclear reactor.  The submarines are air-independent propulsion ( AIP ) powered and do not have to surface to recharge their batteries.  The submarines have a maximum diving depth of 350 m ( 1,150 ft ).  The Arihant class submarines are capable of speeds of 20 knots ( 37 km/h; 23 mph) surfaced and 25 knots ( 46 km/h; 29 mph) submerged.  As of 2016, the Arihant class submarines have a crew of 65 officers and sailors.
The Arihant class submarines are equipped with the B-05 Sagar Missile System.  The B-05 Sagar Missile System uses the Klub-NK land attack cruise missiles ( LACM ) air launched and fired from 212 mm torpedo tubes. There exists in the northern parts of North America a mushroom of a disagreeable smell, and a greenish color, which grows about the stumps of the oak and birch trees in damp ground. This beverage is prepared by roasting a little of the mushroom and then pounding it in a mortar. This powder is then boiled in water, and the result of this is a thick beverage, which is drunk by the Indians.
This description of the mushroom is by the great naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, who visited North America in 1804. The Indians described to him how they had prepared the "drunken thing" and how they used it to relieve the heat of the sun. They also described how it was used as a stimulant.

A biography of Meyerbeer by Leon Botstein went so far as to say : " On the surface, it was an ideal marriage. Beethoven, who was godfather to the couple's first child, was shocked to discover that Meyerbeer, who was supposed to be a brilliant pianist, could not play a single note. "

The fish has a high fat content in contrast to other members of the family. The species has a silvery body with a green hue to it. It has a moderately long body, with a pointed snout with a lower jaw that is slightly projecting over the upper jaw. There are two barbels on the chin, and the eyes are large and protruding. The dorsal profile is convex, and the caudal fin is slightly truncated. There are 16 to 21 dorsal spines, and 12 to 18 dorsal soft rays. The anal fin has 30 to 34 soft rays. The maximum published weight is 7.8 kg (17 lb), and the maximum published length is 200 cm (79 in).

## Distribution and habitat

The species is native to the waters of Japan and Korea, and has been recorded from the Yellow Sea, the Sea of Japan, and the East China Sea. It inhabits depths of 100 to 600 m (330 to 1,970 ft). It is a demersal fish, but it is not known if it has any particular depth preference.

## Biology

The fish form schools at depths of 100 to 200 m (330 to 660 ft).

## Human uses

The fish is cultured and sold commercially as food in Asian countries , including Korea and Japan . The demersal fish is a popular food in Korea  and is widely considered to be a delicacy. Cadmium exposure is a risk factor associated with a large number of illnesses including kidney disease , early atherosclerosis

and multiple myeloma . In this study, we sought to evaluate the relationship between occupational cadmium exposure and the risk of multiple myeloma. Cadmium is thought to be a potent multiple myeloma carcinogen, as cadmium exposure increases the risk for multiple myeloma by roughly 30% .
We performed a prospective case-control study of multiple myeloma cases in the United States, using data from the US National Cancer Institute’s Cancer Prevention Study II Nutrition Cohort (CPS-II Nutrition). The CPS-II Nutrition study was a prospective investigation of cancer and other chronic diseases among 112,971 men and women aged 50 to 74 years who were recruited from 1992 to 1993. All participants were interviewed by trained personnel at their homes, and information was collected on a wide variety of topics, including demographic characteristics, medical history, smoking, and occupational and environmental exposures. Data were compiled from interviews conducted at baseline and biennial follow-up interviews through 2005. One thousand two hundred thirty-four incident multiple myeloma cases were identified from 1993 through 2005. Each case was matched to four control subjects.
We estimated occupational cadmium exposures using a detailed job-exposure matrix based on information provided by the participants. We calculated the median (quartile range) occupational cadmium exposure as 14.0 (5.1, 32.8) μg/m3. We estimated the age-adjusted cumulative occupational cadmium exposure by multiplying the median exposure by the number of years of work and then summing the cumulative exposures among all jobs held during the follow-up period. We estimated the occupational cadmium exposure at each job by multiplying the annual exposure level at each job by the number of years working at that job and then summing the cumulative exposures among all jobs held during the follow-up period. We estimated the maximum occupational cadmium exposure by multiplying the median exposure level by the number of years of work, then summing the maximum exposures of all jobs held during the follow-up period.
We estimated the relationships between occupational cadmium exposure and multiple myeloma risk using multivariable conditional logistic regression models. The primary model included age at enrollment, race, education, body mass index, alcohol consumption, smoking, family history of multiple myeloma, and mean annual income. The secondary model included all the covariates from the primary model plus occupational cadmium exposure. The tertiary model included occupational cadmium exposure and the other covariates in the primary model. The final model included all the covariates in the tertiary model. We performed a sensitivity analysis to assess the robustness of our findings by repeating the analyses using median cadmium exposure as the exposure metric. All statistical tests were two-sided, and statistical significance was defined as a P value < 0.05. Analyses were performed using SAS version 9.2 (SAS Institute, Inc., Cary, NC).

In 2009 , a cladistic analysis of fungal phylogeny was carried out by the French phycologists , Pierre Boistel and François Lutzoni . The Early Neolithic people of Britain placed far greater emphasis on the ritualised burial of the dead than their Mesolithic fo

es. They buried their dead in the ground in a variety of ways, placing the bodies in graves or in simple stone cists. Some of the dead were buried with personal possessions, but most were not. Some of these early Neolithic graves were excavated and examined by antiquarians in the 18th and 19th centuries, and their contents published by the early archaeologists. More often, however, these 'barrows' were left undisturbed, though their exact location was sometimes recorded by map-makers. It was not until the 1930s that these 'barrows' were systematically explored by archaeologists. The result was a reassessment of the role of the Early Neolithic in Britain, and a general re-evaluation of all Neolithic periods.
The most common type of grave, however, was that in which the dead were buried in the ground without a surrounding mound. These were excavated by archaeologists in the 1930s and 1940s, and their contents published in the 1950s and 1960s. In the 1970s, however, a debate began on the role of these 'barrows' and the reasons for their use. The barrows were divided into two types: those that contained no grave goods, and those that did. The former included the fully excavated examples such as those at Hambledon Hill in Dorset, and the fully excavated examples from the southern chalk of England such as those around the Weald, and those from the Wessex region. The latter included the undisturbed examples such as those on the chalk of the Weald and Wessex, the Oxford Clay of the Vale of White Horse, and the Oxford Clay of the upper Thames valley. The division into two types was, however, rather arbitrary, and it was suggested that these barrows should be reassessed.
The debate was hotly contested, and in the end it was the archaeologists rather than the anthropologists who came out on top. This was an important victory, for it resulted in a reassessment of the whole of the British Neolithic, and led to the publication of much new material. Some of this material was soon to be published by the Oxford Archaeology Unit, and this book is a product of that work.

At the Battle of Jutland , she was the first ship in the German line , and Hipper 's flagship , and drew fire from the British

5th Battle Squadron ( HMS Barham , HMS Valiant , and HMS Malaya ) in the first four minutes of the action. As she was 21 knots (24 mph; 39 km/h) faster than the nearest British ship, she was able to disengage and escape.
Windermere was the first ship to receive the Iron Cross 1st class in the Battle of Jutland, awarded to her captain, Wilhelm Souchon.
Souchon was promoted to rear admiral on 17 September 1916 for his success at Jutland.
Souchon was promoted to vice admiral in 1921 and became commander of the German naval forces in Turkey. In 1923 he was appointed to the German Navy High Command as a member of the staff of the Inspector of Naval Forces.
On 1 January 1928, he was appointed commander of the fleet, and in 1929 he became chief of the naval command.
From 1934 to 1935, he was commander-in-chief of the German Navy (Oberbefehlshaber der Kriegsmarine). When Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933, he was considered a pro-Nazi, as he had been a member of the NSDAP (Nationalsozialistische Deutsche Arbeiterpartei).
The first member of the German Navy to hold the rank of Admiral, he was also the first naval officer to be awarded the Nazi Party Golden Party Badge.
He was in command of the German forces during the Battle of the River Plate, the first naval battle of World War II, and the first naval battle of the war in which a battleship was sunk. The defeat was attributed to his decision to take the pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee on a suicidal mission against the Royal Navy force.
On 18 December 1939, he was promoted to Admiral and appointed Commander-in-Chief of the German Navy. He was also a recipient of the German Cross in Gold.
He was promoted to Generaladmiral in 1941 and appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Navy on 30 January 1943.

The main gameplay feature of Crush is the ability to transpose the layout of a level between 2D and 3D representations to reach

the Exit. The player can switch between the two representations (which are given names "N" and "S" respectively) at any time with a press of a button, but the player has to take into account the layout of the level in one representation when switching to the other.

The game's levels are generally non-linear, but there is an order to them, with the player having to reach the Exit before moving on to the next level. Reaching an Exit by using the 3D representation results in a game over, whereas reaching an Exit by using the 2D representation will result in a "win".

The gameplay is partly a platform game, where the player has to avoid "Hazards" (which can be avoided either by jumping over them or by ducking underneath them) and crush "Targets" (which are reached by jumping on them) to reach the Exit on the level. The player has to reach the Exit to proceed to the next level.

### Levels

Levels are assigned to a difficulty level, with the difficulty level being selected by the player. The difficulty levels are "Easy", "Medium", and "Hard", but the levels are not separated into different categories, so all of the levels in a given category (no matter what the difficulty level) are the same.

Levels have a variety of different layouts and themes, with each level having its own layout and theme.

### Hazards

Hazards are objects that cause an instant death if the player touches them. Hazards can be avoided by jumping over them or by ducking underneath them.

A list of Hazards:

* Balls: Balls are objects that float around the level. If the player touches a ball, the player dies.

* Pits: Pits are objects that are fixed to the ground and are unable to be jumped over. If the player touches a pit, the player dies.

### Targets

Targets are objects that can be crushed to earn points. Targets are able to be crushed by jumping on them.

A list of Targets:

* Pits: Pits can be crushed by jumping on them.

* Targets: Targets can be crushed by jumping on them.

### Crushing

Crushing refers to the act of jumping onto a Target to earn points.

### Difficulty

The game has a difficulty setting. The player can select the difficulty level before starting a new game, and the player cannot change the difficulty level during a game.

The difficulty levels are "Easy", "Medium", and "Hard". The difficulty setting does not affect the layout of the levels, with all of the levels being the same in each difficulty level.

### Scoring

The player earns points by crushing Targets. The player can earn a higher score if the player manages to crush more Targets in a level than if the player managed to crush less Targets.

Between 1764 and 1809 , Sweden built six hemmemas . The hemmema became the largest and most heavily armed vessel in the archipe

lego's fleet, illustrating Sweden's commitment to active naval defense of the Baltic Sea against potential enemies. The hemmema was a ship of the line built in accordance with the regulations of the artillerieordning of 1772 .
The hemmema was a relatively small vessel with a length of about 150 feet (45 m) and a beam of about 40 feet (12 m). Its displacement was about 450 tons, and its main battery consisted of 44 cannons in 12 batteries of 3 cannons each, with additional 6 long guns and 4 smaller guns enabling the hemmema to defend itself from small vessels. The hemmema was a three-mast ship (main mast forward, fore mast aft, and mizzen aft), and the main mast was almost 70 feet (21 m) tall. The hemmema had a crew of about 100 men, about half of which were cadets in training.
Between 1764 and 1767, six hemmema were built in the Danish shipyard at Nyland as part of Sweden's naval defense of the Baltic Sea. Five of the hemmema were built as a single class, and the sixth was built as an improved version of the five. The hemmema were used in the Russian War of 1788-1790 when Sweden joined the Russian side of the conflict, and all six were involved in the Battle of Svensksund in 1790. The hemmema were used until 1809 when Sweden joined the Third Coalition against Napoleon and all were converted into warships carrying 44 cannons. The hemmema were not constructed in large numbers and the disadvantages of a ship of this size and design were apparent. The hemmema were too small to be used as flagships, too expensive to maintain, and too slow to keep up with the main fleet. Consequently, none of them were built after 1809.

In 1942 he was again promoted, this time to understudy. On 19 November he understudied Maurice Denham in Richard II. He was on a tour of Sussex that day when he was telephoned from the Old Vic and asked to come back to London at once. He caught a train and rushed to London. He was taken to the theatre and made up. Then he was seated in the stalls to watch the rehearsal.
At the end of the performance he was taken to the stage and introduced to the audience. He did not remember any of this, but he was told he had been "received with cheers and applause". He was then taken to the dressing room and an older actor, who was the understudy for the actor playing King Henry, asked what he had done. "I've been introduced to the audience," he said. "I've been given a round of applause and cheers and I've been taken to the dressing room." "You're the understudy for Richard Burbage," the other actor said.
He was given only a brief rehearsal before the performance, and he was then on stage throughout the performance. Later he was asked to take four lines, and then eight lines. Egyptian writings describe the gods ' bodies in detail . They are made of precious materials ; their flesh is gold , their bone

is silver , their blood is lapis lazuli , their sweat is amber , and their resurrection from the dead is made of copper . The gods are often depicted with human faces, but they have the bodies of animals , birds , reptiles , or fish .

### Egyptian deities

In ancient Egypt , the gods were said to have created humanity from their own bodies. One god , Atum , is described as being encircled by a milky white snake . It is said that he created the world and the first human from the snake.

### Mesopotamian deities

In Mesopotamia , the gods are often described as being composed of gold and silver , and even though they can take on human form , they are more often depicted as winged humans or humanoid animals .

### Greek deities

In Greek mythology , the gods were each said to be made of one or more elements . For example, Demeter and Persephone each had one body and two faces, one of each element.

### Hindu deities

In Hindu mythology , the avatars of Vishnu are said to be made of either jewels, diamond, or the flesh of the goddess Lakshmi.

### Mayan deities

In Mayan mythology, the gods were created from the sun, the moon, and the earth.

### Norse deities

In Norse mythology, the gods are described as having silver or gold bodies. Thor is described as being made of iron, while Odin was made of wood.

### Romano-Greek deities

In Roman and Greek mythology, the gods are often depicted as having animal bodies or parts of animals. Zeus is often depicted with the head of an eagle, while his wife Hera is often depicted with the body of a cow.

### Chinese deities

In Chinese mythology, the gods are said to have bodies made of metal. The most famous example is Guan Yin, who is said to be made of gold.

### African deities

In West African mythology, the gods are said to have bodies made of gold and silver. The most famous example is Olorun, who is said to be made of gold.

### Japanese deities

In Japanese mythology, the gods are said to have bodies made of wood. The most famous example is Amaterasu, who is said to be made of cedar.

### South American deities

In South American mythology, the gods are said to have bodies made of stone. The most famous example is Inti, who is said to be made of gold.

### North American deities

In North American mythology, the gods are said to have bodies made of earth. The most famous example is Tiamat, who is said to be made of clay.

### Oceanic deities

In Oceanic mythology, the gods are said to have bodies made of wood. The most famous example is Rongomai , who is said to be made of bamboo.

### Asian deities

In Asian mythology, the gods are said to have bodies made of wood. The most famous example is Shen Nung , who is said to be made of bamboo.

Minarsih is rescued by Bapak Yasin and his wives. Bapak Yasin takes Banjar to the police station to make a report. Bapak Yasin's wives are shocked to learn that Minarsih is pregnant. Bapak Yasin's wives also learn that Minarsih is now the mistress of Bapak Yasin.
The following morning, Bintang Mas is informed that Bapak Yasin's mistress is giving birth to a baby boy. Bintang Mas tells Bintang Bintang to prepare for the child's birth. Bintang Bintang does not want to do this. She tells Bintang Mas that she wants to give her baby to Minarsih to raise. Bintang Mas is angry. She tells Bintang Bintang that she will do whatever she wants, and that she will teach Minarsih a lesson.
Bintang Bintang gives birth to a baby boy. She tells Minarsih that she will give the baby to her. Minarsih is surprised. She asks Bintang Bintang why she wants to do this. Bintang Bintang tells Minarsih that she wants her baby to be raised by a mother who loves him. Bintang Bintang then leaves. Minarsih raises the baby boy and gives him the name Basoeki ( Basoeki Nael Muhajir ). Basoeki grows up to be a painter like his father.
Bapak Yasin's wives are angry with Minarsih. They want to kill her. Bintang Bintang tries to protect Minarsih. She tells Bapak Yasin that Minarsih is pregnant with Basoeki's child. Bapak Yasin is happy and tells his wives to leave Minarsih alone.
Minarsih and Basoeki have been living together for many years. Bapak Yasin's wives are still angry with Minarsih.

" Ode to a Nightingale " is a poem by John Keats written either in the garden of the Spaniards Inn , Hampstead , London or , ac

cording to some critics , in the garden of Fenton House , Hampstead. 

Keats first wrote a sonnet on the subject and then, almost immediately, expanded it to a full ode. He wrote the poem in the summer of 1819.

## Background

John Keats left medical school in 1815 to embark on a career as a poet, although he only began to publish in 1817. Keats met John Hamilton Reynolds, a friend from medical school, whom he met again in 1818. Reynolds was a poet who critiqued Keats' poems. He encouraged Keats to publish his work in the Examiner and he published his poems as part of a subscription project for Keats' brother, George. He was also a member of the Leigh Hunt circle, which included other poets, such as Percy Bysshe Shelley, and artists, such as Joseph Severn.

In 1818, Keats moved to Pole Street, Hampstead, north-west London. He lived there until 1820, and it was there that he wrote Ode to a Nightingale. John Hamilton Reynolds came to stay, and it was during his visit that Keats wrote the poem.

## Analysis

Ode to a Nightingale is a sonnet whose first 8 lines are an apostrophe, addressed to the bird, and the last 6 lines are a response by the poet to his friend's confusion over the sonnet's apparent end.

Throughout the poem, the poet uses the nightingale as a symbol of death and immortality. In the first stanza, for example, the bird's song is described as "The self-same song that heard before" (line 1), suggesting that the nightingale's song has always been and will always be. The bird is "half-sad" as it sings its "plaintive" song, which suggests that it is aware of how it is perceived by the listener, and that the bird's song is a response to the "unequal match" (line 11) of the listener's mortality and the bird's immortality.

In the second stanza, the poet returns to the melancholy theme with a reference to "ill-fated lovers" (line 13) who have died because of their unrequited love. This stanza also begins to introduce a sense of regret and longing in the listener. The third stanza concludes with the listener declaring that he would rather hear the bird sing to him than to anyone else.

The fourth stanza begins with the listener comparing himself to the nightingale, suggesting that he is just as sad, lonely and unrequited. The listener ends the stanza with the question: "What if the youth should vanish from my sight / And those two lips / Should never more / In this poor bosom repose?" (lines 22–25), suggesting that the listener is afraid that he will die before he can win the listener's love and that the loss of the listener's love will be the end of his life.

In the last two stanzas, the listener begins to hope that the nightingale will sing to the listener to "cheer" (line 29) him in his anguish. In the penultimate stanza the listener compares his "fading" (line 32) and "waning" (line 33) spirit to the nightingale's song, and in the last stanza, the listener asks the nightingale to "forget" (line 35) him and to sing to others, ending with the phrase "If I died" (line 36), suggesting that the listener is contemplating suicide but is afraid to do it.

## Reception

In 1819, Keats sent the poem to Lord Byron, who declared it "magnificent and perfect". It was published in 1820, in Hunt's The Examiner.

To say that the comic book had been a success would be something of an understatement .

By 1993, Hellblazer had been selling around 100,000 copies an issue. It had become a staple of the late-night television chat shows and a regular target for the tabloid press . It even had its own movie tie-in, in the form of _Batman: The Killing Joke_ by Alan Moore and Brian Bolland .
It was, in other words, a success.
So much so, in fact, that Delano had won the Eagle Award for Favourite Comic Book Writer in 1990 . He had even received a letter from an MP, who had been concerned that the comic book was corrupting the youth of the nation.
Delano had always been an outspoken man, and he had often been accused of setting out to deliberately shock his audience. It had been a criticism that he'd often taken great pleasure in ignoring.
'Most people, ' he said, 'have a very narrow, very safe view of the world . They don't want to be confronted, because they don't want to have to look at themselves . '

'I always knew that I wanted to write comic books, ' he said. 'I wanted to tell stories in pictures . '

The Penguins ' needs led them to complete a blockbuster trade on March 1 , 1991 . Cullen was sent to the Hartford Whalers , alo

ng with a first-round draft pick , in exchange for Sergei Makarov , a second-round draft pick , and a fourth-round draft pick . Cullen began his NHL career with the New Jersey Devils in 1986–87 and played for the Devils for four seasons, appearing in 219 games and 216 of them as a regular. Cullen played for the Detroit Red Wings and the Tampa Bay Lightning before joining the Whalers .
Cullen played for the Whalers over 15 games in the 1990–91 season, scoring seven goals and six assist s. The trade was mostly considered a lucky break for the Whalers , who used the first-round draft pick to select Patrik Elias .
In June 1992 , Cullen signed with the Pittsburgh Penguins as a free agent . He quickly established himself as a key component of the Penguins ' front line . He was named to his first All-Star Team in 1992–93 and the Penguins reached the Stanley Cup Finals in 1992, losing in six games to the Chicago Blackhawks .
In 1993–94 , Cullen had career highs in goals (32), assists (41), and points (73), and was voted to the NHL All-Star Game , where he was named the game's MVP.
Cullen played for the Penguins for ten seasons, scoring 336 goals and 726 points in 821 games. He was named to the NHL All-Star Team four times, in 1994 , 1996 , 1998 , and 1999. Cullen played with the Penguins until 1999 , when he signed with the Boston Bruins for a three-year term. He was traded to the Toronto Maple Leafs on February 13, 2003 and retired after the 2003–04 season.
In 2005 , Cullen was inducted into the Penguins ' Hall of Fame .
Cullen grew up in St. Louis , Missouri and played college hockey at the University of Michigan .
Kelly is the son of Penguins' president and CEO David Cullen, former Penguins' president and COO Trevor Cullen, and grandson of former NHLer and coach Ted Lindsay . His brother, Paul Cullen, played at Michigan and in the NHL with the Detroit Red Wings.
Cullen, an avid golfer , was a member of the PGA Tour 's Nissan Open and the Buick Open in 1992 .
Cullen has been married to Debra Lynn since 1990. The couple has two children: Aaron , who played hockey for the Michigan State Spartans , and Brayden.
The Penguins retired Cullen's number 27 in a pre-game ceremony on March 18, 2006 .
In 2007 , Cullen joined the Penguins ' broadcast team as a color analyst for Fox Sports Net Pittsburgh broadcasts.
On November 14, 2009 , Cullen was named as the head coach of the Wilkes-Barre/Scranton Penguins of the American Hockey League . He was relieved of his duties on November 23, 2009 .

In the early years of colonial South Australia , the colonists saw themselves as part of the British Empire and external defenc

e of the region would be provided by the British military. In 1808 Britain had adopted a policy referred to as 'liberal neutrality', which stated that it would not attempt to prejudice the war between France and her allies and would not allow the French to use its ports for the purpose of attacking Britain .
The colonies, however, were exempt from this policy and their ports were at the disposal of the Royal Navy and the military. In 1816, General Sir Ralph Abercromby, the commander-in-chief of the British forces, stated that South Australia would be defended by the military. Governor Sir John Hindmarsh, however, thought that the colony's financial situation would not allow the establishment of a permanent garrison. In 1836, Governor George Gawler decided to form a small military garrison and in 1838 an infantry regiment was formed, with the South Australian Corps (SAC) as the colonial name. The Governor himself was appointed its commander, with the rank of lieutenant-colonel. This garrison was to be supplemented by a detachment of the 40th Regiment, a small corps of mounted riflemen and a detachment of the Royal Artillery.
The outbreak of the New Zealand Wars in 1845 placed an increasing burden on the SAC. It was not until 1847 that Governor George Grey decided that a permanent garrison of 110 soldiers, later increased to 150, would be maintained in Adelaide . They were brought from England by the transport the _Sir William Parker_ , which arrived in November 1848. In 1849, the 40th Regiment left South Australia, but its riflemen were retained and in 1854 became the Mounted Rifle Corps.
In addition to the military forces, the civil power and the colony's police force were to be augmented by the gaoler, who in 1843 became the Chief Police Officer. The gaoler was to be assisted by a magistrate and became part of the colony's police force.
By 1847, the SAC was divided into three battalions, one of which, the Adelaide Battalion, was made up of the regiment's detachment in the city. A detachment of the 40th Regiment, which was to become the 1st Battalion of the South Australia Mounted Rifles (SAMR), was stationed at Port Lincoln and a detachment of the 40th was stationed at Port Adelaide.
Following the establishment of responsible government in South Australia in 1856, the military forces were placed under the control of a minister of defence. A permanent garrison of 216 men and 13 officers was maintained and in 1860 a second battalion of SAMR was raised. During the 1860s, South Australia 's military was the only one in the Australian colonies to be maintained by the colonial government, the others being supported by the British military. In 1870 the colony's military was placed under the War Department.
The 1870s were a difficult period for the South Australian military, and following a disastrous period on the frontier, the SAC was reorganised and was renamed the South Australian Mounted Rifles. By 1879, South Australia had a small and under-funded military, the cost of which was borne by the colonists and not the British government. By 1881, the South Australian Mounted Rifles was only 300 strong and the SAC consisted of 216 men. In 1885, the Adelaide Battalion was disbanded and the SAMR was reduced to 250 men. The following year, the SAMR was reduced to a cadet corps, and in 1888 the SAC was reduced to a state reserve.
In 1890, the Adelaide and Port Lincoln Battalions were reunited and the SAMR was again raised to full strength. Following Federation, the SAMR was placed under the control of the Commonwealth government and the SAC was disbanded.
During the First World War , South Australia played a major role in the defence of the ANZAC beachhead at Gallipoli , and the 1st and 2nd Battalions of the Australian Imperial Force (AIF) were formed in the colony.
In the defence of the Australian mainland, the SAMR was committed to the defence of Sydney and Hobart .

In 1947, the Selective Service Act of 1947 ( Chapter 7, 61 Stat. 36, Public Law No. 80-77) removed the CPS from the federal government and transferred it to the jurisdiction of the states.

Emerson 's essay "The American Scholar" , delivered at the Phi Beta Kappa Society at Cambridge, Massachusetts in 1837 , established him as a leading voice of his generation. He was a leading exponent of Transcendentalism and a mentor to Henry David Thoreau.
The importance of this essay to the history of philosophy is twofold. First, it laid the groundwork for many of the themes and concepts he would develop and expand upon in his sermons and published works. The Arnhem Oosterbeek War Cemetery , more commonly known as the Airborne Cemetery , is a Commonwealth War Graves Commission cem

eteries in Oosterbeek, Netherlands.
It is the largest war cemetery in the Netherlands, and commemorates 1,731 Commonwealth servicemen, many of whom died in the Battle of Arnhem in September 1944.
The cemetery was designed by Sir Frederick Gibberd and the first interments were made in 1946. 2,850 Commonwealth casualties are buried or commemorated in this site.
There are 2,850 Commonwealth burials of the Second World War in this site. 2,818 of them are unidentified.
The cemetery is managed by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.
The cemetery is open daily and admission is free.

With a more streamlined form than other nurse sharks , the tawny nurse shark is believed to be a less benthic , more active swi

Â­mer. In shallow water, or when startled, it will often swim to the surface.
The tawny nurse shark is a large shark, capable of growing to over 14 ft (4.27 m) in length. Its coloration is generally dark brown or grayish, with a yellowish or whitish underbelly. Its back is marked with four rows of dark brown, triangular spots. It has a pointed snout, a short, rounded head, and small eyes. Like all nurse sharks, it has five gill slits.
The tawny nurse shark is found in the tropical western Atlantic Ocean. It occurs from southern Florida and the Bahamas, to southern Brazil, and from the Caribbean to southern Brazil. It has also been reported in the Gulf of Mexico.
The tawny nurse shark is common in estuaries, lagoons, harbors, rivers, and coastal waters. It prefers sandy or rocky bottoms, and is most common at depths of 2-168 ft (0.6-52 m). It may also enter brackish water.
This shark is a nocturnal feeder, hunting on the bottom by touch. It feeds on crustaceans, molluscs, fishes, and other invertebrates.
The tawny nurse shark may be a viviparous , oviparous , ovoviviparous , or oviparous species. It is thought to be oviparous, with the eggs hatching within the mother, who then gives birth to live young. Ovoviviparous, viviparous, or oviparous females give birth to live, young ones. The young are about 20 in (50 cm) long at birth.
The tawny nurse shark is not threatened; however, it is commonly caught by fishermen.

The play opens with Algernon Moncrieff , an idle young gentleman , receiving his best friend , John Worthing , whom he knows as

Bunbury.
 When they part, Algernon reveals that he has created a fictional invalid friend, Bunbury, whom he uses as an excuse to escape from unwelcome social obligations.
 On a train to London, Algernon meets Cecily Cardew , a young girl who has recently inherited some money and begun spending it on improving her estate in the English countryside.
 Cecily, who is in love with Algernon, explains that she is waiting for her cousin, Gwendolen Fairfax , to arrive.
 Gwendolen arrives and, after discovering that Cecily has inherited some money, hopes to marry her for her money and then leave her.
 Gwendolen is forced to marry Jack Worthing, who has recently arrived in the country and is introduced to her by Algernon.
 Gwendolen is delighted when she realizes that Jack is Algernon's brother.
 Jack and Algernon reveal that they have been masquerading as brothers to protect Jack's reputation.  Jack is a respectable member of society.
 When Algernon suggests that he and Gwendolen should marry, Jack refuses and leaves with Cecily.
 Algernon and Gwendolen marry.
 Algernon, who has previously been claiming to be the brother of a clergyman, is revealed to be the clergyman himself.  He returns to his parish.
 The play concludes with Jack and Cecily, who choose to be married secretly and live happily ever after.
 The play was first presented at the Haymarket Theatre in London in 1895, where it ran for 87 performances.  Its success at the Haymarket Theatre prompted a British tour, which began the same year.
 The play has been adapted several times for film and stage.  The first major film adaptation was the 1938 British film The Importance of Being Earnest, directed by Anthony Asquith and starring Michael Redgrave as Jack Worthing and Michael Wilding as Algernon Moncrieff.
 The play is routinely performed by school and amateur theatre companies.

In 1981, the FDA issued a warning that women expecting a baby should not use nonoxynol 9 vaginal creams and gels since it may increase the risk of preterm labor.  In 1993, the Centers for Disease Control ( CDC) recommended that pregnant women should not use nonoxynol 9 or products containing it because of concerns about the possible association of this agent with resistance to the AIDS virus. The hen flea ( Ceratophyllus gallinae ) is the most common flea in their nests . The small , pale house @-@ sparrow flea C. fri

valdszkyi also lives in nests. The larvae both feed on plant materials and animal droppings including feathers.
 Bird fleas are particularly important in the development of bird mites and some other ectoparasites of birds.
 In 1758 Linnaeus used the scientific name Pulex gallinae in his Systema Naturae , one of the first uses of the name ( his spelling was Pulex gallinaceus ).
 In the 20th century two subspecies of C. gallinae were recognised, C. gallinae gallinae and C. gallinae mustelae.
C. gallinae gallinae has a darker greyish brown coloration than C. gallinae mustelae.
The identification of C. gallinae mustelae as a separate subspecies is controversial and in some modern texts it is not recognised.
 The scientific name C. gallinae is derived from Latin gallinae , meaning "hen", to distinguish it from the chickens' flea, C. perniciosus, as chickens were at that time a food source for people, and the flea was considered a pest.
The hen flea is endemic to the Palaearctic region. It is found in most of Europe , Asia, and North Africa . It is also present in Morocco and Algeria ( in the Atlas Mountains ).
Outside these areas it is absent in most of North America , the Caribbean , and the Near East .
Larvae of C. gallinae feed on droppings including bird droppings , both organic and inorganic.
 The life cycle of C. gallinae is completed at temperatures between 15 °C (59 °F) and 25 °C (77 °F). The eggs of C. gallinae are white and elliptical, becoming yellow as they mature.
 The adults are dark brown with a white abdomen.
The species has a wide host range. The main host of the adults is the common pheasant ( Phasianus colchicus).
C. gallinae is the most common flea on chickens .

In 2005 a Canadian study of cockatiels found that they could become infested by C. gallinae larvae.

C. gallinae is a vector of tapeworms of the genus Raillietiella in chickens and other birds .
C. gallinae are known to transmit the bacterium Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis, the cause of Johne's disease , to cattle.
Fleas in the genus Ceratophyllus are also known to be vectors of the gastrointestinal worm Trichostrongylus colubriformis in sheep .
The disease flea allergy dermatitis is caused by C. gallinae or C. brachyurus .
They can also transmit the bacterium Bartonella henselae to humans, who are typically infected by the bite of a cat which is carrying the bacterium. The bacterium can cause a painful skin rash ( Carrion's disease ).

Shortly after Evita 's death , Dr. Pedro Ara was approached to embalm the body . Fraser and Navarro write that it is doubtful t

issue preservation was ever a consideration. The body was removed from the air-conditioned room in the Buenos Aires Racetrack where she lay in state to the Casa Rosada in the afternoon of 27 June 1980. From there it was taken to the Panteón de la Recoleta Cemetery where it was placed in the Duhalde family vault. The body was never subjected to the rigours of a full embalming process.
The first problem for Dr. Ara was what to put in the vault. There was a catafalque of 2.4 metres in height, which had been used for the funeral of the US ambassador to Argentina, Henry Cabot Lodge. Somehow, the Duhalde family found out about it and it was placed in the vault. In the following weeks, the catafalque was changed from the one used for Lodge, to one specifically designed for Evita.
The five-metre-high catafalque was constructed by the sculptor Ildo Meneghetti, and the clever architect, Eduardo Giannini. The catafalque was covered with 12,000 red roses and was adorned with a glass crown. The image of Evita was created by the sculptor Lucio Corvalan.
The funeral mass was held the following day, on 28 June 1980. The Duhalde family, the Peronist party, the military, the Church and the people of Argentina all took part in the funeral.
The coffin was carried on a gun carriage down the streets of Buenos Aires, through the Plaza de Mayo and to the Recoleta Cemetery. A 21-gun salute was fired and the Duhalde family joined the religious service. The military band then played the national anthem and the body of Evita was interred in the family vault.
This was not the end of the story.
Dr. Pedro Ara, the embalmer, had not been given any instructions on how to proceed with Evita's body. During the funeral, the body was covered with a black cloth which had to be lifted so that the coffin could be moved to the vault.
When the pallbearers placed the coffin in the vault, they found the body of Eva Peron sitting upright. This was because of the air trapped in her lungs, which had squeezed her body into a sitting position. Her knees were bent too, which caused considerable discomfort to the people who had to be squeezed inside the vault with her.
The crowds were horrified and shocked, and there were suggestions that Evita had been murdered and that the assassin had dressed her corpse to look as if she had been buried alive. Much to the relief of the people, the body was found to be in good condition, and it had not been rotting.
The funeral was a bit of a shambles and the Duhalde family were sure that the body should be removed from its tomb and placed in a mausoleum.
The body was embalmed on two occasions in 1981, both times before the tomb was visited by the public. The first embalming took place on 23 April 1981, and the second on 22 May 1981.
The first embalming was carried out by Dr. Pedro Ara who had been assisted by Dr. Carlos N. R. Ferreira. The second embalming was carried out by Dr. Carlos A. Vera, assisted by Dr. Carlos N. R. Ferreira. The bodies were placed in the vault in the Panteón de la Recoleta on 23 April 1981.
The first tomb was opened to the public on 17 June 1981. After that, the tomb was opened two days a week. By 1983, the tomb had had 1,350,000 visitors. By 1986, the number had increased to 5,000,000. The tomb was closed in 2006 to undergo restoration work. It reopened on 27 December 2007.
The tomb itself is fairly modest. It is made of stone and has a glass front. There is a plaque on the wall that has the following inscription:
Aquí yace el cadáver de la heroína popular Eva Perón.
El pueblo argentino la despierta y la engrandece.
Juan Domingo Perón.

Postural displays include tall and low poses , pointing , open bill , and wing waving . The ' tall posture ' is used when in cl

ash of wills with another bird.
The ' low posture ' is used when the bird is in a submissive mood, but also protects the bird's vulnerable neck and head.
The ' pointing ' is used when the bird is protecting its territory. In this posture, the bird's eyes and beak are pointed (hence the name).
The ' open bill ' is used when the bird is begging for food.
The ' wing waving ' is used to try and scare the other bird away. Both the tall and low postures are used when birds are trying to attract a mate.

Soil mycorrhizae are  a diverse set of fungi that grow in symbiosis with plant roots.  The soil fungi are members of the phylum Basidiomycota , the same phylum that includes edible mushrooms like shiitake , maitake , and portobello mushrooms.
Members of the class Agaricomycetes  are among the "most common and widespread" soil fungi.  They produce the familiar mushrooms and toadstools.
A number of species of fungi, mostly in the Zygomycetes and Agaricomycetes, are known as plant pathogens.
Many of the more than 10,000 species of lichens are fungi that have formed symbiotic relationships with algae or cyanobacteria.
Fungi are nature's most efficient recyclers and a key part of the nutrient cycle.
The mycelium (singular mycelium) of a fungus is the vegetative part of the organism that often forms the visible part of a fungal colony.  The mycelium is a network of branching threads called hyphae, which share a common source of nutrition. Hyphae may branch extensively, forming a mycelium with a large area.
Mycelium is the part of a fungus that grows and spreads over a large surface area, typically in soil or on other substrates.  The word comes from Greek: mykēs, meaning "fungus", and lēthē, "vegetation".

" Forbidden Fruit " was the last song recorded and produced by J. Cole for his second album , Born Sinner ( 2013 ) . It was rec

oded at The Hit Factory by Ronald " Hutch " Hutchinson and Cole himself. The song was written by Cole, Chris Styles, Ivy Dickens, Jim Jonsin, Willie Taylor, and Ronald Hutchinson. 

Cole's second album , Born Sinner (2013)

It was inspired by his relationship with his then-girlfriend , Melissa Heholt , who later became his wife , and was the first song the couple wrote together.

During the third week of its release , the song became the ninth most downloaded song of the week on the Billboard Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs chart.

## Background

Cole wrote the song with his then-girlfriend, Melissa Heholt. It was written about their relationship. Cole also revealed on the album's tour that he wrote the song about Heholt, who became his wife in 2015. He said "I wrote this song with my wife. I was going through a lot of personal stuff and she was there for me. There are a lot of guys who experience that, they just don't talk about it. She's a very beautiful, strong woman. She doesn't understand why I don't have a lot of songs about her. I guess she knows I'm a bit shy."

## Composition

During the song, Cole uses his voice to sing a soft melody over a slow piano and synthesizer riff.

## Critical reception

Professional ratings

"Forbidden Fruit" received generally positive reviews from music critics. Michael Madden of Consequence of Sound praised the song for its "vocal tone, touching lyrics and emotional delivery", stating that "it's a testament to Cole's growth that this song is more about his wife than himself." Andy Kellman of AllMusic wrote that the song "is a lovely, more delicate narrative, but it's also a slyly ironic lyric, as Cole sings, 'It's amazing how nothing can feel so forbidden'." Ryan Dombal of Pitchfork Media wrote that "Forbidden Fruit" is "a complete opposite of 'Let Nas Down' in every way, and it's one of the album's best tracks." Ryan Middleton of PopMatters wrote that "the best songs on Born Sinner are moments like 'Forbidden Fruit', where the singer's falsetto is allowed to soar over a piano riff that echoes the best of classic soul, or when he's able to let loose with a rapid-fire flow like on 'Power Trip'."

## Chart performance

During the third week of its release, the song became the ninth most downloaded song of the week on the Billboard Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs chart.

## Live performances

Cole performed the song on the 2013 BET Hip Hop Awards on October 15, 2013.

Operational experience had found Blackburn 's Firebrand strike fighter to be far from suited to carrier operations . In particu

- lar, Blackburn 's low-wing monoplane design had proved itself to be of limited use in the confined conditions on deck. The Firebrand was, however, a very fast aircraft and its capabilities were not to be totally forsaken.
Ideally, a new carrier-based fighter would be based on the Boulton- Paul Defiant, a twin-engined, twin- tail aircraft fitted with a turret-mounted machine gun. In the late 1930s, however, the Admiralty had rejected the Defiant design for carrier use because it was considered to have insufficient speed and range. The Power Jets W.1 was also considered but rejected in favour of a Fire- brand design.
The Firebrand was a single-seat carrier strike fighter, powered by two Rolls-Royce Griffon engines. First flown in March 1944, it entered RN service in May that year.
In 1945, the Admiralty decided that the Firebrand would be superseded by a new carrier-based fighter, but before it could be replaced the aircraft had proved itself to be a very effective combat aircraft.
In May 1944, Fire- brand squadrons were deployed to the Mediterranean Fleet, arriving in time to take part in the invasion of the Italian mainland.
The first operational sweep was flown by a lone Firebrand during the invasion of the island of Pantelleria, which was captured on 12 June 1944.
A few days later, Firebrand IIIs from 803 Squadron took part in the invasion of Sicily. Two 803 Squadron aircraft were shot down, but the pilots made forced landings on the island and were rescued by the Royal Navy.
The Firebrand squadrons continued to operate in the Mediterranean for the remainder of the war, carrying out strikes against targets in Italy, Yugoslavia and Syria. In all, 803 Squadron lost nine aircraft, 804 Squadron lost four aircraft.
Following the end of the war in Europe, the Firebrand squadrons were deployed to the Far East. In July 1945, the aircraft flew in support of the British landings on the island of Malaya. In operations against the Japanese, 804 Squadron lost one aircraft, but the pilot was rescued.
During the Battle of Malaya, the Firebrand squadrons, flying from the carriers _Illustrious_ and _Indomitable_ , carried out a number of precision raids against Japanese airfields and gun positions.
The Firebrand squadrons returned to the United Kingdom in the late summer of 1945, but the aircraft continued in operational service with 804 and 807 Squadrons, based on the carrier _Dawn_ , until the end of the war in August 1945.
By the end of the war, a total of 171 Firebrands had been built.

The Firebrand was a single-seat, single-engine monoplane, powered by two Rolls-Royce Griffon 88 engines.
The aircraft was 36 ft (11 m) long with a wingspan of 44 ft (13.5 m), and had a maximum speed of 400 mph (644 km/h). The Firebrand had a service ceiling of 35,000 ft (10,670 m) and a range of 675 miles (1,086 km).
The Firebrand was armed with a 20 mm Hispano cannon in a dorsal turret and with four .303 in (7.7 mm) machine guns in the wings.
The aircraft had a crew of two, the pilot and an observer who doubled as a radio operator.
The Firebrand was the first British naval aircraft to be fitted with four-bladed propellers.
The aircraft were fitted with a 'ski-jump' deck layout, with a 10° 'ramp' at the leading edge of the wing, to improve take-off performance. In addition, the aircraft had a jettisonable tail-hook to assist with carrier landings.
Aircraft from 803 Squadron were also fitted with the AI Mk IV airborne radar.

In a review of the first performance of Parsifal in Brighton in 1924, the Daily Mail commented: 'A few years ago a friend of mine, who is not very familiar with the works of Wagner, wished to be initiated into the fascination of his music. "Fancy taking me to one of those performances of Parsifal," he said, "You know I can't stand Wagner." I was puzzled. "Why not?" I asked. "Well," he answered, "the music is too long and boring, and I think the libretto is silly."
'I had to agree with him. Parsifal is long, and the libretto is silly. The reason why Wagnerism has been so wide-spread is not that Wagner's music is particularly good, but that it is so stupid.
'The story is one of the stupidest and most uninteresting I have ever read. The music is even stupider and more uninteresting, and the play on the whole is a monumental vulgarity.'
Victor de Wolf, in his book Wagner's Ring (1964), also took the view that Parsifal was a failure: 'Wagner should have ended the Ring with the death of Siegfried and the burial of the spear on the top of the mountain. He should not have written the Parsifal music, and he should have left the Wagners to carry on the work.'
It is a pity that neither Mr de Wolf nor the Daily Mail reviewer took the trouble to read the libretto carefully, because the story of Parsifal is one of the most beautiful and fascinating of all the operas. It concerns the quest of the Grail, the mystical chalice, and deals with issues arising from the attempt to find the Grail and to understand the meaning of the Grail's legend.
The Grail, with its implications of purity, of redemption, of sacrifice, of the power of death and of the power of rebirth, is a beautiful symbol of all the most profound and sublime aspects of the human experience, and the story of Parsifal is a remarkable and beautiful one. The libretto of the first performance in 1882 was incomplete, but Wagner completed it before his death in 1883, and the completed libretto was used in the first production of Parsifal in Bayreuth in 1882.
Because the libretto of Parsifal was so complete, the original production in Bayreuth was able to use music which Wagner had written to accompany the action, and the result was a succession of scenes which are among the most beautiful and moving of all opera, and which have an inner significance which is almost unique in opera. The production at Brighton was the first complete production of Parsifal to be seen in England since that of 1924, and it was a delight to be able to see it again.
The music is remarkable in many ways. It is the most abstract of Wagner's music, and yet it is among the most deeply felt. In fact, the music is the most profoundly felt of all, but it is abstract, in the sense that the music is not a representation of literal action, but is rather a representation of the inner significance of the action. The music is beautiful in the abstract sense, and the production in Brighton did not succeed in realizing the full significance of this beauty.
The action of Parsifal takes place in the Land of the Grail, in a castle which is a replica of the castle of the Grail. It is a city in the earth, with the earth itself as the background.
