The 'Dunkerque' was built at the Arsenal de Brest . The keel was laid down on 15 June 1935 and the ship was launched on 14 January 1937 by Madame Marquet-Chavanne (the wife of Jean Marquet, Prefect of Loire-Inférieure). She was commissioned on 20 May 1937 under the command of Capt. (S.) (Cdt) Marcouat.
On 10 October 1939, the 'Dunkerque' was assigned to the Northern Flotilla (FN) (with the 'Strasbourg' and the 'Saint-Louis') and was based at Boulogne-sur-Mer. A year later, on 9 October 1940, she was assigned to the Southern Flotilla (FN) (with the 'Strasbourg' and the 'Jean Bart').
In late 1940, the 'Dunkerque' and the 'Strasbourg' were ordered to leave the British Navy's blockade of the French coast and return to French ports. They were not to be caught in the same trap as the 'Richelieu' and the 'Courbet'.
On 29 November 1940, they set sail from the Channel ports, escorted by the destroyers 'Gloire' and 'Guépard' and the torpedo-boats 'Bourrasque' and 'Marsouin'. However, they were spotted by the British submarines 'Oswald' (Lt.Cdr. R.W. Mack) and 'Sturgeon' (Lt.Cdr. G.S. Stewart). The 'Oswald' torpedoed the 'Dunkerque' at 19,500 yards at 19h16. The 'Dunkerque' immediately turned sharply to starboard and attempted to return fire, but her guns could not be depressed enough to reach the submarine. The 'Dunkerque' was struck on the port side, between 'X' turret and the conning tower. One of the torpedoes hit the engine room, destroying the propeller shafts. The 'Dunkerque' lost power and began to sink. The destroyer 'Gloire' managed to tow her for a while, but the 'Dunkerque' sank at 20h15.
The 'Jean Bart' was launched on 21 June 1938 and commissioned on 11 September 1940 under the command of Capt. (S.) (Cdt) Pierre Guépratte. The ship was based at Toulon (FN) from 1941.
The 'Jean Bart' was ordered to return to French ports on 13 November 1942. She was escorted by the destroyer 'Siroco' and the torpedo-boats 'Bourrasque' and 'Capitaine Mehl'. The 'Jean Bart' was spotted by the British submarines 'Utmost' (Lt.Cdr. R.V.E. Case), 'Unbeaten' (Lt.Cdr. B.J.B. Schofield) and 'Utmost' (Lt.Cdr. R.V.E. Case). The 'Unbeaten' attacked the 'Jean Bart' with a spread of four torpedoes at 19h02. Two torpedoes hit the ship, one between 'B' turret and the conning tower. The 'Jean Bart' lost power and began to sink. The 'Siroco' attempted to tow the ship, but the 'Jean Bart' sank at 20h03.

Prince Albert Kamehameha, also known as Prince Lot Kapuauluohi Kamehameha, (1824–1849) was a member of the House of Kamehameha, and heir apparent to the throne of the Hawaiian Kingdom. His reign was brief, as he was only king for eight months before his death. He was the only son of King Kamehameha III and Queen Kalama.

His father died on November 15, 1854, and Lot was chosen as the successor to the throne on December 11, 1854.[2] He was then elevated to the title of prince on December 13, 1854, and heir apparent on December 26, 1854.[3]

However, in academic circles the study of non-institutionalized religions has been trending away from the anthropological and sociological approaches of the 1950s and 1960s and toward the empirical, historical, cultural, and psychological approaches that are common in the present day. Contemporary scholarship is heavily invested in the cultural turn in the humanities, and it is following in the footsteps of the social historian of religion, the cultural historian of religion, and the sociology of religion. These approaches are arguably more appropriate than earlier approaches for studying what is currently construed as Wicca.
The current determination of what is and is not Wicca is a relatively recent phenomenon. The label "Wicca" was first used in 1954 to describe a group of English Pagans who met regularly in the home of a retired schoolteacher named Gerald Gardner (1884–1964). Gardner and his followers were interested in traditional folk culture and European witchcraft, and they were seeking to revive the practices of earlier generations. The Wiccans Gardner and his followers were a part of a larger movement that has been called the "Stone-Age Revival" or the "Neo-Pagan Revival" (Wasson 1989: 35). This movement consisted primarily of crypto-Pagans, but also included members of other non-institutionalized religions, such as Druids and members of the Theosophical Society. These individuals were interested in traditional folk culture, and they believed that this culture was more authentically "religious" than the Christianity that had become dominant in the West. The Stone-Age Revival was also something of an intellectual movement. The movement was heavily invested in the study of anthropology and comparative religion, and it was inspired by the work of scholars who were attempting to recover the lost religions of the ancient world.

They believed that the Craft was the remnant of the pre-Christian religion of the British Isles. They believed that the survivors of this ancient religion had become "witches" who had been persecuted and killed by the Church. They believed that their religion was a living tradition, and they began to refer to themselves as "Witches." The term "Wicca" was invented in 1954 by one of Gardner's followers, Doreen Valiente, to refer to this religion.
In 1957, Gardner's book _Witchcraft Today_ was published. In this book, Gardner claimed that the religion of the English countryside was the "Old Religion," which had been revived by him and his followers. With the Flood Control Act of 1944, Congress set forth policies and guidelines to prevent further flooding. One of the guidelines was to provide flood control to communities that were at a higher risk.
In 1949, a survey was conducted to determine the location of the proposed levee systems to protect St. Louis. The survey identified the location of the proposed levees and their lengths. With the survey complete, the St. Louis Flood Control Project (SLFCP) was authorized in 1954. The project included the construction of a series of levees, floodwalls and pumping stations. The total cost was $86.5 million.
Construction of the project began in 1958 and was completed in 1962. The project was managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE). Construction of the project was divided into three phases. Phase I, from Jefferson Barracks to the City of St. Louis, was completed in 1960. Phase II, from the City of St. Louis to the Missouri River, was completed in 1962. Phase III, from the Missouri River to the Mississippi River, was completed in 1963.
The project protected 5,550 square miles of land from flooding. The project also provided a route for commercial water traffic on the Mississippi River.
The project was of great importance to St. Louis as it provided flood control for the region. It also provided a route for commercial water traffic on the Mississippi River.

The American pilot was Lieutenant Commander William Burch, who was flying out of Gander, Newfoundland. He reported that he had seen the smoke stacks of a fleet of tankers which were trying to get into the Kola Inlet. His report was ignored by those on the ground, who did not believe that there was such a large fleet of tankers.
The American plane was a Martin PBM Mariner, an amphibious aircraft, which could land on water and be ready to take off again within five minutes. It was a slow aircraft, with a crew of thirteen, and had a top speed of 190 miles an hour. The Mariner had been designed to carry a crew of five, and at the time of the raid was carrying a crew of twelve. After his initial report, Lieutenant Commander Burch was ordered to land close to the American submarine _Grenadier,_ which was moored in a harbour near the Kola Inlet.
Burch was an experienced pilot, but on landing in the dark he crashed into the submarine, damaging the aircraft and injuring Burch himself. He refused to let the crew of the submarine take him to a hospital, and was taken back to Gander, arriving there at 0130, three hours before the raid was due to end. Burch's report was now the only information that the Americans had about the Russian fleet.
The Americans now knew that the Russian fleet was at sea, but they were unaware that two of the tankers, the _Atlantic Conveyor_ and the _Fort St. John,_ were already hit by torpedoes. The raid now had to be called off, and the British Ministry of Defence ordered a recall. No one knew what the Americans knew of the situation, but the RAF received the recall orders at 0145. The raid was now over, and the RAF had suffered five aircraft lost.
Bad weather had now closed in, and the weather conditions were so bad that the Americans decided to recall their aircraft. They did not, however, call off the British aircraft, and at 0225 the weather was sufficiently clear for the RAF to start taking off again. By now the Russians knew what was happening, and their anti-aircraft batteries were now in position and ready to fire at the attackers. The Americans were not in a position to recall their aircraft, and they had to wait until the British had taken off.
The continued attack was totally ineffective. The _Atlantic Conveyor_ and the _Fort St. John_ were now on fire, and their crews were in danger of being overcome by smoke or of being hit by a torpedo as they tried to bring the fires under control. As the attack continued, the aircraft were taking quite heavy anti-aircraft fire, and one of them, a Lancaster, was hit and forced to return to base.
The Russians now started to put their anti-aircraft batteries on to radar, and this information was passed to the RAF. The RAF pilots were now flying blind, and were unable to locate the Russian batteries. They were forced to fly at low levels, and the aircraft were hit by anti-aircraft fire.

His crew were saved, but the aircraft was lost. Another Lancaster was hit and the pilot, Flight Lieutenant Alastair Cunningham, was killed. The remaining Lancasters were forced to fly to Norway to land.

Afterward Ingrid reached peak winds , shear increased and began to weaken the hurricane as it approached the Mexican coast . Th

irty-two people were killed in Mexico and dozens of houses were destroyed.
On September 2, 2003, Ingrid reached peak winds of 185 km/h (115 mph) as a Category 4 hurricane which was the most powerful storm to strike Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula since Hurricane Gilbert (1988) and Hurricane Beulah (1967). It was one of only two Category 4 hurricanes to strike the country and the only one to hit the peninsula. It was the first hurricane recorded to reach the Yucatán Peninsula in 17 years.
On September 3, the storm weakened to a Category 3 hurricane. The storm struck Veracruz as a Category 3 hurricane, causing extensive damage. When the hurricane hit, the Mexican government had already evacuated 12,000 people from the state of Veracruz as a precaution. 1,000 people were left homeless by the storm, and 30,000 people were left without electricity.
A total of 44 people were killed in the state of Veracruz. This was the highest number of deaths from a hurricane in that state in 43 years. 23 people were killed in the state of Tabasco, 5 in the state of Chiapas and 1 in the state of Campeche. 11 people were missing in the state of Veracruz, and 3 were missing in the state of Tabasco.
Ingrid caused 43.3 million U.S. dollars in damage, making it the most expensive hurricane in Mexico. In total, the hurricane caused at least 46 deaths and at least US$2.9 billion in damage. The storm was the most expensive hurricane in Mexico since Hurricane Pauline in 1997.
After landfall, Ingrid weakened to a tropical storm on September 4. The storm moved over the mountains of Mexico and the state of Hidalgo, where it caused more floods. The storm weakened to a tropical depression and dissipated on September 6.
The name Ingrid was retired from the rotating list of names on May 23, 2004. Ingrid was replaced with Idalia for the 2009 Pacific hurricane season.

The scientific name of the oribi is Ourebia ourebi . The sole member of its genus , the oribi is placed under the family Bovida

and the order Artiodactyla . A small antelope of about 70 cm height at the withers , it can weigh up to 45 kg. The oribi has a brown and yellow coat , which changes according to the seasons and is very homogeneous . These are two white triangles above the eyes, a white line on the chest and a white patch on the throat . Its tail is short and thin .
The oribi is found throughout the African continent (South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Zambia, Tanzania, Kenya, Ethiopia, Somalia, Sudan, etc.) in savannah and savannah-forest areas. Its habitat is the open savannah with scattered trees.
In the past, the oribi was abundant. The population has nevertheless greatly declined since the 1970s, especially because of the massive expansion of agriculture and the encroachment of wooded areas. Now it is considered to be an endangered species .
The oribi is a solitary animal that lives in small groups of 1 to 4 individuals. His territory is delimited by urine deposits and dung piles . The males and the females are not territorial.

Thomas Vincent Darden ( born August 28 , 1950 ) is a former American football cornerback , safety , and punt returner who playe

in the National Football League for the Green Bay Packers , Los Angeles Rams , and Atlanta Falcons . Darden was selected in the second round of the 1973 NFL Draft , and was inducted into the Green Bay Packers Hall of Fame in 2017 .
Darden was born on August 28, 1950 in Memphis , Tennessee . He grew up in Chicago , Illinois .
Darden attended Crane Technical High School in Chicago, Illinois . He was a member of the varsity football team, playing both offense and defense. Darden was the all-city defensive back in 1967. He was named Chicago Tribune All-State Honorable Mention and was also an all-city wrestler. Darden attended the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign where he played defensive back for the Illinois Fighting Illini football team.
Darden was selected in the second round (36th overall) of the 1973 NFL Draft by the Green Bay Packers . Darden was the first player from the University of Illinois to be drafted in the first two rounds of the NFL draft.
On September 30, 1973 , Darden made his NFL debut against the Buffalo Bills . He intercepted a pass from quarterback Jim Leopold for a 38-yard gain, which was his first NFL interception. Darden's rookie season was highlighted with an interception return for a touchdown against the St. Louis Cardinals . In 1974 , Darden's first full season as a Packer, he intercepted three passes and also returned 14 punts for 117 yards. In 1975 , he intercepted two passes and also led the Packers with 250 all-purpose yards.
Darden was traded to the Los Angeles Rams in 1976 . He intercepted two passes in 1976 . Darden intercepted a pass from quarterback Jim Plunkett in the first quarter of the 1979 Super Bowl XIV against the Pittsburgh Steelers .
In 1980 , Darden was signed by the Atlanta Falcons . He intercepted five passes, which was the most by a Falcons player since 1971 . Darden's interception total led the team in 1980 and 1981 .
Darden retired from the NFL after the 1982 season .
Darden was named to the Green Bay Packers Hall of Fame in 2017 .

A tropical wave spawned a tropical depression between the Lesser Antilles and Cape Verde on August 7 . It slowly strengthened a

few days later and became Tropical Storm Harvey. It was the first hurricane of the season and was only the second hurricane to be named Harvey. The storm made landfall on the coast of the Dominican Republic as a Category 3 hurricane, but it weakened slightly before it dissipated over land on August 11 .

Hurricane Harvey (1993)

On July 29, the National Hurricane Center issued a special statement on Tropical Depression Three, indicating that the tropical cyclone had become the first hurricane of the season. Harvey was the fourth tropical storm or hurricane to be named in the 1993 Atlantic hurricane season; the others being Bertha, Cesar, and Hortense.

On July 29, the National Hurricane Center issued a special statement on Tropical Depression Three, indicating that the tropical cyclone had become the first hurricane of the season. At 1200 UTC on August 10, the hurricane made landfall near Samaná, Dominican Republic. Early on August 11, the hurricane moved ashore near Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic. A reconnaissance flight indicated that the cyclone had quickly degenerated into a tropical wave; as a result, the National Hurricane Center discontinued advisories on the cyclone.

## Preparations and impact

A tropical storm watch was issued for the islands of Montserrat and Antigua; the watch was discontinued on August 10. A hurricane watch was issued for Guadeloupe; the watch was discontinued on August 10. The storm was expected to impact Puerto Rico, but it did not.

At least one person was killed by the hurricane in the Dominican Republic. About 40,000 people were left homeless by the storm. A total of 85,000 people were left homeless by the hurricane. The hurricane was the strongest to strike the Dominican Republic since Hurricane David in 1979.

Similar games [ edit ]
Barbarian II: The Dungeon of Drax was a major inspiration for Rise of the Triad , which was first released in 1994 for MS-DOS, Amiga , and Atari ST. The 3DO version of Rise of the Triad was the first (and only) 3DO game to make use of the 3DO's CD-ROM drive.
The game was also similar to the 1989 home computer game Dungeon Master , which was released in the same year as Barbarian II: The Dungeon of Drax on the Apple II.
Reception [ edit ]
Barbarian II was positively reviewed when released. In the December 1988 issue of Computer Gaming World , Steve Clarke called it "one of the best games ever," with outstanding graphics and sound. The magazine's software feature "The Role of Computers" declared it "the best, most addictive barbarian game."
In 1996, Computer Gaming World declared Barbarian II: The Dungeon of Drax the 65th-best computer game ever released. The editors wrote, "One of the best barbarian games ever made, this first Ultima Underworld-style 3D dungeon crawler showed how far you could push the 256-color EGA graphics."
In 2000, Computer Gaming World declared Barbarian II: The Dungeon of Drax the 12th-best computer game ever released. The editors wrote, "While it lacked the sophistication of later titles, this was the first of the 3D dungeon crawlers, and for its time it was as good as it gets."
In 2004, Computer Gaming World declared Barbarian II: The Dungeon of Drax the 97th-best computer game ever released. The editors wrote, "This was the first game to provide solid 3D graphics for the PC, one of the first to use pre-rendered backgrounds, and one of the first to introduce WASD-style movement."

The main industries are tourism , agriculture , fishing and forestry . Skye is part of the Highland Council local government ar

ena. The main settlements are Portree, Broadford, Dunvegan, Sleat, Uig, and Tarbert. The island gives its name to the Skye Boat Song .
Island loom large in the human imagination: their stories have been told since time immemorial, and the people who live there have connections that are both ancient and modern.
The island is connected to the mainland by the Skye Bridge , a 2.1 km (1.3 mi) long bridge on the A87 which crosses the channel between Kyle of Lochalsh and Kyle Rhea , and is the shortest bridge in Britain connecting two islands.
Road and rail connections to the mainland are provided at Kyle of Lochalsh and at Glenelg , with a ferry service also available.
The island has a wide range of attractions, including the Cuillin Hills , the Talisker whisky distillery , the Museum of Island Life (which is based in the old County Gaol) and a large number of castles. Other attractions include the Old Man of Storr , the Old Man of Stoer , the Duntulm Castle ruins, the Dunscaith Castle ruins, the Neist Point Lighthouse, and the Dunvegan Castle .
Skye is served by Skye Bridge , which opened in 1995 and enables road traffic between mainland Scotland and the island. The bridge is the shortest of any in the UK connecting two islands, at 2.1 km (1.3 mi) long. It connects the A87 to the A855 , the latter being the main route through the island.
Skye is also served by a ferry service, between Armadale and Mallaig (with a connecting bus service), which takes cars and foot passengers. The ferry service is operated by CalMac Ferries and takes around 30 minutes. A ferry also runs between Uig and Tarbert (with a connecting bus service), from the mainland.

Russian tanks and tanks of the former Soviet Union.
 1915 – 1930s: The civil war in Spain and the Russian-Polish war provided Soviet engineers with plenty of first hand experience with tank warfare.
 1943 – 1945: The Germans in the east and the Japanese in the south provided Soviet engineers with plenty of real-life data on large-scale tank warfare.
 1946 – 1960s: With the resumption of military hostilities between the East and the West, the Soviet Union once again became a pioneer in tank development.
 1970s – 1990s: The continuation of the arms race between the East and the West further increased the need for faster development in armor technology.
In the Soviet Union, the need to develop new armor types was a major factor in the Soviet's designing of new tank models. Soviet engineers were never shy to experiment, as their country was not politically or economically stable. Therefore, they often had to improvise and maintain a high level of innovation in order to keep up with the West.
The Soviet Union was the first country to use experimental armor, known as "sturdy" armor. This "sturdy" armor was made of non-hardened steel plates. The turret was completely covered in this armor, as were the tank body and the hull. The side armor was 12 mm thick and the side armor was 10 mm thick. In most cases, armor thickness stayed at 10 mm. . As a result, early Soviet tanks had much more armor than the comparable French and British tanks.
The Soviet Union was the first country to develop a steel-armored tank, known as "experimental" armor. This "experimental" armor was made of hardened steel plates, which made them resistant to ordinary artillery and bullet impacts. The turret was completely covered in this armor, as were the tank body and the hull. As a result, early Soviet tanks had much more armor than the comparable French and British tanks.
Soviet engineer Nikolai Fedorovich Shashmurin was the first to introduce the concept of a cemented steel armor. The tank body was made from several layers of armor plates, between which there were gaps filled with cement. This would make it harder for the armor to be penetrated by bullets. However, this armor was still relatively soft and could be penetrated by artillery shots.
In the late 1920s, the Soviet Union was the first to develop a cemented armor steel plate. This "cement armor" was made of steel plates that were hardened and then filled with cement. This would make it harder for the armor to be penetrated by bullets and artillery shots. The turret was completely covered in this armor, as were the tank body and the hull. As a result, early Soviet tanks had much more armor than the comparable French and British tanks.

#  **Giraldus Cambrensis**
 _The Itinerary of Archbishop Baldwin through Wales, c._ 1188
Translated by Peter C. Lewis
INTRODUCTION
The author of this text is known to us as Giraldus Cambrensis, or Gerald of Wales. He was born in Wales sometime around 1146. He was educated at Oxford and Paris, and returned to England in the 1170s. He was a friend of Henry II and was appointed the bishop of St Asaph in 1188. In 1191 he became the archbishop of Brechin in Scotland. He returned to England and served as the bishop of St David's until his death in 1223. His work on the history of Wales and his travel narratives are the best sources of information about the medieval history of Wales.
There are several different versions of the text presented here. The first version is the Latin text that was edited by Thomas Wright in 1852. The second version is the English translation prepared by Peter C. Lewis, which is a "new" translation, commissioned by Penguin Books in 1993. The differences between the two versions are not always clear, but the English translation is generally more smooth, and is therefore the preferred version. I have provided a comparison of the two translations in the notes to the text.
This type of travel narrative is known as an itinerary in which the character of the region is described in detail. Medieval readers and writers also created a genre of travel narrative in which the "perfection" of each place is described. See Erin Sullivan, _The Perfection of Medieval Travel Narrative_ (Amsterdam: Rodopi, 2000).

He had, moreover, been made a bishop of the church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and had been sent to the countries over which the Church of St Asaph has jurisdiction. So he determined to take up the duties of his office, even though he was unfamiliar with the characteristics of the country and its inhabitants. He chose to visit it from end to end, and in his journey he sent ahead of him the envoys of the church, who were to make the people acquainted with his coming. He himself arrived at the city of Bristol in the month of September, in the year of our Lord 1188.

Irish writer Garth Ennis then took over the title in 1991 , again from 2000 AD , where he had been working on Judge Dredd . He

wrote  several  stories  set  in  the  same  universe  as  his  popular  series  The  Boys ,  then  teamed  with  artist  Glenn  Fabry ,  who  had  previously  worked  on  Hellboy , on a new version of the 2000  AD  icon  in  2000  AD  Prog 2052  and  Prog 2053  respectively. The new series has featured the return of the mutant alien Judge Death ,  a  continuation  of  the  story  of  the  robot  alien  Judge  Anderson ,  and  an  exploration  of  Judge  Dredd's  past.

In 2006, Ennis began a four-part Dredd story in the 2000 AD Megazine and in 2007 he worked on a Judge Anderson story with artist Dan Cornwell.

### Conceptual development

Ennis has said that he was an avid reader of 2000 AD as a child, which inspired him to become a writer. He said, "I wanted to be a writer from the age of ten or eleven. I'd write a lot of stuff when I was a kid and I suppose I was getting paid for writing from the age of 19 or 20." Converting to Christianity had a major effect on Ennis' writing career, as he said, "I became a Christian about ten years ago. It made me a better writer, because I've thought a lot about my beliefs and why I believe things. I think it's made me more understanding of other cultures and other people's beliefs as well. I'm not particularly religious, but I'm a big believer in not being a dick." Of his writing for 2000 AD, Ennis said that he was "looking forward to it because it's a great opportunity to do something different. I thought I'd like to try doing something for 2000 AD because I've never really done anything for it before, and I thought it would be fun to do Judge Dredd. I'm a big fan of the stuff he does, so it's going to be fun trying to write him." He enjoyed writing for Dredd remarkably, saying, "I just had a ball writing it. I think we're going to do another storyline. There's been a lot of good feedback from it and I think people are going to want to see more."

### Writing style

Ennis has said that he has no preference for writing for 2000 AD over other comic publishers and that he enjoys writing for the characters of Judge Dredd, Punisher, and The Boys, and that he has been pleased with the feedback he has received from his work on The Boys.

A survey conducted by Minnesota's Department for Families and Children's Services shows that men consider child care to be factored into decisions about whether to have children, according to a Star Tribune report.
Among the Minnesota men surveyed, child care was as important a factor as financial concerns and health in deciding whether to have children.
The survey was conducted by the Minnesota Department of Children, Families and Learning and the University of Minnesota's Center for Urban and Regional Affairs.
"While child care has always been a major issue for women, it also is proving to be a major issue for men," the report states.
The survey was based on focus group discussions with 150 Minnesota men.
The men said they would be more likely to hire a nanny or find child care in their home to work than use day care. A majority said they would prefer to use child care for only one child.
The reason, according to the men, is that they'd like to be able to be involved in their child's care and they don't want to leave their child in a large day-care environment.
"We're not going to be able to have two incomes if we have to pay for child care," said one man.

In 1940, the MHSRL was placed under the jurisdiction of the Public Health Service (PHS). During his initial audition , Johnston claimed that he was bullied and victimised from the age of six because of his singing .

He claimed that he had been misdiagnosed with dyslexia at the age of 10 following a background check by the BBC .  However, the BBC later released a statement saying that the audition was "a set-up" to give the impression that Johnston's singing career had been difficult, and that he was never misdiagnosed with dyslexia. Johnston later admitted that he had "invented" the story in order to impress the judges.
During his time on The Voice, Johnston was well known for his "weird" and "funky" style of dressing, which included a purple jumpsuit with a cape, a green and white striped jumper with a colourful tie and a pair of brightly coloured trousers.  He was often teased for his outlandish outfits, with one of his team mates joking that Johnston was wearing "a PE kit" during a live performance.
Johnston was a member of the boy band group, The 2gether Boys,  a group of singers who auditioned for The X Factor in 2005. They reached the Bootcamp stage of the talent show.
At the age of 12, Johnston auditioned for the BBC talent show, Fame Academy, although he was unsuccessful.
Johnston auditioned for the first series of The Voice in July 2012. He sang an original song, "Rise and Fall" and was quickly given a "yes" by all four judges.  He was then put into team Jessie J, and as a result, was the first person in The Voice history to be given a chair turn.  He was put into a battle with another participant, Danny Riley, who sang "One Day I'll Fly Away" from the musical, "Rent".  Johnston won the battle.  In the live semi-final, Johnston successfully made it through the public votes and was put through to the final, where he performed "Rise and Fall".
Following the show, Johnston signed a record deal with Universal Music,   and in September 2012, released a cover of the song "Little Talks" by the Icelandic group, Of Monsters and Men.  He also performed the song on the final of The Voice, which was broadcast live on BBC One on 28 October 2012.  In January 2013, Johnston was announced as one of the acts selected to perform on the BBC's Sound of 2013 event.

After 1986 , the Jewish Community of Zagreb began to consider a Jewish cultural center and a memorial synagogue . Two architect

ural competitions were held, but they did not result in satisfactory results .
A Jewish community
 1.2.1 1941-1945
 1.3 1945-1986
 1.4 1986-present
The Jewish Community of Zagreb was founded in January 1868, and on October 23, 1872, Emperor Franz Joseph I issued a decree on the legalization of the Jewish Community of Zagreb .
The Jewish Community of Zagreb was a member of the World Union of Jewish Communities from 1920 to 1941 .
 1.2.1 1941-1945
During the German occupation, the Jewish community was persecuted, as were all other Serbian ethnic groups. The synagogue was converted into a warehouse and used by the German army. In 1942 the synagogue was blown up. Many Jews were killed in the Jasenovac concentration camp .
 1.3 1945-1986
After the Second World War, the Jewish Community of Zagreb was restored in 1946 and has been functioning as the only Jewish community in Croatia ever since. There was no synagogue at that time. In 1947, the community bought a house on the corner of Vlaška and Šubićeva streets and converted it into a synagogue .
In 1948, the Jewish Community of Zagreb was expelled from the World Jewish Congress because of the political position of the State of Israel within the United Nations .
 1.4 1986-present
Under communism, the Jewish community was banned and its membership list was revised. In the 1980s, the Jewish community was revived again. The community acquired the premises of a former gas station as a center and began considering a memorial synagogue .

Architectural competition
The first competition was held in 1990. Three architects participated in the competition: architects I. Levi (Israel), D. Katz (Israel) and E. Zilberman (New York). The jury, chaired by architect Ivo Štakula, was unanimous in its decision and awarded the first prize to the project of the Israeli architect I. Levi .
The second competition was held in 1995. Eight architects participated in the competition: architects Z. Huber (Germany), E. Katz (Australia) and I. Levi (Israel), as well as architects V. Balog, M. Buzulj, N. Erfurt, D. Sokolović and T. Vrdoljak from Croatia. The jury, chaired by architect M. Vulić, declared the project of architects Z. Huber and V. Balog to be the best, and awarded the first prize to the architect Z. Huber .
In 1997, the Architects' Association of Croatia held a public poll among its members. The winning architect was Z. Huber .
The Jewish community decided to construct a memorial synagogue according to the winning project of the architect Z. Huber . The project was shaped in 2000. The construction of the memorial synagogue began in 2006. The memorial synagogue was built with the support of the Republic of Israel, the City of Zagreb, the Croatian Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Croatian Ministry of Culture, the World Union of Jewish Communities, the Federation of Jewish Communities of the CIS and the World Jewish Congress.
The opening of the synagogue was scheduled for April 2008, but was postponed to May 11, 2008.
The memorial synagogue was built in the center of the Jewish Community of Zagreb, on the corner of Vlaška and Šubićeva streets .
The memorial synagogue was designed by the Canadian architect Peter Eisenman and the Croatian architect Ivan Štraus. The synagogue is an asymmetrical cube with a height of 23 meters, with an irregular shape and an irregular window. It is built from concrete, steel and glass. The interior is characterized by natural light in the form of a window of 20 m 2 in the facade.

The British 9th Division, which had arrived in Egypt in September 1914, was formed in Cairo at the end of October 1914 as part of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force. Disembarking in Alexandria on 16 November, it was sent to the Suez Canal zone, where its main role was to defend the canal from a possible Turkish land attack.
After the canal had been secured and the threat of a Turkish advance removed, the 9th Division was ordered to proceed to Mudros in the island of Lemnos, in the Aegean Sea, to form part of the force which was to be sent to the Dardanelles. Driven out of the Dardanelles by the Allied fleet and the Turkish Army, the Gallipoli landing force moved to Lemnos, where the 9th Division was first landed on 31 March 1915.
The Gallipoli campaign began on 25 April 1915 with a disastrous landing on the peninsula and the subsequent attacks on the Turkish positions. The first landings by the British were carried out by the 29th Division, which had been formed in Egypt in 1914.
The first battle of the Gallipoli campaign, 25 April 1915, was a complete failure. The landing force was led by the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC), which had to land on a narrow beach after their transport ships were delayed by the weather and then scattered by a Turkish destroyer. The ANZACs had to advance through heavy fire and were therefore forced to take cover in the trenches that they had come to hold. Over the next seven weeks the 9th Division, under Brigadier-General (later Sir) E.L. Smyth, played a significant role in the struggle for dominance on the beaches.
It was not until 4 June that the 9th Division was fully in action, as the first troops of the 42nd (East Lancashire) Division were withdrawn to the Peloponnese to fight in France. The 9th Division was now in action all along the line, with the 29th Division taking over the left sector of the beaches. The 9th Division's role was to cover the withdrawal of the 29th Division's right sector, and to relieve some of the 29th Division's troops on the left.
Fighting behind the line, the 9th Division was involved in a number of operations, including the capture of the Turkish redoubt known as 'Hill 60' and the erection of a new redoubt, 'Hill 80', in its place. The capture of Hill 80 was 'the only real success achieved by the British during the campaign'.3

Competitive gliding in the UK takes place between May and September . Regionals are local competitions , organised and run by o

ily clubs. Competitions are run to a strict set of rules, which are written down. Pilots are also expected to fly by a set of codes of conduct, which are designed to ensure that competitors can compete safely.
 The Association of Gliding Clubs ( AGC ) is the governing body for gliding in the UK and is responsible for organising the National competitions, the British Gliding Championships, the British Gliding Team and the British Gliding Open. The AGC also has responsibility for developing gliding in the UK and for ensuring that the rules and codes of conduct are followed by all pilots.
 The AGC is managed by a Council, which is composed of the Chairman, who is appointed by the AGC , a Treasurer, who is appointed by the AGC , the Secretary, who is appointed by the AGC, and the Chairman of each of the Regional Associations.
 The Regional Associations are responsible for the selection of the pilots who will represent the UK in the European and World Championships. They are responsible for all competitive flying except for the National competitions, the British Gliding Championships, the British Gliding Team and the British Gliding Open.
 The Regional Associations are composed of the Chairmen of the oily clubs within their region.
The "Rules of Gliding " are the rules that govern all competitive gliding in the UK. They are written and administered by the AGC . They can be found on the AGC web site.
The Regional Associations are responsible for the organisation of the "Regional Championships ". These competitions are organised and run by the Regional Associations with the assistance of the oily clubs within their region. They are typically held over a weekend and are usually open to all pilots, subject to the rules and codes of conduct.
The Regional Associations are also responsible for the selection of the pilots who will represent their region in the European and World Championships.
The oily clubs will provide the organisation and equipment necessary for the competitions over which they have responsibility.

The stingray is a slow-moving, bottom-dwelling fish. It does not have swim bladders and is not able to float.

From the early 1980s , Khoo tried to pursue a Master of Business Administration ( MBA ) degree from various universities , but

was rejected on several occasions  as he was not a citizen of the United States . He claimed  that he was rejected because he was a foreign student and not because of his race .

He then applied for admission to the University of Rochester and was admitted in 1981. Khoo was reportedly the first Asian American to receive his MBA from the University of Rochester,  and he was subsequently accepted to the University of Michigan Law School.

## Career

Khoo is a lawyer and investor . He is co-founder and managing partner of the $10 billion firm, Orchard Capital Management. He also founded and was chairman of the board of directors of Orchard Capital Bank, a commercial bank that failed in 2009.

### Career in investment

Khoo has been a principal of a number of private equity funds including Nautic Partners, which he founded in 1993, and ABRY Partners, where he was a founding partner.

He has been an investor in a number of companies including Rite-Aid, PetSmart, and AMC Entertainment. He was also a board member of the Rite-Aid Corporation  from 2001 to 2007 .

### Career in banking

Khoo was chairman of the board of directors of Orchard Capital Bank, a commercial bank that failed in 2009. He became involved in banking after the 2008 financial crisis .

## Personal

Khoo's father was born in China but emigrated to Malaysia to escape the Japanese invasion of China. His mother was born in Malaysia.

Khoo was born in Singapore and grew up in Malaysia. He attended a United World College of Southeast Asia in Singapore. He completed his undergraduate education at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland. He was 24 years old when he received his MBA degree.

Khoo is a member of the board of trustees of Johns Hopkins University and the board of directors of Johns Hopkins Medicine. He is the owner of the professional basketball team, the Sioux Falls Skyforce.

Khoo is also a philanthropist. In 2017, he pledged $33 million to the University of Rochester, the largest donation in the school's history.

Main article: List of Crash Bandicoot characters

Crash Bandicoot in the game.

While Domoina was moving through South Africa , it drew an area of moisture from the northeast , which produced heavy rainfall

between the 19th and 21st of January 1999, over Mozambique. The rainfall resulted in flooding that killed at least 1,000 people and displaced over 1 million.
In the aftermath of the floods, a study was published in 2000 by the American Geophysical Union , titled 'The Mozambique flood of January 1999: A case study of synoptic impacts of tropical cyclones on rainfall' and written by Josefino C. Comiso , Marcelo A. Pinto and Richard A. Hewitson (2000). The study investigated the synoptic impact of tropical cyclones on rainfall, and suggested that it is possible to predict the effects of tropical cyclones on rainfall over South Africa and Mozambique, although the exact mechanism is still uncertain.
The study concluded that the floods were caused by a combination of factors. The study also found that the frequency of such flooding events is increasing in Mozambique, and that the development of a disaster-resistant government is necessary in order to mitigate the damage.

In the management of first and second @-@ degree burns , little quality evidence exists to determine which dressing type to use

for each burn. Surprisingly, many clinical studies have focused on this issue because of the importance of burn management to the healthcare system. The aim of this review was to evaluate all randomized and non-randomized controlled trials investigating the effect of the type of dressing used in the first 24 h after burn injury on the healing of first and second degree burns.
(a) In first degree burns, the use of an occlusive dressing is more effective than the use of a non-occlusive dressing in reducing the healing time.
(b) In second degree burns, the use of an occlusive dressing is more effective than the use of a non-occlusive dressing in reducing the healing time.
Six databases were searched from their inception until February 2003. Results were subjected to two rounds of screening, first by title or abstract, and then by full text. Studies that included patients with burns or wounds were excluded. The quality of the trials was assessed using the Jadad scale.
Five studies compared the effect of an occlusive dressing with a non-occlusive dressing in first degree burns and four studies compared the effect of an occlusive dressing with a non-occlusive dressing in second degree burns. There was inconclusive evidence that the use of an occlusive dressing is more effective than the use of a non-occlusive dressing in reducing the healing time in patients with first degree burns. There was no evidence that the use of an occlusive dressing is more effective than the use of a non-occlusive dressing in reducing the healing time in patients with second degree burns.
The effect of the type of dressing used in the first 24 h after burn injury on the healing of first and second degree burns is inconclusive.

The T30 also served during the Allied invasion of Sicily in 1943 , the war in Italy in 1944 , and possibly in the Pacific . It

was replaced in the early and mid-1940s by the M2 Half Track and the M3 Half Track. It was used  by the British Army during the Burma campaign against the Japanese .
The T30 had a crew of four, including the driver and commander. The driver and the commander sat on a raised bench at the front of the hull, above the engine compartment. The driver sat on the right, and the commander on the left; both had a roof over their heads. After the war, the driver's hatch was removed and the commander's hatch was moved to the right. Later models also had a front-mounted .50 cal (12.7 mm) machine gun. The gunner sat on a raised armor plate behind the hull on the right, and the assistant gunner sat on a raised armor plate behind the hull on the left. The gunner and assistant gunner could operate the .30 cal (7.62 mm) machine gun mounted in the hull roof; the gunner also could operate the .50 cal (12.7 mm) machine gun mounted in the hull roof.
The T30 was armed with two .30 cal (7.62 mm) Browning Machine Guns.

a twelve-hour period. This created localized flooding, which resulted in five deaths and 4,500 homes being destroyed. The storm later produced heavy rainfall in Zimbabwe , which resulted in further flooding and damaged 1,500 homes.
The storm then entered the Republic of the Congo and passed over the capital Brazzaville . It was there that the rainfall and subsequent flooding was most severe, with 900 mm (35 in) of rainfall falling in 24 hours, and 4,500 homes being destroyed. Individual rainfall totals in the city reached 540 mm (21 in), which was the highest amount ever recorded in the country. Prior to this, the highest amount of rainfall ever recorded in the Republic of the Congo was 375 mm (14.8 in). Heavy rainfall caused further flooding in the Democratic Republic of the Congo , Zambia , and Malawi .
In Mozambique , 52,000 people were made homeless as a result of the flooding. Heavy rains also caused flooding in Botswana , South Africa , and Lesotho , which resulted in the deaths of 48 people. The storm also caused severe flooding in Zimbabwe , where 15 people were killed and 60,000 people were made homeless. The rains caused severe flooding in South Africa, where 10 people were killed.
The cyclone caused 223 deaths and left 22 people missing. Additionally, 143,000 people were made homeless, 1,500 homes were destroyed, and 500,000 acres of crops were damaged. In the Republic of the Congo, 18 people were killed, and 50,000 people were made homeless. Damage in the country amounted to $100 million. In Malawi, the rains caused severe flooding, which resulted in the deaths of 38 people and left 75,000 people homeless. Damage in the country amounted to $100 million. In South Africa, the rains caused severe flooding and landslides, which resulted in the deaths of 12 people and left 20,000 homeless. Damage in the country amounted to $60 million. In Lesotho, the rains caused severe flooding and landslides, which resulted in the deaths of 11 people. Damage in the country amounted to $20 million.

A large number of molecular alterations are under study for their prognostic impact in AML . However , only FLT3 @-@ ITD , NPM1

M30 , and TP53 mutations are currently incorporated in the WHO criteria . A significant number of AML cases are lacking these mutations. Therefore, additional prognostic markers are necessary for the risk classification of AML patients.
 AML is a heterogeneous disease of various biological subtypes, which are distinguished by their prognostic and therapeutic factors. The most common subtypes are M0 , M1 , M2 , M3 , and M4 . Patients with M0 subtype usually have an excellent prognosis and constitute ~5-10% of all AML cases. M0 is defined by normal karyotype , negative expression of NPM1 , and normal expression of CEBP alpha . These patients have a better response to intensive chemotherapy and are therefore considered as an excellent prognostic subgroup.
 In contrast, patients with M1 , M2 , M3 , and M4 AML are treated according to the risk group they belong to. The M1 subgroup is characterized by the presence of FLT3 @-@ ITD mutation. These patients have an intermediate prognosis and are often treated with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. In the M2 subgroup, the expression of NPM1 M30 mutation is a good prognostic factor. The M3 subgroup is characterized by the NPM1 wild-type (WT) and CEBP alpha WT, and is associated with a poor prognosis. The M4 subgroup is characterized by the presence of TP53 mutation and is also associated with a poor prognosis.
 The prognostic factors for AML are based on the initial cytogenetic analysis of bone marrow. However, this analysis is time-consuming and therefore not applicable for routine diagnostic use. Therefore, the prognostic markers must be analyzed at the time of diagnosis .
 The prognostic impact of the expression of NPM1 WT was first reported in 2005 . NPM1 WT has been reported to be present in 65-80% of cases . However, it was not incorporated in the WHO criteria for AML. Furthermore, the impact of NPM1 WT in the prognostic classification of AML was not studied in detail. Therefore, we performed a study to evaluate the prognostic impact of NPM1 WT in AML patients.
 To investigate the prognostic impact of NPM1 WT in AML, we retrospectively analyzed the medical records of AML patients from 2006 through 2012, which were diagnosed at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University, China. All patients were included in the study after they had signed an informed consent form. All patients were treated according to the standard guidelines.
 The diagnostic and treatment procedures for AML patients were approved by the Second Affiliated Hospital, Soochow University's Committee on Human Experimentation. The study was performed in accordance with the rules set forth in the Declaration of Helsinki. Informed consent was obtained from patients for the participation in this study.
 We defined AML M1 , M2, M3, and M4 patients based on the WHO classification criteria . The medical records were reviewed to obtain the following data: age, gender, initial white blood cell (WBC) count, hemoglobin (Hb), platelet count, and International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS)-R score. Cytogenetics analysis was performed at the time of diagnosis. The expression of NPM1 WT was investigated by immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining. In addition, the expression of FLT3 @-@ ITD , NPM1 M30 , and TP53 mutations were determined by Sanger sequencing.
 The expression of NPM1 WT in the bone marrow biopsy was examined by IHC staining. The IHC staining was performed as previously described .
 The level of expression of NPM1 WT was evaluated by a pathologist. For each biopsy specimen, 100-200 fields were examined for the expression of NPM1 WT. The expression of NPM1 WT was considered to be positive when the protein was demonstrated in more than 50% of the nucleated cells. " Livin ' the Dream " was written by story editor Niki Schwartz @-@ Wright , marking her second writing credit for the series ,

following " Sibling Revelry ". In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter , Schwartz Wright discussed her work on the episode, saying, " This is a self-contained story. We were able to look at what we've done with the family over the last two seasons and kind of re-examine what's important. There's a lot of touching and re-examining of what's important in life, which is not only the family that you create but the family that you're born into. " It was directed by series star and executive producer Christopher Lloyd , marking his fourth directing credit for the series.

## Reception

### Viewers

In its original American broadcast, "Livin ' the Dream" was seen by an estimated 1.72 million household viewers and gained a 0.5 ratings share among adults aged 18 to 49, according to Nielsen Media Research. This means that 0.5 percent of all households with televisions watched the episode. This was a 4% increase in viewership from the previous episode, which was watched by 1.65 million viewers with a 0.5 in the 18-49 demographics.

### Critical reviews

"Livin ' the Dream" received mostly positive reviews from critics. Alan Sepinwall of Rolling Stone wrote, "This may be the most optimistic, uplifting episode of 'Breaking Bad' to date, and it's wonderful, and I'm sure many of you will enjoy it. I'm also sure that a lot of you will be left scratching your heads."

Molly Eichel of The A.V. Club gave the episode an "A" and wrote, "The final season of Breaking Bad has been building to a crescendo—and it's not a bad time to start thinking about the end of the show. It's not just that the main characters are all making huge moves, but that the show itself is becoming more confident in its exploration of its themes. "Livin ' the Dream" is an episode that could have been heavy-handed, but instead is nothing if not a surprisingly beautiful and thoughtful hour of television." Sean T. Collins of The New York Times wrote, "It's only the second episode of the final season of 'Breaking Bad,' but it feels like a real turning point. It's the first time in a long time that the episode's first third felt like it was just existing in its own little movie bubble. The first half of the season has largely been spent reestablishing the status quo and setting up the fall. But something about this episode feels like it belongs in its own universe, and I have no idea how that world will connect to the one that's been established."

Nick Harley of Den of Geek gave the episode a 4 star rating out of 5 and wrote, "Much like 'Blood Money,' 'Livin ' the Dream' sees the series turn a corner, taking a step outside of Walt's world to show us how his actions are affecting the people around him. I'm not sure if this is a permanent shift in the series' structure or simply a one-off, but it's an incredibly effective change of pace."

The opening sequence of the video features Jay Z as a passenger in a car speeding along Mission Road in Los Angeles , where he

and punches the dashboard in frustration.  It then cuts to a funeral, where Beyoncé and her bridesmaids all walk down the aisle, past mourners and a casket. She then turns around and walks back down the aisle with family and friends.  Beyoncé's father, Matthew Knowles, is the officiant of the fake funeral, and is seen giving a speech before Beyoncé emerges from the casket. Beyoncé, with her hair in cornrows, is dressed in a white bridal gown and veil.  The video then cuts to a scene of Beyoncé and Jay Z dancing in the streets of Los Angeles.  The music video ends with Beyoncé performing the song on stage with a saxophone.
 The music video received mixed reviews from critics.  Many critics praised the visuals and emotional aspect of the video, but some criticized the concept.  Jocelyn Vena of MTV News explained, "As soon as the clip begins, the visuals tell a story. The camera tracks Bey's face as she watches her wedding party from a window. Inside, the room is filled with tears. She walks down the aisle of the church and joins her family in mourning. The video then transitions to Bey and Jay walking through L.A. carrying on as if nothing happened. The clip ends with the star belting out the song onstage."  Edna Gunderson of USA Today wrote, "Beyoncé and Jay-Z's music video for 'Crazy In Love' features both of them in wedding dresses in a clip that suggests they're marrying each other on the spot. Well, they already are, sort of. This video is a fiction, but it's not fiction for nothing."  Ryan Dombal of Pitchfork Media wrote, "The video almost seems to mock the concept of marriage and the wedding industry in general, but that's not what Beyonce and Jay-Z are about. The video is a metaphor for their love, and a metaphor for love in general."  Tanner Stransky of Entertainment Weekly wrote, "At first, the video seems to be all about Beyoncé's wedding to rapper Jay-Z (who in the real world was married to R&B singer Rihanna at the time), but as the clip continues, it's revealed that the video is actually about how their relationship is doomed."  In 2014, Spin named the video the 100th best music video of all time.
 "Crazy in Love" was nominated for three awards at the 2004 MTV Video Music Awards: Best Female Video, Best R&B Video, and Video of the Year.  "Crazy in Love" won the Best R&B Video award over "Hey Ya" by Andre 3000, "The Real Slim Shady" by Eminem, "Slow Jam" by Usher, and "You're All I Need to Get By" by Method Man and Mary J. Blige.  Beyoncé performed the song on the American television show, The Tonight Show with Jay Leno, on May 11, 2003.  She performed "Crazy in Love" on the U.S. television show, Saturday Night Live, on May 17, 2003.  "Crazy in Love" was performed on The Oprah Winfrey Show and on Live with Regis and Kelly on May 19, 2003.  The song was performed on the U.S. television show, American Idol, by Beyoncé on May 28, 2003.  Beyoncé and Jay Z performed the song on the American television show, The Today Show, on June 18, 2003.

1939 , she provided cover for troop carrier aircraft delivering supplies to Franco's Nationalist forces .
She fought at the Battle of Britain in 1940 and was badly damaged by German bombs at Dover on 28th June. She was later refitted for service in the Pacific , but was sunk by an American submarine in August 1944.
She was built by Hawthorn Leslie and Company, at Hebburn-on-Tyne .
She was laid down in January 1936 . She was launched on 28th January 1937 . She was completed in September 1937 .

The 1940 Atlantic hurricane season was a generally average period of tropical cyclogenesis in 1940 . Though the season had no o

minous designation like the Great Hurricane of 1900, the season saw the most significant storm in the Gulf of Mexico since the 1926 Miami Hurricane. The season produced seventeen tropical cyclones, of which thirteen became hurricanes. The Average Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) for the year was about 100 units.
The season officially began on June 1, 1940, and officially ended on November 30, 1940. These dates conventionally delimit the period of each year when most tropical cyclones form in the Atlantic basin.

Nationally important deities gave rise to local manifestations , which sometimes absorbed the characteristics of older regional

divinities . The accumulation of deities during the course of time , however , did not result in the haphazard accumulation of temples - a phenomenon which is often a characteristic of Hindu temples . The temple - and therefore the deity - were the essential factors in the popular imagination . The deity , moreover , was a personification of a particular quality ; thus a deity could be of the type of a child , a woman or a male , or of an animal ; each type was associated with particular traditions and rites , and each might assume various identities in different places . During the course of the first half of the sixth century the deities of the localities were placed on a common footing , and the imperial cult superseded the local cults . It was at this time that the various deities were given a common title , and it was then that the temples of the deities were assembled in the imperial cities . The temple was a symbol of the deity , and in the temple , moreover , the deity was represented in a particular form in which he or she could be approached . The temple , therefore , was the essential element in the worship of the deity . The deity was the great personal god of the land , and he had to be approached through a particular representative who acted as his agent and could communicate with him . This representative was the priest , who in turn acted as the intermediary between the people and the deity . There were thus three categories of persons who were concerned with the worship of the deity - the divine representative , the priest and the people .
The people in turn were divided into two groups : the first group was composed of those who had access to the sanctum of the deity , and the second group of those who did not have access , and who were therefore not allowed to enter the precincts of the temple . The latter group , although not allowed to enter the temple , could participate in the cult , and this participation was of a twofold nature . First , the people could participate directly in the rituals of the temple . Second , they could participate by making offerings of the various kinds of foodstuffs which were used in the rituals .
The popular cult was thus composed of two elements : on the one hand , it was a cult which consisted of the rites and ceremonies performed by the priest in the sanctum of the temple , and on the other hand it was a cult which consisted of the food offerings which were made to the deity by the people . The popular cult , however , was not merely a cult of the temple ; it was a cult of the deity , and the cult in the temple was the main element in the popular cult . The popular cult , moreover , had many aspects to it . There were, for example, the offerings which were made to the deity , or to the priests , by the people ; there were the festivals which were held in honour of the deity ; there were the offerings of charity which were made by the people to their priests and to the deity ; there were the prayers which were offered to the deity . The popular cult , moreover , was not only a cult of the deity , but it had other aspects as well , and thus we find that the people also worshipped the temple when they went to the temple , and during festivals the people would take part in the processions which were held in honour of the deity .
The most important aspect of the popular cult , however , was the cult of the temple , and the cult of the temple was the cult of the deity . The cult of the deity , moreover , was not merely the cult of the temple , but it was also the cult of the people . In the 1930s Idloes Owen , a singing teacher and conductor , ran an amateur choir , the Lyrian Singers , based in Cardiff . In

1954 he founded the National Youth Choir of Wales , a mixed-voice choir which included all of Britain's major Welsh-speaking regions. The choir's first public performances came in 1958, and it has given regular concerts and broadcasts since then. In 1994 the choir was renamed the National Youth Choir of Great Britain .
The choir is made up of singers aged 16 to 25 years. It is composed of three groups: Welsh, English and Scotish. They each meet up once a month for rehearsals and concerts.
The choir has performed in many countries including the USA, Canada, Russia, Italy, France, Germany and Brazil, as well as throughout the UK. In 1995 it was awarded the prize of Best New Artist at the Classical Brit Awards. In 1996 it was awarded the Queen's Golden Jubilee Medal for its services to the music industry in the UK.
The choir has recorded a number of albums, including some works by John Tavener and Karl Jenkins (both Welshmen), and has made a number of television appearances.
In 2009, the choir received the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Medal.

Baron Riedesel caught up with Fraser around 4 pm , and insisted that his men could not go further before making camp . Fraser ,

on the other hand , was adamant that they should push on ; the Baron had lost a day on the march , and the force was running short of supplies . Fraser protested that they were within reach of the objective, and that the Hall was only a few more miles away. Riedesel had to concede that Fraser was right , but he was adamant that they should make camp in the next valley . He also said that Fraser should try to get some food from the local settlers ; there were none within easy reach , and the garrison , it was said , had suffered badly from starvation and disease . Riedesel would not allow any of his men to be maltreated by the settlers , and he asked Fraser to make it clear that he himself would make no distinction between German and American settlers .
The two men had a long discussion , but Fraser could not persuade the Baron to budge from his decision to make camp . Riedesel made it clear that he was not blaming Fraser for the shortage of provisions , but he was certain that the men would suffer if they went any further . Fraser , for his part , said that he was prepared to take the risk , and to march straight on to Fort George .
The situation was resolved by the arrival of a small party of Americans led by Daniel McGregor, who had been sent out by Colonel Johnson to bring back news of the British position . McGregor and Fraser had a good deal to discuss , and they agreed that the Americans should accompany the British force for the rest of the way to Fort George.
The Americans were brought into the main body of the column at this point ; they were given their own wagons and horses , and were told to travel at the head of the column .
 Riedesel had hoped that the American settlers would be able to supply the column with food , but they had little to offer ; they were suffering from the same shortage as the British, and were down to their last few provisions. The Americans were not over-friendly to the British soldiers , and the men of the King's Royal German Regiment were particularly resented.
 The Americans were not keen on fighting for the British , but they were also reluctant to fight for the Americans , who had been responsible for the destruction of their settlements in the Mohawk Valley .
 The Americans were now so short of supplies that they had to travel as light as possible. They had little food , and no tents , bedding , or winter clothing .
 The Americans had little idea of the direction of Fort George , and were forced to travel by night and hide by day under the cover of thick forests.

 Professor Innis was an economist and social scientist whose research focused on the social determinants of economic growth and development. Innis took a major part in the founding of the Department of Economics and Political Science at the University of Toronto.  The department included the first Canadian academic chair in political science. Innis was also the first Canadian academic to focus on media studies and the impact of mass media on society.
 Professor Innis was born on November 22, 1885 in Toronto , Ontario , to Thomas Innis, a lawyer, and Lillian Innis (nee Rickard), a nurse and teacher. Innis received his early education in Toronto, and while he had no formal university education, he attended lectures at the University of Toronto and later lectured at the university himself.
 Innis received his PhD from Columbia University in New York City . His dissertation was entitled _The Problem of Meaning in the Nineteenth Century_ and was supervised by the American economist and social scientist, Henry Charles Taylor .
 Professor Innis' research on the social determinants of economic growth and development had a major impact on the social sciences in Canada. Innis' work also influenced many other social scientists who were interested in the impact of mass media on society and the economy.

A story was told that Ælfric introduced monks into the cathedral church of Christ Church , Canterbury , replacing the secular c

athedral canons. In the account, Ælfric was a monk who was raised to the see of Canterbury by the king. The monks were the king's own monks. Ælfric was thereafter accused of heresy by the cathedral canons and was forced to write a letter to the king in his own blood in an attempt to get the king to pardon him. The letter was a plea to be allowed to return to his monastery, and the king granted his request. A separate account of the death of Ælfric was that he was the monk who was forced to defend himself against the king's bishops . This account had Ælfric being forced to fight to the death against a champion chosen by the king, then being given the choice of death or exile, and then choosing exile.
The story of the origin of the Benedictine monastery at Abingdon , which was founded in the early 10th century, is that Ælfric was a monk who was in exile in the time of King Æthelred . Ælfric was a teacher of reading and writing who for 20 years taught the monks at Æthelred's court before being invited by Æthelred to be abbot of a new monastery at Abingdon.
The stories of Ælfric's origins and career thus present his career as one of exile and penance.
The accounts of his death preserve the idea that he was a monk who was forced to defend himself against the king's bishops. In one account, the king's bishops travelled to Abingdon and told Ælfric that he could either fight a champion chosen by the king, or be banished. Ælfric chose to fight, and was wounded in the leg. The king's bishops then tried to convince Ælfric to agree to the king's proposal that he be allowed to return to his monastery, but Ælfric refused. One of the bishops then tried to cut off his head, but Ælfric's friend, the bishop of Winchester , struck the bishop down with his staff. The king's bishops then broke Ælfric's leg, and he died of the wounds.
The accounts of his death present his death as the result of a fight that he was forced to fight.
The accounts of his death present the story of his death as a martyrdom, and the stories in his life present his life as one of exile and penance. This suggests that the stories of his life and death were based on a legendary poetic narrative.
One account of his death, from the 13th century, has it that Ælfric was brought to Canterbury and buried in the cathedral there. It also has it that his body was removed from Canterbury and buried in Winchester in 1106. The account then goes on to say that the monks of Winchester spent years praying to Ælfric to be allowed to move his body back to Canterbury. The account says that Æthelred, who was king in 1106, was the king who granted them permission to move Ælfric's body. The account also says that Æthelred's son, Henry I, was the king who ordered the reburial of Ælfric's body in Canterbury.
The story thus presents Ælfric's death and reburial as the result of a prayer by a community.
A manuscript of Ælfric's life was produced in Winchester in the mid-12th century. This manuscript has the story of the removal of Ælfric's body from Canterbury to Winchester in 1106. In the manuscript, it is said that the king who granted permission to remove Ælfric's body from Canterbury was Henry I.
When the story of the removal of Ælfric's body from Canterbury to Winchester was written, Ælfric's body had been buried in Winchester for more than a century.

ara Scar. At the time he claimed it was one of the best-preserved Roman forts in Britain. Wheeler had planned to continue excavating at Sara Scar in 1922, but in August he received an offer from the Egyptian authorities to excavate on behalf of the government in Egypt at Amarna. The offer had come from Lord Carnarvon, who had recently recovered the tomb of Tutankhamen, and the excavations were to be directed by Howard Carter. Wheeler had always wanted to direct an expedition in Egypt, and he accepted the offer.
Wheeler's excavations at Amarna were made possible by the Egyptian Antiquities Service's decision to take on a large-scale programme of excavations in Egypt. Finding work for archaeologists had been a long-term problem in Egypt. The Egyptian Antiquities Service had been created in 1858, and from the beginning it had been the intention that it should put archaeology on a secure  footing. However, the service's most important work was the conservation and maintenance of the country's monuments, and it was not until 1908 that the service put an end to its practice of sending the country's antiquities to the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. In 1910 the Antiquities Service set up an excavation department, and by 1912 had decided to launch a programme of excavation of all the sites mentioned on the Rosetta Stone. This project was known as the 'Campaign of Monuments' and was designed to restore and conserve the monuments mentioned on the Rosetta Stone.
The campaign had been planned at a time when the country's financial resources were desperately stretched, and it was decided that the project should be launched as part of the general national reconstruction scheme following the First World War. In July 1919 Lord Cromer, who had been the British High Commissioner in Egypt for over twenty years, visited London with a request for financial aid. In September the British government granted £100,000 to the Egyptian government to start the project. The money was to be used to restore the Rosetta Stone, the Pharos lighthouse at Alexandria and the beam used to light the Olympic flame in Paris in 1924. The money was also used to help restore the temples of Esna and Philae and to conserve the monuments at Deir el-Medina and the temple of Karnak. The campaign of monuments was intended to make the monuments safe for tourists, but also to provide employment for Egyptians, and in 1919 the Antiquities Service recruited the first batch of Egyptian archaeologists. A second batch was recruited in 1920.
The Antiquities Service decided to launch excavations at Amarna, the site of the royal city built by Akhenaten and his wife Nefertiti. The city had been abandoned after Akhenaten's death, and was later covered by the desert. In 1891 Amarna was rediscovered by a group of Italian archaeologists. The city was being excavated at the time Wheeler visited, but because the Antiquities Service did not have funds for a large-scale programme of archaeological excavations it was decided to take over the work and to employ the Italian archaeologists. The excavations at Amarna were to be directed by the Italian archaeologist Pietro Della Valle. Della Valle had been excavating at Amarna since 1904, and he had found a stone _stela_ which referred to Akhenaten and Nefertiti. The stela was inscribed with the names of Akhenaten's children, and it was the first evidence that the royal family had been buried at Amarna. The stela was also the first archaeological evidence to suggest that Nefertiti had died.
The excavations at Amarna were an enormous success, and when Wheeler left Amarna in 1922 he had found a large number of objects from the royal family's palace and from the tombs of the royal family's servants. Wheeler's excavations at Amarna have been described as 'the most exciting and productive season of his career'. A distinguishing feature of the Sclerodermatineae is the diversity of morphologies within the group . The hymenomycete genera B

iscogniauxia , Scleroderma and Sclerotium are all important in agriculture, forestry and horticulture, but they also include the intriguing "water molds" , and the infamous "dark raisin rot" [1, 2].
Dark raisin rot of grapes (Prunus: Vitis vinifera) is the most severe and widespread disease of table grapes in the world. The disease begins as a brown, gelatinous lesion on the rachis of clusters of berries. It is particularly serious in regions where grapes are grown in temperate regions with high humidity, such as in the northeastern USA (e.g., New York) and in Mediterranean regions (e.g., Spain and Italy). Infections occur in rachis tissues or on berries, and can spread rapidly to adjacent clusters. In most cases, the raisins are unmarketable because of their dark color, and the entire cluster often is discarded. This disease is caused by the fungus Sclerotium rolfsii (teleomorph Biscogniauxia rolfsii), and is transmitted by splashing rain or overhead irrigation.

The Allied Powers (Allies) were the countries that opposed the Central Powers (Axis Powers) in the First World War. While not a formal alliance in the legal sense, the common interests of its members caused them to co-operate militarily, financially, and diplomatically. The war had been continuing since July 1914, but the official coalition between the Allied Powers only began with the outbreak of the war in Europe on 3 August 1914 with Britain, France, and Russia agreeing to the formal Allied system of orders of battle under the Triple Entente. The Entente Powers were initially Dominion and colonial states of the British Empire, as well as Russia. By 1915, Italy had joined the Entente Powers. In 1916, Japan joined the Entente Powers and in 1917, the Entente Powers were joined by the United States.
Allied forces were commanded by British General Sir Douglas Haig. The Allies were ultimately successful, with the defeat of Germany and her allies in 1918.

Hurricane Humberto was an intense tropical cyclone that affected the Azores and Europe during September 2019. The origins of Hurricane Humberto were from a tropical wave that exited the coast of Africa on September 11 . After moving across the Atlantic Ocean, the wave slowly developed into a tropical depression on September 19. The depression strengthened into a tropical storm on the next day. Due to favorable environmental conditions, the storm rapidly intensified and became a Category 4 hurricane on September 22. After the hurricane reached a peak intensity of 160 mph (260 km/h), it underwent an eyewall replacement cycle and weakened to a Category 2 hurricane. The storm rapidly weakened and became a Category 1 hurricane before making landfall near Pico, Portugal on September 24. Humberto degenerated into a remnant low after crossing the coast.
Hurricane Humberto caused moderate to severe damage to the Azores and Portugal. In the Azores, Humberto caused significant damage to crops and infrastructure. In Portugal, Humberto caused more than 1,300 damaged or destroyed dwellings. The total damage caused by Humberto was estimated at €25 million (2019 euros). In response to the storm, the Portuguese government declared two states of emergency.
On September 11, a tropical wave exited the coast of Africa and moved westward. The wave was initially only producing light showers while it was in the Eastern Atlantic. The wave gradually organized into a tropical depression on September 18, while it was located about 450 miles (720 km) south of the Azores. The depression was assigned the identifier 13L.
A Hurricane Hunter aircraft flew through the storm and found that it had become a tropical storm. Humberto developed into a hurricane on September 22 and reached Category 4 on September 23, with 155 mph (250 km/h) winds. The storm underwent an eyewall replacement cycle and weakened to Category 2 intensity at 21:00 UTC, with 115 mph (185 km/h) winds. Humberto reached its peak intensity on September 24, after making landfall near Pico with 160 mph (260 km/h) winds. The hurricane became extratropical after making landfall in Portugal. The extratropical cyclone then crossed the Iberian Peninsula, before being absorbed by a larger system on September 29.
