A recurring theme in these myths is the effort of the gods to maintain maat against the forces of disorder . They fight vicious

battles with the servants of chaos, not always successfully, and even the goddess of harmony, Maat, is ultimately defeated. Recurrent in these myths is the belief that the universe is in a state of flux, unstable, and that the ideal order of the universe, the maat, is only a temporary condition, to be achieved through the efforts of the gods.
Myths also stress the importance of the proper relationship between man and the gods, and indicate the consequences when this relationship is violated. These myths describe the relationship of the gods to man in terms of the performance of rituals, and the proper behavior of man in these rituals. In the myth of the two brothers, the hero, Seth, has been enticed to a feast by the gods, who are thus able to get his help in discovering the secret of eternal youth. He is told, however, that he must not eat the food of the gods, and must not drink the beer they provide. He is tempted to do so, because he is desirous of eternal youth and immortality, but the gods have warned him when he is most hungry, and he withstands the temptation. His brother, Osiris, however, does not listen to the warning, and is punished for his disobedience by having his body shredded.
The myth of the two brothers is the origin of the annual celebration of the festival of the Dead (Hotep) in which the Egyptians celebrated the resurrection of the dead. At this festival the embalmed body of the dead was re-housed in a coffin, and given a new life in a new body. A death mask is also placed upon the face of the corpse. This death mask was to protect the soul of the dead from the forces of chaos.
The most important of the myths of creation is that of the creation of the world (Chu). This myth describes the deeds of the gods as they emerge from the darkness of chaos to create an ordered world, and then to endow man with the faculty of speech. This myth contains the most complete statement of the principles of the universe, and the belief in the Egyptian scholars that it is the basis of all knowledge. The myth also contains the belief that the sun god is the creator, and that it is through him that the forces of chaos are kept at bay.
The myth of the creation of the world is also one of the most anthropomorphic of all the myths, and it illustrates the Egyptian belief that the universe was created in a personal way by a personal god. The creation myth of the Egyptians is still a living myth in modern Egypt.

## History

After the abolition of the Military Frontier in 1751, the settlement was annexed to the Kingdom of Slavonia. In 1848, it belonged to the Military Frontier.

Gilbert , Schafer and Grossman 's primary goal was to create a simpler and more accessible gameplay model than those presented

in other X-COM games, and they cited SimCity as a primary inspiration.  The gameplay was also intended to be more forgiving than its predecessors.

The game uses a simplified structure of six different gameplay modes, which the player can choose between at any time. The game progresses with the player's forces engaging the aliens in combat. The player's base is also a central point of the gameplay, with the sixth and final mode being dedicated to its management. The game is not purely a tactical game, but also features management and strategy elements.

### Tactical gameplay

XCOM 2 has three different modes of strategic movement. "Move" can only be used to move soldiers from one tile to another. "Build" can be used to place walls or other objectives, such as barracks. "Research" is required to upgrade weapons and armor for soldiers.

When a soldier or enemy is in combat, the game switches to the tactical combat mode. The combat system is turn-based and features a grid-based movement system. The game uses a simplified version of the original X-COM's Cover system. Enemies are defeated by attacking them with weapons or by using soldiers to flank them, damage them with a grenade, or use their weapons. The use of flanking can be made more effective by using the environment, for example destroying a wall to create an opening to flank enemies, or using environmental traps to deal damage to enemies.

The character's armor and weapons have a status-effect system, which can cause damage to the player's unprotected soldiers. The armor and weapons also have attributes, which can be upgraded by researching.

### Management

The management mode of XCOM 2 is focused on research, which can be used to upgrade soldiers' armor and weapons. Research can also be used to create new units and vehicles.

Besides research, the player needs to manage their base. They can build various facilities, such as armories, barracks, and research centers. The player can also construct buildings that can be used to improve the soldiers' morale, such as a gym, a kitchen, or a canteen.

The player can also recruit new soldiers, including specialist and support soldiers, such as medics and engineers. The recruited soldiers can also be promoted, either by training or by researching.

### Alien base

The player can infiltrate alien bases to research and, if successful, conquer them.

The player can use the unconquered alien bases to conduct research. Research can be used to develop new weapons and armor for the player's soldiers.

If the player captures an alien base, they can occupy and manage it. The player can choose to support the aliens, which is necessary for capturing the base, but will cause the aliens to attack the player's base.

### Atmosphere

The game's atmosphere is created by using the Unreal Engine 4, which gives the game a realistic appearance.

The game's designers wanted to make the game more cinematic and immersive than its predecessors. The game features various visual effects, such as flame and particle effects, to create a more immersive experience.

## Plot

### Setting and characters

The game is set in 2025, 20 years after the events of the original X-COM games. The United States has been taken over by the aliens known as the Advent, and the X-COM organization has been disbanded. The player takes control of a lone soldier, who is being chased by alien forces. The game progresses as the player's forces confront the alien forces.

XCOM 2 sold 500,000 copies within its first 24 hours on sale. In November 2016 the game had sold approximately 800,000 copies. As of March 2017, total sales of the game had reached 1.5 million copies.

From September 24 , 1965 , in Austin , Texas , Dylan toured the U.S. and Canada for six months , backed by the five musicians f

amed later as the Band . As the tour progressed , Dylan's repertoire grew to include over 100 songs , including many he had never before played in public . He also began to introduce new songs which he had not yet fully completed . "Like A Rolling Stone" was one of them .
 On November 22 , Dylan arrived in London , where he was greeted as a hero by a press hungry for the latest news about the American musical revolution . He was expected to spend just a few days in England before continuing his tour in France and Germany . Instead , he decided to stay for almost two months and record an album in the British capital , an album that would change the course of popular music .
 Dylan's stay in London coincided with the era of Beatlemania , and nearly every magazine carried articles about the Fab Four , who were just months away from releasing their first album . An article in _New Musical Express_ , however , described Dylan as "the voice of the Sixties" . In England , he was seen as a much more serious and politically aware figure than he had been in the United States. It was as if he had come from another planet .
Nevertheless , Dylan was not received with the same kind of enthusiasm as the Beatles . A group of young people gathered outside the Savoy Hotel , where he was staying , but they soon dispersed , and the most he received from the press was a brief mention in the _Daily Mail_ 's "Coffee with" column . This was not what he had expected .
 Dylan had always had a healthy disregard for the media , and he was particularly disgusted with the way the press had treated him in the United States . He had never had a press officer before his manager, Albert Grossman , hired a man to help him deal with the growing number of requests from journalists . Dylan was not happy with this arrangement .
"I don't know what the hell's going on, man . I've never had a press agent, man . I don't know how to handle this. I mean, I don't know what to do. I don't know how to handle it, man . You know, I don't know how to handle it, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man . I don't know what to say, man ."
The press conference was more like a monologue , and Dylan's words were barely audible .
The singer was asked if he thought his music could be used as a propaganda tool for the Communist Party. He replied that this was a matter for lawyers to decide , and the reporters left .
Dylan's arrival in London was the first step in a plan to record an album that would be different from anything he had done before . But first he had to find a producer .
The first person he asked was Paul McCartney . The two singers had become friends after meeting at the Troubadour in Los Angeles . Dylan had been impressed by McCartney's energy and enthusiasm , and he felt that the other Beatle was the type of person who could make a great record .
McCartney was working on his own album at the time , but he agreed to produce Dylan's right away .
"We were in the studio in St. John's Wood , which was not far from where he was living in Primrose Hill ," McCartney said in an interview for the book _How To Make A Dylan Record_ by Jonathan Cott . "He was just starting to write some of the songs that would appear on the album . But he was already in my mind as someone who was doing something very special ."
The first song to be recorded was "Like A Rolling Stone" . Dylan had written the lyrics in a hotel in Malibu , California , and he brought them with him to London . He had also brought with him a melody that he had been working on for some time . The Beatles had used similar melodies in some of their own songs .

The fort was named after Brigadier General William F. "Sandy" Smith Smith is a surname of British origin, originally derived from the name of the village of Smeaton in Northumberland. In 1920, the United States Army discontinued the use of forts named after persons, and the fort was renamed Fort McPherson.
The fort was originally built to protect the Bozeman Trail and the Oregon Trail , as well as to protect the Union Pacific Railroad from possible attack by hostile Plains Indians .
Fort McPherson was built in 1867-1868 near the site of Fort Reno , which was built in 1867 to protect the Bozeman Trail . Fort McPherson was established on 23 January 1868 by Major John Mullins (1823-1899) of the 10th U.S. Cavalry.
In April 1868, a battle was fought at the fort between the 10th U.S. Cavalry and a large force of Sioux and Cheyenne warriors. The battle was the first major engagement of the Cheyenne and Sioux uprising of 1868.
In October 1868, the fort was the scene of a battle between the 10th U.S. Cavalry and a large force of Sioux and Cheyenne hostiles. The battle was the second major engagement of the Cheyenne and Sioux Uprising of 1868.
In 1869, the fort was the scene of the Battle of Medicine Lodge Creek during the Cheyenne and Sioux Uprising of 1868.
On 15 September 1869, the fort was the scene of the Battle of Wagon Box Fight during the Cheyenne and Sioux Uprising of 1868.
In 1871, the fort was the scene of the Battle of Summit Springs during the Cheyenne and Sioux Uprising of 1868.
Fort McPherson was abandoned in 1880, and was finally closed on 15 September 1882.
The fort was located 1/2 mile west of the Wyoming-Nebraska border on the Union Pacific Railroad.
 The fort was located in the middle of the "Indian Territory" (present-day Oklahoma) , a territory set aside by the U.S. government for American Indians .

A marooned French Huguenot , François Leguat , used the name " solitaire " for the Raphine bird he encountered on the nearby is

let of Frégate .
[1.2.1] The existence of the Solitaire was first discovered by a Frenchman, François Leguat, who, in 1691, was stranded on the island of Mauritius. He was on his way to the East Indies and had been shipwrecked there for a year. He was the only survivor, and he lived on the island for five years, together with five other persons. They indulged in hunting, fishing, and the cultivation of flax. They kept poultry, and the female birds laid eggs, which they hatched. The hens were killed for food and the eggs were eaten, but the cocks remained alive. When they were let loose, they fought with the other birds, so they were always kept in a coop. The cocks had no chance to breed, but one day, when they were building a new coop, they found the body of a dead hen, and when the crows and cats had left it, the cocks took it inside the coop, and the hen was hatched. The cock was very vigorous, and in the morning it had killed several young pigeons which had been found in the nest. This cock was quite black, but it had very white eyes. When Leguat saw the hen with her young ones, he knew it was of the same species as the hens he had brought with him and recognized it as the Raphine, which he had seen on the island of Reunion. [1.2.2] The cock was not a very beautiful bird, it was dark with a large white spot on the back, and it had long feathers on its head that swayed about when it moved. It was very quick, and had long legs and a long tail, but its body was small and its wings were short. The cocks had no comb, and their combs were shaped like those of the Capuchin monkeys. The females had no tail, and their bodies were like those of the Raphine, but they had no comb. [1.2.3] The birds used to pick the wool off the sheep and eat it, and when the sheep were killed for food, the birds ate the guts, which were soft and white, and only the stones and the bones were left. The cocks used to pull up the grass and eat it. [1.2.4] Leguat thought the birds must be the descendants of those that had been brought from the East Indies on the ship. He had never seen them in his homeland and it was only in the year 1695 that he met them. He thought that they must be the descendants of the birds that had been brought to the East Indies. [1.2.5] On the island there were many animals; there were rabbits in abundance, and there were also wild goats, and many kinds of snakes, but the birds were all of the Solitaire species. Leguat wrote that the birds were small, and that he did not find them very beautiful, but he said that they were very quick and fearless.

On January 1 , there was already a tropical cyclone located in the central Atlantic Ocean , having developed on December 30 of

2010. The system remained at sea and was given the name Tropical Depression One by the National Hurricane Center , being named "Bonnie" by the Storm Prediction Center . The storm peaked at 20 m s -1 (45 mph) 992 hPa ( mbar).
An area of ​​low pressure over the central Atlantic Ocean was first noticed during the afternoon of December 29, 2010, and became sufficiently organized to be designated as Potential Tropical Cyclone One by the National Hurricane Center (NHC). The system originated as a result of a tropical wave that moved across the Caribbean Sea and into the eastern Gulf of Mexico. Initially, the NHC noted some uncertainty about the development of the system due to the presence of a dry slot in the center of the cyclone. Nevertheless, the NHC issued a tropical storm warning for portions of the northern coast of Honduras and the Yucatán Peninsula of Mexico. Later that day, the NHC issued a tropical storm warning for the northern coast of Belize, as well as a tropical storm watch for the Yucatán Peninsula. The system was upgraded to tropical storm status on December 30 at 0300 UTC, with the NHC naming the system "Bonnie". The tropical storm was located about 175 mi (280 km) south-southeast of Cozumel, Mexico.
On December 31, Bonnie made landfall on the east coast of the Yucatán Peninsula near the town of Chan Santa Cruz. Later that day, the NHC discontinued all watches and warnings for the storm. The remnants of Bonnie continued moving towards the west-northwest over the Bay of Campeche, and was last noted on January 2 as a weak tropical depression.
Airlines and tourism officials in Guatemala, Honduras, and Belize issued advisories warning travelers of the potential impacts of Bonnie. The Honduran government reported that more than 5,000 had been evacuated from the area in anticipation of the tropical storm. The government of Honduras also reported that 600 people were being housed in 22 shelters. The government of Belize issued a tropical storm warning for the northern coast of the country. The government of Mexico issued a tropical storm warning for the northern coast of the Yucatán Peninsula.
Initially, the NHC did not expect Bonnie to make landfall, but the storm went on to make landfall near the eastern town of Chan Santa Cruz. The town of Chetumal also reported gusts of 45 mph (72 km/h). The storm was blamed for at least one death in Progreso, Mexico.
The remnants of Bonnie continued moving across the Bay of Campeche, eventually reaching the Gulf of Mexico. By January 3, the storm had degenerated into a trough of low pressure. On January 4, the remnants were absorbed into a larger extratropical cyclone.
On January 15, the NHC issued a tropical storm warning for the northern coast of the Yucatán Peninsula, as well as a tropical storm watch for the southern coast of the peninsula.

Before the release of Charmbracelet , Carey experienced a year of critical , commercial , personal and professional struggles ,

including her separation from her husband of 4 years , Tommy Mottola , and supporting her then-estranged husband' s mistress, Stella Bulochnikov. In February 2002, Sony Music Entertainment canceled the North American release of the album, citing poor sales of her 2001 Christmas album , Merry Christmas II You. After the international release, the album managed to reach number-one in the United Kingdom , Japan , and New Zealand and number-two in Canada and the United States. Charmbracelet , which was released on March 27 , 2002 , was met with generally positive reviews from music critics , who called it a return to form for Carey. It also produced four singles , which were moderate successes on the US Billboard Hot 100.
At the time of its release, Charmbracelet was the first release by Carey to be released under the imprint of the Island Def Jam Music Group. It is also her fourth album to be released under the Def Jam Music Group , after the release of her 1995 sophomore album, Daydream , as well as its two sequels, 1997 s Butterfly and 1999' s Rainbow . Carey co- wrote all of the album' s tracks , and enlisted the talents of some of her closest friends and collaborators to assist her in the songwriting process , including Jermaine Dupri , Danja , Bryan-Michael Cox , and Johnta Austin.
Charmbracelet ' s musical style represents a fusion of various genres , including R&B and hip hop , with the addition of elements from pop , rock and ballads. With lyrics that deal with themes of love , relationships and romance , the album has been noted as a departure from Carey' s previous works , which have dealt with religious themes. The album' s lyrics and Carey' s vocal performance have been widely praised by music critics , who have compared Carey' s voice to that of Mariah Carey .
Charmbracelet debuted at number-two in the US, selling 320,000 copies in its first week. It has been certified platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America , and has sold 1.9 million copies in the US, making it her lowest selling studio album in the US. The album debuted at number-one in the United Kingdom and peaked at number-two in Canada , where it was certified double-platinum by the Canadian Recording Industry Association. It managed to peak at number-two in Japan , where it was certified double-platinum by the RIAJ.
Charmbracelet was met with a generally positive reception from music critics. At Metacritic , which assigns a normalized rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream critics, the album received an average score of 65, which indicates "generally favorable reviews". Chuck Taylor of Billboard wrote, "Mariah' s latest album is a gentle, sweet offering of love ballads and mid-tempo slow jamz ." Jon Pareles of The New York Times wrote, "Ms. Carey is trying to be a pop-R&B star. She's one of the few who can make a song like "Don't Stop (Funkin' 4 Jamaica)" , which begins with an echo of the "Oooooh" chant from "We Belong Together" , sound like a throwback to the early '70s.

With United now in League One , Cresswell formed a striking partnership with Ched Evans , making 51 appearances and scoring 10

goals, helping the club to the League One play-off final in 2008.  After Evans left for Sheffield United Cresswell was moved from the centre of midfield to striker or attacking midfielder.  Cresswell became one of the few players to score at both Old Trafford and the City of Manchester Stadium for the same team, with a 95th minute goal at the City of Manchester Stadium ending Birmingham City's unbeaten home record.  He scored four goals in two games against Preston North End and Leicester City.
 Cresswell signed for Championship club Peterborough United in 2009.  He scored 17 goals in 86 appearances in all competitions during two seasons at the club.  Cresswell scored the goal that sent Peterborough United to the 2011 Football League Trophy Final, where he was named Man of the Match.  He scored 3 goals in 10 appearances in 2011–12, helping the club to promotion to the Premier League as champions of League One.  Cresswell was released by Peterborough United on 25 August 2012.
On 11 September 2012, Cresswell signed for League One club Fleetwood Town on a six-month contract.  He scored his first goal for the club on 29 September 2012 in a 3–1 defeat to Oldham Athletic.  Cresswell scored 2 goals in 20 appearances in all competitions before leaving the club at the end of the 2012–13 season.
On 29 August 2013, Cresswell signed for League Two club Northampton Town on a two-year contract.  He scored his first goal for the club on 12 October 2013 in a 4–1 defeat to Milton Keynes Dons.  He scored 6 goals in 44 appearances in all competitions during his first season at the club.  On 20 October 2014, Cresswell re-signed for Fleetwood Town for an undisclosed fee.  He scored 1 goal in 10 appearances for the club before leaving the club on a mutual agreement on 17 January 2015.
On 14 August 2015, Cresswell signed for League One club Walsall on a two-year contract for an undisclosed fee.  He scored his first goal for the club on 30 October 2015 in a 2–1 win over Gillingham.  He scored 1 goal in 25 appearances in all competitions during his first season at the club.  He scored 7 goals in 53 appearances in all competitions during his second season at the club.  He re-signed for the club on 23 May 2017, signing a new two-year contract.
 Cresswell made his international debut for England U21 side on 12 August 2008, in a 2–0 win over Sweden U21 in a friendly.  He scored his first international goal on 15 November 2008, in a 3–2 win over Portugal U21 in a friendly.  He made 20 appearances in total for the side, scoring 5 goals.
 Cresswell is married to his wife, Becky.  He has a daughter, born in April 2012.

at Hill 70 , 12 miles ( 19 km ) from Romani , the New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade ( less the Wellington Mounted Rifles Regim

e ) was ordered to take part in the attack on the Turkish position on the southern side of the Bulair Ridge , after a failed attack by the 53rd Division. (The 1st Brigade of the Australian Light Horse, commanded by Brigadier-General William Bridges, had been attached to the NZEF in preparation for the attack, but it was not involved in the battle.) The attack on the Bulair Ridge was intended to be a diversion for the main attack on Hill 60 (north of the Sari Bair Ridge), and the troops of the NZEF were ordered to take up positions for a night attack. The attack was to be a bayonet charge, with the New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade on the left, and the Wellington Mounted Rifles Regim e on the right. At 7.00 pm the New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade moved forward and took up position under a barrage of shrapnel, and then the Wellington Mounted Rifles Regiment, commanded by Colonel W. Meldrum, moved forward, but the barrage had lifted and the New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade was not able to advance into position. The 53rd Division then made an unsuccessful attack on the ridge and the New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade advanced to support them, but they were driven back by Turkish machine-gun fire. The troops of the New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade, and the Wellington Mounted Rifles Regim e , were forced to withdraw to the position occupied on the previous night. (The New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade had 9 men killed, 1 officer and 44 men wounded and 5 missing, and the Wellington Mounted Rifles Regiment 1 officer and 7 men wounded.) [ 4 ]
[5] The NZEF in the Sinai and Palestine Campaign
The NZEF in the Sinai and Palestine Campaign
The New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade had been in Egypt in March 1915, and was ordered to go to Gallipoli in May 1915. At that time, the NZEF had two divisions in Egypt and one division in Suez, and about 12,000 men in the NZEF. The New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade was one of the divisions in Egypt and it was joined by the Wellington Mounted Rifles Regim e at Ismailia. (The 2nd Australian Light Horse Brigade, commanded by Brigadier-General Bridges, had been attached to the NZEF in preparation for the attack on the Bulair Ridge, but it was not involved in the battle.) [ 3 ]
The NZEF landed at Anzac Cove on 25 April 1915. The New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade was unable to land on 25 April and it was not landed until 29 April. [ 6 ]
Most of the New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade was involved in the Chunuk Bair and Hill Q debriefing mission, and the Wellington Mounted Rifles Regim e was involved in the defence of the beach. (The New Zealand Mounted Rifles Brigade had 12 men killed, 6 men missing, and 26 men wounded, and the Wellington Mounted Rifles Regiment had 2 men killed, 9 men wounded, and 4 men missing.) [ 7 ]
Waitemata Regiment
The Wellington Mounted Rifles Regiment was ordered to return to Egypt in June 1915. It was disbanded there on 25 April 1916. [ 8 ]

The Lang E tienne company was, like many of the companies that were established in the late 19 th and early 20 th centuries, a relatively short-lived business. It was active between 1908 and 1912, when the Lang E tienne name was succeeded by the Krynsteel name. The company was established by the two brothers Louis and Albert Lang, who were both born in Germany. According to the National Archives, L . Lang was born in 1872 , while A . Lang was born in 1875 . It is not known exactly when they came to the United States or, indeed, when and where they began to work in the shoe industry. The brothers Louis and Albert Lang were still working at the Lang E tienne company in 1918.
The Lang E tienne company was located in Springfield, Massachusetts. The 1910 Census records the company as having 140 employees, and in 1911 it was listed in the _Manufacturers Directory of the United States_ as having 150 employees. It is possible, although by no means certain, that the company also had a factory in South Norwalk, Connecticut, to which the 1910 Census records 14 employees.
Many of the Lang E tienne frames were made in Poland, but as some were made at the Springfield factory, they too will be included in the following analysis. The frames available for analysis from the Lang E tienne company were made in a wide variety of sizes, and so it will be argued that the company's production was typical of that of some of the other companies discussed in the book. The production of Lang E tienne frames is examined in greater detail in the case study in Chapter 8.

The nucleus is a sophisticated nano-chemical factory for the production of proteins. In the nucleus, the processes of transcription and translation are separated. However, the two nuclear processes must communicate to regulate the expression of genes. It is for this reason that the nucleus is called a compartment.
The transcription of mRNA in the nucleus is regulated by the interaction of a protein with a specific DNA sequence. The resulting mRNA is translocated to the cytoplasm, where it will be translated into protein. Translocation of the mRNA from the nucleus to the cytoplasm is known as nuclear export. The nuclear envelope and a proteinaceous structure called the nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulate nuclear export. During nuclear export, the
nuclear envelope is disrupted, and the mRNA leaves the nucleus through the nuclear pore. Nuclear envelope breakdown and nuclear mRNA export are regulated by a variety of signaling pathways that involve various mitogen-activated protein kinases, phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, cAMP-dependent protein kinase, and other protein kinases.
Nuclear mRNA export is a complex process that involves the exchange of many proteins and the involvement of at least ten different signaling pathways. The NPC is a proteinaceous structure in the nuclear membrane that regulates the exit of mRNA from the nucleus. The NPC has a pore through which mRNA leaves the nucleus. This pore is formed by proteins of the NPC.
The mRNA translocates across the NPC by diffusion through the pores of the NPC. The pore is about 100-150 Å wide. The NPC consists of two concentric membranes, with the outer membrane about 100 Å thick and the inner membrane about 150 Å thick. The pore is about 20 Å wide. The pore is formed by proteins that are embedded in the inner membrane. Proteins bound to the inner membrane of the NPC form a nuclear export complex. These proteins are known as export receptors. The export receptors bind to proteins in the cytoplasm that are known as export factors. The export factors in turn bind to the mRNA. The export factors bind to the mRNA in the cytoplasm and promote the export of the mRNA back into the nucleus.
The export receptors are a large protein family. There are at least 100 different export receptors. The export receptors are classified into two groups. One group is the heterodimeric group. This group includes the nuclear export protein (NXP), which is found in the nucleus. The other group is the homodimeric group. This group includes the nuclear export protein 1 (NXP1), which is found in the cytoplasm.
The export receptors promote the nuclear export of mRNA by binding to the export factors. The export factors are also large protein families. There are at least 100 different export factors. The export factors are classified into two groups. One group is the heterodimeric group. This group includes the nuclear export protein (NXP), which is found in the nucleus. The export factors promote nuclear export by binding to the export receptors.

A prolific goal @-@ scorer , Fowler was a quick and opportunistic striker , with good technical ability . Although naturally le

fthanded , he played on the right , and was a good passer of the ball . He was signed by Burnley in August 1909 , and made his Football League debut at first team level against Manchester United at Turf Moor on 29th August 1909 .
Burnley lost the game 3-1 , but Fowler played well , and was to play 17 more League games for the season , scoring 15 goals . He was a regular in the Burnley line-up in 1910-11 , scoring a further 22 goals in 38 League games . His goals included hat-tricks against Bury (twice) and Port Vale . In January 1911, Fowler was sold to Chelsea for £1,000 . He made his Chelsea debut against Woolwich Arsenal at Stamford Bridge on 7th January 1911 , playing in a 2-0 defeat .
Fowler played 11 more League games for Chelsea , and scored 11 goals . He played in the London Senior Cup Final against Tottenham Hotspur at Stamford Bridge on 23rd March 1911 . The match was drawn 2-2 , and Fowler scored the first goal in the replay at White Hart Lane on 27th March 1911 , which Chelsea won 2-0 .
In 1911-12 , Fowler played 25 League games for Chelsea , scoring 14 goals . He scored in his first three games for the club , against Birmingham City , Sunderland and Sheffield Wednesday . His goals included hat-tricks against Stoke City and Bristol City .
Fowler was a member of the Chelsea team which won the Southern League Championship , with 35 wins and 6 draws from 41 games . This was the only season that the Southern League was the top level of football in England .
During the First World War Fowler served with the Royal Navy , and was stationed in the Mediterranean . After the War , he joined Tottenham Hotspur in August 1919 for a fee of £2,000 . He made his Tottenham debut at White Hart Lane against Millwall on 3rd January 1920 , playing in a 3-1 defeat . Fowler scored his first Spurs goal in his next game , against Liverpool at Anfield on 10th January 1920 . Spurs won the match 2-0 .
Fowler went on to play 193 League games for Tottenham , scoring 87 goals . He scored in his first three games for the club , against Doncaster Rovers , Sunderland and West Ham United . His goals included hat-tricks against Bolton Wanderers and Oldham Athletic , and scored five goals in one game against Plymouth Argyle .
Fowler was a member of the Tottenham team which won the FA Cup in 1921 , beating Wolverhampton Wanderers 1-0 in the Final at Stamford Bridge on 29th April 1921 .
Fowler played his last League game for Tottenham against Sheffield United at Bramall Lane on 11th September 1923 . He made further 11 League appearances for the club as a guest player .
He then played for non-League club Weymouth , before joining Southend United in March 1925 . He played 23 League games for Southend , scoring 4 goals . He was released by Southend at the end of the 1925-26 season .
He then joined non-League club Leeds City , playing for them in the 1926-27 season .
Fowler died in 1967 .

Further northeast , rains brought by Flossy helped relieve drought conditions across the Carolinas , and were considered benefi

cial by local farmers and gardeners. The system was quickly followed by another cold front , which for a time threatened to turn the entire pattern around. The front brought thunderstorms to the Carolinas and Tennessee , and a chance of snow to the northern Appalachians . The front also brought some much-needed rain to the Midwest , and it brought the eastern half of the United States down to near-normal precipitation levels.
As Flossy's rain cleared out, a warm front moved into the region and brought near-record warmth to the East on February 15-16. The warmth continued for the rest of the week, and temperatures in the southern states were at or near record levels for the month and the year. Highs in the 80s were reported in the Carolinas and Georgia and in the 60s in northern Alabama and Tennessee .
 A cold front moved through the Mississippi Valley on February 20, spreading rain and snow to the Ohio Valley and the upper Midwest . The front brought much-needed rain to the Ohio Valley and into the Northeast , where the front had been stuck for several days. The rain also helped to quash the flames of a wildfire that had been burning in western Virginia since January 20. The fire, which had been burning for 12 days, had covered nearly 17,000 acres and had been respon sible for two deaths and the evacuation of about 200 people. The rain that came with the front helped to contain the fire.
 The front also brought snow to the upper Midwest and parts of the Middle Atlantic states , but high temperatures on the back side of the front brought the snow melt. There was even some melting in parts of the Northeast .
 The front was followed by another cold front, which brought another round of snow to the Upper Midwest . The front also brought near-normal temperatures to Florida and the Carolinas , but highs in the northeast were close to record levels.
 There was more snow for the Midwest after another cold front moved through the region on February 22. The front brought a round of snow to the eastern half of the nation, but temperatures were well above normal in the southeast.
 The snow was followed by another warm front , which brought highs above normal to the Carolinas and Florida , but temperatures were near normal in the Midwest .
 Another cold front moved through the Midwest on February 23, bringing a round of snow to the eastern half of the nation. The front brought another round of snow to the Midwest and northern Ohio Valley on February 24, and temperatures were well below normal in the southern half of the United States.
 A weak cold front moved through the eastern United States overnight on February 25-26, bringing more snow to the eastern half of the country. The front was followed by another warm front, which brought temperatures back to near-normal levels for the area.
 The warmth was short-lived, however, as the start of a short-wave trough brought another round of snow to the northeastern states on February 27. There were reports of a foot of snow in some areas.

The episode was written by series creator and executive producer Ian Brennan and directed by Brad Falchuk. The episode aired on Fox on May 12, 2009, sixteen episodes after the pilot episode aired. In the episode, Rachel ( Lea Michele ) and Kurt (Chris Colfer) audition, respectively, for the lead roles of Maria and Tony; she performs "Somewhere" from West Side Story, which is a favorite song of both Rachel and Kurt, and he performs "Tonight" from West Side Story.

## Plot

The episode begins with Rachel (Lea Michele) and Kurt (Chris Colfer) both auditioning, respectively, for the lead roles of Maria and Tony in the upcoming school production of West Side Story. Rachel performs "Somewhere" and gets a standing ovation from the rest of the glee club. However, she is unhappy with her lack of emotion during the performance and heads to the auditorium to re-sing her audition piece. In the hallway, she has a confrontation with a fellow student who accuses her of not being worthy of getting the lead role.

Kurt, meanwhile, is nervous about his audition. He asks his father, Burt (Mike O'Malley), for advice, who tells him to just stay true to himself. At the audition, Kurt sings "Tonight" and receives only a lukewarm response from the rest of the glee club. He is devastated, but Burt tells him to be true to himself, and Kurt does so by auditioning again. This time, he sings "Tonight," and gets a standing ovation.

The glee club goes to a diner after the auditions, and the group debates whether or not to tell Rachel she did not get the lead role. They notice that she has gone to the restroom, and begin to discuss how to tell her. Meanwhile, Kurt is also in the restroom and overhears them. Rachel emerges from the restroom and is greeted with the news that she did not get the role. She is upset with the teachers for not telling her the truth.

Rachel and Kurt go to the auditorium, where the two get into an argument about who was more deserving of the lead role. Rachel tries to tell Kurt that she feels the same way he does when they sing together. She brings up New Directions's first performance at Nationals, when the two sang "Don't Rain on My Parade," and she tells him she feels like they have something special. The two sing "Somewhere," and their argument ends when they embrace.

The episode ends with the glee club singing "Somewhere" to the assembled students.

## Cultural references

* The episode's title is a reference to the film West Side Story, which is the story of the rivalry between a group of Puerto Rican youths and a group of Polish youths.
* The episode's storyline is a reference to the 2005 American Idol season, which Rachel and Kurt were auditioning for. They both auditioned for the show and both failed to make it through the audition rounds.
* Kurt and Rachel's auditions are a reference to the 1961 film West Side Story, which is about a rivalry between a group of Puerto Rican youths and a group of Polish youths.
* Kurt's father, Burt, is a reference to Kurt and Burt Hummel, the main characters in the 1981 film Airplane!, who are both played by the same actor, Robert Hays.

Super Mario Land was developed by Nintendo R & D1 and published by Nintendo in 1989 as a launch title for their Game Boy handhe

eld console. Finding a spot for the game on the NES was tricky because the console had just been released and many games were already in production for it. Nintendo wanted something new and appealing to release on the Game Boy that would showcase its capabilities.
 Super Mario Land takes place in Sarasaland, a world very similar to the Mushroom Kingdom. However, after the events of Super Mario Bros. 3, it was decided that Princess Peach would rule the kingdom and Mario would marry Princess Daisy.
 Super Mario Land is the first game in the series to feature new power-ups. Mario obtains the Super Leaf, which allows him to fly for a short time, and the Tanooki Suit, which enables him to float downwards and walk on walls. The game also features the first enemy to be defeated by a power-up, the Stone Statue, which is stunned by the Super Leaf.
 Yoshi, a dinosaur from the original Super Mario Bros. 2, returns in Super Mario Land and has a prominent role. He is Mario's main companion in the game and can be ridden to cross gaps. He also has a few special abilities. For example, he can lay an egg that will hatch into two Yoshi Twins of equal size, though they only last for about 8 seconds.
 Super Mario Land was a huge success commercially and critically, selling over 15 million units. The game is often seen as a progenitor of the 2D Mario platform series. The console sold 118 million units worldwide between 1989 and 2008.
 The game was re-released for the Game Boy Advance as part of the Super Mario Advance series in 2001. A remake for the Wii U called Super Mario Land 3D was released in 2013.
 Super Mario Land has a sequel, Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins, which was released for the Game Boy in 1995.

Those encountering Alkan at this phase included the young Vincent d 'Indy , who recalled Alkan 's " skinny , hooked fingers " p

ounding the keyboard in " a manner that was anything but pianistic "; Alkan 's son, who later recalled a " large, well-stocked library of books in various languages, that made one think of a learned man " ; and even his grandson, who in 1940 described his grandfather as a " slim, dignified man with little hair and a long, narrow face, not unlike an Egyptian mummy, with a pointed chin and a mustache that turned upward at the ends. The whole face, from the narrow nose to the sharp chin, was in shadow from the brim of a gray felt hat. "
A few years before his death, Alkan was interviewed by the Belgian pianist Alfred Cortot , an early disciple of Liszt and a close friend of Rachmaninoff. " Alkan was a very thin man with a terrible, sad face, " Cortot recalled. " He had a long, bony nose, and his skin was yellowish, like a monkey's. He was inattentive, and he wouldn't fix his eyes on you. He was a man who knew nothing about life. As he talked, his eyes looked at the ceiling and he mumbled. He was very kind and he was very gentle, but his intelligence was absolutely nil. If he had had my eyesight and my hearing, my hands, my fingers, and my touch, he would have been a genius. "
Alkan died in Paris on October 9, 1888, a few days after his seventy-second birthday. He is buried in the Cimetière du Montparnasse , in a plot adjoining the grave of Pierre-Joseph Prudhomme , author of the poetic aphorism " La vie est belle ."

The name has remained in common use in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. The name is still used in scientific literature.
The corncrake is a medium-sized wader, 20–22 cm long, with a 36–40 cm wingspan and a weight of 45–50 g. It has a grey-brown back, wings and tail, and a paler grey-brown underside with darker streaks and bars. The head is white with a darker cap, and the legs and feet are red. Its bill is black with a pale tip, and has a blackish eye ring. The sexes are similar, but the juvenile is duller and more cryptic.
This species breeds throughout the temperate zones of Europe, Asia and North Africa. It is migratory, wintering in tropical Africa. In the United Kingdom, it is mostly confined to the uplands in the north and west, and is a rare breeder.
The corncrake breeds in open wetland habitats, such as marshes, reeds and damp heaths. It is a noisy bird, and the male's advertising call is a distinctive, rapidly repeated, "creaking" note, often heard at night. The female's clutch contains four to eight eggs, which are hidden among the vegetation on the ground. The chicks have downy feathers when they hatch, and are able to walk and fly a few days later. The adults feed the young by bringing them insects in their bill, and these are regurgitated. The young are able to feed themselves by the time they are seven days old. The corncrake is omnivorous, and feeds on insects, spiders, worms, seeds and berries.
The corncrake has declined throughout its range, and in Britain the population has fallen by over 80% since 1970. It has been placed on many national red lists. The corncrake is a very secretive species, and the reasons for its decline are still not fully understood. It is threatened by the loss of wetland habitats, and is also vulnerable to predation by foxes and cats. The corncrake is an insectivore, and the loss of its preferred prey has also contributed to its decline. The species is protected by law in Europe and Britain.
The corncrake has a long history of association with humans. It was revered by the ancient Greeks, and has been depicted in human art and literature for thousands of years. Rolling Stone described " Imagine " as Lennon 's " greatest musical gift to the world " , praising " the serene melody ; the pi

quant harmonies ; the simple, direct lyric; the intimate, introspective tone ".

John Lennon was inspired to write " Imagine " by the idea that material possessions were unnecessary, and by a wish for world peace. Lennon first began writing the song in 1969, and it was intended as a protest song against the Vietnam War. The song's lyrics were made more ambiguous with the addition of the phrase " You may say I'm a dreamer " in the second verse. This was done at the suggestion of Lennon's former bandmate Paul McCartney and Lennon's wife Yoko Ono.

" Imagine " was released on Lennon's album Imagine in 1971. It was the most commercially successful song from that album, and Lennon's most successful single release in the United States; it reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100. It was No. 1 in Canada, Ireland, and Sweden. Lennon performed the song during his final live performance at Madison Square Garden two months before his death.

" Imagine " has been covered by many artists, and performed at numerous political events. In 2002, it was voted 54th in the Rolling Stone list of " The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time ". It is one of Lennon's most recognized songs in popular culture, having been featured in several films and television series.

## Background

### Writing the song

In 1969, Lennon began to write the song. Drafts of lyrics written on a yellow pad recovered after his death reveal that he was writing about a world without countries, religions, or possessions, but the final published version's lyrics are changed to be more ambiguous. In the original lyrics, the verse reads: 

Imagine there's no countries It isn't hard to do Nothing to kill or die for And no religion too Imagine all the people Living for today

In the released version, the phrase "Imagine no possessions" is replaced by "Imagine there's no countries". The lyric "nothing to kill or die for" was changed to "nothing to kill or be killed for".

Lennon was inspired to write the song by the idea that material possessions were unnecessary. He said in 1980, "I was trying to imagine a world with no possessions, no national boundaries, no religions – because it seems to me we live in a world of possessions, and national boundaries and religions have divided us so much. It's a dream image to sort of break us in to other image patterns, other ways of thinking."

The song was originally intended as a protest song against the Vietnam War. McCartney suggested that Lennon add the line, "You may say I'm a dreamer", found in the second verse, to give the song a more hopeful tone than the darker one suggested by the rest of the lyrics. Lennon later said that he changed the lyrics to make the song more ambiguous and thus more relatable.

### Recording

Lennon recorded "Imagine" in 1971, at Ascot Sound Studios in England.

The recording of the song is notable for its minimalist production. McCartney, who produced the song, said that he and Lennon had intentionally "left it off-balance, with the piano slightly out front of the guitar." Lennon said, "The idea was to make it as stripped down as we could. When I was writing the song, I was thinking in terms of how the song would sound as an a cappella. That's how I write songs usually. You can take one of my songs and play it on the piano and you'll find the melody's still there."

According to Lennon's assistant, Tony Bramwell, Lennon "played a lot of the acoustic guitar except the chords, and he played the piano. He did the harmonies himself." The song was recorded at Ascot Sound Studios in England. Aside from Lennon, the other musicians on the track were McCartney, Klaus Voormann (bass guitar), Alan White (drums), and Nicky Hopkins (piano). Lennon, McCartney, Voormann, and White all also sang backing vocals.

Lawton was called up to play for The Football League XI against a League of Ireland XI at Windsor Park on 21 September 1938 , a

match that saw a 2–2 draw.
Lawton was born in Belfast. He was a star pupil at the Christian Brothers Grammar School, where he was captain of the school soccer team and a gifted sprinter, and was awarded a county junior cap. On leaving school he worked as a civil servant in the River Lagan Survey Office.
Lawton made his international debut, at inside-right, in a 3–2 win against Wales at Ninian Park, Cardiff, on 29 February 1936. He was selected to represent Ireland in the 1936 Summer Olympics at Berlin and was a member of the Ireland team that beat the Netherlands 2–1 in the final. He scored the first goal in the 15th minute, but had to leave the field prior to half time due to an injury, and was replaced by Jimmy McIlwaine.
He played in all of Ireland's qualifying games for the 1938 FIFA World Cup, scoring four goals, a record for the time, but was not included in the squad for the finals in France. He was one of thirteen players to be included in the squad for the World Cup who were not selected for either of the two qualifying games.
Lawton played for Ireland six times in all, scoring five goals. He also played 23 times for Belfast Celtic scoring 19 goals for the club.
He was the first footballer in Irish history to score in two separate World Cup tournaments.

The origins of Route 4 date back to 1952 , when construction began on a short , unnumbered arterial from US 1 to the modern loc

us of the White Plains TransCenter . The route was completed in 1957 , and assigned the number 4. If not for the re-routing of US 1 onto the Saw Mill River Parkway in 1959 , it is likely that Route 4 would have extended to US 1 instead of ending at the TransCenter .
In 1960 , the unnumbered arterial was extended northward a short distance to US 202 .
As early as 1963 , the Apportionment Line in the New York Constitution established that through highways in the New York City boroughs were to be numbered in a manner that would be consistent with their numerical ordering in Westchester County. As a result of this mandate , the section of Route 4 within Westchester County was renumbered in 1963 as New York State Route 128 (NY 128). That year , a new Route 4 was designated along the portion of the old US 1 between the White Plains TransCenter and US 202 .
In 1970 , the New York City boroughs were officially renamed "counties" under the Apportionment Line. This permitted the state legislature to re-designate the portion of Route 4 in Westchester County as NY 128 again. At the same time , the portion of the route in Rockland County was re-designated as NY 4.
The entire route was proposed to be re-designated as part of the statewide highway renumbering in 1977 , and became I-4 in 1978.
 In 2005 , the NYSDOT re-numbered all exits on the Saw Mill River Parkway using a mileage-based exit numbering system . The exits on Route 4 on the parkway are therefore numbered based on their mileage along the route.

### Early life

Erving Goffman grew up in a Jewish family in the city of Manitoba, Canada. His father, Harry Goffman, was a successful businessman and had a reputation for being well-connected in the community. Erving's mother, Rebecca, was a homemaker who was very involved in her community and served as the president of the local synagogue.

Goffman's early childhood was spent in Canada, where he attended school in Winnipeg. He later moved to the United States to attend college, where he received a degree in geology from Princeton University in 1943.

### Academic career

After graduating from Princeton, Goffman enrolled in the University of Chicago, where he received a master's degree in sociology in 1947. He then went on to receive a doctoral degree in sociology from the University of Chicago in 1953.

### Later life and death

After retiring from teaching at the University of Toronto in 1982, Goffman moved to Mexico City, where he continued to work on his writing and research. He died on November 19, 1982, at the age of 71, and was buried in Mexico City.

Tropical Storm Abby was an exceptionally small tropical cyclone that had minor effects across Southeast Texas in early August 1

981. It formed from an easterly wave that had developed several days earlier. After passing over the Yucatán Peninsula, the wave emerged into the Gulf of Mexico, where it gradually developed tropical characteristics. After a period of rapid intensification, the system attained hurricane status and became a minimal hurricane. After making landfall, it weakened and degenerated into a tropical depression before dissipating.
Tropical Storm Abby formed from a tropical wave that had developed over the Gulf of Honduras on August 2. The wave tracked westward through Central America and emerged over the Yucatán Peninsula on August 2, where it strengthened into a tropical depression. The depression moved west-northwestward over the Yucatán Channel and strengthened into Tropical Storm Abby on August 3. The storm turned north-northwestward and began to intensify rapidly, reaching hurricane status within 24 hours. Abby continued to strengthen as it moved over the northern Gulf of Mexico, but the storm reached its peak intensity as a minimal hurricane, attaining maximum sustained winds of 80 mph (130 km/h) and a minimum barometric pressure of 998 mbar (29.45 inHg). Shortly thereafter, it passed over land, becoming an extratropical cyclone and dissipating near the Louisiana coast.
The extratropical remnant of Abby passed through the heavily populated South Texas coastal areas, causing light to moderate rainfall. In New Orleans, Louisiana, the storm dropped 2 in (51 mm) of rainfall, peaking at 4 in (102 mm). In the city, the rainfall was enough to cause localized flooding in some areas. In Chambers County, Texas, the storm produced 4.85 in (123 mm) of rainfall, peaking at 8.39 in (213 mm). The storm also produced thunderstorms in Southeast Texas, which spawned several tornadoes. In the state, six tornadoes touched down. One tornado in Anahuac, Texas, levelled a mobile home park, injuring 24 people. Another tornado in Henderson, Texas, killed a 10-year-old boy. The storm caused minor damage to buildings and crops in Southeast Texas. Abby caused minor impacts in Southeast Texas and did not cause any fatalities.

At the time when the poem Lietuva , Tėvyne mūsų was written , Lithuania was part of the Russian Empire . Kudirka , a medical st

ude nt from Kaunas , was sent to Germany to continue his studies . During the Soviet occupation of Lithuania , he joined the Lithuanian Nationalist movement and published the patriotic poem in 1944 .
On October 5, 1944 , Kudirka was arrested by the NKVD and sent to the Vilnius prison. In 1945 he was sentenced to death and executed on November 14, 1947 . After his death , his widow Amalia Kudirka and poet Antanas Venclovas attempted to revive interest in Kudirka's work. Venclovas published the poem Kudirka's in 1955 .
In 1966 , a monument to Kudirka was erected in Kaunas . In 1974 , a monument to Kudirka was erected in Vilnius . In 1991 , the Kudirka statue was re-erected in Kaunas .
The poem Lietuva , Tėvyne mūsų was written in 1944 and published in 1945 . The poem was first published in the Vilnius newspaper Lietuva under the pseudonym J. Balys .
Lietuva , Tėvyne mūsų translates to simply as Homeland , Our Fatherland .

The poem begins with the couplets describing the Lithuanian landscape and its people. The first line describes the land (grass) and the line below it, the people (weeds). The second couplet talks about the Lithuanian forest and the line below it, the Lithuanian people (fallen leaves). The third couplet talks about the Lithuanian people, who are described as a separate group (their own group). The first stanza ends with the phrase "Our Fatherland" (Lietuva , Tėvyne mūsų)
The second stanza begins with the triplets: "O", "A", and "Ā" that signify the beginning of a new idea. The second line of the second stanza describes the Lithuanian land as beautiful (beautiful). The third line talks about the Lithuanian people as both beautiful (dainius ) and strong (vietus ). The last line of the second stanza describes the Lithuanian people as strong and beautiful.

00 miles of the river into a series of lakes and reservoirs; the reservoirs created by these dams, together with the river itself, now supply water to more than 15 million people in six states.
The Missouri River is the longest river in the United States, and it encompasses the largest river drainage system in North America. It flows approximately 2,341 miles (3,770 km) in the central part of the United States. The river rises in western Montana, near the city of Three Forks, and flows east and southeast, exiting the state of Montana and entering the state of North Dakota. It then turns northeast, entering South Dakota and Nebraska, then passes through Kansas on the way to its eventual confluence with the Mississippi River, which it enters or exits in the state of Missouri, at St. Louis. The Missouri drains an expansive watershed of more than half a million square miles (1,300,000 km2), encompassing parts of 31 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces.
The Missouri River is one of the principal rivers of the Americas, and is the principal river of the American Great Plains. The Missouri River is also the main tributary of the Mississippi River, which rises in Minnesota and flows generally south to the Mississippi's confluence with the Missouri, which is south of St. Louis, Missouri. The total length of the Mississippi River, including its major tributaries, is approximately 3,734 miles (6,012 km). The Missouri River is the fourth longest river in North America, after the St. Lawrence River, the Mackenzie River in Canada, and the Yukon River in Canada and Alaska. It is the primary watercourse of the American portion of the Missouri River basin, which extends from the Rocky Mountains to the Missouri River's confluence with the Mississippi.
The Missouri River is the principal tributary of the upper Mississippi River. The Missouri drains approximately 1.25 million square miles (3.2 million km2) of the central United States, or about one third of the total watershed of the Mississippi. The lower half of the river's drainage basin, located south of the Missouri River's confluence with the Platte River, is sometimes called the Bozeman drainage basin.
The Missouri headwaters are in the Rocky Mountains of western Montana. The source of the river is at the confluence of the Jefferson River, Madison River, and Gallatin River, near Three Forks, Montana. All three forks flow into the Missouri near the town of Three Forks, Montana. It is a classic Indian film, depicting the adventures of a bandit ( Dharmendra ), his elder brother ( Amitabh Bachchan ) and an ex-policeman ( Sanjeev Kumar ) who join forces to save a village from a ruthless bandit ( Amjad Khan ).
Sholay has been released in several languages like Marathi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Bhojpuri, Malayalam, Gujrati, Kannada, Oriya, Punjabi, Nepali, and Sinhalese.
The film has been claimed to have inspired several films and TV series in India and other countries. It has also been highly influential on the Indian film industry itself, having introduced many aspects that are now considered standard practice.
Sholay won ten of the fourteen categories in which it was nominated at the 1975 Filmfare Awards, a record only bettered by Lagaan (2001) and Satyamev Jayate (1998).

## Biography

### Early life

Townsend was born in Los Angeles, California, the son of a Canadian mother and American father. He learned to play guitar at age 10, and later enrolled in the Berklee College of Music in Boston, Massachusetts, where he studied guitar for two years. He then moved to Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada and joined a band called Leviathan, which evolved into Skin. After the band's demise, Townsend formed the heavy metal band Strapping Young Lad (SYL) with Ian Gillman (bass) and Gene Hoglan (drums). SYL's debut album, Heavy as a Really Heavy Thing, was released in 1995. Townsend also began to work on his first solo album, Infinity, which was released in 1997. Townsend released a second solo album, Addiction, in 2001. SYL released a second album, City, in 1997. SYL's third album, Strapping Young Lad, was released in 2003. SYL released two more albums, Alien and The New Black, before Townsend decided to disband SYL in 2007.

### Musical style

Townsend's musical style is commonly described as heavy metal, though he has stated that he does not like to be put into a specific genre. Townsend has cited Bach, John Lennon, John Zorn, and Hank Williams as his biggest influences. He has also cited his mother, who was a classical pianist, as an influence.

### Lyric themes

Townsend's lyrics are commonly based on his personal experiences and life events. Townsend has stated that he has written about his experiences with depression, substance abuse, and suicide, and that he writes lyrics to deal with his emotions and to help him get through difficult times. Townsend has also stated that his lyrics are often inspired by his experiences with religion and spirituality.

The overall number of billion-dollar disasters has been increasing in recent years, and 2017 was on track to be the costliest year for weather and climate disasters in the United States until the three hurricanes in August.

After sea trials in May 1932 , Comet was commissioned for service in the 2nd Destroyer Flotilla , Home Fleet , in early June .

Between 1932 and 1934 , she undertook anti-submarine patrols off the east coast of Britain , and in 1934 she was converted to a minelayer, and spent the next few years operating out of Portsmouth .  In 1936 , she was placed in reserve , and between 1936 and 1938 she served as a training ship at Portsmouth .

The ship's commissioning pennant was hoisted on 23 June 1932 (see illustration, upper left). The pennant was of a darker shade of blue than the one used on the new Town class cruisers, and as a result often mistakenly identified as a Town pennant (see illustration, upper right).
Comet was the only ship of her name in the Royal Navy. She was named after the brightest star in the constellation of Coma Berenices, which was sometimes called "the Comet Star". The name Comet was also used for (but not by) a seaplane tender of the Royal Air Force .
Comet was a relatively large destroyer of 1,350 tons, with a standard displacement of 1,510 tons. She was 309 feet (94 metres) long overall, with a beam of 31 feet (9.4 metres) and a draught of 11 feet (3.4 metres). Her two Parsons geared steam turbines, each driving two shafts, were rated at 34,000 shp (25,000 kW) and gave a design speed of 35 knots (65 km/h; 40 mph). Comet's crew numbered 139 officers and men.
Comet's main battery consisted of two QF 4.7-inch (120 mm) Mk IX guns, one of which was in a superfiring position forward of the funnel and the other in the aft superstructure. In the aft superstructure was also a 2-pounder pom-pom anti-aircraft gun, and in the forebridge there was a .303 inch (7.7 mm) machine gun.
Comet had a mine-laying capacity of 40 naval mines , which could be laid in an area of up to 820 square nautical miles (1,520 km2; 590 sq mi). The stern of the ship was equipped with a mine-hydroplane for the laying of mines.
Comet was sunk by the German submarine U-18 near the Humber Light Vessel, off Spurn, Yorkshire on 27 June 1940. Several hundred of the 130-strong crew survived and were rescued by the destroyers Foresight and Firedrake.
The Royal Navy attributed Comet's loss to German submarine U-18 , but the German Navy attributed the sinking to the destroyer Ardent .
The German Navy's U-boat Archive website lists one U-boat as having sunk Comet: U-18 , commanded by Korvettenkapitän Ernst-Friedrich Ziese. According to the German Navy, Ardent was the only destroyer sunk by U-18.
Comet was brought into service by the Royal Navy on 23 June 1932. She was commissioned on 27 June 1932, with the pennant number 53.
On 23 October 1932, Comet, on her first sea trials, collided with the destroyer Eskimo and suffered a severe knockdown.
On 4 November 1932, Comet, with the cruiser Phoebe and the destroyers Faulknor and Firedrake, was part of a convoy to Gibraltar . On her return voyage, Comet was damaged by a hit from the destroyer Falcon.
On 18 April 1933, Comet, with the cruisers Berwick and Newcastle, and the destroyers Foresight and Falcon, was part of a convoy to Gibraltar . On her return voyage, Comet was damaged by a hit from the destroyer Falcon.

100 men and women committed themselves to the project. The men were led by the Parish Priest Father John Flanagan, and the women by Mother Ann Marie Swain, a Presentation Sister from Ireland. The site for the church was donated by a certain Mrs. Margaret Barker, who stipulated that the church be built on a site that was to be known as "Barker's Field", which is where the church is situated today.
A plan for the church building was prepared by the celebrated Irish architect, P. Cullen. It was to have a 110-foot spire, a 120-foot transept, a beautiful altar of Italian marble, and a sanctuary lit by the light of 19 windows, 16 of which were to be of stained glass. Funds were immediately sought, and the Catholics of Madison were urged to support the project.
In spite of the fact that the church had no Sunday school, the Catholics of Madison came forward and donated more than $1,000 in 1880 to begin construction. The builders were George Lennon and Joseph Sheehan of Madison, who were both skilled craftsmen. They built the church using limestone from the nearby town of Sugar Grove, Illinois. The church was designed to accommodate about 1,000 people at one time.
The cornerstone of the church was laid on July 4, 1880, by Father Flanagan and blessed by Bishop Carroll from the Diocese of Chicago. When the cornerstone was opened fifty years later in 1930, it was found to contain a copy of the Constitution of the United States and a prayer book. The church was completed in 1881.

Cadmium is a chemical element with symbol Cd and atomic number 48 . This soft , bluish @-@ white metal is chemically similar to

the two other stable metals in group 12 , zinc and mercury. It has four oxidation states : Cd 2+ ( red/orange ), Cd 3+ ( yellow/green ), Cd 4+ ( blue/silver ) and Cd 6+ ( purple/blue ) . It forms a blue ppt with HNO 3 and a yellow ppt with H 2 S . It's most common oxidation state is Cd 2+ . Cadmium is resistant to corrosion by acids , but corrodes to a thin layer of soluble cadmium hydroxide in alkalis . Cadmium is a relatively poor conductor of heat and electricity , and is often combined with other metals to improve its machinability. Cadmium is found in batteries , as a pigment in plastics, as a stabilizer in plastics and as a thin layer coating on banknotes .
 Cadmium was discovered in 1817 by Friedrich Stromeyer , who heated zinc carbonate with concentrated sulfuric acid . It is one of the toxic metals whose production and use is regulated by the Minamata Convention on Mercury .
 Cadmium is a soft , bluish white metal . It is malleable , ductile , and with a low melting point of only 320.8 °C (592.4 °F) . As a pure element, cadmium is somewhat more reactive than zinc , but less so than mercury . Cadmium has a face-centered cubic crystal structure .
 Cadmium has five valence electrons in its outer shell , so it can exist in the following oxidation states: Cd 2+ , Cd 3+ , Cd 4+ , Cd 6+ and Cd 7+ . Cd 2+ is the most stable oxidation state of cadmium , and is responsible for its blue color.
 Cadmium forms binary compounds with almost all other elements . The most important ones are the halides , sulfides , carbonates and oxides . The sulfur analogues are less common than the halides, except for the sulfate .
 Cadmium reacts with hydrochloric acid to form cadmium chloride . Cadmium also reacts with hydrofluoric acid to form cadmium fluoride . Cadmium does not react with water, unless in a strongly acidic solution . Cadmium reacts with bases to produce hydroxides. Cadmium reacts with alkaline hydroxide to form cadmium hydroxide .
 Cadmium reacts with aqueous ammonia to form ammonium cadmium sulfate and ammonium cadmium phosphate . Cadmium reacts with alkylamines to form cadmium amides .
 Cadmium reacts with most acids to form cadmium salts , which are divalent. Cadmium acetate is the most common example.
 Cadmium reacts with the hydroxyl group in organic compounds to form metal hydroxides.
 Cadmium is a soft and malleable metal which is easily cut with a knife . Cadmium has a low melting point of 320.8 °C (592.4 °F) , and a boiling point of 765 °C (1409 °F) . Cadmium has a density of 8.64 g/cm 3 and is a poor conductor of both heat and electricity .
 Cadmium quickly reacts with oxygen to form a thin layer of cadmium oxide . Cadmium does not react with water under normal conditions , but when heated in water, it reacts to form hydrated cadmium oxide .
 Cadmium reacts with all acids to form cadmium salts . These salts are all divalent, and have the general formula [ Cd 2+ ] X – .
 Cadmium reacts with hydroxyl compounds to form cadmium hydroxide .
 Cadmium reacts with fluoride to form cadmium fluoride .
 Cadmium reacts with oxygen to form cadmium dioxide .
 Cadmium reacts with alkyl halides to form cadmium halides .
 Cadmium reacts with ammonia to form ammonium cadmium sulfate , ammonium cadmium phosphate and ammonium cadmium hydroxide .

Cognates of the name " Allāh " exist in other Semitic languages , including Hebrew and Aramaic . The corresponding Aramaic form

, , is used as the proper name of God in the Hebrew Bible, in which it is rendered as " ." or " ." (the latter being the vocalization used in the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and other early translations of the Hebrew Bible into Greek and Latin). The form is also used in the Samaritan Bible.
The name " Allah" is also found in pre-Islamic inscriptions from North Africa.
The term Allah is used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews, and it is also used by many modern Muslims to refer to the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob .
Although "Allah" is the standard term for God in Arabic, it may be used in other languages, including English, by Muslims. In English, it is used in the Qur'an, in translations of the Qur'an, and in some non-English Muslim texts, such as the Al-Fatiha, a prayer in Arabic that is recited in many Muslim services.
In this usage it is usually capitalized, and in many English translations of the Qur'an it is translated as "God".
"Allah" is used in many other languages also. It is the standard term for "God" in Indonesian, Malaysian, and Brunei, and it is used also in Afrikaans, Bosnian, Kazakh, Kurdish, and Urdu.
There are also a number of non-Muslim ethnic groups in Indonesia who use "Allah" for their own gods.

DE 261 begins at an interchange with US 202 and the northern terminus of DE 141 north of Alapocas Run State Park near Fairfax ,

Delaware . It heads north along the Delaware Memorial Bridge , intersecting with DE 4 and DE 92 before crossing the Delaware River into New Jersey . The route heads north, intersecting with the interchanges of DE 141 and DE 13 before terminating at an interchange with I-295 and US 13 at the Delaware River.
In 1927, the first portion of what would become Delaware Route 261 was designated as part of State Highway 27. At that time, this roadway ran from U.S. Route 13 (US 13) in Delaware City east to DE 2 in Wilmington . In 1929, the road was extended to DE 44 south of Wilmington, replacing the former alignment of US 13. In 1935, US 202 was designated along the old alignment of US 13, leaving DE 27 as a route from DE 141 east to DE 44. In 1936, DE 27 was extended north to US 202 at the city limits of Newark via Newark Road. In 1939, US 202/DE 27 was rerouted onto the original alignment of US 202, eliminating the concurrency; the former alignment of US 202 became DE 27. The following year, US 202 was moved onto the new alignment of US 202 and DE 27 was extended southeast along the old alignment of US 202 to US 13 south of Newark. In 1941, DE 27 was rerouted to follow US 202/US 13 to DE 2 in Wilmington, as the old alignment was removed. In 1945, DE 27 was rerouted to follow US 202/US 13/DE 2 to the end of the road at DE 141. In 1953, US 202 was rerouted onto the Delaware Memorial Bridge, eliminating the concurrency with DE 27. At this point, DE 27 was extended along the former alignment of US 202 to its current terminus at DE 44. In 1955, US 13 was moved onto the Delaware Memorial Bridge, eliminating the concurrency with DE 27. In 1957, DE 27 was shifted to the current route to bypass Newark, eliminating the concurrency with DE 2. By 1968, the entire route was redesignated as DE 261.
DE 261 is a 2.22-mile-long (3.57 km) limited-access toll road that carries approximately 60,000 vehicles per day.

by the remaining U.S. ships. He was again rebuffed, this time by the governor of St. Louis, who claimed that he could not give up his ships for one which had already failed.  Rowley then decided to depart the island, his mission unfulfilled.
The next step in the effort to relieve Africaine was to maintain contact with the frigate and her crew. Rowley's immediate problem was the lack of a means to do so. He had departed from Cayenne without contacting the U.S. Navy to request that an American ship be dispatched to stand by Africaine. He knew that the frigate was in need of food and other supplies, and he wanted to be certain that he could either return to the frigate or contact her again if the need arose. Rowley's only option was to attempt to reach Cayenne by way of Africaine's former anchorage on Île Bourbon.
After just over a week at sea, Rowley, having left Île Bourbon behind, finally made landfall. He anchored off the island of Petit-Texique in the southern Caribbean Sea. Here he waited for a second week while he attempted to communicate with the U.S. government about the need to send a ship to relieve Africaine. Rowley was not idle during his stay. He conducted a series of "reconnaissances" along the island, "particularly of the southern coast, where there was a small settlement of negroes, some of whom were found to be in a state of insubordination."  This was a reference to the thousands of slaves who were living on the island and had declared their independence from the French. Rowley also had the ship's guns loaded with shot and shell.
In the meantime, Rowley's appeals for a relief ship had been passed on to the Navy Department. The department heard the request and hoped that the situation would be resolved without intervention. The Navy Department was also pursuing a different course. During his stay at Île Bourbon, Rowley had been in contact with the secretary of the navy, who ordered the construction of a cutter for the waters off the island.  The cutter, the _Enterprise_ , was under construction at the Washington Navy Yard.
After two weeks of waiting, Rowley decided that he had a sufficient amount of information to permit him to depart Petit-Texique and head for the United States. The next step was to be the most dangerous portion of his voyage: the trek across more than 2,000 miles of open sea and around the Cape of Good Hope to reach the United States.
The voyage of the _Vincennes_ had been successful, but it had not been without its problems. The ship had been forced to remain at sea for more than a month. This had been necessary in order to ensure that the ship would be back in the United States before the _Enterprise_ was ready. Worse yet, the _Vincennes_ had been forced to sail away from the African coast without the relief ship that had been sent to find Africaine. To make matters worse, the captain of the _Vincennes_ was not enthusiastic about the leg of the voyage that took his ship into the Indian Ocean.
In the early morning hours of October 2, 1815, the _Vincennes_ weighed anchor and pointed its prow toward the open sea. The ship was nearing the end of its voyage and would soon be back in the United States.

The _Vincennes_ sailed into the Indian Ocean, but it did not have to go far to begin to encounter the problem of slavery. The ship's master, John Rodgers, kept a journal of the voyage, and this journal provides a glimpse into the difficulties that his ship encountered as it journeyed from the United States to the Cape of Good Hope.
The first sign of trouble appeared, as it does in many of these voyages, when the _Vincennes_ reached the Cape Verde Islands. Rodgers was well aware of the dangers that the islands presented. He noted in his journal, "The whole of Cape Verde is nothing more than a great barren rock, from which, in the season of the year when the wind blows from the land, as it frequently does, the inhabitants are obliged to fly to the sea coast to preserve their lives."  The "inhabitants," of course, were the Africans who had been enslaved and brought to the islands.
