The Dangerously in Love Tour was the debut concert tour by American recording artist Beyoncé . Although the tour was intended to promote Beyoncé's debut solo album Dangerously in Love, it prominently featured songs from Destiny's Child . The tour began in North America on May 2, 2003 and concluded in the United States on September 16, 2003. The tour grossed a total of $60,000,000.

The Dangerously in Love Tour was Beyoncé's first solo concert tour. The concerts were originally scheduled to consist of 35 performances and was booked to begin on April 26, 2003 in Washington, D.C. at the MCI Center . However, the tour was extended by 11 performances so as to include more cities. Beyoncé performed in 46 cities across the U.S. and Canada with opening acts, the J-Kwon , Mario and J-Boog . Beyoncé's performances consist of a mix of Destiny's Child songs and her solo songs. The tour's setlist was a playlist of these songs, with Beyoncé performing three songs from her then-upcoming album.
Beyoncé's stage performance was such a success that it earned her her first Grammy Award for Best Contemporary R&B Album in 2004. The Dangerously in Love Tour was filmed and was released on home video on November 11, 2003. The tour was nominated for Best R&B Tour at the 2004 Soul Train Music Awards .
On October 15, 2003, Beyoncé was scheduled to perform in Ottawa , Ontario at the Corel Centre . However, the performance was cancelled due to the lack of ticket sales. Fans who purchased tickets before the show's cancellation received a refund.
Although the Dangerously in Love Tour was Beyoncé's first concert tour, the tour quickly became a major commercial success. The tour grossed $46 million from 35 performances in North America alone. The tour was Beyoncé's first headlining tour and included 46 performances. The highest grossing concert of the tour was in San Antonio , Texas at the Alamodome . This concert grossed $1,250,816 and was the highest grossing concert in the tour's history. The Dangerously in Love Tour also broke the record for the highest grossing tour for an artist in the history of the Corel Centre. The tour entered the 2003 Pollstar's Year End Tour Rankings at #18, ranked #15 on Billboard's Top Tour Money Makers of 2003 and ranked #10 on Billboard's Top 20 Concert Tours of 2003.

Bob Dylan was born Robert Zimmerman on May 24, 1941, in Duluth, Minnesota. His mother, Beatrice Stone, was a high school teacher, and his father, Abraham Zimmerman, was a Russian Jewish immigrant who worked in a shop as a lumber salesman.
Dylan 's parents divorced when he was six, and, after living with his maternal grandfather, he moved in with his father and stepmother in Hibbing, Minnesota.
Dylan has said that his father was a hard-drinking, abusive man who frequently hit him, and that his stepmother was a cold, domineering woman.
Dylan was educated at Hibbing High School, where he became interested in the works of Woody Guthrie and, later, Jack Kerouac. He began performing in coffee houses as a folk singer in 1959 and, in 1960, he moved to New York City, where he changed his name to Dylan .

The 19th @-@ century writer Samuel Lewis said that the rebuilt church " forms a very good specimen of the early English style o

/ architecture."
The original building, constructed of rubble masonry with a crafted limestone roof, was erected in the 13th century. It was remodelled in 1711 by the architect William Price. The rebuilt church is of yellow brick with a limestone roof. There is a slate roof to the vestry.
The church was declared redundant in 1995 and passed to the Churches Conservation Trust.
Both the parish and the village were originally named after the church. The name is of Anglo-Saxon origin meaning the "church of St Swithin".
The church is built in the Anglo-Norman style. It consists of a chancel, nave, north aisle and south porch.
The church has a Perpendicular style west tower. The tower dates from the 14th or 15th century. The tower has a clasping buttress on the west face.
The tower houses a single bell. The bell was cast by Thomas Mears in 1794 and weighs 14 cwt. The bell was formerly the parish church of St Mary the Virgin in Ballymena but was transferred to the church at Antrim.
The church has a 15th century font with a shaft carved with a pelican. The font has a scalloped and a ribbed design.
Inside the church is a 15th century tomb chest.
There is a churchyard cross located in the churchyard. The cross is a 14th century cross head. The cross head has a carved shaft which is decorated with foliage and bosses.
The church is surrounded by a 19th century wall. The wall has a wrought iron gate and railings.
The churchyard is surrounded by a 19th century railings.
There are six grave markers within the churchyard.
The grave markers date from the 19th century and include a headstone in memory of the Reverend John Henry Maunsell and a headstone in memory of William and Anna McCarter.

The Wilhelm Busch Prize is awarded annually for satirical and humorous poetry . The Wilhelm Busch Society , active since 1930 ,

has been awarding the prize since 1950 . The prize is named after Wilhelm Busch (1832–1908), a German author, artist, and illustrator, who is best known for his book Max and Moritz . The prize is awarded by the Wilhelm Busch Society in cooperation with the Alfred Toepfer Foundation F.V.S. and the German Publishers and Booksellers Association (BdV).
The prize is endowed with 10,000 euros and is intended for “the poet, who has achieved the best artistic performance in the field of satirical and humorous poetry with the publication of a book”. The jury is made up of five members: two representatives of the Wilhelm Busch Society, two representatives of the Alfred Toepfer Foundation and one representative from the BdV.

The best @-@ known feature of the Church of Christ Pantocrator is the rich and colourful decoration of its exterior walls . The

vast majority of its 500-odd square meters are covered by a mural to which the richly decorated domes give even more dynamism. The theme is the life of Christ, with the most important episodes presented in the form of narrative scenes, and the lesser events worked into the details of the ornamental motifs. The mural was painted in the 14th century on the order of the Emperor Andronicus II Palaiologos, who himself is represented at the centre of the composition, standing before the Icon of Christ Pantocrator. The Emperor is shown giving the order to begin work on the mural, with a group of Stonemasons (exemplified by their tools) carrying out the work.
The richly decorated dome of the church is known as the 'Pantocrator' because of the mural representing the Christ Pantocrator in the central bay of the drum. The decorative scheme is a sophisticated and highly original one, with the four equal-radiused domes each carrying a distinctive mural in the central bay of the drum. The domes of the narthex are each painted with a scene from the Gospel of St John, the central bay of the south dome with a representation of the Evangelist himself, and the north dome with the mural of the Pantocrator. The western bay of the drum is decorated with a panel showing the Emperor Andronicus II Palaiologos giving the order to the Stonemasons (with the Stonemasons themselves represented in a figure at the centre of the mural). The remaining bays of the drum bear mosaics.
The mural of the Pantocrator shows the Christ with the right hand raised in blessing, the left hand holding the Gospels. The scene is framed by two angels, one on each side. They hold the scroll of the Apocalypse and the Evangelist's symbol, the eagle, in their hands. Christ's head is crowned with the halo, and he wears a royal diadem on his forehead. The mural shows the Christ as the Pantocrator, the 'Ruler of all', with the right hand extended in blessing. The composition is set against a background of a golden-yellow sky, while the Christ's white robe is depicted in light blue hues. The mural is framed by a deep blue border.

The upper part of the mural presents two angels, one on either side of the central scene. The angels are of a quite large size, with a tall, slender body, and a large head with almond-shaped eyes, a small nose and a long elongated chin. By age five , she began performing on stage at the famous Tokyo 's Bunka Kaikan Concert Hall .  She made her professional debut in 1962 at the age of seven , and by the time she was nine , she had recorded more than 30 , 000 songs in the Japanese market .  She gained international attention in 1971 with her first single , " I 'm in Love " , which was number one for three consecutive weeks in Japan .  In 1973 , she became the youngest person ever to win the Japan Record Award , and by age 13 , she was the only person to ever win it three times .  She also won the Japanese Record Association 's " Gold Disc Award " in 1972 and 1973 , and in 1974 , she was the first Japanese pop star to receive an " RIAJ Gold Disc Award " for selling more than 100 , 000 copies of her album .  She is the only Japanese artist to ever receive all three awards in a single calendar year .  In 1974 , she became the first female to receive the " Japan Record Association " 's " Special Award " for selling more than three million records .  She also received a " Special Award " in 1975 for selling more than four million records .  In 1976 , she became the first Japanese artist to receive the " RIAJ Grand Prix Award " .  She also received a " Special Award " that same year for selling more than five million records .  In 1977 , she received a " Special Award " for selling more than six million records . In the earlier part of the 19th century the area which is today Minnesota was not recognized as a single entity . The Mississip

i River was the boundary between what was then the Northwest Territory and what was then Wisconsin Territory. It was a time of great change in the United States and the Territory of Minnesota was created at a time when there was great interest in the West.
In 1849 gold was discovered at Sutter’s Mill in California. This discovery caused great interest in the West, and in 1851, the Fremont Expedition was organized. The purpose of the expedition was to find a railroad route from the Missouri River to the Pacific Ocean, and find a passageway between the Missouri and the Platte Rivers.
The Fremont Expedition was made up of forty people; consisting of army officers, government officials, scientists and journalists. The Expedition was organized in Washington, D. C. and the party left that city in 1851. The first part of the journey was made by water, on the steamboat, the Yellowstone. On the way to the Pacific coast, the Yellowstone stopped at St. Louis, and the party transferred to the steamboat, the California. The expedition landed in San Francisco on August 21, 1851.
Because of the interest generated by the Fremont Expedition, Congress decided to send another expedition, the Kearny Expedition, to explore the West.
The Kearny Expedition was organized in Washington, D. C. on June 13, 1852. The party consisted of 181 men made up of officers from the U.S. Army, journalists, scientists, and prospectors. The party left Washington, D.C. on June 21 on the steamboat, the General Jessup. The party landed in St. Louis on July 7. The party stopped at Fort Atkinson, Wisconsin Territory. After leaving Fort Atkinson, the party came to Fort Snelling where a meeting was held with Colonel Henry Sibley and Captain John H. Steele, commanding officers at Fort Snelling. They decided to explore the region from Fort Snelling to the Pacific Ocean.
In July 1852, Colonel Henry Sibley, Captain John H. Steele, and Lieutenant James W. Marshall, left Fort Snelling on a steamboat called the Minnehaha. The expedition travelled through the Minnesota River Valley, and on July 30, the expedition arrived in Fort Snelling.
The Kearny Expedition was a success. The Steamboat Minnehaha, the second steamboat to enter the Minnesota River, and the first to go as far as Fort Snelling, transported settlers and goods from Fort Snelling to St. Paul.
The Kearny Expedition was the first organized exploration of Minnesota, and the first organized expedition to the West Coast.

In the autumn of 1968 the US Marines had to clear the area around Con Thien, a village in the eastern part of South Vietnam near the eastern approaches to the Demilitarised Zone. The objective was to cut the Vietcong supply line to the village and, if possible, to the North. But the task was made more difficult by the terrain. The area was full of bamboo and rushes, which could be used as cover, and there were many tunnels and caves in the area which could be used as hiding places. The area was also heavily mined and there were many booby-traps.
In the spring of 1969 a group of Marines, commanded by First Lieutenant Robert Gideon, was sent to reconnoitre the area and scout out the booby-traps and mines. They were supposed to use a helicopter to take them in and out but the helicopter was destroyed by ground fire and the Marines had to find a way to get in and out by themselves. They were dropped in a field and quickly surrounded by the Vietcong. One by one the Marines were killed and Lieutenant Gideon was shot in the head and killed. The Marines were unable to get out and the area was mined and booby-trapped.
For the next year the Marines at Con Thien were pinned down and under constant attack. The village was not captured for another year.
The Con Thien operation was one of the most difficult and controversial operations the US Marines have ever undertaken. In the end, though, they were successful. The operation at Con Thien was the first US operation that made extensive use of the new US 'aerial mine clearance system', which used helicopters to carry out the clearance of mines. The loss of the helicopter and the difficulty of getting the Marines out of the area were a warning of the dangers of using helicopters for operations in difficult terrain.

Banksia violacea grows in a range of habitats in south-western Western Australia. It grows in sandy-clay, sandy-loam and clay soils. It grows in well-drained soils. It grows in mallee, woodland, shrubland and heathland. It grows on sandy soils near the base of granite outcrops.
The species epithet violacea means violet and refers to the flowers.
The main threat to the species is probably fire, although it is also threatened by agriculture and clearing.
Banksia violacea can be propagated from seed or cuttings. Cuttings should be taken from healthy, mature plants in spring. Seeds can be collected in late summer and autumn.
Banksia violacea is a good species for the garden. The flowers are attractive and the plant is reasonably hardy. It is also reasonably fast growing and should not be difficult to establish.
The species was first formally described by Carl Meissner in 1849 in Hooker’s Journal of Botany and Kew Garden Miscellany. The type specimen was collected by John Gould near the Gingin River in Western Australia by James Drummond.

In the 1945 election , the Communists were unopposed because the other parties abstained . Once in power , the Communists intro

ded a number of reforms . They all aimed at reducing the power of the bureaucratic elite . They introduced a system of private industry , and sought to abolish all remaining feudal rights . While some of the Soviet Union 's Asian satellites were ruled by single-party communist states , Vietnam was ruled by a coalition of nationalist and communist parties . The nationalists were led by Ho Chi Minh . The Communists were led by Vo Nguyen Giap . The coalition was known as the Democratic Republic of Vietnam , or the DRV . In 1956 , the Communists attempted a coup d ' etat against the nationalists . However , the coup failed , and the nationalists continued to rule the country . In 1957 , they renamed their country to the Socialist Republic of Vietnam . In the 1950 s , the United States began to fear that the Soviets were gaining too much influence in Vietnam . They funded the South Vietnamese army and the Vietnamese nationalists . The fighting in the south became so intense that the DRV decided to invade the south in 1965 . This became known as the Tet Offensive . The DRV was quickly defeated , and the war escalated . Nevertheless , the Vietcong continued to fight against the government in the south . The United States became involved in the war , and sent 500,000 soldiers to the Vietnamese countryside . In 1968 , the North Vietnamese launched the Tet Offensive II . In the south , the DRV forces made minor gains . However , they suffered heavy casualties . On the other hand , the Vietcong forces were more successful . They inflicted heavy casualties on the South Vietnamese army . In 1969 , the United States began to withdraw its troops from Vietnam . The South Vietnamese army was defeated in 1973 . In 1974 , the United States withdrew its remaining 40,000 soldiers from Vietnam . In 1975 , the DRV invaded the south . The north took Saigon in 1975 . The DRV became the Socialist Republic of Vietnam . The war cost the United States sixteen billion dollars and cost both sides hundreds of thousands of soldiers . The war ended in 1975 with the DRV taking power .
On the one hand , the Vietcong, the DRV, and the United States all fought for their political ideals . The Vietcong and the DRV fought for communism . They wanted to spread their political ideology throughout the world . The United States fought to preserve the status quo , and to prevent the spread of communism . On the other hand , the United States and the DRV both fought to maintain their political power . The United States was fighting to preserve its political power in Vietnam . The DRV was fighting to unify Vietnam under one communist government . Nevertheless , the war was a failure for the United States . While they did not lose the war, they did fail to achieve their political and military goals . The United States did not achieve democracy , and it did not prevent the spread of communism . Nevertheless , the North Vietnamese did achieve their goal of uniting Vietnam under one communist state .
The war had significant negative effects on both sides . However , the United States suffered the most . The war was hugely expensive . The United States spent sixteen billion dollars on the war . The war also had a highly negative impact on the American economy . The war created inflation , and caused the U.S. dollar to depreciate . As a result , the United States had to increase its national debt . However , the war had a negative impact on the Vietnamese economy as well . The war destroyed Vietnam's infrastructure . As a result , the war devastated the Vietnamese economy . Nevertheless , the Vietnamese economy recovered from the effects of the war .

period.

## Construction

The Derfflinger was built by the Kaiserliche Werft Kiel (Imperial Shipyard, Kiel) starting in 1913. She was named after Karl Friedrich von der Marwitz, leader of the "Freikorps der 180000" (Free Corps of the 18,000) which was the first German unit to enter Berlin on 22 November 1918, and which placed the Kaiser under house arrest.

## Service history

Her successful career was interrupted when during the Battle of Jutland she was badly damaged by British fire. She was repaired at the end of the war, and recommissioned in 1919. The ship was used as an accommodation ship after the war. In 1923, she was towed to the German Navy's base at Lorient on the west coast of France.

### Interwar

In 1922, the German Navy, now renamed the Reichsmarine, renamed the ship to Lützow, after Otto von Lützow, a famous naval hero during the Napoleonic Wars. In 1934, the ship was renamed again to Thüringen. In 1938, the ship was converted to a training ship for naval cadets and renamed Horst Wessel.

### World War II

Main article: Naval activity in the Baltic during World War II

The Horst Wessel in the port of Memel, 1941

On 19 October 1944, the Horst Wessel was commissioned as a flak ship in the Baltic Sea. On 31 October, she was attacked by Soviet torpedo boats, but the attackers were driven off by the Horst Wessel's 105mm guns and AA guns. On 21 January 1945, a Soviet submarine attacked the Horst Wessel, but the submarine was driven off by the ship's guns.

On 24 January 1945, the Horst Wessel was sailing from Kiel to Pillau when she was attacked by a Royal Air Force bomber. The ship was so badly damaged that she was sunk by her own crew. The ship was salvaged by the Soviet Navy and renamed the Projekt 20 (Проект 20) on 11 April 1945. She was refitted at the Baltiysky Zavod in Leningrad, and commissioned on 22 August 1945.

### Soviet Navy

The ship was refitted at the Baltiysky Zavod in Leningrad, and commissioned on 22 August 1945. She was renamed the Volkhov (Волхов) on 17 October 1945, and the Molotov (Молотов) on 19 February 1946. She was renamed Peoples Volunteer Guard (Народный Восток) on 19 March 1948. The ship was decommissioned on 15 July 1950.

In 1837, Spon made a series of 24 drawings of the cathedral and surrounding area for his friend James Bremner .
In 1838, Spon made a series of twelve watercolour views of the cathedral and its environs .
In 1854, Spon made a series of four drawings of the cathedral and surrounding area . In 1855, he made a further series of six drawings of the surrounding area .
Spon was the author of a number of works of local history.
Spon's contemporary, James Bremner , was impressed by Spon's drawings of Elgin.

## Aftermath

The government of Vietnam was criticised by the United States and the European Union . The European Union called for an independent investigation into the incident . The United States Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said that the United States was "deeply concerned" about the incident . The US State Department issued a statement saying that the recent Vietnamese government actions "raise concerns about Vietnam's commitment to respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms, including freedom of assembly and freedom of expression." The State Department also said that "the rights of all Vietnamese citizens to peacefully assemble and express their views, as well as other internationally accepted human rights and fundamental freedoms, must be respected."

The government of Vietnam issued a statement saying that the protesters had "defied the law" and "deliberately violated social order and discipline" . The government also said that the protesters had "forcibly attacked and injured a number of police officers and soldiers", and that the use of force by the police was "necessary".

## Plot summary

The novel takes place in the 18th century, more particularly in the last quarter of it. The narrative begins with the arrival of a 16-year-old boy, Damodar, on the streets of Thane. He is brought up by a low-ranking police officer, Sartaj, whose wife, Jijabai, takes pity on him. Jijabai's father is Shivaji's prime minister, Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath, a powerful figure in the Maratha Empire.

Damodar grows to manhood and becomes a devotee of Ramakrishna and Vithoba, as well as a devout Muslim. He becomes both an accomplished guitarist and an incisive critic of political and social institutions, and the novel is a series of meetings between Damodar, Sartaj and Jijabai, and the many people he meets and encounters with, among whom are the Peshwa himself and the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Damodar's interpretations are pessimistic, and he is an uncompromising critic of social and political injustice, in particular the subjugation of women and the oppression of the poor.

Truth in Numbers ? Everything , According to Wikipedia , an American documentary film , explores the history and cultural impli

cations of Wikipedia , the online encyclopedia that has been called " the largest and most popular general reference work ever compiled by human beings " by The New York Times . The film depicts Wikipedia's early history , beginning with its inception in 2001 , its growth to an estimated 17 million articles in over 250 languages , and the increasing controversy surrounding it. In 2007 , the Wikimedia Foundation , the nonprofit organization that operates Wikipedia , received its first major grant of $1.3 million , which sparked accusations from some that Wikipedia has become a " propaganda machine " . The film also looks at how Wikipedia is viewed in the academic community and how it is used to edit Wikipedia articles. The documentary , which was directed by Seth D. Michaels and produced by Andrew Denton , premiered at the 2011 Tribeca Film Festival on April 26 , 2011 , and was released on iTunes and Amazon.com on April 29 , 2011. The film was released on DVD on August 24 , 2011.

 Truth in Numbers ? Everything , According to Wikipedia 

## Synopsis

The film shows the history of the development of Wikipedia , including the origins of the project , the funding , and the editing . It also discusses the role of the community , and the criticism that it has received. It includes interviews with Jimmy Wales , the founder of Wikipedia ; Larry Sanger , the co-founder and former chief editor of Wikipedia; David Weinberger , the author of Everything Is Miscellaneous: The Power of the New Digital Disorder ; John Seely Brown , the author of The Power of Pull: How Small Moves, Smartly Made, Can Set Big Things in Motion ; and others.

Emily's father, Nigel appears in 2010, and turns out to be the killer. Nigel tries to set up Jamie for the murder, but Jamie again survives and he and Emily finally get together.

Emily is seen a few times in 2011, as she has moved to the United States.

The Patriarchal Cathedral features a triple apse , the central part of which matches the apse of the original basilica on the s

lopes of the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem. The church is rectangular in shape, with a square-shaped sanctuary (4.27 meters) and a flat roof.
The church does not contain a dome, but is topped with a cupola (4.27 meters in diameter and 12.65 meters high). The cupola is decorated with 16 windows. The exterior of the church is predominantly white with a few isolated spots of blue. The windows are adorned with 164 stones in the shape of a cross. The style of the church is reminiscent of the churches of the Hagia Sophia and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.
 The Patriarchal Cathedral is situated in the compound of the Moscow Kremlin in the Moscow's Red Square. The cathedral stands on Ivanovskaya Square. The Patriarchal Cathedral was consecrated on November 26, 1656, at the Dormition Day, by Patriarch Nikon of Moscow. 

## History

 The first cathedral on the site was built in 1451. The cathedral was constructed in the Byzantine style. The cathedral was destroyed in 1547 and rebuilt in the following year. After the Russian conquest of Kazan in 1552, the cathedral was rebuilt and turned to a mosque. The cathedral was converted to a Russian Orthodox Church in 1561, with the name Church of Our Lady of Kazan. The church was again rebuilt in 1631, and then in 1645. In 1654, the cathedral was rebuilt and the bells were added. The cathedral was consecrated in 1656.

The cathedral is located on the place of the first Moscow kremlin Church of Our Lady of Kazan (Russian: Церковь Богоматери Казанской в Кремле) (1451–1547). It was the largest Russian Orthodox cathedral in Moscow and one of the largest in Europe. The 1532 fire destroyed the church, and it was rebuilt. In 1551, it was converted to a mosque. It was converted into a Russian Orthodox Church in 1561, with the name Church of Our Lady of Kazan (Russian: Церковь Богоматери Казанской).

The cathedral was rebuilt in 1631, and again in 1645. In 1654, the cathedral was rebuilt and the bells were added, and in 1656 it was consecrated.

The Patriarchal Cathedral was consecrated on November 26, 1656, at the Dormition Day, by Patriarch Nikon of Moscow.

## Interior

The main altar was decorated with a large iconostasis. Above the altar was a great icon of the Mother of God, the iconostasis was adorned with 36 icons of saints and the icon of the Mother of God, covered with silver, gold, and precious stones. The walls of the cathedral were adorned with icons. The interior was decorated with carvings. The cathedral was adorned with 164 stones in the shape of a cross on the windows.

The Blackburn B @-@ 48 Firecrest , given the SBAC designation YA.1 , was a single @-@ engine naval strike fighter built by Blac

-burn Aircraft between 1943 and 1946. It was the first British jet fighter to be produced in quantity.
In 1945, the Italian manufacturer Fiat began to produce the B @-@ 48 under licence as the Fiat G.80 , but it remained a minor production aircraft. During the war, 26 were produced in Italy.
The first prototype B @-@ 48, RR.188, was powered by a Bristol Centaurus, but the Centaurus had a very high fuel consumption and the prototype was re-engined with a Rolls-Royce Derwent V. The Derwent was also not suitable as it suffered from frequent engine failures.
In early 1945, a prototype YA.1 was fitted with a Rolls-Royce Griffon 83. This engine proved to be more reliable than the Derwent, and the YA.2 and YA.3 production aircraft used the Griffon 83. The Griffon 83-powered YA.2 and YA.3 were the only production variants to be fitted with a bulged fuselage, due to a change in the wing planform and rudder shape. Later production aircraft had a more streamlined fuselage.
The Blackburn B @-@ 48 was the first jet fighter produced in large numbers by the British. The Royal Navy ordered 160 examples, plus 250 Sapphire trainer aircraft. The Royal Air Force ordered 210. The Blackburn was the only jet fighter available to the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force in the immediate postwar period until the de Havilland DH.100 Sea Vampire became available.
The Royal Navy began to receive B @-@ 48s in May 1946 and the RAF in September 1946. The B @-@ 48 was later joined by the Gloster Meteor and the de Havilland Sea Vampire in the RAF and Royal Navy. The B @-@ 48 was operated by No. 602, 603 and 604 Naval Air Squadrons and No. 1307 and 1308 Naval Air Squadrons.
The RAF operated the B @-@ 48 until 1952, followed by the Royal Navy until 1953. The B @-@ 48s from Royal Navy, Royal Air Force and Royal Auxiliary Air Force squadrons were commonly used for photo reconnaissance.
The Blackburn B @-@ 48 was exported to the Indian Air Force.
The Blackburn B @-@ 48 was powered by the Rolls-Royce Griffon 83 or 85. The Griffon was a liquid cooled, 18-cylinder, supercharged, all-aluminium radial engine, rated at 4,035 hp (3,005 kW) for take-off. The engine drove a three-bladed, constant-speed propeller through a reduction gearbox.
The B @-@ 48 could fly at a speed of 478 mph (770 km/h) at 18,000 ft (5,500 m). The service ceiling was 38,000 ft (11,580 m). The B @-@ 48 had a range of 522 nm (598 mi, 963 km).
The B @-@ 48 could climb to 10,000 ft (3,048 m) in 4 minutes 15 seconds. The aircraft had a maximum ferry range of 615 nm (706 mi, 1,137 km).
The B @-@ 48 had an endurance of 1 hour 50 minutes at 18,000 ft (5,500 m).
The B @-@ 48 had a wing span of 36 ft 7 in (11.16 m), a length of 33 ft 2 in (10.11 m) and a height of 14 ft 6 in (4.42 m). The dry weight was 13,408 lb (6,123 kg) and the maximum take-off weight was 17,050 lb (7,735 kg).

Tessa became involved in a love triangle with British Egyptologist Howard Carter and his wife, Lady Evelyn Herbert. Tessa and Evelyn became close friends, but Tessa fell in love with Howard, whom she described as "a wonderful man". Tessa and Howard had an affair, and in 1923 she became pregnant with his child. Howard wanted to marry Tessa, but Evelyn would not allow him to divorce her. Tessa's pregnancy ended in a miscarriage.
In 1925 , Tessa left Howard and returned to England , where she died a year later.
Wheeler was married for a third time in 1929 to Mary Layard , the daughter of the archaeologist Sir Austen Henry Layard . Mary was a qualified archaeologist , and the pair worked together on excavations in Greece and Cyprus. During the Second World War , Wheeler led the British School of Archaeology in Jerusalem , and the pair travelled together in Egypt and Mesopotamia . Mary died in 1975 .
During World War II , Wheeler was dispatched to Egypt to try to salvage as many British relics as possible. During his time in Egypt , he discovered the tomb of Amenhotep II .
In 1952 , Wheeler retired from his position as Director of the British School of Archaeology in Jerusalem . He died on 15 March 1966, after a short illness, at his home in Sussex . His funeral was held at St Margaret's Church in Rottingdean .

His use of data-collection and reporting methods in archaeology has largely defined the discipline.

Sir Curtis Gregory Riley Mackay was a British archaeologist. He was a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries and a member of the Royal Geographical Society.

In 1795 , François Alexandre Frédéric visited Spanish Hill while en route to Canada . He described the hill as " a mountain in

the shape of a sugar loaf, covered with a thick wood crowned with a square fort , where the Spaniards once placed one of their principal posts , in the way of the fur trade ." No trace of the fort remains today. It is now known that the fort was built in the 1600s by the French to protect their fur trade with the Algonquin people.
In 1800 the fort was taken over by the British. Fort Masson was a very important part of the defence of the Rupert's Land region, which was part of British North America until 1870. It was also a waypoint for explorers and traders going to the West.
In 1796 , Alexander Mackenzie built a small fort on the other side of the river from Fort Masson. It was called Fort Fork . Mackenzie called the area " the Forks of the River " , and this is how Winnipeg was named.
In 1799, John Ballantyne wrote that " Fort Fork is situated 22 miles above Fort Masson on the north or right bank of the River, and is about a mile above the confluence of the Red River with the Assiniboine, which is about 100 miles from Fort Dauphin ."
In 1818, Scottish fur trader Simon Fraser also passed by Fort Masson and Fort Fork when he explored the headwaters of the Fraser River in British Columbia .
Fort Masson is now a Provincial Heritage Site and is located in the heart of The Forks National Historic Site.
Sources: "The Province of Manitoba", by John A. FitzGibbon, 1906, pp. 156-57; "The Upper Red River Settlement," by John Ballantyne, 1819, p. 31.

Charles Cardell ( 1892 – 1977 ) was the founder of a Pagan Witchcraft tradition that rivalled that of Gerald Gardner 's in sout

heastern England in the 1950s.
He was born in Liverpool, and worked as a barber. He was one of the earliest initiates of Gardner's Wica in 1939 and was Gardner's first High Priest. He was influential in the establishment of the Gardnerian tradition, and also the Cochranian and Alexandrian traditions. He was also an occultist of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn.
He was also a founding member of the Fellowship of Isis, and later became one of the founders of the Chthonian Order, a school of Wicca, which he founded with fellow Gardnerian High Priestess and author Doreen Valiente.
Cardell died in 1977.
He is author of:
The Witches' Bible.
The Magical Philosophy of the Western Mystery Tradition.
The Magical Path.

Jane Guildford was born on 22 August 1508 or 1509 as the daughter of Henry Guildford and his wife Anne Conyers . Her father was one of the great nobles of the North and had the title Earl of Surrey . He was the son of the head of the earldom, Thomas Guildford , and his wife, the heiress of the barony of Rothley, Alice Neville , the granddaughter of William Neville , 1st Earl of Salisbury . Jane's mother, Anne, was the daughter of Thomas Conyers , Lord Conyers , and Elizabeth Percy , 8th Baroness Percy .
Jane's father had been sent to the Tower by Henry VIII in 1536 for having supported the Pilgrimage of Grace and remained in the Tower until his execution in 1537 .
Jane's paternal grandfather was Sir Edward Guildford , the younger son of Thomas Guildford and his wife Elizabeth FitzHugh . Sir Edward married Alice Cockayne . Their daughter Jane was the mother of Jane Guildford.
Jane's maternal grandfather was Sir Thomas Conyers , the son of Sir Richard Conyers of Horden and his wife Jane de Vaux .
Jane's maternal grandmother was Elizabeth Percy , the daughter of Thomas Percy, 7th Earl of Worcester and his wife Elizabeth FitzHugh .

1538 – 1547: Tenant lady
In 1538, Jane became Countess of Northumberland on the death of her father-in-law , John Dudley (the son of Edmund Dudley ).
Jane and her husband, John, were both strongly in favor of the Protestant Reformation . Jane and her husband were a controversial couple. In 1535, she accompanied her husband to Calais to make a speech to the Protestant lords. And in 1539, she and her husband were excluded from the English court for a while because they had forbidden their daughters to join the household of the Queen, Katharina Parr .
Jane and her husband became strong supporters of Edward VI . In 1547, Jane and her husband were arrested for high treason and for having supported Princess Elizabeth . They were released in 1549, but they were forced to go into exile until they were recalled in 1553 .
1547 – 1553: Widow of Edward Seymour
On 22 August 1547, the day of Jane's birthday , her husband, John Dudley, died. She was appointed to the widowhood of Edward Seymour, 1st Duke of Somerset in 1547 .

Aretusa was laid down at the Cantiere navale fratelli Orlando ( Orlando Brothers ' Shipyard ) in Livorno on 1 June 1889 , and w

ass launched on 22 August 1890 . She was then completed in January 1891 .

She was named after Aretusa , the mythological nymph and river in Syracuse .

She was built for the Società di navigazione a vapore ( S.N.V. , Steam Navigation Company ) and originally served the Naples – Palermo – Genoa route.

In 1901, she was acquired by the Lloyd Austriaco di Navigazione ( Austrian Lloyd Line ) and in 1902 she was transferred to the Vienna – Istanbul – Port Said – Genoa line.

### Austrian Lloyd

In 1906, she was transferred to the Trieste – Istanbul – Port Said – Naples – New York line.

### Second World War

She was requisitioned by the Italian Regia Marina ( Royal Navy ) and converted to a troopship , and served in the Mediterranean.

She was transferred to the Armistice Commission in December 1945 , and was scrapped in 1949 in Livorno.

## Biography

Toirdelbach succeeded his brother Domnall as King of Meath from 1052 to 1066 . His brother's death was to be avenged by his sons who would rule in Meath for thirty years from 1066 to 1094 . In 1052 , Toirdelbach married the widow of his brother, Bé Binn, daughter of Donnchad mac Briain, King of Munster .

In 1067 , he was involved in the Battle of Moyry Pass, a failed attempt to drive the English out of Ireland . In 1075 , Toirdelbach drove Gofraid from the kingship and Ireland itself . There is uncertainty concerning the circumstances of his death, which might have occurred in 1086 , 1087 , or 1088 .

## Family

* Mael Sechlainn mac Toirrdelbach Ua Briain (died 1121)

Toirdelbach was succeeded by his son Mael Sechlainn.

LONG AND HONOURABLE SERVICE
Ex-Sergeant W. H. Weir
A well known resident of Stuart Park, Mr. Wm. Henry Weir, who has been very ill for some time, died in hospital on Monday last. The late Mr. Weir was born in England, and enlisted in the South Australian Volunteer Militia in 1885. He served in the South African war and was stationed at Pretoria for four years, returning to Adelaide in 1900. He was a member of the South Australian Mounted Infantry for twenty years, and during the last war he enlisted in the A. I. F. in 1915, seeing active service at Gallipoli and France. On account of illness he was invalided home in 1916, and on his return he settled at Stuart Park, where for the past twenty-seven years he was employed on the railway. For some time he was a member of the Stuart Park State School committee. The late Mr. Weir leaves a widow, three sons, and a daughter. A service was held at the Stuart Park Church of England on Wednesday afternoon, and the remains were interred in the Port Pirie cemetery.

Hellblazer boosted the popularity and image of the occult detective fiction genre and shaped it to its modern form . Many moder

ately successful occult detective authors, such as Simon R. Green and Tim Pratt, have cited Hellblazer as an influence.  The series has been called "the greatest comic book ever published",  and "the most literate and sophisticated"  comic book to be published in the 1980s.
The magical elements of Hellblazer have been compared to those of the Seventies occult detective fiction novels of John Constantine's creator, urban fantasy writer John Niles. The character of Constantine has been compared to those of many other occult detectives, such as Harry Potter, the Doctor, Swamp Thing, Hellboy, and Alan Moore's characters Zatanna and The Demon.  And Constantine has been compared to occult detectives en masse, with the comparison of the character to the occult detectives of the 1980s being cited as a reason for the genre's resurgence in the 21st century. The Good Terrorist is a novel by the British author, journalist and peace activist Doris Lessing. It tells the story of a group of anarchist terrorists in London who are attempting to overthrow the British government. The principal characters are an American woman (Elena) and her lover (Kelman), the latter a British anarchist.
The book was highly controversial at the time of its publication, with some readers and critics deeming it a disguised confession of Lessing's own beliefs and subsequent activities; others, on the other hand, considered the book to be a thinly disguised critique of the British government.
The novel was adapted into a 1988 British movie of the same name, starring Jodhi May as Elena, Rufus Sewell as Kelman, and Adrian Dunbar as Llewellyn. In 2000 it was adapted as an opera by the composer Philip Glass and the librettist Christopher Hampton. In 2006, the book was the focus of a critical essay by novelist Jonathan Lethem in The New Yorker.

Alkan was a virtuoso pianist and composer . His piano compositions are among the most difficult to perform. Alkan's compositions are noted for their harmonic complexity and emotional intensity. ### Personal life

Alkan was a friend of the pianist Sigismond Thalberg. He was also a friend of the composer Hector Berlioz , with whom he had a falling out in 1839. Alkan was also a friend of the pianist Charles-Valentin Alkan , whom he had once tutored.

### London of 1858

It is reported that Alkan was in London at this time. During his visit to England, he is said to have accommodated himself in the "Britannia Hotel" in Oxford Street , where he spent some time in his room, being only seen in the street. One morning, however, the door was found shut, and on entering the room, the window was found open, and the piano (upon which stood a decanter of brandy), the window, and the piano-stool removed. The "Times of London" published a paragraph on the unfortunate occurrence. It was then supposed that Alkan had committed suicide, although the supposition was denied by his friends. There is little doubt, however, that he fell over a wall on the street, and was killed.

After ending his work at Verulamium , Wheeler turned his attention to the late Iron Age hill @-@ fort of Maidan Castle near to

the town of Launceston in Cornwall and to the late Iron Age enclosure of Tintagel Castle on the north Cornish coast. It was at these sites that he revised his view of the Iron Age, which he had previously characterized as a period of stagnation. He argued that the Iron Age was an era of rapid change and that the Iron Age landscape was a complex one.

The Dartmoor Project, as Wheeler called it, consisted of surveying and excavating in 4683 square miles of Dartmoor, Devon, England. This was the largest survey and excavation project in the United Kingdom up to that time. The results of this project were published in the series Dartmoor Excavations. It was also the first systematic excavation of a prehistoric site in the United Kingdom.

### 1920s

In the 1920s Wheeler's work on the Iron Age enclosure of Tintagel Castle and the late Iron Age hill fort Maidan Castle made him rethink his view of Iron Age Britain as a period of stagnation. In his reports on Tintagel he argued that the site was occupied in the Roman period, something that had previously been thought impossible. In his report on Maidan Castle, Wheeler argued that Iron Age Britain had been a period of rapid change.

### 1930s

In 1932 Wheeler published The Archaeology of Roman Britain. This was his first major work on the Roman period and was based on the work of the Dartmoor Project. The book proved popular and is still in print. It was, however, the subject of much criticism.

In 1935, Wheeler was appointed as the first County Archaeologist of Cornwall. He held this post until 1945.

### 1940s

In 1940, Wheeler was appointed as the Director of the British School at Rome. He held this post until 1948.

### 1950s

In 1951, Wheeler was appointed as the first Director of the British Academy. He held this post until 1958.

### 1960s

In 1966, Wheeler was appointed as the Vice-Chancellor of the University of London. He held this post until 1969.

## Personal life

In 1920, Wheeler married Dorothy Longstaff. They were married until Dorothy's death in 1969.

## Legacy

The archaeological sites that Wheeler worked on are still popular tourist attractions. Tintagel Castle is owned by English Heritage and is one of the most popular archaeological sites in the United Kingdom. Maidan Castle is owned by the National Trust and also remains popular.

The name Mogadishu is derived from the Arabic expression "The city of Islam" or "the city of peace" .
The earliest written record of the name Mogadishu is found in the 13th-century writings of Arab geographers and historians Ibn Sa'id, al-Idrisi and al-Umari . These suggest that the name  Mogadishu was originally applied to a village or small town on the coast of the Indian Ocean .
In addition, the earliest known written record of Mogadishu is a 14th-century letter written by the Venetian explorer Marco Polo , who wrote about Mogadishu in 1293 in his book The Travels of Marco Polo . In this account, Marco Polo described Mogadishu's port as being "the greatest and most important of all the ports of the Indian Ocean".
In the early 16th century, the city was visited by the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama , who described the city in his book The Book of the Conquest of the Canary Islands and the Overseas. According to da Gama, the Somali leader of the city, the Sultan of Mogadishu, was an ally of the king of Portugal. Da Gama named the city Mansa Mogadishu , meaning "King of Mogadishu".
In 1846, the first British consul to Mogadishu was appointed by the British government .
During the Turks and the Omani era, Mogadishu prospered as a trading port. The city was an important centre for the Arabian slave trade , with the slave trade continuing into the colonial period . In 1905, a British steamer called the SS Salumbar collided with a small Somali vessel and sank off the coast of Mogadishu, killing 130 Somalis .
During the colonial era, the Italians bombed Mogadishu in 1925 in a failed attempt to capture the city from the British-controlled Somaliland .
In 1928, the city became part of the British-administered Somaliland Protectorate .
In 1960, the city and the Somaliland Protectorate became independent from Britain. Mogadishu became the capital of the new state of Somalia.

The regiment was formed in the aftermath of the First World War to restore cavalry regiments to their pre-war establishments and was classified as a yeomanry regiment . In 1939, the regiment was mobilised for service in the Second World War and trained for the role of armored reconnaissance as part of the 5th Armoured Brigade. During the war they served in North Africa initially as part of the 7th Armoured Division and later as part of the 22nd Armoured Brigade.

## Aston Villa

### Football

Aston Villa are a professional association football club based in Aston, Birmingham, England, that plays in the Championship, the second tier of the English football league system. Founded in 1874, they have played at their home ground, Villa Park, since 1897. They were the first football club in the world to become a limited company, in 1897.

Villa have had a long-standing rivalry with Birmingham City, and a more recent rivalry with West Bromwich Albion. The club's traditional kit colours are claret shirts, sky blue shorts, and white socks. The team's anthem is "Glory, Glory Villa" and the club's mascot is a bull terrier named Jack, who is a reference to the club crest.

Villa have won the League Championship seven times (the most recent in 1981), the FA Cup seven times, the Football League Cup five times and the Football League Second Division once. The club has a long-standing affiliation with German club 1. FC Köln, and have a number of players and coaches who have been loaned to the club.

The Altar of the Kings was also the work of Jerónimo Balbás , in Mexican Baroque or Churrigueresque style . It was begun in 171

5, and finished by Balbás himself in 1725, but it was not until 1767 that the sculpture of the bas-reliefs was finished.

The Altar of the Kings is a monumental work of art, of the highest level of the Churrigueresque style . It is considered the most important work of the architect and sculptor Jerónimo Balbás in the city.

## The altar

The altarpiece is a monumental work, 6.75 m high and 11.50 m wide. The altar is made of walnut and crystals, and has a large central tabernacle with the image of the Virgen del Rosario, protector of the city, and a large sculpture of a Crowned Christ (Virgen del Rosario) and the Kings of the East.

In the altarpiece are depicted the twelve apostles, the Virgin Mary, the Christ Child, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Saint James the Greater, Saint James the Minor, Saint Jerome, Saint Thomas, Saint Stephen, Saint Anthony of Padua, Saint Anthony of Egypt, Saint Augustine, Saint Bernadette, Saint Francis of Assisi, Saint John the Evangelist, Saint Matthew, Saint Mark, Saint Luke, Saint Thomas, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Joseph, Saint Peter, Saint John the Evangelist, Saint James the Greater, Saint John the Major, Saint John the Minor, Saint Anthony of Padua, Saint Anthony of Egypt, and Saint Peter.

The bas-reliefs are made of limestone and were sculpted by Manuel de Cabo and Pedro Ortega.

The base of the altar has a sculpture of the Virgin of the Rosary, flanked by the Kings of the East, and topped with the image of the Virgin of the Purification, patron saint of the city.

In the main door of the altar there is a sculpture of the Crucifixion.

Owing to the abrupt nature of Abby 's development on August 7 , residents had little time to prepare for the storm . According

to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) , Abby made landfall in North Carolina as a Category 1 hurricane. Abby weakened to a tropical storm, then transitioned to a post-tropical cyclone, before it made landfall in Maryland.
  Abby killed 78 people, damaged or destroyed 2,440,598 homes and businesses, and caused $ 20.5 billion in damages (in 2018 dollars). Although this figure is below the normal threshold for a Category 1 hurricane, it is still above the 1980 1985 average of $ 15.5 billion.

On August 6, a tropical depression formed off the coast of North Carolina. It moved northward and became a tropical storm, with the name Abby, on August 7. The storm moved parallel to the coast of the Carolinas during the day of August 7, before making landfall in New Hanover County, North Carolina, at around 18:00 UTC that same day. The storm moved inland and made landfall in Carteret County, North Carolina, at around 20:00 UTC. Abby was then downgraded to a tropical depression, and further weakened to a remnant low on August 9.

Abby was the first tropical cyclone to form in the Atlantic Basin during the 1980 1985 season.

## Preparations

The North Carolina Department of Transportation closed the Cape Fear Memorial Bridge on August 7 to all traffic to conduct bridge repairs.

## Impact

See also: List of North Carolina hurricanes (1980–present) § Abby

Hurricane Abby caused almost $ 20 billion in damages (in 2018 dollars). The effects of the storm were felt in many areas of the Atlantic Coast, the Gulf Coast, and Central Florida.

### North Carolina

Upon making landfall, the hurricane damaged or destroyed 55 homes in North Carolina.

Wind damage in the Outer Banks left 95% of the houses damaged or destroyed. Damage was evaluated at $158 million in 1985 dollars. A total of $332 million in damages was reported.

The storm caused seven deaths in North Carolina.

### South Carolina

In South Carolina, the storm caused six deaths.

### Florida

In Florida, the storm killed five people.

On the coast of Côte d 'Ivoire , Scully sits in her tent studying detailed photographs of the spacecraft half @-@ buried on the

beach . She has been living here for the past three months , waiting for the opportunity to take samples . During this time , she has been accompanied by a small team of scientists , a photographer and a television crew . The area is situated near the village of Sassandra on the Atlantic coast of Côte d'Ivoire . The ship is the size of a soccer field and is covered in a thick layer of sand . It was discovered by a fisherman who was diving to find a sunken canoe near the village of Azaguié . The initial investigation by a French team of archaeologists and marine engineers has failed to determine the true origin of the ship . The photographs show the outline of a ship with an oval hull and a tall superstructure . In addition , there are also traces of a large wooden wheel and the lower part of a mast .
 Flat-bottomed ships were developed in the Mediterranean in ancient times and used to transport olive oil and wine . These vessels were capable of sailing in the open sea . The discovery of a ship of this kind in Côte d'Ivoire is an intriguing finding . Further investigations are now under way to try to determine the age of the ship and if it had been involved in trade .
  Shipwreck hunters do not only find old wrecks in shallow waters , but also in the deep ocean . A deep-sea vessel is usually located on the seabed in 2000 meters of water or more . It is covered with sediment and often barely visible . Even though there are now machines that can map the sea floor , the location of a shipwreck is often found by chance . In 2017 , a team of divers discovered what is thought to be the oldest shipwreck in the world in a Turkish bay . The ship , which was built in the 2nd century BC , was loaded with gold and silver when it sank . The divers discovered the remains in the Marmara Sea . The ship was probably transporting cargo between the Black Sea and the Aegean Sea .
In the 1820s , a new account of the Biddenden Maids was published , which claimed that a gravestone marked with a diagonal line

in the middle was the actual grave of the sisters. The tale was popularized in the 1850s by the Reverend John Cobb , a clergyman in Kent , who offered a £100 prize for anyone who could prove the story was untrue. Cobb claimed that the story was false because it was impossible for the sisters to be twins, as they were born in different years. The claim was based on a 1779 census of the town.
In 1947 , the descendants of the Biddenden Maids were contacted about a film that was being made about the mysterious sisters, and an investigation was launched into the provenance of the story and the validity of the claim. The descendants were successful in proving that the sisters were twins, and that the 1873 gravestone was not their grave at all. The gravestone that Cobb had claimed was their grave was in fact their parents' grave, and the actual gravestone is at the bottom of a ditch.
The investigation uncovered a number of discrepancies in the story, including the fact that the sisters were buried at St Mary's Church, and not St Augustine's, as had been previously claimed. The church has two sets of twins interred, and it is possible that the two sets of sisters were mixed up in the confusion over the story.
The sisters' grave was discovered and opened in 1949. A copy of the gravestone was made and placed in the Biddenden church, while the original was put in the church in Burwash. There were no markings on the gravestone, but its inscription was written out in modern handwriting. The gravestone was not even in the original church, but had been moved after the death of the sisters, by their parents, to the church in Burwash.

The mating season is the period when the most offspring are produced. The time when reproduction occurs is linked to the availability of food. In the northern hemisphere, the mating season is from May to August. In the southern hemisphere, it is from November to March .
Mating occurs when the female is in heat . Males seek out females and attempt to mate with them. The female uses her sharp claws to scratch the male and express her displeasure.
Gestation lasts 21 to 24 days. A litter includes 1 to 8 pups. Twins are common. The litter is born in a den and the pups are born blind and deaf. The mother nurses the young but later leaves them to fend for themselves.
The population of the Arctic tundra fox is declining . There is a growing demand for their pelts to make coats. The foxes are also hunted for sport by people in the Arctic.
The Arctic fox is a very social animal. It lives in a pack of 5 to 10 animals. These packs are made up of females and their young. Males live alone in a den during the winter months. They are nomadic and move about according to the season. They often live in loose packs. There is a hierarchy within the pack. The dominant female leads the pack and controls the males.
The Arctic fox is an omnivore . It feeds on berries, grasses, lichens, small mammals, carrion, and insects.
The Arctic fox has many predators including the golden eagle and the Arctic wolf .
The Arctic fox is important in the ecosystem. It helps to control the population of some small mammals.

The company 's men , a mixture of former French paratroopers , ex @-@ Foreign Legionnaires and young adventurers , had trouble

integrating into a " normal " Army unit.  Their training , under the command of Captain Pierre Meinertzhagen , was made difficult by the difficulties of the terrain and the climate. The desert , to the men of the company , was like a foreign continent.
Because of their poor knowledge of the North African terrain , many of the men of the company died of thirst or hunger after getting lost during long marches.  This situation was aggravated by the lack of leadership and the poor training of the men.
It was only after the 1940 defeat and the consequent disaster of the British and French armies, that the company was integrated into the British 11th Battalion of the Royal Scots.  In 1942, the men of the company were incorporated into the 1st Battalion of the 15th /19th Battalion of the KOSB, under the command of Lieutenant Colonel David Stirling, who became the founder of SAS.
After their first operations in Libya , the men of the company participated in the famous  Operation Flipper , which was the first sabotage operation of the SAS in the Axis territory of Italy .
The company of 10 men was dropped on a cliff overlooking a bridge on the road to Barga , near Ponte Nizza ( Tuscany ) .  The mission of the company was to destroy the bridge and the road for a period of 48 hours, so as to allow the advance of the Allied forces to be carried out easily.
The men of the company were to be dropped at 24,000 feet, but the parachutes opened too late and the men landed at 10,000 feet.  Two men were killed and two others injured.  The company commander, Captain Pierre Meinertzhagen , was injured and had difficulty landing safely.  He was eventually arrested by Italian soldiers.  Three men died of their injuries and the other eight were captured.
The men of the company were imprisoned in the town of Grosseto and after a few months in prison, were transferred to the prison of Regina Coeli , in Rome , where the Company Commander , Captain Pierre Meinertzhagen , was imprisoned.
The Company Commander and his men were taken out one by one and shot.  The date of execution was 13 May 1942.

## Design

See also: Type IIA submarine

The design for the 'A' class submarines was based on lessons learned from previous classes. The power plant was upgraded with a more powerful range of Vickers V12 diesel engines, and the electrical system was overhauled with a larger capacity battery and a more powerful generator.

The boats were 56-metres (183 ft 9 in) long, had a beam of 5.5 m (18 ft 1 in) and a draft of 3.7 m (12 ft 2 in). They displaced 649 long tons (659 t) on the surface and 807 long tons (820 t) submerged.

The 'A' class submarines had a crew of 44 officers and men. They had a diving depth of 100 feet (30.5 m) and could dive to a depth of 180 feet (55 m).

For surface running, the power plant consisted of two 600-brake-horsepower (447 kW) diesel engines and two 420-bhp (313 kW) electric motors. The submarines had a maximum surface speed of 13 knots (24 km/h; 15 mph) and a submerged speed of 9 knots (17 km/h; 10 mph). When submerged, they could operate for 50 nmi (93 km; 58 mi) at 4 knots (7.4 km/h; 4.6 mph).

The boats were armed with six 18-inch (460 mm) torpedo tubes and carried a total of 16 torpedoes.

In cool , moist areas ranging from 4 @,@ 800 feet ( 1 @,@ 500 m ) to 6 @,@ 800 feet ( 2 @,@ 100 m ) , Douglas fir is predominan

t. We have mapped an area of 117 s quare miles (304 s quare km ) , showing more than 1 ,000 ,000 acres (400 ,000 ha) of forest.
Much of this forest is on the slopes of volcanic mountains. Elevations range from 500 feet (150 m ) to 5 ,000 feet (1500 m) above sea level. The major volcanic areas are shown in the accompanying map.
 The climate is very moist and foggy. Average annual precipitation ranges from 100 inches (250 cm) at lower elevations to 220 inches (560 cm) at higher elevations.
This area is divided into 13 districts, of which all are within the area shown on the accompanying map.
The areas within the districts are indicated on the map by the numbers which refer to the map keys.
The district in which the majority of the Douglas fir is located is known as the Klamath District. This is an area of approximately 1 ,300 square miles (3400 square km) and includes most of the area covered by the map.
The elevations of the mountains are generally above 4 ,000 feet (1200 m) and the climate is characterized by cool summers and cold winters.
The district is divided into 6 management units.
In the western Klamath National Forest the Douglas fir is generally found in humid areas of the high altitude slopes of the Cascade mountains.
In the eastern Klamath National Forest, Douglas fir is found on the western slopes of the Siskiyou mountains.
Management units are indi cated by numbers which refer to the map keys.
We have evaluated the Douglas fir stands in terms of their production potential (as a source of commercial timber) and in terms of their environmental quality (as a source of environmental goods and services).
We evaluated the environmental quality by relating a stand's production potential to the number of acres that the stand provides for other uses.
The area east of Williams contains 436 ,000 acres (177 ,000 ha) of timberland but 250 ,000 acres (100 ,000 ha) of this land has been placed in the wilderness and off-limits to commercial timber production.
This leaves us with 186 ,000 acres (75 ,000 ha) of timberland in the eastern Klamath National Forest.
The area west of Williams contains 473 ,000 acres (191 ,000 ha) of timberland.
Two-thirds of this timberland has been designated as wilderness and is off-limits to commercial timber production.
This leaves us with only 150 ,000 acres (60 ,000 ha) of timberland in the western Klamath National Forest.
The 150 ,000 acres (60 ,000 ha) of timberland west of Williams is a very important source of commercial timber production for the Klamath National Forest.
The eastern Klamath National Forest contains 436 ,000 acres (177 ,000 ha) of timberland.
More than 250 ,000 acres (100 ,000 ha) of this timberland has been designated as wilderness and is off-limits to commercial timber production.
This leaves us with only 186 ,000 acres (75 ,000 ha) of timberland in the eastern Klamath National Forest.
Therefore, the eastern Klamath National Forest contains an important source of commercial timber production.
In 1990 , we evaluated 150 ,000 acres (60 ,000 ha) of timberland in the eastern Klamath National Forest in terms of its environmental quality.
In the eastern Klamath National Forest, the acreage of commercial timberland that has been designated as wilderness and off-limits to commercial timber production is roughly equal to the amount of commercial timberland that remains.
The remaining timberland in the eastern Klamath National Forest is a very important source of commercial timber production.

During the Song dynasty , the city of Bianjing had three enclosures : the outer city wall , the inner city wall , and the palac

elike inner enclosure. The three walls were connected with eight gates and were protected by a moat . The city wall had a circumference of about 6 kilometres (3.7 mi) and was about 7 metres (23 ft) tall and 10 metres (33 ft) thick. It took about 300,000 workers to build the city wall, and it was completed in 1121 . The city wall was renovated several times, and the total length of the city wall was 16.5 kilometres (10.3 mi).
 Bianjing was the capital of the Jin dynasty , and it is known as the "Southern Capital" because the capital of the Jurchen Jin dynasty was in Manchuria (in present-day northeastern China).
 The city wall of Bianjing was built during the reign of Emperor Huizong of Song .
 The city wall of Bianjing was destroyed in 1214 during the Mongol invasions of the Jin dynasty .

Normally, the British Royal Navy operated a policy of ' continuous at sea ' , whereby a fleet would remain at sea until a threat was no longer present. An exception was the base at Scapa Flow , where the fleet could be based securely, in the knowledge that the fleet would be safe from invasion or attack.
As it was, the British fleet in Scapa Flow was attacked by U-boats , and after the surrender of Germany , many of the ships were scuttled in the deep waters of the Scapa Flow.
The first British battleship to be laid down after the end of the naval arms race, HMS _Victory_ was completed in 1765.
She was built at a cost of £ 135,000, and was commissioned as flagship to the First Sea Lord, Admiral Sir John Jervis.
The ship served as flagship for the First Sea Lord until 1830, when her role was taken over by HMS _Cumberland_.
The ship was not considered obsolete until 1835, and she was used at the Battle of Lissa in 1811, under the command of Admiral Sir John Duckworth.
After being decommissioned in 1824, she was rebuilt into a training ship, and she served in this capacity until the start of the First World War.
HMS _Victory_ was converted into a first-class battleship in 1905, and she served in this capacity in the First World War.

## Plot

The game centers on the titular character, Gomez, who is a cube with a human-like face, arms and legs. Gomez is a typical child who resides in a small town with his parents and has a dog named Copper. Gomez finds his way to a magical book which transports him to a fantasy world that is based on his own town.

## Development

The game was originally intended to be a 2D side-scrolling game, with the player controlling Gomez as he moved through the 2D space. However, as he began working on the game, Fish wanted to make a game that was a 3D platformer that incorporated classic platformer mechanics. Fish is also known for his love of the Nintendo Entertainment System and other classic games.

During the development of the game, Fish did not want the game's soundtrack to be curated, with him wanting the game to have a soundtrack that was created from music recorded by the team working on the game. Fish also wanted to recreate the feeling of playing a classic platformer, with the game having new music being played when the player is entering a new area or once the player has passed a certain point in a level.

The game's initial development was funded by Fish and other members of the development team. During the development of the game, Fish was given help from several people who were interested in the game and helping out the development, with Fish giving the game's development to his team to help develop the game.

## Release

Fez began development in 2008. The prototype was first shown at the Penny Arcade Expo (PAX) 2008. The game was then shown at the PAX 2009 and PAX East 2011. During the development of the game, Fish had to take time to work at his day job, which was working as an animator for Cartoon Network. Fish also had to deal with his personal life, including having a child. The game was released in February 2012.

Fez was released on the PlayStation 4 and PlayStation Vita in May 2014, and on Microsoft Windows, Xbox One and Xbox 360 in October 2015. The game was released on macOS in July 2016.

The game was released on Nintendo Switch in September 2018.

Fez received "generally favorable reviews", according to review aggregator Metacritic.

Fez won the Grand Prize at the Independent Games Festival, as well as the Seumas McNally Grand Prize for Excellence in Story at the 2011 IGF Awards. It was also nominated for the Innovation Award at the 2011 IGF Awards.

A tropical disturbance persisted from November 18 to November 22, 1941. The weather remained non-tropical until December 1, when Hurricane Ione completed a transition to a tropical cyclone. The storm then headed northward, strengthening to a Category 3 hurricane on December 5. Hurricane Ione then took a slight northeastern turn, while its strength began to decrease. By December 7, the storm had been downgraded to a Category 1 hurricane as it accelerated eastward. Ione then accelerated southeasterly, and moved offshore the United States East Coast. Its intensity remained at Category 1 intensity until it weakened to a Category 2 hurricane on December 10. Ione then began to weaken at a faster rate, and was downgraded to a tropical storm on December 11. Late that day, the storm made landfall on the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The storm quickly weakened to a tropical depression, and was absorbed by another storm on December 13.

## Preparations and impact

A tropical depression in the Caribbean Sea on November 18 was devoid of any deep convection. As a result, the system was not recognized until the following day. The system drifted westward. An air reconnaissance flight was dispatched to survey the system on November 22. The reconnaissance flight found that the system had no deep convection. The system began to organize as it entered the Gulf of Mexico on November 23. Upon entering the Gulf, the system began to intensify. The system subsequently became a tropical storm on December 1.

The storm brought high tides to the central and eastern coasts of Florida. Heavy rains fell in the Florida Keys. The storm also brought strong winds to the Florida Keys.

### United States East Coast

Hurricane Ione approaching the East Coast

The hurricane produced gale-force winds in the Florida Keys. On December 7, it brought high tides to the North Carolina coast. The storm continued northeastward, bringing heavy rains to North Carolina. The storm brought rain to North Carolina and Virginia. Heavy rains were reported in South Carolina.

The Internet meme Rickroll , where a link is given to a seemingly relevant website only to be directed to a music video of sing

ers Rick Astley and MC Hammer performing the song " Never Gonna Give You Up ", has been criticized as an example of a clickbait article.

"Rickroll" redirects here. For the song, see Never Gonna Give You Up. For other uses, see Rick Roll.

## Origin and usage

The meme originated in 2007, when blogger Brian Krebs received an e-mail from a man who claimed to have hacked his computer. The e-mail contained a link to a music video by Rick Astley, "Never Gonna Give You Up". The email then said, "I have sent you a virus, I've taken over your computer." The email then said, "I am sending you this message because I have something very important to tell you. You have been RickRolled!"

In 2013, the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) gave "Rickroll" a definition. The OED defined "Rickroll" as a "prank or practical joke involving the tricking of a person into clicking a link which then directs them to the music video for Rick Astley's 1987 song 'Never Gonna Give You Up'". The OED's definition of "Rickroll" as a word was met with criticism and controversy, with some critics arguing that the definition was too narrow, as the term "Rickroll" can be used to describe any prank that involves someone being redirected to a music video, and that the definition failed to reflect the overall popularity of the meme.

As of 2014, "Rickroll" had become a popular Internet meme mostly in English-speaking countries, and had been used widely on forums, chat rooms, and social networking sites such as 4chan, Reddit, Facebook, Twitter, and Tumblr.

## Criticism

The Internet meme Rickroll, where a link is given to a seemingly relevant website only to be directed to a music video of singers Rick Astley and MC Hammer performing the song "Never Gonna Give You Up", has been criticized as an example of a clickbait article. The Telegraph's Sam Levin wrote that "Rickroll" is "a viral prank that has been around for a while", and that it "works in a similar way to other popular viral internet pranks."

## Reception

### Critical response

The seventh season of 24 has been met with overwhelmingly negative reviews. Many critics have stated that the season had too many problems with its storyline and characters, such as making the main character Jack Bauer unlikable by making him too brutal and uncaring, and the fact that some of the characters are not developed.

IGN gave the season a 2 out of 10, calling it "the worst television season ever". The review said that "The season's biggest crime is that it is boring. ... The entire season is nothing but a long, drawn out, painfully slow, and unbelievable search for a chemical weapons plot that is completely uninteresting. ... Everyone in this season is a cardboard cutout of a character."

In a review of the season, the A.V. Club gave the season a C+, stating that "In recent years, 24 has had a bad habit of giving us bad seasons, usually followed by a decent season. But this time, they've managed to go from bad to worse. It's as if they've decided to make the seventh season as inconsequential as possible, giving us a plot with no real stakes and no sense of urgency. ... The anti-terror overtones of the show have always been a bit dubious, but this season has gone over the top."

The A.V. Club later ranked the seventh season as the second worst season of any TV series in history.

### Awards and nominations

In 2010, the seventh season of 24 was nominated for, but did not win, the "Worst TV Series" award at the 30th Golden Raspberry Awards.

### Post-playing career

Jordan returned to his front office position in October 2001. In 2003, Jordan, along with majority owner Jerry Reinsdorf and team president Michael Reinsdorf, led a group that purchased the Hornets from George Shinn. Jordan's ownership lasted for six seasons, until the Hornets were sold to Tom Benson in 2010.

Jordan was the Hornets' primary owner of record, but the Benson-led group maintained control of basketball decisions. On June 5, 2007, Jordan, along with Reinsdorf, was named to the executive committee of the NBA.

On April 15, 2010, Jordan announced his retirement from the Hornets, citing that his duties with the Charlotte Bobcats and the Washington Wizards had left him too much time away from his family.

### Charlotte Bobcats

On January 12, 2007, Jordan was named majority owner of the Charlotte Bobcats. The team was valued at $275 million at the time. When Jordan purchased the team, the Bobcats were in the midst of a 13-game losing streak, and had a 4–28 record. Since then, the Bobcats have made the playoffs in two of the next three seasons (2008, 2010). The Bobcats made a 20-game improvement in their record over the 2006–07 season, and won 44 games in 2008–09, the most in their history. Jordan is the third African-American majority owner in the league, joining Vivek Ranadivé of the Sacramento Kings and Micky Arison of the Miami Heat.

### Washington Wizards

On October 2, 2010, Jordan purchased a minority stake in the Washington Wizards from majority owner Abe Pollin's estate for a reported $250 million. Jordan and Pollin had a long-standing friendship, and Jordan had served as the Wizards' vice chairman since 2001.

### Chicago Bulls

In 2020, Jordan exercised his right of first refusal to purchase majority ownership of the Chicago Bulls from Jerry Reinsdorf. Jordan's purchase closed on May 17, 2022.

### Charlotte Hornets

In September 2021, reports surfaced that Jordan was in talks to purchase the Charlotte Hornets, which were put on the market for an estimated $1.5 billion. On October 20, 2021, it was reported that his group was the preferred bidder for the team. In December 2021, the league had approved the purchase of the Hornets by Jordan and his group, but the NBA was still in talks with other potential bidders on the team. On January 4, 2022, the NBA approved the purchase of the Hornets by Jordan and his group for $925 million.
