More than 200 artists have recorded cover versions of " Imagine " . Joan Baez included it on 1972 's Come from the Shadows and

1974's Diamonds and Rust . The song was used in a 1991 episode of The Simpsons .

### The Beatles

The Beatles' version was recorded on 26 May 1971 at Trident Studios in Soho, London. According to George Martin, the Beatles had recorded the song with John Lennon on lead vocals on 30 May. Martin preferred Lennon's version, but the group decided that the song should be sung by Ringo Starr. In the end, they decided to combine both versions and merge the two takes into one. Starr's version is the one that appears on the 1971 album Imagine.

#### Background

Yoko Ono and Lennon had been in a relationship for over a year by the time they recorded "Imagine". The song was a 1971 collaboration between Lennon and Ono, and in its lyrics it envisioned a world without religion, nationalism, or materialism.

In 1980, Lennon told Rolling Stone:

"Ringo's... was the one I preferred. It sounded more like a song. John's was good. But when we went into the studio, we had problems, because I couldn't sing it anymore. I had been singing it in my head for weeks. I had sung the song so many times that I couldn't sing it anymore. It sounded like I was imitating myself, which is not a good idea. Ringo sounded like he was singing the song."

#### Recording

The Beatles recorded "Imagine" on 30 May 1971 at Trident Studios. The band recorded the song shortly after the completion of the 1970 album Let It Be. The song was one of the few Lennon-penned originals to be recorded by the group during their final period. A version of the song featuring Lennon on vocals was recorded, but Lennon preferred Starr's take. Lennon would go on to say in 1980:

"I think it's a better song when he (Ringo) sings it. It's more like a song. My version sounds like me trying to sing. Ringo's sounds like a song."

The Beatles' version was produced by George Martin and engineered by Geoff Emerick. The band was joined in the studio by Lennon's wife Yoko Ono, who contributed backing vocals to the song. The production features a timpani drum played by Alan White, along with a sitar played by Eric Clapton.

#### Release

The Beatles' version of "Imagine" was released on 11 September 1971 as the second single from the Imagine album. The song was the first single the Beatles released with a songwriting credit for Lennon and Ono. The song was released on the Imagine album, which was their last album of new material to be released. The single peaked at Number 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart, making it the first Top 10 hit for the Beatles since the 1968 single "Hey Jude". The song also peaked at number one in Canada and the United Kingdom, and reached the Top 10 in Australia and Ireland.

"Imagine" was released as a non-album single in the United States. The song's release as a single was a departure from the group's previous practice of including only album tracks on their singles. The single was also notable for being the first Beatles single to feature a songwriting credit for a Lennon-Ono song. The single peaked at number 4 on the Billboard Hot 100.

### Paul McCartney

On 16 September 1971, McCartney released his version of the song as the first single from his debut album McCartney, with "Another Day" as the B-side. His version of "Imagine" peaked at number 12 on the Billboard Hot 100 and number 11 on the UK Singles Chart. McCartney later included the song on his 1973 album Red Rose Speedway.

The President of the Republic ( Croatian : Predsjednik / ica Republike ) is the head of state ; he or she is directly elected according to the Croatian Constitution for a five-year term. The President of the Republic appoints the Prime Minister, upon the recommendation of the National Assembly, and he or she may also, in extreme cases, dissolve the assembly. The President of the Republic also represents Croatia abroad and receives foreign ambassadors on his or her behalf.
The President of the Republic may be removed from office in two situations : if he or she is unable to perform his or her duties, he or she may be temporarily replaced by the President of the Parliament, and in the event of impeachment, the President may be suspended from office, and the Constitutional Court may declare him or her permanently removed.

The position of President of the Republic was first established in 1990, following Croatia's independence from Yugoslavia. The Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, which was adopted in 1990, did not establish any specific method for the election of the President. However, the Constitution stated that the President should be elected in the first round of voting, if the number of votes for any candidate exceeded 50% of the total number of votes cast. The Constitution also established that the President may be removed from office by a two-thirds majority vote of the National Assembly.
The first President of the Republic was Franjo Tuđman.
The Constitution was amended twice in 1997 and 2000 to reflect the formation of a bicameral National Assembly (replacing the unicameral parliament), and to also establish a five-year term for the President of the Republic. Following the amendment of the Constitution in 2000, the President of the Republic is elected according to a two-round election system. The first round is held on the same day as the parliamentary elections, and a second round is held if no candidate obtains more than 50% of the votes in the first round. The second round is held two weeks after the first round.
Presidential powers and duties
The President of the Republic represents the Republic of Croatia in its international relations and, in accordance with the Constitution, appoints and dismisses ambassadors, consuls and heads of international organizations, on the basis of the advice of the Government of Croatia. The President may also approve international treaties and agreements, after ratification by the National Assembly, and declare a state of war.
The President may also invite the National Assembly to dissolve itself, and in such a case, the President may form a caretaker government, and call early parliamentary elections. However, the President may not dissolve the National Assembly more than once a year. The President of the Republic may also refer a bill to a referendum, and also call a referendum on a bill, if the President believes the bill is in the interest of the republic.
The President of the Republic may also dismiss the Government of Croatia, and appoint a new government, after consulting with the President of the Parliament. In the event of a deadlock in the National Assembly, the President of the Republic may invite the President of the Parliament to form a new government.
The President may also declare a state of emergency, and appoint a member of the Government to represent him or her in that capacity. Finally, the President of the Republic may issue an amnesty, in accordance with the Constitution.

r subjugates or co-opts the heroine; " the thriller " , in which Raffles confronts a threat to his life or liberty; and " the detective story " , in which he seeks to unmask the author of a crime. " 'The Story of a Newspaper'," Raffles for the Liberal journalist, is a detective story, but it is also a dark comedy, and it is in comedy that I believe we may find the key to Raffles's charm.
It is a comedy of manners, in effect, a farce, at least if we are willing to regard the social world as a stage and the depiction of social relations as a form of drama. The story places Raffles's world on a stage where it is both controlled and exposed. It depicts the relations of these characters to one another as scenes of farcical action, in which a series of events is staged for the purposes of comedy and satire, and in which the audience, like the characters onstage, is called upon to laugh at the follies and to make sense of the chaos.
The story takes place in a flat in Lambeth. It is a room in which everything is out of place, where the furniture is squeezed in by the window and the acting is hampered by the imperfect stagecraft and the lack of a proper scrim. It is a room in which Raffles's clowning is met with the solemnity of a solemn farce, and in which the central character is a clown, a comic figure whose career as a criminal is more a matter of entertainment for the audience than a topic for serious discussion.
The story is set in the year 1897. It is a time of transition for London society, one that is both in the past and already in the future. It is a society whose moral convictions are being challenged in the courts, a society that is threatened by the growth of the mass media, and a society that is about to be undone by the impending war in South Africa.
The room in Lambeth is a space in which the audience can watch the decline and fall of a society that has lost its own sense of humour. It is a space in which a man can be set on trial for his crimes, a man whose crimes are the crimes of a gentleman, and who is sentenced to death.

(the "bible" of poetry) in a contemporary idiom. The "bible" would involve the rules of metre and diction, while the "heaven" would be the realm of poetic inspiration and genius. "The Love Song" is described in this way:
> The Love Song is about the difficulties of love and the difficulty of knowing how to love, but it is also about the difficulty of writing poetry. It is a poem about writing poetry, in a sense, and it is a submission of a poem to the poetic dicti—the rules of poetic diction and metre—and that is why the poem is a difficult poem. (Jones 1971)
For Jones, the poem is a "meaningful allegory" that is "a struggle between the two sides of the poetic nature, the dicti and the heaven" (1981).
> In the poem, the poet is standing in the realm of dicti, which is a hell, in order to get to the realm of heaven, the place of poetic inspiration, and in order to get to the realm of heaven, the poet must first submit to the dicti—the rules of poetic diction and metre—and that is what he is doing. (1981)
John Hollander, similarly, asserts that "The Love Song" is a reworking of the Miltonic dicti in a modern idiom. He describes the "dicti" as "rules of poetic diction and verse" that "seem to be the poet's demon." In the poem, "the poet is constrained, tortured, by them." The Miltonic dicti are also the "dictatorship" of the poem. The poem is a struggle against the dicti, a struggle for freedom of expression. The "dicti" are the "heaven of the poem." The poem is a struggle to reach the "heaven" and to express one's feelings.
> In the poetic dicti, the poet in the poem is standing in the hell of the poem, and in order to get to the heaven of the poem, the place of poetic inspiration and freedom of expression, the poet must first submit to the dicti, and that is what he is doing. (1976)

Typical of Meyerbeer 's innovative orchestration is the use in Robert le diable of dark @-@ toned instruments – bassoons , timp

ani , and a pedal celesta (an instrument invented only in the 1870s) – to suggest the eerie aura of the setting. In the love duet of Act III, the bassoons and pedal celesta suggest the feelings of the main characters.
Other characteristics of Meyerbeer 's style are the alternation of lengthy instrumental passages with secco recitatives. His early operas combine many aspects of German, French, and Italian musical styles.
Meyerbeer 's later operas, which were performed at the Paris Opéra beginning in 1860, were in the Italian style. His first grand opera in the Italian style, L 'Africaine (1865), was a failure. The next year, he traveled to the United States to conduct performances of his operas. Robert le diable was the first opera presented by the New York Metropolitan Opera Company in 1883.

Bernard Perusse of The Gazette described the book as " more superficial but more positive " than the 2006 biography Van Morriso

n & Me , which was written by Ron Fournier, a former editor-in-chief of the National Journal .  Fournier's book was criticized in the Canadian media for its uncritical approach to Bush, while Perusse said of the book that " it only deals with the good sides of Bush, which made it feel a bit like a campaign brochure. 

" I think we need to show the world that we're not as bad as what's being said, " Bush told The Canadian Press. " I think it's important for us to show the world we're not the bad guys. " 

## Synopsis

The book is a collection of Bush's speeches and public appearances, interspersed with commentary from the president in which he describes his decision-making process. A foreword by Bush's father, George H. W. Bush, was included in an updated edition of the book. 

The book is divided into seven chapters:

* " From the Heart: My 9/11 Vow"
* " We Will Not Forget: The War on Terror"
* " Rebuilding America: Economic Security"
* " Freedom & Freedom's Enemies: Foreign Policy"
* " America's Promise: Health Care"
* " Serving the People: Education"
* " Supporting Our Troops & Their Families: Our Military"

## Reception

The book was reviewed by Andrew Cohen of The New York Times, who praised it as an " absorbing" book that " succeeds in a way that many political books fail, which is to explain the mind of the president of the United States, " and described it as " a serious, earnest and thoughtful accounting of a presidency that is far from over and whose history is still being written. " 

The book was also reviewed by James Traub of The New York Times Book Review, who described the book as " a collection of speeches and statements that were meant to be inspirational, " and concluded that " despite the occasional overweening rhetoric, this is a surprisingly reflective and revealing book. " He added that " though the book is in many ways a campaign brochure, it is also a reminder of the difficult choices the president has faced. " 

In his review of the book for Newsday, David Brooks described the book as " a curious collection of speeches and commentaries. " He added: " The book's analysis of the terrorism issue is an interesting amalgam of the best and worst of Bush's thought process. He takes a cautious and humble approach to the war on terrorism. But his approach to the broader war against global terrorism is naive. " 

Henry M. Paulson, Jr., who served as the 74th United States Secretary of the Treasury from 2006 to 2009, wrote in his review of the book for The Wall Street Journal that " the book is a valuable resource for those trying to assess the state of the nation and the challenges that lie ahead. " He concluded that " the book is a timely reminder that making tough decisions must be tempered by the need for compassion and empathy. " 

Some reviewers were critical of the book. Anthony Zurcher of The Christian Science Monitor described the book as " a collection of largely self-serving speeches and commentaries by a president in a hurry to make the case for his actions over the past six years. " He added that the book " does not exactly redefine the public's perception of the president as a man of the people, the man of faith who sees the world as he does. " 

David Frum, a conservative political commentator, wrote in his review of the book for The Washington Post that " the book is disappointing, in many ways. " He added: " I had hoped that Bush would be candid on the record about his most serious mistakes. Instead, he seems to be trying to deny that he has made any. " He concluded that " this book will be read as the president's last effort to bend the record in his favor. It is not a successful effort. " 

Joshua Micah Marshall of The New York Times wrote that " the book is essentially a campaign document, designed to shore up the president's support among his base. " He wrote: " The book's core is a series of speeches and statements by the president, which are interspersed with comments in which the president explains and defends his actions. "

at was called "expert systems" (the name was coined by John McCarthy in 1983). The key building block of expert systems was the knowledge base, which contained the rules that described the expert's knowledge of the real world. In the 1980s, AI researchers discovered that the expert knowledge could be represented as a set of rules that specified a set of axioms, the logical implications of which defined more axioms, and so on, in a chain of logical implications that could be summarized as a set of first-order logic sentences. The expert knowledge could be represented by some set of axioms, and the expert system could be viewed as the process that followed the rules to generate sentences in the set of axioms, which all had the same logical form.
The first expert systems were prototypes of expert energy management systems and expert knowledge-based computer-aided design systems. In 1982, Thomas L. Petrie and others at MIT completed a project called Expert Systems for Knowledge Workers (ESKW), the first prototype of an expert system. The project was funded by the United States Office of Naval Research. The project was an effort to automate the knowledge of a design engineer, which was represented by the engineering knowledge base that specified the design of a new aircraft. In 1983, the project was extended and expanded into the Knowledge-Based Engineering System (KBES) project.
In 1983, the White House announced the Strategic Computing Initiative (SCI). The goal of the SCI was to create the first large-scale expert system. The SCI provided funding for the construction of a prototype system, called the Knowledge Level Artificial Intelligence System (KLAIS). KLAIS was to be an expert system that could design and build an aircraft. The SCI funds were used to construct KLAIS in the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The KLAIS project was a collaboration between MIT, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Lincoln Laboratory (MITLL), and the United States Air Force Office of Scientific Research. Transmembrane proteins can also serve as ligand transport proteins that alter the permeability of the cell membrane to small mo

ieties, such as lipids. These proteins help to break down lipids and are essential for the normal functioning of the body. One such protein is the very large lipoprotein-related protein (LRP). LRP is found in the golgi body, and its function is to transport lipoproteins, such as chylomicrons and high-density lipoproteins (HDL), and apolipoprotein E from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell's membrane. This protein also transports apolipoprotein A1, which is an important protein for the formation of VLDL (very low density lipoprotein).
Roughly half of all known proteins contain transmembrane segments. These proteins mediate the transport of molecules through the membrane and are important in cellular signaling. Examples of these proteins are the ion channels, G-protein–coupled receptors, and transporters.
 Ion channels are proteins that allow the passage of a specific ion across the membranes that separate the inside of the cell from the outside. The movement of ions through the membrane can be initiated by a variety of stimuli such as the binding of a ligand, a change in pH, or a change in membrane voltage.
The function of the ion channels is to allow the flow of specific ions through the biological membrane. The flux rate of ions through the membrane is referred to as ion permeability. This rate is affected by the ion's charge and concentration.
The ion channels are classified into two major groups: inward and outward. Inward channels conduct positive ions, such as sodium and potassium, from the outside of the cell to the inside. Inward channels open when the concentration of positive ions inside the cell is higher than the concentration outside the cell. Outward channels conduct negative ions, such as chloride, from the inside of the cell to the outside. Outward channels open when the concentration of negative ions outside the cell is higher than the concentration inside the cell.

N @-@ 88 starts at the Nebraska – Wyoming state line in Banner County , where WYO 151 ends , and travels northeast . The road q

ue r t e r s the state's southern border with Colorado and crosses the North Platte River before entering Rocky Mountain National Park . The highway continues through the park and, beyond the park boundary, intersects U.S. Route 34 and U.S. Route 40 . It ends at U.S. Route 85 near Walden in Jackson County .

This article is about the section of U.S. Route 85 in Wyoming. For the entire route, see U.S. Route 85.

## Route description

Southern terminus

US 88 begins at the Nebraska state line south of Banner, where the route continues as Nebraska Highway 151. From its southern terminus, the route travels north and northwest to intersect US 30 and SH 25 . The route continues through North Platte and crosses the North Platte River before entering Rocky Mountain National Park . The highway continues through the park and, beyond the park boundary, intersects US 34 and US 40 . It ends at US 85 at an intersection with Wyoming Highway 130 near Walden in Jackson County.

The entire route is a part of the National Highway System, a system of roads important to the nation's economy, defense, and mobility.

## History

US 88 was first signed in Wyoming in 1926. In 1929, the route was extended east to US 16 at Cheyenne. US 88 was routed on a more northerly alignment in 1936, replacing US 20. On June 25, 1960, US 88 was replaced by US 85.

Temples , where the state rituals were carried out , were filled with images of the gods . The most important temple image was

the god- king , who was honored as the embodiment of the godhead . In the Egyptian temples , the god- king was always shown as a human figure , seated on a throne , while the gods were represented in the form of gigantic statues .
The temple platform , on which the images were displayed , was called naos ( Shrine ) , while the inner sanctum , in which the image of the god was located , was called sanctuary . The Egyptians believed that the gods were not located in the sanctuary , but in the naos . The naos and the sanctuary were separated from each other by a wall called mystagogical .
The Egyptians believed that the sanctuary was only a symbolic representation of the godhead . The high priests represented the gods in the form of the god- king . The high priests were priestly princes who were politically supreme in the land . The high priests were also responsible for the state rituals in the temple . The high priests of the Egyptian state religion were always men ; the women were only allowed to take care of the cult of the goddess Isis , who was especially important for the royal family .
The Egyptians also believed that the gods only had a physical body , the so-called  " body of fire " , in the sanctuary . They believed that the gods were not located in the temple , but in the naos . When the Egyptians entered the temple , they only saw the naos , but not the sanctuary . In the sanctuary , the god- king was thought of as a real person , not as an image .
The temple in Egypt was a sacred place , where the gods came down to earth in the form of the god- king , and where the king of Egypt was thought of as a god himself .

 The 2006 Peach Bowl was the 39th edition of the Peach Bowl, an American college football bowl game held on January 1, 2006, at the Georgia Dome in Atlanta, Georgia. The game featured the East Carolina Pirates of Conference USA and the Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets of the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC) . The 2006 Peach Bowl was a rematch of the 2004 game. East Carolina defeated Georgia Tech 58–40. East Carolina running back Chris Johnson finished the game with 223 rushing yards , 32 receiving yards , and 153 return yards fumble, and 4 touchdowns. The game set the record for most points scored in a bowl game with 100, but was tied in 2014 with the 2014 Fiesta Bowl (50–49).
East Carolina had opened the season with five straight wins, but lost four of their next five games. In their final conference game on November 18, 2005, the Pirates lost to Marshall 24–13. East Carolina head coach Ruffin McNeill was hired as the head coach for the ECU football team on December 1, 2004, after the firing of Skip Holtz.
Georgia Tech opened the season with a 24–21 loss at Virginia Tech. The Yellow Jackets lost three of their first four conference games as well, including a 21–17 loss to North Carolina . Georgia Tech finished the season with a five-game winning streak. They defeated West Virginia 45–44 in the 2005 Gator Bowl.
The game was a rematch of the 2004 Peach Bowl, which Georgia Tech won 45–28.
The Yellow Jackets wore their standard white jerseys with gold pants. The Pirates wore their white jerseys with navy pants.

On the first drive of the game, Georgia Tech quarterback Reggie Ball was sacked in the end zone by East Carolina's Darius Reynolds, giving the Pirates a safety.
Chris Johnson returned the next kickoff 100 yards for another touchdown, and the game was over early in the first quarter.
The Yellow Jackets finally scored on their next possession with a 41-yard touchdown reception from Ball to Calvin Johnson. Georgia Tech kicker Brandon Coutu missed the extra point, and East Carolina led 16–6.
Chris Johnson returned a Georgia Tech punt 20 yards to the Yellow Jacket's 41-yard line, but the Pirates were unable to score. Later in the quarter, Ball threw an interception to East Carolina's Johnathan Baker at the Yellow Jacket's 34-yard line. East Carolina needed only three plays to score on a 31-yard touchdown pass from quarterback Patrick Pinkney to Kevius Bryant. East Carolina led 22–6.
Georgia Tech scored again on their next possession with a 12-yard touchdown pass from Ball to Calvin Johnson. The Yellow Jackets failed to convert the extra point, and East Carolina led 22–12.
The Pirates scored again on their next possession with a 25-yard touchdown pass from Pinkney to Kevius Bryant, extending the lead to 29–12.
Georgia Tech scored again with a 2-yard touchdown run from Tashard Choice. The Yellow Jackets converted the extra point, and the Pirates' lead was cut to 29–19.
Chris Johnson returned the next kickoff 71 yards to the Yellow Jacket's 25-yard line. Three plays later, East Carolina scored on a 5-yard touchdown pass from Pinkney to Kevius Bryant. East Carolina led 36–19.

## Behavior

The chimpanzee is highly social , using visual and aural communication as well as touch . This species has a dominance hierarchy . Females are generally dominant over males. Adult males are dominant over juvenile or sub-adult males.

## Reproduction

Chimpanzees are polygynous , and females give birth to one infant every four to six years. Females are sexually mature by the age of 8 or 9, and males by the age of 12. Chimpanzees use a variety of communication and sexual signals to attract mates. The female has no interest in mating with males other than her dominant male.

## Conservation

Chimpanzees are threatened by habitat loss and commercial hunting . Their status varies between regions. The eastern and central chimpanzee subspecies have been hunted to extinction in most of their range. The western chimpanzee subspecies is not threatened. Commercial hunting of chimpanzees is illegal, but it continues in some areas. The chimpanzee populations are declining due to habitat loss.

The conservation of chimpanzees is a difficult challenge for conservationists. Due to habitat loss and commercial hunting, chimpanzees have been classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. The Declaration of the Great Apes convened in 2000 by the World Conservation Union and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) has been a major step in chimpanzee conservation. The meeting was successful in focusing conservation efforts on chimpanzees and other great apes.

The Southern Way Link Road ( Welsh : Ffordd Gyswllt y Ffordd Deheuol ) , generally known simply as Southern Way , was built in

1999 to provide a quicker link between the A470 at Troed y Rhiw and the M4 at Cardiff. It also serves as a link between the A4232 at Whitchurch and the A470 at Llanishen. The road is 4 km long, and is largely grade-separated. It has junctions with the A470 at Llanishen and the A4232 at Whitchurch.
The road was authorised by the Welsh Office in 1991, under the direction of the Wye Valley Area Transport Study, which also included plans for the A468 Newport Eastern Distributor Road. The road was built between 1996 and 1999, at a cost of around £40 million. The project was part of the Welsh Office's £1.25 billion black route programme, and was a key part of the Welsh Office's transport policy for South Wales.

On August 5, 1945, the Manhattan Project leaders, General Leslie Groves , and the Manhattan Project Overseer, Major General Kenneth Nichols, met at Building 81 to decide the fate of the plutonium core of the Fat Man bomb .
On August 6, 1945, Building 81 was the site of the Trinity test , the first detonation of a nuclear weapon in history. General Groves and Major General Nichols observed the test themselves from the site, while a large number of scientists and technicians from the Manhattan Project witnessed the test in a vantage point 10,000 feet (3,048 m) away.
 The purpose of the Manhattan Project was to develop an atomic bomb.
 It was based on research that began in 1939 and continued through 1945 at numerous laboratories and sites throughout the United States.
 The project was led by the U.S. Army under the leadership of General Leslie Groves. Although major research and production took place at three sites: the Los Alamos Laboratory , the Oak Ridge National Laboratory , and the Hanford Site, there were also lesser-known operations at other sites, including: the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory , the Chicago Metallurgical Laboratory , the Phillips Laboratory, the University of California Radiation Laboratory, the University of Chicago Metallurgy Research Laboratory, and the Columbia University Radiation Laboratory.

The Woodward case , formally known as Hebert v. Comair , was set for a punitive damages jury trial July 19 , 2010 . In that tri

al a civil jury awarded $10.5 million in punitive damages to the plaintiff, $100,000 in compensatory damages, and $100,000 in attorney's fees and costs. Comair appealed to the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals where it lost. The Elev enth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's findings that Comair knowingly and intentionally caused the plaintiff severe emotional distress. The Elev enth Circuit Court of Appeals also affirmed the trial court's finding that the plaintiff was entitled to punitive damages in the amount of $10.5 million. The Elev enth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's findings that the plaintiff was entitled to compensatory damages in the amount of $100,000 and attorney's fees and costs in the amount of $100,000, and remanded the case to the trial court for a new trial on only these two issues. Comair appealed the Elev enth Circuit Court of Appeals's ruling to the United States Supreme Court, which declined to hear the appeal. So, Comair continued to appeal.
And appeals they did. The state of Ohio , as the plaintiff, argued that Comair's appeal was nothing more than a frivolous appeal. As such, the state of Ohio moved the Ohio Supreme Court to dismiss Comair's appeal for lack of jurisdiction. The Ohio Supreme Court agreed. In an opinion filed January 20, 2012 , Comair's appeal was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
This case has been long and hard fought. It represents the first time in state history that a state appellate court has considered whether a jury's award of punitive damages was excessive. It also represents the first time in state history that a state appellate court has considered what constitutes a frivolous appeal.
Despite the finality of the Ohio Supreme Court's holding, this case is not over. The case against Comair (and its parent company Delta Air Lines) is not over. In fact, it is more likely to be just beginning. The case continues in a federal court.
The federal lawsuit against Comair/Delta Air Lines is still pending. The case in the federal court is based on the federal Tort Claims Act (TCA). The TCA prevents the federal government from being sued in its own courts for injuries or damages caused by its employees while acting within the scope of their employment. However, the TCA provides an exception.
1. The employee or agency of the Government, while acting within the scope of his office or employment, subjects the citizen of the United States to the deprivation of any rights, privileges, or immunities secured by the Constitution and laws.
2. Such citizen has been injured by such action.
3. The injury was proximately caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the employee or agency of the Government while acting within the scope of his office or employment.
4. The injury occurred on land owned or controlled by the United States.
The trial court ruled that the federal TCA did not prevent the plaintiff from filing suit. The trial court also found in favor of the plaintiff on the claims against Comair.
The trial court found that Comair's conduct, if found to be intentional, would have caused the plaintiff to suffer severe emotional distress. The trial court also found that there was no proof that the plaintiff's conduct, if found to be intentional, would have caused Comair's conduct.
The trial court also found that Comair's conduct was not justified. The trial court found that Comair's conduct was outrageous and that Comair had no good faith basis for its conduct. Finally, the trial court found that Comair acted with reckless disregard for the plaintiff's rights.
On appeal, the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's finding that Comair's conduct was outrageous. The Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals remanded the case back to the trial court with instructions to enter findings of fact and conclusions of law on the issue of whether Comair's conduct was outrageous. The Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals did not rule on the trial court's other findings.

On October 15 , 1915 , the Historical Society of Bradford County , Pennsylvania , dedicated a memorial on Spanish Hill in honor

of the Confederate soldiers who gave their lives in defense of their country. It was a simple ceremony. The county's mayor spoke of the ties between the two countries' peoples. The head of the county historical society spoke of the hope that lessons would be learned from the War Between the States . A member of the county's board of supervisors laid a wreath at the base of the monument. Another wreath was placed at the base of the flagpole that stood atop the hill. After a moment of silence, a bugler played "Taps."
The next day, the mayor of Bradford County and the president of the county historical society traveled to New York City to attend a meeting of the General Lee Confederate Memorial Association.
In February 1916 , nine months after the dedication, the president of the historical society, along with the mayor and a few other local leaders, traveled to Richmond, Virginia , to attend the dedication of the Monument to the Confederate War Dead in Hollywood Cemetery. They were joined by several other Pennsylvania delegations. It was a solemn occasion. A community bereft of its sons and daughters had erected a monument to those lost. The survivors gathered in silence to reflect on the cost of war.
The following year, the president of the historical society traveled to Waynesboro, Pennsylvania , for the dedication of the monument to the Confederate War Dead in Penn Hall Cemetery.
Several years later, in 1920, the president of the historical society traveled to Gettysburg to witness the dedication of the monument to the Confederate War Dead in the National Cemetery.
In 1921 , the county's mayor traveled to Baltimore to attend the dedication of a monument to the Confederate War Dead in Mount Olivet Cemetery.
The story of these monuments is not a story of martyrs, but of healing. It is a story of remembrance and reconciliation. In the aftermath of war, these citizens from a little-known county in Pennsylvania chose to remember the dead and to express their hopes for reconciliation among the living. They did so by erecting monuments to those who had fallen in the War Between the States . And in the process, they helped to heal the wounds that many in their community carried.
But there is another story that is also worth telling. The story of how these monuments came to be erected. What were the circumstances of the time that led to the creation of these monuments? Who was responsible for their design and construction? What were the hopes and dreams of the men and women who dedicated them?
These were the questions that I sought to answer when I decided to write a book on the Memorials to the Confederate War Dead of Bradford County , Pennsylvania. I was struck by the profound respect these small-town Pennsylvanians had for the men and women who had fallen in the War Between the States. They honored their dead by erecting monuments to them. They did so despite the fact that there seemed to be little support for the Confederacy in their community. These Pennsylvanians were not motivated by any political or economic agenda. They acted out of a sense of duty to their fallen comrades. They believed that those who had laid down their lives in the defense of their country deserved to be remembered. They believed that those who had died in the War Between the States belonged to the same nation that they did. They believed that the best way to honor the dead was to memorialize their sacrifice. And in the process, they helped to heal the wounds that had been inflicted during the war.
This book is the story of the men and women who dedicated the monuments to the Confederate War Dead in Bradford County , Pennsylvania. It is a story of remembrance and reconciliation. It is a story that deserves to be told.

Dota 2 includes a matchmaking system , which is measured by a numerical value known as " matchmaking rating " ( MMR ) . MMR is

100 points. The overall MMR of all players in a game is displayed in the game lobby before the game starts. MMR is calculated using a weighted average of wins, losses, and games played, and is adjusted based on the player's skill level in a game. MMR is recalculated every two weeks. Weighting of wins and losses is based on the difference between the MMR of the two teams involved.
MMR is used in many game modes, including Ranked Matchmaking. In Ranked Matchmaking, the MMR of players is displayed on the in-game scoreboard, along with a rating icon. Players with an MMR below 1185 are denoted with a green icon, players with an MMR between 1185 and 1314 with an orange icon, players with an MMR between 1315 and 1530 with a yellow icon, and players with an MMR above 1530 with a blue icon. Players with an MMR below 1185 are generally placed in a competitive matchmaking queue; players above 1530 are placed in a casual matchmaking queue.

The matchmaking system was officially released on November 19, 2012.

In 1950 Alan Turing published a landmark paper in which he speculated about the possibility of creating machines that think . H

uge strides have been made in computer technology since then, but the problem of building an artificial intelligence is far from solved. In fact, the problem has become more complex, not less. The main reason is the rise of an entirely new field: nanotechnology, which has revolutionized our understanding of the very nature of material objects.
If you're like most people, you probably think of matter as something solid and indivisible. The table you're sitting at, for example, is a block of wood. It's not a bunch of little pieces of wood. But if you examine it closely, you'll find that it is indeed made of little pieces of wood held together by glue. A table is a macroscopic object, but it can be decomposed into smaller objects, or _building blocks_ —in this case, the wood and the glue.
Now, imagine a little machine that can make copies of itself. This is a pretty simple machine in some ways: all it has to do is chip away at its own building blocks. The machine can make copies of itself if it carries enough supplies with it. In this case, the supplies are copies of itself. The machine can thus divide and multiply until it eventually disappears. For a while, however, it is a real danger to the rest of the universe.
The natural question to ask is: Can the machine make any other kind of object? If it can, then it's not a machine at all; it's a _factory_. This is important because it shows that the concept of a macroscopic object is an illusion. In fact, a macroscopic object is just a collection of microscopic objects. We often refer to matter, or material objects, as _stuff_. But what is stuff? If you take a piece of wood, for example, and break it down into its fundamental building blocks, you'll find that it's not just wood; it has lots of other stuff in it, too.
The most elementary building block of the universe is the atom. Atoms are made of even smaller building blocks called _quarks_ , which are held together by even smaller building blocks called _gluons_. Atoms are, in turn, held together by even smaller building blocks called _electron_ neutrinos, which are in turn held together by even smaller building blocks called _electron_ neutrinos—and so on and so on.
What we call "stuff" is actually the result of a gigantic chain of building blocks that goes back an infinite number of steps. In other words, stuff is not really there; it's just a label we apply to the result of a sequence of transformations.
The idea that stuff is not really there is an unsettling one, and it's easy to lose sight of it. However, it has profound implications. For example, if stuff is not really there, then it is not possible to understand the universe without understanding how to manipulate it.
The question, then, is: What is the fundamental unit of matter? If matter is built up from smaller building blocks, how do these building blocks get put together? Is there a fundamental building block? Is there a fundamental force that holds matter together?
In the early 1970s, scientists carried out an experiment in which they bombarded a certain kind of glass with atomic particles. The glass turned out to be made of two kinds of atoms, which were held together by a force that was different from the forces that held the other atoms together. The force that held those two kinds of atoms together was called the _strong force_. As the name suggests, the strong force is very strong. It is a billion trillion trillion times stronger than gravity.
The strong force is the result of a quantum field, which is a mathematical object that acts like a wave—a wave that is responsible for holding two kinds of atoms together. The wave, in turn, is the result of a chain of building blocks that goes back an infinite number of steps.
In 1982, David Gross and Michael Green published a paper in which they proposed that matter is made up of even smaller building blocks called _quantum fields_ , which are held together by even smaller building blocks called _gluons_. These fields and gluons are a billion trillion trillion trillion times smaller than atoms.
In 1995, David Gross, Frank Wilczek, and David Politzer shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for their work on quantum fields. The following year, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to David Gross, David Politzer, and Frank Wilczek for their work on the strong force.

the National Portrait Gallery, London , for his portrayal of Warham's successor, Cranmer, which was painted around 1533. [4] A more immediate inspiration for Cranmer's portrait may have been the 1528 Portrait of Anne Boleyn , also in the National Portrait Gallery, by Hans Holbein, which closely resembles Cranmer's pose.
The Cranmer portrait clearly shows the influence of the Tudor court painter Hans Holbein, who was at the time working out of England. The pose recalls Holbein's portrait of Anne Boleyn, and Cranmer's gesture of reading the Bible also recalls the gesture of Holbein's portrait of Boleyn, which shows her with a book of devotions in her lap. The Cranmer portrait thus calls attention to the fact that the subject shares his royal predecessor's piety and learning, and suggests that Cranmer will play a role in the reign of his royal patron, Henry VIII, similar to the one that Anne Boleyn played in the reign of her royal patron, Henry VIII.
The portrait of the 1534 coronation was commissioned by the king, not by Cranmer. It is the only extant likeness of the king at the coronation and the only likeness of Henry Vlll wearing the imperial crown.
In 1540, Cranmer commissioned a further portrait of himself, which he had engraved by William Brooke, 10th Baron Cobham. This is a full-length portrait that shows the archbishop in his episcopal robes. [4]

After completing his schooling at the Joachimsthaler Realgymnasium in Berlin, he began to study law and medicine at the University of Berlin, but concentrated on his musical studies, and soon began to study composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter at the Singakademie. At the age of 14, he began composing songs for the services of Berlin's two Protestant congregations. He also began to compose instrumental works, including the cantata The Slave ( Der Sklave ) and the opera Boadicea (1816).
Meyerbeer's first opera, Robert the Devil ( Der Flugsprunch ), was performed at the Berlin State Opera in 1817, but was not a great success. Meyerbeer also began to write for the piano; his first composition for this instrument was the Fantasia in C major .

Meyerbeer's next opera, Le pardon de Ploërmel ( The Pardon of Ploërmel ), was performed in Paris in 1825; it was successful, but not as successful as his earlier works. In 1827 he composed his opera, Robert Sempere ( Robert Sempere und die beiden Cousins ), which was not performed until 1840.
Meyerbeer's next opera, The Huguenots ( Les Huguenots ), was first performed at the Paris Opera in 1836; it was a huge success, and established his reputation in France. His opera, The Fairy's Circle ( Das Rheingold ), was performed in Berlin in 1839, but failed to meet with the same success as his earlier works.
Meyerbeer's last opera, The Woman without a Shadow ( Die Frau ohne Schatten ), was written in 1843; it was not performed until 1856, and was not as successful as his earlier works. After this, he retired from composition and turned to painting.
Meyerbeer died in Paris on 2 May 1864. He was buried in the Cimetière de Montmartre .

In the 1986 film, which was in color, the cast included Joan Plowright, Rupert Everett, Colin Firth, Judi Dench, Tom Wilkinson, and Nicholas Farrell. The 1999 television adaptation starred Rupert Everett, Colin Firth, Anna Chancellor, Dame Judi Dench, and Zoë Wanamaker.

The play is a comedy of manners, very much a product of its time, and a very English comedy. It is the story of the relationship between two young men—Jack Worthing and Algernon Moncrieff—and the lengths to which they go to hide the fact that they have, in fact, been leading double lives for some time.
The play opens with Jack Worthing on the telephone telling his friend Algernon Moncrieff that he is on his way to see him. Croatia was first subdivided into counties ( Croatian : županija ) in the Middle Ages . The divisions changed over time to refl

ect the political and territorial changes of the region.
The Kingdom of Croatia and the Croatian Parliament ( Sabor ) were reestablished in 1527, and remained so until the death of the last Croatian king, Ferdinand I , in 1567.
The Kingdom of Croatia was formally united with Hungary as the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia from 1868 to 1918.
On 10 April 1907, the Croatian Parliament adopted the "Statute of Autonomy" ( Stjepan Radić ) , which established a limited parliamentary autonomy for Croatia within the Kingdom of Hungary.
On 29 October 1918, the South Slavs of the Kingdom of Dalmatia, the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia and the Kingdom of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs proclaimed the unification of the three kingdoms into the new State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, which was renamed the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes after the Serbian army invaded the country, and then the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929.
The Kingdom of Croatia ( Croatian : Kraljevina Hrvatska ) was a state in the Balkans that existed from 1918 to 1941 .

The Piper Aviation Museum exhibits aircraft and aircraft equipment , documents , photographs , and memorabilia related to Piper

Aircraft and the aviation industry in general.

The Piper Aviation Museum is located at the Piper Aircraft headquarters in Vero Beach, Florida , a few miles north of the city's Municipal Airport (VRB). When the museum was founded in 1986, it was located in the second floor offices of Piper Aircraft, and it was accessible only to Piper employees. In 1995, Piper Aircraft moved its headquarters to the Tree-to-Sea Business Park, and the museum moved to the first floor of Piper's new building. It was then open to the public.

The museum's collection, located in 13,000 square feet (1,200 m²) of space, includes more than 100 aircraft and airplane parts, 800 photographs, 100 periodicals, and 200 memorabilia items. The museum also has a library with books and periodicals related to aviation.

The museum was closed between 2007 and 2011, due to the financial difficulties of Piper Aircraft. The company was sold in 2012, and the museum was reopened to the public on September 22, 2012.

## Exhibits

The museum's exhibits include Piper aircraft, including a Piper J-3 Cub, a Piper J-5 Cub, a Piper L-4 Grasshopper, a Piper L-4 Cub, a Piper PA-18 Super Cub, and a Piper PA-28 Cherokee.

The museum also has an exhibit on the famed aviator Amelia Earhart (1897-1937), including her Piper J-5 Cub.

Seventeen-year-old high school student, Kate "Katie" Armstrong, the daughter of a doctor named Diane Armstrong, gets involved in a mystery after finding a dead body on the riverbank of the Delaware River. Katie goes to the morgue to see the body and is shocked to see that the body is all washed up and clean, except that it's missing a hand. Katie also finds a note that says "Please help me" written on the palm of the hand.
When Katie goes back to the morgue, she sees that the body is gone, and the police are not doing anything about the note. Katie sets out to find the body and the person who wrote the note. She discovers that the body is an amputee, and that the note was written by the poltergeist who is haunting the morgue. Katie and her friend, Max, find the body and discover that the body is the missing girl, Rose. Katie and Max also discover that the poltergeist is the ghost of a homeless man named Richard.
Katie goes to Ocean City to find her missing father. She discovers that her father is dead and that he was murdered. Katie investigates her father's death and finds that the murderer is a man named David Carver. Katie discovers that Carver is a serial killer, and that he is murdering the homeless people in Ocean City. Katie manages to stop Carver from killing any more people.

The evidence for male monogamy is not as strong as the evidence for female mate-guarding. But it is a bit stronger than the evidence for female monogamy.
Several species that are promiscuous are semelparous. (Semelparous means that each female may mate only once, and dies after a single reproductive cycle.) This is not the case for species that are monogamous. Monogamous species can mate many times, and the males can have many mates. But the monogamous species are usually polygynous, which means that only one male is allowed to mate with a female.
Male-only monogamy is apparently rare in animals (although there are some exceptions) and seems to be avoided by most female animals. As long as females have extra resources (to feed and care for the male), they will usually have extra resources to begin breeding at a younger age and have more young. So, in an evolutionary sense, it doesn't make sense for a female to be monogamous if she can be polygamous. In most species, males are more likely to be monogamous than females.

In species that are male-only monogamous, mate-guarding is usually a form of mate-choice by the female. She mates with the male that is most likely to provide the best care and support for her and her young. In species that are female-only monogamous, mate-guarding occurs in at least two ways. First, mate-guarding is often a form of mate-choice by the female. She mates with the male that is most likely to support her and her young. Second, mate-guarding is a form of parental care. The female does not allow other males to mate with her offspring.

Rio de Janeiro is located in the southeastern region of Brazil, at latitude 22°26'28" South and longitude 43°11'48" West .  The city is located in the state of Rio de Janeiro.  Geographically , the city is located on the shores of the Atlantic Ocean , with the Bay of Guanabara and the islands of Paquetá , and in the Serra da Carioca hills .  The city is the capital of the State of Rio de Janeiro .  Rio de Janeiro is Brazil's second-largest city and its third-most populous .  The Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Area was home to over 11 million people, the third largest in Brazil .
Rio de Janeiro has a tropical climate , with high temperatures and high humidity during the summer , and high temperatures and low humidity during the winter.  The climate is classified as a tropical savanna climate , which is characterized by high temperatures for most of the year .  The city's climate is affected by the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn , which run through the Atlantic Ocean , fluctuating with the seasons.  The climate also varies due to the fact that Rio de Janeiro is located in the temperate zone , so the temperatures are not as extreme as in the areas of the tropics .  There are four distinct seasons in Rio de Janeiro .  The summer season , which extends from December to March , is characterized by high temperatures and high humidity .  Temperatures reach 30 ° C (86 ° F) during the day and 22 ° C (72 ° F) at night .  During this period, the city also receives occasional floods or tornadoes .  The winter season , which extends from June to August , is characterized by cool temperatures and low humidity.  Temperatures range between 16 °C (61 °F) and 22 °C (72 °F) during the day, and between 10 °C (50 °F) and 14 °C (57 °F) at night .

@-@nal consistency. His playing style is based on his amazing footwork and ability to move explosively side to side.
 Federer was born on August 8 , 1981 in Basel , Switzerland , to Swiss tennis player Robert Federer and South African former professional , Lynette Federer. He was introduced to tennis at the age of eight by his father and trained in the Basel Tennis Club from 1989 to 1998 .
 Federer is the only player in the Open Era to have reached at least the semifinal of every Grand Slam tournament. He has won 17 Grand Slam titles , the second-most in history for a male player and the third-most in the Open Era. He is also the only male player to have defeated all other male players who are currently in the top 100 . He also holds the record for the most ATP World Tour titles won with 57.
 Federer is the only player to have won the Wimbledon title eight times. He is also the only player to have won the Australian Open four times and the Wimbledon title four times consecutively . He has also won the men's singles title at the Olympics four times .
 Federer is known for his remarkable footwork , unusual stroking style , and powerful serve. He has been credited with popularizing the "one-handed backhand" . Federer has had a longstanding rivalry with Novak Djokovic , Rafael Nadal , Andy Murray , and Tomas Berdych .
 Despite his success on the ATP Tour , Federer has rarely played in the Davis Cup , as he is most comfortable playing at the Grand Slam tournaments . He has a record of 16-4 in Davis Cup play .
 Federer was ranked number one in the world for a record 310 weeks , including a record 237 consecutive weeks . He is the first player in the Open Era to achieve a career Grand Slam and a career Grand Slam in men's singles , having won the Australian Open in 2004 , the French Open in 2009 , the Wimbledon in 2003 , 2004 , 2005 , 2006 , 2007 , 2009 , 2012 and 2017 and the US Open in 2004 , 2005 , 2006 , 2007 , 2009 , 2010 and 2011 .

Early examples of Anglo @-@ Saxon art are largely metalwork , particularly bracelets , clasps and jewellery , that has survived

in large quantities from interments in bogs in the Netherlands and Denmark. Some of the most well-known of these treasures are the Sutton Hoo hoard and the Vendel hoard . Much of the metalwork is in the form of runic inscriptions, which are still being deciphered.
##
 The first written evidence of Anglo-Saxon art is from the Latin Gildas' _On the Ruin of Britain_ , written around 570. It refers in a dismissive manner to a style of painting that Gildas saw in Brittany, saying that it was not even on a par with the style of a potter's apprentice. The art of these painters was to be found in the churches built by British bishops on their return to the north of Gaul.
 The next reference to Anglo-Saxon art is in the _Martyrology_ of Alcuin , the scholarly adviser to Charlemagne, who in 779 sent a mission to the court of the Northumbrian king. Alcuin was interested in the art of the Northumbrians, and he records that King Æthelred had two men named Ceadwalla and Æthelwolf. This group of artists who worked from the 780s onwards are known as the 'Ceadwalla group', and their style is referred to as the 'Northumbrian style'.
##
 The art of the King Alfred group, which includes the _Bald's Leechbook_ and the _British Museum Cotton MS Titus A_ , is a continuation of the Northumbrian style.
 The art of the Wessex group, which includes the _Exeter Book_ and the Psalter of Æthelwold, is a development of the previous two styles.
##
 The earliest manuscripts in the Anglo-Saxon style have a decorative feature known as an 'initial' that delineates the opening of a section of text. The initials of the Insular style are usually decorated in the form of a plant, with interwoven tendrils and leaf-like forms. The earliest Anglo-Saxon initials are in the King Alfred group, and are examples of 'intricate', 'deep' and 'tendrilled' initials.
 The Anglo-Saxon art of the Wessex group uses tendrilled initials for the first two lines of text on the page, and the third line is decorated with an 'interlace' initial.
##
 The Northumbrian style is described as 'the Tenth-century style'. The earliest surviving manuscripts of this style are the Lindisfarne Gospels and the Book of Durham, both of which date to the ninth century.
 The Wessex group is described as the 'Eleventh-century style'. The earliest manuscripts belonging to this style are the Exeter Book , the Psalter of Æthelwold , and the _Bald's Leechbook_.
##
 The 'Anglo-Saxon style' is the form of decoration that developed in England during the period 1050–1150. The earliest surviving manuscripts of this style are the _Echternach Gospels_ and the _Fulda Bible_.
##
 The Norman Conquest of England in 1066 resulted in a new form of decoration, which was primarily derived from the Anglo-Norman style of the eleventh century. The earliest surviving manuscripts of this style are the _Eadwine Psalter_ and the _British Library Cotton MS Nero D.IV_.

## Specification

The museum is housed in the original battery magazine of the site, a large brick building with a corrugated iron roof. The building is also known as the Battery Magazine and is located adjacent to the coast road, near Llanrhidian. It is a Grade II listed building, designated on 23 July 1975.

## History

### Fort Glanville Battery

The battery was built in 1869, and was intended to assist in the defence of Swansea Harbour against a potential French invasion.

The battery was first manned in 1869 and was completed in 1877. The fort was manned and maintained by the Royal Artillery until 1926. The fort was then used as an observation post until 1968.

### Museum

The fort museum opened in 1973 and is run by the Fort Glanville Historical Association. The museum displays include a full size model of the fort as it would have been prior to WWII, the armament of the fort as it was in 1877, and a small collection of photographs.

### Glanville Fort Lighthouse

A small lighthouse was built at the fort in 1876, and was manned by a lighthouse keeper. The lighthouse was lit for the first time on 1 December 1876, and was manned by the Royal Corps of Signals. It was decommissioned in 1922, and the light removed. The building was converted in 1937 for use as a generator shed. After decommissioning the fort in 1968, the lighthouse was restored and reopened as a museum in 1973. The lighthouse is now a Grade II listed building.

## Transport

The museum is located only 0.5 miles (0.80 km) from the A483 road.The museum is on the coastal path between Llanrhidian and Llanrhidian Beach.

In May 1938, the water level reached 19.1 ft (5.8 m), the highest level ever recorded in Florida. The water level stayed high for several months and then fell gradually. The extended dry season brought the water level below 15 ft (4.6 m) within a year, which was the low point since construction.
The water level in the lake rose to 16.7 ft (5.1 m) above sea level, and the lake level has never returned to its pre-dam height, but has varied between 10 and 16.7 ft (3.0 and 5.1 m) above sea level.
The dam's power station has the largest capacity of any U.S. hydroelectric facility, and it provides much of the electricity used by the Las Vegas Valley.
The dam was completed and dedicated on March 1, 1935. At the time, it was the world's largest dam. However, time has seen the Hoover Dam surpassed by the Itaipu Dam on the Brazil-Paraguay border, the Three Gorges Dam in China, and the Grand Coulee Dam in the United States. The dam is 726 ft (221 m) high, 1,244 ft (379 m) long, and has a crest elevation of 726.4 ft (221.4 m). The dam's foundation, near the bottom, is 660 ft (201 m) below the crest. The dam is 660 ft (201 m) thick at the base and only 3 ft 6 in (1.07 m) thick at the top. The dam's weight is estimated to be 6,600,000 short tons (6,000,000 long tons; 5,900,000 metric tons).
The dam was designed to withstand water pressures in excess of 300,000,000 lb (1,360,000,000 kg; 1,400,000,000 short tons) per square foot (1,400,000,000 kg/m²). As a result, the dam was built with 5.5 million cubic yards (4,200,000 m3) of concrete, 726,000 cubic yards (557,000 m3) of structural steel, and 32,500 cubic yards (25,100 m3) of hydraulic cement.

" Ode on Indolence " is sometimes called upon as a point of comparison when discussing Keats 's other poems . Charles Wentworth

Dilke makes the following claim about it in the preface to _Poems of_ _Arthur Hallam_ ,
_"_ _Ode_ _on_ _Indolence_ _is_ _not_ _a_ _good_ _poem,_ _but_ _contains_ _some_ _good_ _lines_ _and_ _sentences_ _and_ _expressions,_ _and_ _has_ _the_ _merit_ _of_ _not_ _being_ _a_ _bad_ _poem._ "
The poem is not well known (though is quoted, it seems, when there is a need for an example of laziness). It is certainly not as well known as his other odes, which have been anthologized in _The_ _Oxford_ _Book_ _of_ _English_ _Verse_ and also in _The_ _Oxford_ _Book_ _of_ _English_ _Prose_ _and_ _Verse_. _Ode_ _on_ _Indolence_ is in the latter collection, but in the former it has been replaced by his odes to _Autumn_ and the _Season._
For the uninitiated, the poem is a discussion of the nature of indolence, which he locates in the human soul. While the imagination is active, the body is inert, and the body is inert while the imagination is active. The distinction between body and soul, however, is not particularly important to Keats, whom we know from other poems is a materialist. The essential point he makes about indolence is that life is best spent in what he calls "the vale of soul-making," which is in fact a "vale of soul-destroying." The poem is a long list of criticisms of various vices and habits of life, to which he is opposed, and a number of propositions about how a human life should be lived.
The poem is very conservative. It is heterogeneous in that it is a list of points of view, rather than a coherent text, but it is conservative in its basic ethical principle: we should be better than we are.
"Ode on Indolence"
When the soft zephyrs,
That kiss with silver lips the glassy wave,
Soothe the long-suffering mariner,
And make him smile to see the foaming crests
Of waters, calm, and dancing in the sun,
While the gay dolphins bounding o'er the main
Plunge down again, and sparkle, as they dive;
And the sweet-sounding shell,
That murmurs to the ear
Sounds of its native sea;
When these and all things seen and unseen
Hung in mid air,
Laughed to behold the mild content
Of him who only loves, and loves the hues
Of love, and loves the calm unruffled breast
Of those, who like himself are only loved,
And only love, and are beloved only:
Then the soul would seem to say,
"Be thou at peace;
For here is that serene retreat,
Which never-ceasing thought can reach,
Nor ever-active power o'erleap;
Here let me rest for ever."
But alas!
Even in this solemn hour,
Even here, where all things silent were,
From the still depths of slumber roused,
Briskly he arose,
And, with a heart elate,
Went forth to meet the stern alarms
Of active life, and do his part
In its perpetual wars.
For what is Indolence,
If it be not the mind's consent,
To suffer life's incessant dream
To pass from brain to brain?
Life pulses to and fro,
And, like a wave, rebounds

Jifna was known as Gophnah ( In Hebrew גופנה ) at the time of the First Jewish @-@ Roman War , and after its conquest became a

Byzantine colony .

## History

Jifna lies in the administrative region of Gush Etzion in the Judean Mountains south of Jerusalem. At the time of the First Jewish Revolt against the Romans, 66-70 AD, it was a Jewish settlement by the name of Gophnah (Gufna) and was part of the Idumean Kingdom. 

In the Byzantine period, Jifna was a village named Gophna and was part of the Judean district of the province of Palaestina Prima.

### Arab period

Prior to the 1920s, the population of Jifna was extremely small, and the village was mostly used for grazing sheep. Between 1922 and 1926, Arab villagers from the nearby villages of al-Khader and Beit Jala planted numerous olive trees in the village's fields, which was previously covered in barley and wheat.

### British Mandate

During the British Mandate, Jifna was allocated to the Jewish National Fund (JNF) under the terms of the 1929 Land . As a result, Jifna's population declined from 130 in 1931 to 49 in 1945.

### 1948 to 1967

Main article: Battle of Jifna

During the 1948 Arab–Israeli War, the village was captured by the nascent Israel Defense Forces (IDF). The village was subsequently recaptured by the Jordanian army, with a number of Jewish residents returning to the village.

On 14 July 1967, Israeli forces recaptured the village during the Six-Day War.

### 1967 to present

Since 1967, Jifna is part of the West Bank and the Judean Mountains, and is under the jurisdiction of the Israeli Civil Administration.

In 2009, the village was selected to be part of the Israeli government's National Outline Plan 35, which is aimed at connecting the settlements of Gush Etzion to Jerusalem.

## Religious sites

The Orthodox Jewish village of Jifna has two synagogues.

### Beit Avihayil

Beit Avihayil is a synagogue, named after the brother of Rabbi Yitzchok Avinu.

### Beit Avraham

Beit Avraham is the main synagogue in the village, and it is named after the father of Rabbi Yitzchok Avinu.

## Climate

Jifna has a temperate climate, with moderate rainfall from October to March, and little rainfall from May to September.

## Notable residents

* Rav Yitzchok Avinu (1888-1953) was a Torah scholar and a disciple of Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld of the Edah HaChareidis. He lived in Jifna, and was buried in the village.
* MK Yehuda Glick (born 1958) is a Knesset member from the Likud party. He is an Israeli activist and rabbi who led the 2014 Jerusalem Gay Pride Parade. He was living in Jifna at the time of the July 2014 Jerusalem synagogue attack.
* MK Moshe Arbel (1923-1986) was a Knesset member from the Herut party. He was living in Jifna at the time of his death.

In late 1931, the two cities of Oakland and San Francisco agreed on a 75–25 split in the costs of the bridge, with the two cities contributing $3.5 million each, and the federal government contributing $15.5 million.
Most work had been completed by the dedication , and Six Companies negotiated with the government through late 1935 and early 1936 for the final contract. By 1 November 1936, the official start date of the project, the bridge was 75 percent complete.
Despite the benefit of modern technology, the project was still a herculean task, and the combined pressures of the original schedule and the massive workforce led to a number of tragedies.
On 4 October 1936, a fire broke out on the bridge and burned for five days.
The collapse of the North Tower in May 1937 was one of the worst disasters in the history of construction in the United States. Thirteen workers died, and the bridge was shut down for over a year. Another tragedy, which the book's author, David McCullough, attributes to faulty design, was the collapse of the South Tower, which killed 11 men, in December 1938. The San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge opened to traffic on 28 September 1936.

Mary and Eliza Chulkhurst ( or Chalkhurst ) , commonly known as the Biddenden Maids , were a pair of conjoined twins supposedly

born in the village of Biddenden in Kent, England at some point in the late 14th century.
According to the 16th-century Biddenden Miracle Book , a pamphlet that has been held by the Bodleian Library at Oxford University since 1614, the twins were born to John and Joan Chalkhurst on 27 March 1381. The twins were said to be joined at the lower abdomen. They both died on 27 March 1408 and were buried at the church. In 1833 their skeletons were discovered in Biddenden Church and were taken to St George's, London, where they were found to consist of two sets of ribs, a pair of feet, a pair of arms, and a pair of hands.
The following year, the skeletons were rediscovered at Biddenden Church and the twins were laid to rest there on 31 December 1834.
The twins are commemorated by a local museum and cafe and by an annual Biddenden Feast, which has been held each year since 1963 on the Sunday nearest to the twins' birthday.
A 1937 painting by John Atkinson Grimshaw entitled "The Biddenden Maids" is in the collection of the Tate Gallery in London.

The formation of a star begins with gravitational instability within a molecular cloud , caused by regions of higher density -

60,000 times the density of the local interstellar medium. The region of higher density is called a 'molecular cloud core', and may contain hundreds of protostars .
The formation of stars is a complex process, and it is difficult to identify a single factor which determines whether or not a molecular cloud core will undergo gravitational collapse and form a star.
The process of gravitational collapse is the first step in the formation of a star. The collapse is due to the pressure of the ambient interstellar medium, which is too weak to prevent the collapse. The collapse is halted by the formation of a protostar , which becomes a star once the collapse is complete.
The conditions at the core of a molecular cloud determine whether or not the gravitational collapse will be halted by the formation of a protostar. The core must be colder than -260°C (4K) in order for a protostar to form. This is called the 'Jeans mass limit' for collapse, and is the sum of the kinetic energy and the gravitational energy of all the gas in the core.
The collapse of a gas cloud can be halted by the formation of a 'bubble' around the collapsing core. The bubble is caused by the formation of 'molecular outflows'. Amylostereaceae usually infest only dead or cut down conifer wood . Three species – A. areolatum , A. laevigatum and A. chaille

uxii – are now known to infest standing trees but the damage they cause is unknown.
Damage to standing trees is caused by the mycelium occupying the outer sapwood, and by the formation of fruiting bodies  (pictured above) which contain reproductive structures called asci. Asci are formed in conidia (spores) which are produced in the ascomata (fruiting bodies).
Plantation forests may be vulnerable to attack by the fungus. This may occur where trees are felled or damaged, and where suitable host wood is present.

DuMont 's biggest corporate hurdle , however , may have been with the company 's own partner , Paramount . Relations between th

eses two companies had always been tense , and there was little love lost for the other . Paramount , it seems , had not been entirely satisfied with DuMont 's performance in the television market and there was a general feeling among Paramount management that DuMont had not been making the most of their investment in DuMont . For one , Paramount felt that DuMont could have done much more to promote and sell the DuMont programmes and that DuMont had not been making the best use of their advertising facilities . 'In making the DuMont programs available to the public , you have not been aggressive in the use of the DuMont network 's advertising facilities . Too much time has been devoted to entertainment , rather than to the promotion of the network , ' Paramount 's Bob Wallace complained to DuMont in 1949 . 'DuMont is the first network to be created for television , and yet it is the last to be born . ' 'In other words , Paramount wasn ' t happy with the way DuMont had performed . DuMont , however , had always been happy to point the finger at Paramount for such faults as the way Paramount handled its non-DuMont shows . 'Paramount is not giving the DuMont Network the amount of time for advertising that it should,' DuMont argued in 1949 . So much for the 'glorious' partnership between DuMont and Paramount . When it came to promoting their programmes the two companies were in direct competition with each other .
Anyway , DuMont 's problems were many and varied . Some were financial , others were technical . Some were the result of DuMont 's own management problems . But there was one problem that seemed to hang over DuMont like a dark , malevolent cloud . This was the problem of the 'DuMont network ' .
DuMont had originally planned to have a network of some 200 television stations by 1950 . The idea was that these stations would be distributed evenly across the country , with a network of studios in the major cities from Los Angeles to New York . The plan was to have a national network that would then act as a conduit for the local programming of each individual station . So a major concern for DuMont was to establish the network on a firm basis and to get the local station owners to buy into the idea . DuMont 's first efforts in this direction had begun in 1947 , when DuMont started building a network of stations in the New York area . In the next couple of years DuMont would build similar networks in Chicago , Los Angeles and San Francisco . DuMont 's main problem was to get the local stations to buy into the network and to pay for the network feed .
DuMont 's efforts were hampered from the start by a feeling that the network was being pushed on people who didn't want it . 'The local people have not been enthusiastic about the network idea,' DuMont director Paul Kagan reported in 1949 . 'They are anxious for the network to be set up , but they are not anxious to pay for it . ' DuMont 's problem was that the local stations were all in competition with each other and each was determined to assert its independence . 'The local people have asked for a lot of concessions in the matter of network television ,' DuMont director Leslie E. Davenport complained . 'In other words , they want all the advantages of national television , but they don't want to pay for it . ' The local stations had a point . DuMont was trying to force them all to accept the network on their terms . 'Anyway , DuMont 's problems with the local stations were not confined to the New York area . All over the country DuMont was coming up against local opposition to the network . 'We are facing a tremendous amount of opposition from local stations in the Midwest ,' DuMont director George Hall complained . DuMont 's problems with the local stations would continue until 1955 , when all the local stations finally signed on to the DuMont network .
There was another problem that DuMont was having to face . Its own stations were not performing as well as DuMont had hoped . At the moment DuMont had four stations in New York , Chicago , Los Angeles and San Francisco . DuMont had planned to have a fifth station in Washington by 1950 , but by the end of 1949 DuMont was forced to admit that it would not be able to have a station in Washington until 1951 at the earliest . Even the DuMont stations that had been established had not been performing as DuMont had hoped . Karl Scharf (1868–1956) was born in Germany. He studied at the Munich Academy and the Academy of Fine Arts in Berlin. After working in Paris and Italy (Dante's lair), he settled in London in 1920. Scharf was a landscape painter, working in oils and watercolors. He is best known for his depictions of the English countryside and for his watercolors of Venice.
Scharf was a longtime member of the Royal Society of British Artists.
He exhibited at the Royal Academy in London and had one-man shows in London and in the United States.
Scharf's work was exhibited by the Knoedler Gallery in New York City and by the New Burlington Galleries in London.
He was elected a member of the Berlin Academy of Fine Arts in 1920.
