The Yellowstone River flows from the Absaroka Mountains in Wyoming to the Missouri River in Montana, a distance of 672 miles. It's the longest free-flowing river in the lower 48 states, and its waters are clear and clean, unlike the muddy Missouri. The splendor of Yellowstone can be seen on a map: the river's source, the Absaroka, is the highest mountain range in the country, peaking at 13,804 feet in the Grand Teton National Park. The river flows through the Yellowstone National Park, where it is fed by seventy-one hot springs, geysers, and two of the world's largest lakes, Old Faithful and Yellowstone. The Yellowstone is the youngest national park in the United States, created in 1872. One year later, the hot springs, geysers, and mud pots were designated a National Park. The park is about the size of Rhode Island, 3,470 square miles, and in 1873 it was almost filled with the smoke from wildfires. But the Yellowstone River was cool and clear.
It was the summer of 1873, and Dr. John Warren, the clerk of the United States Court in Helena, Montana, was on his way home from the capital when he saw something in the distance. It was a large herd of buffalo. Bison. The herd was so large that he could not see the other end of the herd. It stretched across the Yellowstone for miles and miles. It was a buffalo stampede. The bison had been driven out of their normal habitat by wildfires and drought, and they were fleeing the fires and drought in search of water and grass.
The herd continued to move as the sun set and the stars came out. Warren hurried to find a place to spend the night. He was on horseback, and he had no idea where he was. He was hundreds of miles from home. He was lost and alone. He was in Yellowstone.
For the first time since 1825, when the Lewis and Clark expedition arrived in the Northwest Territory, the vast wilderness of Yellowstone was opened to the public. The federal government in Washington, D.C., had decided to protect the land, but they were not going to close the area to people. It was too vast to be closed to people. There was no way to protect the land from the threat of development. The best way to protect it was to allow people to go in and see it.
But the people who went into Yellowstone were not the kind of people who would write letters to the government about the beauty of the wilderness and what it needed to be preserved. The people who went into the wilderness were the kind of people who did not write letters to the government. They were the kind of people who went into the wilderness to kill buffalo.
The buffalo herds were on the brink of extinction. Bands of Indians had killed them for food and clothing, and white men had killed them for sport. They had killed so many that there were no more. The government had turned the land over to the people who wanted to kill buffalo. The buffalo hunter was born.
The buffalo hunter was a cowboy and a hunter, a good shot, and a man who was not afraid to get into a fight. The buffalo hunter was a man who knew the land and who had lived with the land all his life. The buffalo hunter was a man who rode a horse and was dressed in buckskins. He was a man who wanted to make a living and was willing to risk his life to do it.

Written by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807-1882) , the poem " The Arrow and the Song " was first published in the collection Ballads and Other Poems (1841) . It is divided into five six-line stanzas.
The poem " The Arrow and the Song " is a ballad about a medieval knight who falls in love with a maiden, writes songs about her, and then becomes enamored of another woman. The poem is in the form of a dialogue between the knight and his lady who asks why he does not write her songs anymore. The knight tells her that he only has enough love for one woman.
The poem has been set to music by a number of composers. In 1845, Henry Bishop set the poem to music as " The Harp that Once through Tara's Halls " . In 1861, Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg set the poem to music as " I Love You" . This is the setting that most people are familiar with.

The 13 C-containing amino acids are labeled by growing the cells in the presence of 15 N-free 13 C-containing amino acids. These amino acids are not incorporated into the cellular proteome at the same rate, though. The incorporation of arginine and proline is relatively fast, whereas that of leucine, valine, and glutamate is relatively slow. Taking advantage of this difference in the incorporation rates of 13 C-containing amino acids, we can quantify the synthesis and localization of proteins by using two different 13 C-labeled amino acids.

Passengers traveling from Western to Northern Norway had to transfer from Braathens SAFE to SAS in Trondheim . Both airlines sa

iled the northern route from Trondheim to Tromsø , Kirkenes and Bodø .

In 1962, Braathens SAFE (with the parent company Braathens) entered into a joint venture called Braathens SAFE SAS (BS-SAAS) for the joint operation of services between Trondheim and the northern capital cities of Tromsø , Kirkenes and Bodø . The service was named "SAS Nord" and the airline's aircraft and uniforms were painted in the SAS colors, but the flight operation was controlled by Braathens.

In 1971 the service from Trondheim to Tromsø and Kirkenes was withdrawn. Also in 1971, the Norwegian government allowed Braathens SAS to operate flights to Oslo , but the agreement was terminated in 1972. The service to Bodø was suspended in 1974, and the whole "SAS Nord" service was terminated in 1976.

The Industrial Revolution led to extensive mechanization , resulting in a shift from home manufacturing to large @-@ scale fact

ories. Further industrialization, the adoption of divorce and legalized abortion , in addition to the advent of effective birth control , led to falling birth rates , precipitating the present-day "ageing population" problem. The Industrial Revolution also helped create the notion of leisure time, which has led to the leisure industry.
In the 18th century, the Enlightenment challenged the Christian world view. The Enlightenment encouraged the liberation of women and the abolition of slavery . The Enlightenment also promoted reason and free will , natural rights , tolerance , fraternity , and separation of church and state . The Enlightenment was marked by a growing skepticism regarding supernatural claims , a rise in deism , and the development of natural philosophy into a science .
The first half of the 19th century saw a gradual shift to democratic ways of governing , with many nations establishing republics , abolishing monarchies , and adopting liberal constitutions. The 18th-century Enlightenment was followed by the 19th-century Age of Revolutions in Europe. Major revolutions took place in France in 1789, Haiti in 1804, and in many nations in Europe between 1815 and 1848. The 1848 revolutions were a series of political upheavals throughout Europe. These uprisings were triggered by major social and economic issues including the Revolutions of 1848 in France, the Palmer Raids , the Paris Commune , the establishment of the German Empire , and the Meiji Restoration in Japan.
In the second half of the 19th century, the world experienced rapid economic, cultural, and political change. Starting around the year 1870, the British Empire was at its height, followed by the French and Russian Empires. Capitalism and colonialism expanded throughout the world. The process of de-industrialization began in 1913 when the United Kingdom became an imperial power. The First World War began in 1914 and ended in 1918, with the signing of the Treaty of Versailles.
The First World War was a major turning point in world history. It was a global conflict of unprecedented scale and carnage . The total number of deaths from all causes is estimated to have been over 38 million. The war left approximately 20 million wounded. About 60 million Europeans were displaced. The Allied powers won the war. In the wake of the conflict, the League of Nations was formed to maintain future peace.
The Second World War followed the First World War , lasting from 1939 to 1945, with a total of 60 million to 85 million people killed. The war culminated in the defeat of the Axis powers , and the establishment of the Cold War between the Allies and the Soviet Union . After the war, the world was divided into two main blocs, the Western Bloc and the Eastern Bloc. This opposition eventually led to the rise of communism in China, Eastern Europe , and the Soviet Union . The Cold War continued until 1991, when the USSR was dissolved.
The 1960s and 1970s were marked by economic expansion and the rise of the developing world, with an end to colonialism and the creation of new nations. Protests against the Vietnam War sparked numerous anti-war movements. The 1970s were also characterized by a period of economic stagnation, known as stagflation , due to the Arab oil embargo.
The 1980s were marked by the beginning of the International Space Station , the fall of the Berlin Wall , and the end of the Cold War through the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. In the 1990s, post-Communist states began to establish democratic governments. The end of the Cold War resulted in the beginnings of globalization . At the same time, the late 20th and early 21st century are characterized by increased concern about environmental issues.
The 21st century has been characterized by a rise in nationalism , tribalism , and populism . Globalization has continued and the stock market crash of 2007-2008 was followed by a slow economic recovery. The rise of social media has altered the way in which information is disseminated.

The tawny nurse shark is widely distributed in the Indo @-@ Pacific region . In the Indian Ocean , it is found from KwaZulu @-@

Natal , South Africa in the east to Japan in the west . In the Pacific , it is found in South China Sea , Taiwan , Philippines , Indonesia , Papua New Guinea , Solomon Islands , Vanuatu , and Australia . It is also reported to be a resident of the western Atlantic Ocean .
the tawny nurse shark is a large animal reaching lengths up to 3.2m . The coloration is pale brown to yellowish tan with darker bands on the sides and a darker blotch on the upper sides of the pectoral fins . The dorsal and tail fins are a darker brown .
The tawny nurse shark is found from 70m to 700m deep . It is usually solitary but sometimes in small groups . It is nocturnal , feeding on crustaceans , cephalopods , worms , and fishes . It is slow moving .
The tawny nurse shark is oviparous , breeding in the spring and summer . The female produces 20 to 50 eggs , which are covered with a gelatinous substance . The eggs are about 14cm in diameter and are attached to the female's body by a string . The eggs hatch after 12 to 15 months .

Allosaurus meriani was described in 1870 by Greppin as a species of Megalosaurus , based on a tooth from the Late Jurassic of S

insheim, Germany.
Shinji Sato in 1976 found that the tooth was from a different species, and in 1995, he renamed it in honor of the geologist Karl Merian.
Allosaurus meriani was a bipedal carnivore that lived in the late Jurassic period. In spite of that, other dinosaurs of that epoch were much bigger, reaching a length of 25 meters and a weight of 40 tons.
It had a length of about 6 meters, a height at the hip of 1.6 meters, and weighed about 1.8 tons. Its arms were about 2.5 meters long, and its tail was almost as long. It had small arms, which is unusual in predatory dinosaurs, and it had two claws on each of its three-toed feet. A large crest ran along its back.
It had a narrow skull with a large, bony protuberance, the bourrelet, in the front of the upper jaw. The crest, though, was the most distinctive feature. It was over 20 cm long and had two bony projections, or keratins, on each side.
The species was described from a single tooth which was discovered in the late 19th century. The tooth was relatively large and had been broken in two, splitting the crown in half. It was found in the Hettangian–Sinemurian section of the Solenhofen Formation of Sinsheim, a site famous for its numerous Jurassic fossils. The tooth was then housed in the collection of the Naturhistorisches Museum in Vienna before it was described by Greppin in 1870. Sato in 1976 noted the unusual shape of the tooth and compared it to other theropod teeth. He noted that it was more similar to the tooth of the large theropod Allosaurus than to those of the smaller Megalosaurus.
Sato further noted that the tooth had been incorrectly described by Greppin as belonging to a Megalosaurus and that it was actually a distinct species. He also noted that the tooth was not the only Allosaurus tooth in the collection, and that it had been part of an assortment of bones that were determined by Greppin to be Megalosaurus. Sato therefore redescribed the tooth in 1995 with the genus name Allosaurus, as he considered it to be a distinct species. He further noted that it was an unusual tooth in the genus, as it was much larger than the typical teeth.
The type specimen of A. meriani is the holotype, BSP AS 54266, which consists of the left upper tooth from near the glenoid cavity. The tooth was broken in two, splitting the crown in half. It was found in the Lohmeyer Clay Member of the Solenhofen Formation, in the town of Sinsheim in the Rhenish Hesse region of Germany. This formation is part of the Hettangian–Sinemurian boundary. The formation is known for its numerous fossils and it is considered to be among the most important fossil localities in the world.
The generic name Allosaurus is derived from the Greek words allos (άλλος), meaning "different", and sauros (σαύρος), meaning "lizard". The specific name meriani is derived from the geologist Karl Merian (died 1887), who was involved in the collection of the specimen by the Museum für Naturkunde in Berlin.
The skull of A. meriani was described only from the holotype tooth. The tooth itself had a length of 52 mm, and was 39 mm wide at the base. It had a relatively large crest, which was 25 mm long. It had two distinct keratins on each side of the crest, which were 9 mm long, 6 mm wide and 1 mm thick. The dentition was typical of theropods, consisting of a single row of conical teeth. The tooth was relatively long compared to other teeth in the genus, and the crest was the most distinctive feature.
The tooth was the only fossil of Allosaurus meriani known to science, and it was discovered in Germany. However, Allosaurus fossils have also been found in the United States, and the same tooth morphology has been found on other continents.

education.  The Education Act 1944 also provided for the establishment of a Secondary Schools Council to advise the Minister of Education on matters of secondary education, and to co-ordinate the provision of secondary education in each area.  The Council's aim was to remove all discrimination in secondary education, and to provide a wider educational experience for all pupils.  However the Act did not abolish the grammar school system, which was still considered the best form of state secondary education by many teachers and parents.  The first secondary schools to be established under the Act were later called "comprehensive" schools, but this term was not used until the 1950s, when it was frequently used by newspapers to describe the new education system.  The schools were called "secondary modern" schools in the Act.
 The Education Act 1944 was amended by the Education Act 1947, which abolished the 11-plus examination for secondary modern schools, but retained it for grammar schools.  The Education Act 1944 was also amended by the Education Act 1948, which provided for some grammar schools to become comprehensive.
The 1944 Act was repealed by the Education Act 1944 (Amendment) Act 1953 which included a clause to abolish all school fees in 1955.  This Act was itself repealed by the Education Act 1962.

Arundel House was originally the town house of the Bishops of Bath and Wells . It was owned by William FitzWilliam , 1st Earl o

f Southampton , and, while his nephew, Charles Howard, 1st Earl of Carlisle , was ambassador in Paris, it was leased to the French court. As an ostentatious display of courtly taste and the new science of taste, in 1702 the house and grounds were transformed by the architect William Talman and the landscape architect Charles Bridgeman . The gardens were later described by William Stukeley as 'the best in England'.
The estate was sold to the Crown in 1731 and the house demolished in 1760, the grounds being laid out as a pleasure ground by 'Capability' Brown .
The gardens were sold to the City of London in 1887 and were partly laid out as a public open space.
The site is now occupied by the headquarters of the Institute of Directors .
The gardens were opened to the public on 4 July 1990.

Her political mettle and ambitions for her husband were however to be more severely tested following the Liberal victory . Rose

bery needed support from the Conservative Party to keep his combination in power, and this he knew would be tenuous. By the summer of 1895, Conservatives, including the king, had become restive about the prime minister's conduct of foreign policy, particularly his policy towards France and the Entente Cordiale.* Radicals too, who controlled the Labour Party, were also increasingly disenchanted. The Liberal split and the government's eventual fall were a consequence of the king's and Conservatives' falling out with Rosebery over the Entente Cordiale. The king, by then convinced that the Entente Cordiale had left England dangerously exposed to France, raised the issue with his private secretary Sir Francis Knollys, who told him that 'Lord Rosebery's views were very different'. When the king asked him to arrange a meeting with Rosebery, Knollys replied: 'I do not think it would be good for the government if the Duke of Devonshire, Lord Salisbury, Lord Rosebery and Lord Balfour all met together in a small room.' The king was enraged and Lord Salisbury was forced to resign. Rosebery was left in charge, but his political future was now doubtful.
After the Conservatives and the Liberals had agreed to form a coalition government, Rosebery's chances of remaining in office looked slim. His supporters, like his wife, were distressed. 'If some of those old heroes of the Liberal Party were still alive,' wrote Lady Rosebery, 'they would have risen in their graves to remonstrate.' In the end, Rosebery's political career was further curtailed when he was appointed a lord of the Admiralty after the coalition came to power.
When the Liberal leader, Lord Rosebery, came to see her in 1894, he spoke with apparent sincerity of his intention to push for women's suffrage. The Liberals had already won over the Scottish women's suffrage movement. In 1893 they had passed the franchise bill for Scotland, the first of its kind in the world. This move, as we have seen, had been in part a consequence of female pressure on the Liberals. Lady Rosebery now had to pull her weight. 'My husband was very anxious to know what women thought,' Lady Rosebery told the suffragist movement. 'He has been studying the question of women's suffrage very carefully, and is anxious to bring it before the House of Commons.' When Lady Rosebery agreed to serve on the executive committee of the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies (NUWSS), she was the only woman in the committee, and she became vice-president in 1895. She also served for a short time on the executive committee of the Women's Franchise League, and agreed to speak for the NUWSS in the House of Lords. Lady Rosebery asked her husband to take the lead in the House of Lords on the issue. 'I am doing all I can to make him speak in the House of Lords,' she wrote in 1895, 'but I am afraid he will not be allowed to do so, as they only allow one member to speak.'
Lady Rosebery's own faith in her husband's commitment, however, was not so strong. At home she was now critical of his willingness to give priority to the NUWSS over his own political career. She was also sceptical about the Liberal Party's commitment to women's suffrage. 'I think it is not likely that the Liberal Party will do anything for Women's suffrage,' she wrote to Gertrude Tuckwell in 1895. 'But I am doing all I can to induce them to do something.' It was an ironic position for her to be in, as she had been the one who had persuaded her husband to support women's suffrage. She now felt that his political ambitions had come to outweigh his commitment to women's suffrage. In 1895 she told Gertrude Tuckwell: 'I think the duke would like to do something for women's suffrage, but he is afraid to do it, and I am afraid he will not do it.'

ball as one of the major talking points ahead of the season.
With Marcus Trescothick having moved to Nottinghamshire for 2009 and Ian Blackwell promoted to the professional ranks, Somerset had a new opening pair for the 2009 season.
The pair, of course, had previously played together at Glamorgan and were joined by their captain, Marcus Trescothick.
However, it was the capture of South African James Harris from Nottinghamshire for a fee of £250,000, that saw Somerset sign one of the most sought after players in England. Harris was signed as a direct replacement for Ian Blackwell who had been promoted to the professional ranks.
In addition, Somerset also had a new overseas player when the South African wicket-keeper-batsman, Justin Kemp, joined in a short-term deal.
Somerset's 2009 season was to include a tour of Uganda.
Trescothick, who was now captain, was selected for England's ODI squad for the summer and in the absence of Marcus Trescothick, Alec Stewart was named as Somerset's new captain.
In Somerset's first match of the season, against Middlesex, a new-ball partnership between McCoy and Harris proved to be a winning one. Somerset were setting a small target  and with the ball swinging, the new-ball pair were able to work through Middlesex's top order.
Having taken 5 wickets between them in the first innings, McCoy and Harris were able to repeat their performance in the second innings.
Somerset's 2009 season was to be a successful one, with the side finishing in the top four of the County Championship.  The side also reached the quarter finals of the Friends Provident Trophy.

## Plot

The episode starts with a man who lives in the suburbs, named "Suburban Dad", who has a wife and three kids. While watching television, he is exposed to a commercial for the "Itchy and Scratchy" cartoon show on television. The family are fans of the show, and every day, he leaves with his kids to go to the "Itchy and Scratchy" theme park. However, while there, he always leaves his kids with others, and spends most of the day at the bar.

The next day, the family go to the theme park. While there, Homer and the kids play a game where they shoot water cannons at each other. Homer leaves the kids to go to the bar, and after a while, the kids ask the park employees to take them to their father. The park employees bring them to their father, who is now in the bar. Homer is told that his kids are waiting outside, but he says that if they wait another five minutes, he will come, and the kids leave. Homer goes to the bar, where he and his friends drink beer. Meanwhile, the kids are still at the park, and Bart, Lisa, and Maggie begin to get hungry. Bart then tries to go to the bar, but the bartender tells him that he is not allowed in, because he is underage. Bart then tries to go to a cafeteria, but it is closed.

As Bart and the kids are getting hungry, for some reason, Bart's hair turns white. The kids begin to wonder why Bart's hair is turning white, and begin to walk around the park, which is now closed. While they are walking, Lisa asks Bart what happened to all the workers of the park, and Bart says that they all left, because their jobs were ruined. After Bart's hair stops turning white, he and his siblings start to walk back to their car, and Bart notices a sign that says "No Children Allowed", and goes into the bar.

After this, Homer gets a phone call from the kids. He is told that they are hungry, and Homer tells them to wait for ten more minutes, and he will be right there. After Homer and his friends leave the bar, the kids ask the park employees what is going on, and they tell them that the park is closed. The kids begin to wonder why their father is not there, and Bart realizes that their father is in the bar. Bart, Lisa, and Maggie go into the bar, where they are surprised that their father is in there. Bart then tries to convince his father to come home, but Homer tells him that he is not coming home. Bart then tries to go into the bar, but the bartender tells him to stop, saying that Bart is underage, and Bart is thrown out of the bar.

Bart kicks and screams, and after a while, he is thrown out of the bar. Bart then begins to walk home, and soon after, the kids leave the park, and start walking home. After a while, Bart and Lisa convince Maggie to take off her clothes, and they all begin to walk home. After a while, Bart and his sisters are stopped by police officers, who arrest them, and take them to jail. Bart then realizes that he forgot to pack their things, so he goes to the park, where he is stopped by the park employees. Bart then asks for his things, and when he is told that he must leave, Bart tells him that he forgot his clothes.

The park employees then take Bart's clothes, and he goes to the cafeteria, where he eats dinner. After eating, Bart and his siblings are released from jail, where they go home, and the episode ends with Homer saying that next time, they will be taking the kids to the park.

He also thought that Sphaerothorax was a close relative of Dimetrodon, and so he placed them both in the order Sphenodontia .
In 1971 , the Russian paleontologist Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska named and described a large iguanodont , probably older than Dimetrodon , which she named Sphaerothorax . However, in 1978 , the American paleontologist Robert Bakker named and described another large iguanodont , and this time he named it Sphaerothorax. **
In 1981 , the American paleontologist Peter Dodson named and described a toothless, antlered dinosaur . The Battle of Monte Cassino was a costly series of four assaults by the Allies against the Winter Line in Italy held by Axis forces during the Italian Campaign of World War II. The intention was a thrust to the Liri Valley in central Italy; three of these assaults were launched from the town of Cassino, in the region of Lazio.

For other battles, see Battle of Monte Cassino (disambiguation).

The first assault was launched on 17 January 1944 by the New Zealand 2nd Division, early in the Italian Campaign. Three further attacks followed in February, March and May; the last was launched by the Polish 2nd Corps. It was two years after the armistice of Cassibile, after the Italian Campaign had already lasted for nearly two years.

The town of Cassino and the abbey on Monte Cassino had been destroyed during the Allied bombing of strategic targets in central Italy in the months before the campaign, but the town was built up again after the war.

## Background

Main article: Battle of Anzio

The Battle of Monte Cassino was a part of the broader Battle of Anzio which began on 22 January 1944, when the Allies launched Operation Shingle, with landings at Anzio and Nettuno. The Allies' aim was to break through the Winter Line and drive north towards Rome. Despite initial successes, the Germans managed to contain the Allied advance into a small bridgehead at Anzio.

On 4 February, the Allies launched Operation Lustre, a diversionary attack on the Germans' flank and rear. This was the first of four assaults on Cassino; the second was launched on 15 February, the third on 11 March, and the fourth and final assault to break the German line at Anzio was launched on 12 May.

## Battle

### First assault

Monte Cassino in mid-1944

#### Initial attacks

Further information: Battle of Anzio § New Zealand assault on Monte Cassino

The first of the assaults on Monte Cassino was launched by the New Zealand 2nd Division on 17 January 1944. It was intended to be a diversionary attack, in support of Operation Shingle, to draw enemy forces away from the battle for Anzio, but it was not successful.

The Allies had hoped that the attack, combined with Operation Shingle and Operation Corkscrew, would break through the German defences on the Winter Line and enable the capture of Rome. The attack was launched by the New Zealand 4th Brigade, with the New Zealand 6th Brigade in support. The attack was preceded by an artillery preparation, which included both medium and heavy calibre guns, followed by an air raid. The attack was intended to be launched in three phases, with the first and third phases consisting of attacks by infantry. The second phase was to be a tank attack, with the infantry following up the tanks' advance.

The attack was initially successful, but German reserves were brought up, and the attack stalled. The New Zealanders were then pushed back, and the position was held by the 4th Brigade.

The 1st New Zealand Division's attack was successful, but the 4th Brigade was heavily counterattacked, and lost 220 officers and men. In the end, the attack had not broken through the German line, and the New Zealanders remained in their positions.

The assault was one of the first uses of the American M4A2 Sherman "Jumbo" tank, which had a large 76 mm gun instead of the 75 mm gun, which was standard on the M4 Sherman tank. This allowed the Sherman tank to break through the German defences.

### Second assault

Bad weather prevented the planned attack on 15 February, but the attack went ahead on 15 March. The assault was launched by the 46th Infantry Division. The assault was a failure, and the Americans were pushed back. On 11 March, the Poles of the 1st Armoured Division were ordered to relieve the exhausted 46th Infantry Division.

### Third assault

Monte Cassino was of strategic importance not only because of its position on a ridge between the Liri Valley and the town of Cassino, but also because it was a communications hub.

### Coins struck at Philadelphia

The Philadelphia Mint began striking gold dollars on October 13 , 1849 , the same day that the first silver dollars were struck . The first gold dollars bore date 1849 , and the date was changed to 1850 in 1850 . On the obverse was the image of Liberty , facing left , wearing a Phrygian cap and holding a staff in her right hand and an olive branch in her left hand . The reverse showed an eagle with its wings outstretched , perched on a rock . The denomination was inscribed in Roman numerals , LIBERTY . The engraver was Mint Chief Engraver James B. Longacre , who later designed many other American coins .

### Coins struck at New Orleans

The New Orleans Mint struck gold dollars from 1850 to 1854 . The New Orleans dollars were identical to the Philadelphia dollars except that the word CENTS was added above the denomination in Roman numerals . The first New Orleans dollars were dated 1850 , but the date was changed to 1851 in 1851 , then to 1852 in 1852 . The New Orleans Mint struck only three dated 1853 ( the last year of issue for the New Orleans Mint ) , which were then dated 1854 .

The 130th's mission was to provide support to the regiment during Operation Desert Storm. The 11th Regiment was charged with capturing Kuwait City from the Iraqis. The 130th Engineer Brigade was responsible for constructing a bridge across the Iraqi-Kuwaiti border to allow the regiment to cross the desert and link up with the 1st Armored Division, which was then besieging Iraqi forces at the Rumayla oil field.
The 130th was commanded by Colonel James K. Kessler, a 39-year-old former drill instructor in the Army. Kessler, who had commanded the brigade in the 1980s during a yearlong deployment to Germany, was a tall, strapping man with a booming voice and a big smile. He was known for his jokes and his love of country and the Army. A West Point graduate, Kessler had served in Vietnam and had earned a Silver Star for valor in combat. When he was assigned to the 130th, Kessler told his staff that he had no problem swimming across the Persian Gulf. "I don't know how deep it is," he said, "but I'll get across."
On December 24, 1990, the 130th Engineer Brigade received orders to deploy to Saudi Arabia. The brigade was ordered to leave within three days and to include 125 combat engineers in its ranks. The order was given at 8:00 A.M. on the twenty-fifth. There were no extra tickets available, so Kessler and General Edward Mercer, the state adjutant general, left for Washington, D.C., on the twenty-sixth on separate flights. Kessler's first stop was to visit his wife and two daughters at their home in Manassas, Virginia, before he flew to Dulles Airport. He had not seen them since Christmas Eve and had only a few hours to say good-bye. "I'm going overseas," he told his wife, Donna, over dinner. "I'll be back in a couple of weeks."
"You know what I'm thinking?" Donna asked.
"What's that, honey?"
"You're going to get killed."
"I'm not," Kessler said. "I've been in the service for twenty-four years and I've never been killed. I'm not going to start now."
At Dulles, Kessler caught the first flight to Frankfurt. He arrived on the twenty-seventh and headed to Ramstein Air Base where he found a room at the Air Force Inn. Kessler's flight to Saudi Arabia was scheduled for the next morning. He said good-bye to his wife and daughters and took a cab to the air base. He arrived at 7:00 A.M. The flight was scheduled to depart at 10:30 A.M., but the airport was a chaotic scene. There were soldiers, sailors, and Marines everywhere. The terminal was packed with people, and the noise was deafening. Kessler was tired and hungry, but excited. He was about to do something he had never done before—go to war.
Kessler waited two hours to board the flight. He had time to have breakfast and catch a few hours of sleep. He soon found himself sitting next to two young privates who were also headed for Saudi Arabia. The two privates were travelling alone. They had no family with them and were going to see their first combat. Kessler tried to put them at ease by telling them what to expect. "Don't worry, the war won't last long," he said. "It'll be over in a couple of weeks."
The three men boarded the plane and took their seats. The plane taxied to the end of the runway and began to roll. After a short time, it lifted off and headed toward the desert.

He was the son of Abraham Zimmerman and Beatrice Stone . His father, a high-school graduate, worked as an electric-appliance repairman. His mother, a graduate of the University of Minnesota , was an elementary school teacher. Dylan had three siblings, all older: two brothers, David and Jacob , and a sister, Mary . The family moved to Hibbing, Minnesota in 1949, where Dylan's father worked in the iron mines until the family moved to Duluth again in 1952. He took up the harmonica at age 10, and began writing songs at the age of 12. 2.2 Musical career Beginnings In his early teens, Dylan dropped out of school and began performing in Duluth clubs with harmonica players Mickey Nelson and Al Osteen. Nelson introduced Dylan to the music of Woody Guthrie, which was to have a profound influence on his music. In January 1960 , Dylan went to New York City , where he began performing alone in coffeehouses . In April 1961, Dylan met Joan Baez at a club on MacDougal Street . Baez had just had a major hit with a song by the writer Rolf Cahn, in which she had changed the sex of the subject so that it was a man. She was performing " With God on Our Side " , which Dylan had heard at the Gaslight . Dylan and Baez became romantically involved, and Baez introduced him to her manager, Albert Grossman. In April 1962, Dylan's debut album, Bob Dylan , was released on Columbia Records. It was produced by John Hammond , the legendary talent scout, who signed Dylan to the label . The album was not a commercial success, but it brought Dylan to the attention of the folk community in the Greenwich Village neighborhood of Manhattan. On the album, Dylan recorded two of his best-known songs, " Subterranean Homesick Blues " and " Like a Rolling Stone ", which are considered to be the beginning of his electric era. His next album, Highway 61 Revisited (August 1965), featured a backing band that included Mike Bloomfield , Al Kooper , and Sam Lay . By the early 1970s , it was uncertain whether the kakapo was still an extant species . At the end of 1974 , scientists located

50 birds and proposed naming the species the ' bird of the century ' . A number of ornithologists and bird-lovers , including Sir Peter Shand of the Department of Conservation , were invited to select the name for the species. Some of those attending the meeting , including Peter , suggested the name ' kakapo ' ; the decision was taken to consult the Maori people who had a great knowledge of the names of birds in their language .
The kakapo is the largest parrot in the world and the only flightless parrot.
It is native to New Zealand, and has been called the parrot of the night. It is threatened by predation from feral cats and rats.

On September 15, the Joint Typhoon Warning Center began issuing advisories on Tropical Depression 22W, located about 950 nmi (1,760 km) to the east of the island of Luzon in the Philippine Sea. At 0000 UTC on September 16, the agency began issuing Tropical Storm 22W advisories. The agency ceased to issue advisories on the storm on September 18, as it weakened below tropical storm force winds. The JMA issued its final advisory on Tropical Storm 22W as it traversed the Luzon Strait on September 17, though the JTWC continued to issue advisories until September 20.

Relay races are the only track and field event in which a team of runners directly compete against other teams . Typically , a

4 × 100 m relay is composed of four runners, each of whom contributes a length of 100 m. The first runner leaves the starting blocks and runs the distance in the fastest possible time. When that runner crosses the finish line, he or she delivers a baton to the second runner, who then begins to run. When the second runner reaches the finish line, the baton is passed to the third runner, who then completes the distance. Lastly, the fourth and final runner runs the distance, and the race is ended when he or she crosses the finish line.
The time of a relay race is typically recorded in seconds and is the combined time of all four runners. The team with the fastest time wins the event. The world record for 4 × 100 m relay is 36.84 seconds, held by the United States since 1993.
Relay races are also run at shorter distances. In 4 × 200 m, the team with the fastest time is declared the winner.

After the 3rd battle of Yellow Sea, in 1905, the Japanese Government ordered a new modern battleship from the British to replace the old battleship Hizen . In 1905, the Japanese Government signed a contract with Armstrongs to build of two new ships of the Dreadnought class. A year later, the Japanese Government ordered two more of the same type from Armstrongs. These ships were called the Shikishima class. All of the four ships were built in the Elswick yard. They were launched in 1906 and 1907. They were completed in 1907 and 1908. They were the first Japanese battleships to use the Whitehead torpedoes.
The ships were armed with ten 12-inch guns and eight 6-inch guns, housed in four twin turrets. They had a top speed of 21.5 knots. During World War I, the ships were used to patrol the Sea of Japan. In 1919, the Imperial Japanese Navy decommissioned the vessels, and they were broken up for scrap.

Active patrolling by mounted troops continued throughout the period leading up to the battle , but by early July , there were n

horses available for this purpose. 46 This meant that the ring of active patrolling could not be maintained, and the cavalry resorted to a series of outposts that were located in the high ground. In each case, the cavalry held the high ground until they were relieved, and then fell back to the next position. Each position was placed so as to cover the ground which had been covered by the cavalry patrols in the past, and each position was held until relieved. 47
It is important to understand that the cavalry was not patrolling the 3000 yards of the valley in the traditional manner. It was moving on tracks that crossed the valley floor, and at times only a single track existed, with the cavalry alternating between the two sides of the valley. The reason for this was that the ground was covered with scrub, and the tracks were the only way to get around it. 48
This system of patrolling meant that the cavalry was not moving up and down the valley as a unit, but moving from one position to another in a series of leaps and bounds. 49 These leaps were not made at random. They were dictated by the ground over which the cavalry had to move. 50

In 2013 and 2014 , auction house sales demonstrated the high cultural value attached to Dylan 's mid @-@ 1960s work , and the r

arity of his early work. The two sets of manuscripts—the Columbia Records acetates and the Basement Tapes—attracted incredible attention, and both were sold for enormous amounts. The acetates, previously thought to be lost, realized a high price, in part because they reveal another version of the same songs, not to mention noises, laughter, and studio chatter. The Basement Tapes manuscripts were even more surprising, for they were also thought to exist only in the fabled Columbia Records tapes.
Their sale was controversial, in part because the sale of manuscripts is unprecedented in American music history, but also because both sets of manuscripts were from the same collection. The Columbia tapes were sold by the original owner, the collector Clinton Heylin, who had bought them from the original owner, Dylan's manager, Albert Grossman. The Basement Tapes manuscripts were sold by the original owner, the collector Paul Coury, who had bought them from the original owner, Dylan's then manager, Jeff Rosen.
In the case of the Columbia tapes, the manuscripts prove how carefully Dylan and the musicians worked in the studio. The artifacts are a significant addition to our understanding of Dylan's process: we can see and hear Dylan working with the musicians, hearing the musicians' suggestions, and working through the songs. Although the Basement Tapes manuscripts do not reveal Dylan and the musicians working in the studio, they are still significant because they reveal how Dylan worked with words and music, and how he worked alone, and how he worked with the musicians.
The Columbia acetates reveal how Dylan and the musicians worked in the studio, and the Basement Tapes manuscripts reveal how Dylan worked alone, and with the musicians.
For 2015, I will be focusing on the years 1961–1963, including Dylan's early 1960s songs, his first albums ( _Bob Dylan_ , 1962, and _The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan_ , 1963), and his first live performances.
In this volume, I will be concentrating as much on Dylan's music as his lyrics, but I will also be attending closely to the words, paying close attention to the stories Dylan tells, the stories he leaves out, and the stories listeners and readers construct. I will be looking at how Dylan's early work is both a product of its time and a commentary on its time. But I will also be looking at how Dylan's early work reflects and comments on the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s.
I will be talking about Dylan's early work in the context of American history, in the context of popular music, and in the context of American culture. This book will not be a biography, or a scholarly study. This book will be, in part, a story of what it is to be an artist.

In 1913, however, the Revolution split into two factions: a reformist one led by Venustiano Carranza and a Communist one led by Zapata. The latter, in an effort to bring more of the country under his control, launched a campaign of terror against the rural areas that were loyal to Carranza, seeking to intimidate the revolutionaries into switching sides. Zapata's men often raided small towns, killing those who opposed him and leaving their bodies scattered around the town square. In some cases, they also killed women and children. Most of the victims were hanged from a telegraph pole or a church bell. The movement was not just a matter of revenge against the landowners, but also a way of terrorizing the population into accepting the revolutionary project.
For many years, the army had grown increasingly powerful in Mexico. In fact, the army had been the only entity within the state to have a monopoly over the use of force. This was why the Revolution had to fight against the military from the very beginning, and why it was so difficult to disarm and dissolve the institution. In 1915, Zapata was assassinated in a battle against the army.

On the one hand, we had the Constitutionalist forces, headed by Carranza and supported by the conservative political elite in the country, who wanted to preserve the old political system. Orozco, also known as Cabeza de Serpiente, or Snake Head, advocated a system of federalism that would allow the regions to administer themselves and maintain their autonomy. A tropical wave originated from the coast of Africa on August 2 . The following day, it developed into a tropical depression east of Cape Verde . After six hours , it strengthened into Trudy , a tropical storm . On August 5 , Trudy made its first landfall near the coast of Casamance in Senegal with winds of 45 mph (75 km/h). It continued to move westward while gradually weakening. At 06:00 UTC on August 7 , Trudy made landfall near Mbour, Senegal with winds of 35 mph (55 km/h). The next day, Trudy degenerated into a remnant low.

After Nicholson 's April 1915 commissioning , she sailed off the east coast and in the Caribbean . After the United States ente

red World War I , she operated out of Newport, Rhode Island, and Hampton Roads, Virginia, as a training and patrol ship .
On 2 July 1917, Nicholson received orders to proceed to Brest , France, in company with Old Colony and North Dakota . She arrived at Brest on 26 July and was placed in commission, France, under the command of Commander John R. B. Fletcher.

### World War I

Nicholson was assigned to the 6th Naval District and operated off the French coast until 5 November 1918. She returned to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on 13 November and was decommissioned on 18 November 1918.

### Interwar period

After a brief period of training duty out of Newport, Nicholson was decommissioned at Philadelphia on 4 July 1919. She was then moved to the 11th Naval District and operated out of Galveston, Texas, until 15 October 1921.

Nicholson was transferred to the cruiser squadron of the Pacific Fleet on 15 October 1921 and operated with cruisers of the Pacific Reserve Fleet at San Pedro, California, until 13 January 1922, when she was again placed in commission, in reserve, in the 11th Naval District. She was placed out of commission in reserve on 24 May 1922.

### World War II

Nicholson was recommissioned on 20 November 1940 and joined the Neutrality Patrol on 18 December. She patrolled the coast of Venezuela from 18 December 1940 through 27 June 1941.

On 28 June 1941, Nicholson sailed from New Orleans, Louisiana, bound for England. On 12 July, she arrived at Liverpool and was assigned to the British Admiralty. She joined the naval forces defending the British Isles and operated in the eastern and western approaches to the British Isles until 18 December 1941.

Nicholson then returned to the United States and remained in idle status at Norfolk, Virginia, until 29 May 1942, when she sailed for the Mediterranean.

On 2 July 1942, Nicholson joined Tortoise , HMS Pindar , HMS Sirius , and HMS Waterhen in Operation Harpoon, a convoy of 14 merchant ships carrying supplies to Malta. This operation occurred on the eve of Operation Pedestal, a convoy of 14 merchant ships carrying supplies to Malta. The convoy was attacked by RAF bombers and German and Italian warships. By the morning of 9 July, all but one merchant ship had been sunk. The next day, the German battleship Tirpitz shelled the convoy, and the escorting British destroyer HMS Jervis was sunk.

On 11 July, Nicholson rendezvoused with the convoy and acted as the outer escort. She engaged a German torpedo boat that attacked the convoy. Later that day, she fought a night action with the Italian destroyer Maestrale. The next day, Nicholson, along with the other escorting British destroyers, HMS Express and HMS Tartar, engaged a German destroyer and sank her.

On 14 and 15 July, Nicholson fought night actions with the Italian destroyer Maestral and the German destroyer Leopard, respectively. Both German destroyers were heavily damaged and forced to withdraw.

On 15 July, Admiral Philip Vian ordered Nicholson to proceed to Malta, leaving the convoy to the British destroyers Tartar and Express. Nicholson arrived at Malta on 17 July.

Nicholson continued escorting convoys between Malta and Alexandria, Egypt, until 10 September, when she was assigned to escort duty in the Aegean Sea until early in 1943. Nicholson then returned to the Mediterranean and performed escort duty in the eastern Mediterranean. On 26 March 1943, she collided with the British destroyer HMS Jervis and sank.

Hornung 's prose is widely admired for its lucid @-@ yet @-@ simple style . Oliver Edwards , writing in The Times , considered

1978's A Bridge Too Far 's "easily the best non-fiction book I have read this year" .
But Hornung's style is not without its detractors, who point out the occasional anachronism or accidental error. Historian and critic Richard Holmes has criticised Hornung for his tendency to overstate, and Norman Mailer , in his review of Falklands , called him a "very English purveyor of the old adage that everything is relative".

The Magdalen imagery further draws on the idea of Christ as the word , represented by a book , with the Magdalen as the reader

or listener. In her most famous painting (1513) , there is a figure on the right hand side looking down, with her hands on her ears. The idea of the book and the preacher continues throughout the series, and appears again in the 1535 painting, where Christ sits beneath a tree , a book on his lap. In the last painting (1543) , the Magdalen sits in a church and looks up at Christ, while her eyes are closed, as if she is listening to his words. In this way, the series can be seen as a representation of the various stages of the human soul, or the soul s journey to paradise.
The Magdalen is a recurring figure in the work of Lucas, and the series is the only one to feature her in all five paintings. She also appears in the 1540 'Miraflores', and in two of the 'Margot' paintings (1520-21). Given the importance of the Magdalen series to Lucas' work, it is perhaps surprising that so little is known about it. Although there are records of Lucas s work at the Vatican and in the chapel of the Palazzo Farnese , there is no mention of the Magdalen series. This is all the more surprising given the popularity of the theme at the time, and the fact that Lucas was a close follower of the more famous Andrea Mantegna, who produced a series of five paintings of the Magdalen between 1490 and 1496.
In fact, it is only from the 16th century that Lucas becomes better known, and a number of his paintings were identified as being by him. The first record of this is from 1549, when the public attention he received from his work in the 'Margot' series led to a description of his work in the 'Venus and Adonis ' series, which was published by Giorgio Vasari in 1550.
Much of what is known about Lucas s work has come from Vasari s account of him in the 'Vasari Lives'. He was not a prolific painter, and yet his work has been described as 'excessive in design but incomparable in execution' . Despite this, Vasari s account was not a description of the 'Magdalen' series itself, but of the work in the 'Venus and Adonis' series, which was commissioned by Lorenzo de Medici. This has led to some confusion about the artist s name, as Lucas was frequently referred to as 'Lucas Gherardini'. It is only in later accounts that his name is given as 'Lucas Cranach the Elder'.
With the exception of the 'Magdalen ' series, Lucas s work was focused on religious themes, and often focused on the life of Christ. Most of his surviving work is either religious or mythological, and was produced either for private clients or for religious institutions in Germany.
At the beginning of the 16th century, he worked in Augsburg, but by 1505 he had moved to Wittenberg. Shortly after this, he began to produce a series of paintings for the Lutheran Church in Wittenberg , which included a number of 'works of Christ', including the 'Temptation of Christ', 'The Last Supper' and 'The Ascension'.
Lucas s style was influenced by both the Northern European tradition of the late Gothic and the Italian Renaissance. In his early work, his style was more Gothic , and he was influenced by Dürer and Albrecht Dürer. However, by the 1530s his style was more Renaissance , with clear, strong lines and a naturalistic style.

William Etty , the seventh son of a York baker and miller , had been an apprentice printer in Hull . On completing his seven @-

year apprenticeship in 1804 , he left his native city for London , where he was taken on by the publisher Ackermann , who was printed a series of 18 aquatint etchings of ' Historic and Romantic Scenes ' , with descriptive text by Etty himself. The scale of the works was far higher than any available in England at the time , and they were widely reproduced in book and magazine form . It is significant that Etty's contemporary , the artist George Cruikshank , after studying the Ackermann engravings , began producing a series of etchings himself , with a similar subject matter .
Etty's etchings were often based on classical or Biblical subjects , but were nevertheless considered to be scandalous in their time . 'The Children of Israel in the Wilderness' (1805) , for example , portrays a group of naked women and children , and was consequently attacked by the clergyman Dr. A.W. Gronow . Etty's style of female nudity is curiously detached , given his youth and the fact that he had never seen naked women in the flesh . The naked female figure , in Etty's work , is often not a subject in itself , but a setting for the main figure or action . Etty's works were largely ignored in his lifetime but , by the end of the century , he was considered to be one of the most important English artists .

Co-creator Allan Burns was born in 1933 in Chicago, and studied at the Los Angeles branch of the University of Chicago, where he was a member of The Second City improv group. In 1957, he joined CBS television in New York as a researcher and writer, before moving to Los Angeles a year later to become a writer and script editor for the _Mary Tyler Moore Show_ (1970). An episode of the _Mary Tyler Moore Show_ , 'The Shopping Problem', made use of a 1966 short film by Bob and Ray, 'The Pedestrian Problem', in which a man is run over by a car while crossing a zebra crossing and is then sued by the driver. Burns incorporated the gag in a scene in 'The Shopping Problem' in which a couple (played by Ed Asner and Mary Tyler Moore) cross a zebra crossing and are struck by a car. The two actors have often been quoted as saying that the episode is the funniest they have ever made.
Burns created _Mary Tyler Moore_ with his fellow _Mary Tyler Moore Show_ writer and co-producer James L. Brooks. He co-created _The Munsters_ with Jerry Ziegelman, who had been a writer on _The Mary Tyler Moore Show_ , and had created the short-lived sitcom _The Bill Cosby Show_ (1969) with Burns. Later, Burns co-created _The Mary Tyler Moore Hour_ (1979), and _The Golden Palace_ (1992). Burns died in 2013.
_Mary Tyler Moore_ also had a strong _Munsters_ connection in the form of the comedy duo Bob and Ray, who starred in two episodes, 'The Shopping Problem' and 'The Painting Problem'.

In 1964, Burns, Ziegelman and Brooks decided to write a series based on a 'family of monsters'. However, 'we didn't want a horror series', Burns recalled. 'We wanted a series that would be like _The Beverly Hillbillies_ or _The Honeymooners_.'
What they came up with was a kind of Victorian horror family, similar to the Addams Family, but with a more European horror tradition, and their _Munsters_ characters were loosely based on the Frankenstein family. 'We felt that if we were really going to do a show about monsters, we should make them as normal as possible,' Burns explained. 'We didn't want them to have fangs or claws, but just to be different looking.'
The Burns/Ziegelman/Brooks team then had to come up with a title for their series. 'We wanted something that would have a double meaning,' Burns said. 'It had to be funny, and it had to have a meaning that would last.'
Having chosen the title _The Munsters_ , the team then had to come up with a way to introduce the characters to the audience.
'We didn't want to do the typical opening for a horror show, with the family meeting in the castle, with the monster in the lab, or the traditional _Dracula_ shot with the monster in the coffin', Burns recalled. 'We weren't trying to do a horror movie. We wanted to make a situation comedy, and we wanted something that would lead you into the show and tell you about the characters.'

## Plot

Two brothers, Raj (Rajesh Khanna) and Shankar (Shammi Kapoor), live in a village in the Punjab. Their father (Raaj Kumar) is a poor farmer, who brings up his sons with a spirit of sacrifice and love. Raj and Shankar are often at odds, as Shankar is an unruly and aggressive person, while Raj is a disciplined and studious boy. One day, their father steals a few kilos of gold from the village moneylender (Pran) to buy a new bicycle for Raj. Raj is thrilled, but his father is dismayed because he has already lost his bicycle, which he accidentally sold to the moneylender to save his crops.

Raj and Shankar's father is arrested by the police, but the brothers escape from custody. In the forest, they are recruited by a band of outlaws who are stealing gold from the moneylender's treasury. Shankar is sent to steal the gold, which he does. However, his loot is stolen from him by a thief, and he is injured in the process. The leader of the gang (Prem Chopra), who is Raj's friend, is angry with Shankar and orders him to be killed. Shankar barely survives the attack.

Raj learns that his father is dead, and that his two brothers are now murderers. Raj decides to find Shankar and save him. Shankar is now living in the forest, and his only friend is a wild bear. Raj reaches the forest and pretends to be a forest ranger who is interested in Shankar's well-being. Raj, who is not a criminal, is also able to get Shankar's bear friend to like him. In one scene the bear shakes hands with Raj, which makes Raj popular with the villagers. After Raj is able to save Shankar from being attacked by the gang, Shankar admits his guilt and Raj is able to save him from the gang.

The film ends with Raj and Shankar's mother (Nirupa Roy) giving the gold they had stolen back to the moneylender.

Varanasi ( Hindustani pronunciation : [ ʋaːˈraːɳəsi ] ) , also known as Benares , Banaras ( Banāras [ bəˈnaːrəs ] ) , or Kashi

( Kāśī [ ˈkaːʃi ] ) , is a city in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.  It is the holiest city (among Hindus) and the oldest continuously inhabited city  in the World.
Varanasi is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists and Jains. Hindus believe that death at Varanasi brings salvation  and the Hindus who die here are cremated on the banks of the Ganges. The city's religious importance to Hindus has made it a pilgrimage site for a large number of Hindu devotees, especially at the festival of Shivaratri.
The city is known as the "holy city of India"  and the "eternal city of India",  and is famous for its many ghats , particularly the Dashashwamedh Ghat . Varanasi is mentioned in the Rigveda , one of the four sacred texts of Hinduism.
Originally known as Kashi (Sanskrit: काशी , ), the city has a history spanning more than 3,000 years. The Varanasi of Buddha's time was known as Kushavati (Sanskrit: कुशावती ) . The city has been a cultural and religious centre in North India for several thousand years, and played an important role in the development of Buddhism and Hinduism.
Varanasi has been a great centre of learning in India for several thousand years, and many influential religious leaders, philosophers and musicians were born in the city. The Kashi Naresh (Maharaja of Kashi) was a hereditary king and ruler of Varanasi.
The city of Varanasi is situated on the left bank of the River Ganges, in the State of Uttar Pradesh in North India, 320 kilometres (200 mi) southeast of the state capital Lucknow . It is 838 km (520 mi) southwest of the national capital New Delhi. The present-day city of Varanasi is spread over an area of 38.6 square kilometres (15 sq mi).
Varanasi lies between 25° 10' and 26° 32' north latitude, and between 82° 55' and 83° 38' east longitude. It is situated 120 km (75 mi) to the southeast of the Himalayas. The river Ganges enters the plains of North India at Haridwar 170 km (110 mi) to the northwest, and while flowing past the city of Varanasi, divides itself into many distributaries.
The climate of Varanasi is characterised by extreme variation of temperature. The summers are hot and dry and winters are cool and temperate. The summers start from March and last till June. During the summers, the daytime temperature varies between 35 °C (95 °F) and 47 °C (117 °F). The winters start from November and last till February. During the winters, the daytime temperature varies between 14 °C (57 °F) and 25 °C (77 °F).
The monsoon rains occur from June to September. The Varanasi monsoon rains are known for their electrical storms and thunder, which occur during the evenings. The annual rainfall is around 116 cm (46 in).
During the monsoon, the city of Varanasi is prone to flooding. The flooding occurs due to the heavy rainfall and also due to the inefficiency of the drainage system.
The inhabitants of Varanasi are known as Varanavahis or Banarasis. According to the 2011 census, the population of the city of Varanasi is 1,084,033, up from 1,039,130 in the 2001 census. The male population is 559,630, while the female population is 524,403.

To perform in vitro analysis , a protein must be purified away from other cellular components . This process usually begins wit

h a homogenization of the cells, which breaks them up into a suspension containing smaller subcellular structures. The suspension is then run through a centrifuge to separate these components; the supernatant fluid, or "cell extract," contains the macromolecules. The supernatant fluid can now be studied for the presence of the protein under investigation. To do this, a solution of the protein must be prepared.
In the past, the protein was solubilized in a detergent and the solubilized detergent-protein complex was then isolated from the detergent. This procedure, known as detergent solubilization, was very common for dry-weight measurements, but it did not work well for kinetic analysis or determination of equilibrium constants.  The 1996 Olympic Games in Atlanta will be remembered for a number of reasons, not least the fact that they were the first Olympic Games to be held in the United States of America. But they will also be remembered for the doping scandals that rocked the athletics programme. The 2000 Games in Sydney were tainted by the death of Steve Smyth in the marathon, and the 2004 Games in Athens were affected by the terrorist bombing in the Olympic village. The 2008 Games in Beijing were affected by the Olympic torch relay being disrupted by Tibetan protesters. But it was 2012 in London that saw the most serious doping scandals of all.
Athletics was, by some margin, the most affected sport. An investigation into the 'rudimentary, unsophisticated' methods used by the Russian anti-doping agency ( RUSADA ) led to the discovery that the Russian national team had been using performance-enhancing drugs ( PEDs ) with the full knowledge of the Russian authorities. The Russian athletics team was banned from the Olympics in Rio.
It later came to light that the Russians were not the only ones using drugs to gain an advantage. The Australian sprinter Dane Bird-Smith was banned for four years after being found to have used the banned stimulant modafinil.
The 'golden age' of the women 's hammer throw began in 1986 when Yuriy Sedykh, the Soviet shot putter, was banned for life – and later jailed – after admitting to having taken anabolic steroids. The ban was later reduced to four years, but Sedykh was unable to compete in the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona, or the 1994 World Championships in Gothenburg.
Yury Sedykh, shot putter, was banned for four years after admitting to having taken anabolic steroids.
The women 's hammer throw 's first recorded winner was the Russian Tamara Press, who won the gold medal at the 1952 Olympics in Helsinki. She won a silver medal at the 1956 Olympics in Melbourne and at the 1960 Olympics in Rome. She was Olympic champion in 1964 in Tokyo and again in 1968 in Mexico City. She was the first athlete ever to win the same event at four successive Olympics. She was also the first track and field athlete to win at three successive Olympics.
Before Press, the only women 's hammer throw records were held by American women in the early 1900s. The first woman to throw over 35 m ( 114.8 ft ) – the standard for entry to the Olympics – was Melinda Boyer. She threw 35.1 m ( 115.1 ft ) in 1913 and 35.6 m ( 116.8 ft ) in 1916.

The story of the development of airplanes is fascinating for so many reasons. The history of airplanes is a good example of how one man's ideas can influence the course of history. The story of flying is not so much a story of science and technology as it is a story of human ambition and creativity. If you are interested in history, aviation history is a good place to start.
The earliest flights were of course performed by birds. Humans began trying to fly at about the same time that the first men started writing. The first documented references to attempts to fly using human power date back to the 7th century BC.
The first prototype of a flying machine was constructed by a man named Daedalus and his son Icarus circa 1400 BC.
The first successful manned flight was on November 3, 1896. The pilot was a man named Alphonse Pénaud. The flight lasted a little over 100 feet and was flown in a glider.
The first successful powered flight was on December 17, 1903. The pilot was a man named Wilbur Wright. The powered flight lasted 12 seconds and was flown in a plane called the Wright Flyer.

There have been numerous descriptions of their generally unaggressive nature . Sweeney ( 1961 ) wrote they are so docile that t

ame animals are often kept as pets. Nocturnal in their habits, they are normally found at night in underground burrows or in tree cavities, but they have been known to climb trees and bask in the sun . The short legs, powerful claws, and large feet indicate that they were probably omnivorous, scavenging and eating invertebrates, seeds, fruits, and roots . Sweeney ( 1961 ) described them as having a "delicate, slender body" with a rounded snout and a short, tapering tail. They had small, round ears and were covered with long, soft fur.
The fossil record of the genus _Nesophontes_ is extensive, and fossils have been found from the Pleistocene to Holocene in the Caribbean Islands as well as in Mexico, the Bahamas, and Florida. In addition to the 16 species that have been described, there are 14 species from the Caribbean that are not described but known from partial skeletons and skulls . Early descriptions of the fossil record are summarized in Ameghino ( 1877 ), and full descriptions are found in Lund ( 1878 ), Blainville ( 1886 ), and Gervais ( 1874 ).
Several species of _Nesophontes_ , especially the larger _N. major_ and _N. superstes_ , have been described as having several subspecies. For example, _N. major_ has been divided into the subspecies _N. major major_ , the type species, _N. major cusucoensis_ , and _N. major bairdi_ . Some of the smaller species, especially _N. edithae_ , have been divided into subspecies as well.
Several species of _Nesophontes_ have been described from the Caribbean Islands, including _N. callidus_ from Puerto Rico, _N. batonganus_ from the Bahamas, _N. gracilis_ from the Bahamas and Cuba, _N. hypomicroides_ from Puerto Rico, _N. major_ from the Bahamas, Puerto Rico, Dominican Republic, and Cuba, _N. micropus_ from the Bahamas and Cuba, _N. nesophilus_ from the Bahamas and Bermuda, _N. nesophonus_ from Cuba, _N. ossiferus_ from Bermuda, and _N. superstes_ from Cuba . Species have also been described from mainland Mexico and Central America, including _N. caribensis_ , _N. cognatus_ , _N. leonardi_ , _N. morenoi_ , _N. ophiodon_ , _N. palaeohyla_ , _N. pallidus_ , _N. rex_ , _N. robustus_ , _N. rufus_ , _N. stratigalus_ , _N. suazae_ , and _N. webbi_ .
_Nesophontes_ is phylogenetically close to several genera in the subfamily _Nesophontinae_ , including the genus _Paramyomimus_ , which is restricted to the Caribbean Islands . The extinction of the genus has been related to human activity, especially the introduction of hogs, dogs, and cats, which preyed on juvenile _Nesophontes_ , and the introduction of non-native plants, which displaced the native vegetation on which the rodents fed . The extinction of the genus is also related to habitat destruction, as subspecies of _Nesophontes_ , such as _N. major_ , were found in the understory of tropical forest, which was cleared for farming and for building homes .
Although the genus is now extinct, there have been several recent descriptions of new species of _Nesophontes_ from the Caribbean Islands, including _N. edithae_ and _N. hypomicroides_ from Puerto Rico, and _N. micropus_ from Cuba . The research on these species, although not focused on the genus _Nesophontes_ , is important, as it contributes to our knowledge of caribou species.

The International Olympic Committee ( IOC ) officially launched the bid process for the 2016 Summer Olympics and Paralympics on

27 July 2006, after the 2006 Summer Youth Olympics in the city of Peking, China. The deadline for bids was 14 September 2007, and the IOC selected Chicago, Madrid, and Tokyo as candidate cities, as well as New York City, which withdrew its bid before the deadline. The final selection of the host city was made on 6 July 2009 at the 121st IOC Session in Copenhagen, Denmark.  The bid by Chicago was considered by many to be the most economically viable and the least controversial of the five cities that had bid for the 2016 games.

2016 Summer Olympics and Paralympics bid scandal

In September 2009, the IOC Ethics Commission of the IOC was convened to investigate allegations made by the IOC's then-president, Jacques Rogge, about an alleged bribery scandal involving Olympic officials from the various bid cities. In January 2010, the IOC commission concluded that IOC president Jacques Rogge had "failed to show the degree of impartiality expected of him as IOC President".  In March 2010, the IOC Ethics Commission recommended that "the IOC President should have recused himself from any involvement in the evaluation of the bids for the Olympic Games 2016 because of his direct involvement in the bidding process and because of a possible conflict of interest".

## Events

### Initial bid process

In July 2004, the IOC announced that it would pursue an Agenda 2010 plan, which would involve an official bidding process for the 2016 and 2012 Summer Olympics. The first step was to select the host cities for the 2014 Winter Olympics and the 2014 Summer Youth Olympics. Vienna, Austria, and Oslo, Norway, were awarded these Olympics, respectively, in July 2007. After that, the IOC began the official process for the 2016 Summer Olympics and Paralympics.

On 27 July 2006, the IOC officially launched the bid process for the 2016 Summer Olympics and Paralympics after the completion of the 2006 Summer Youth Olympics in Peking, China, the host city for the 2008 Summer Olympics. The deadline for bids was 14 September 2007. In September 2006, the IOC received five official bid books from cities that intended to bid for the 2016 Olympics. The five cities that bid and were subsequently selected for further consideration were Chicago, Madrid, Tokyo, New York City, and Rio de Janeiro. The IOC evaluated the five cities and selected three of them to bid officially for the 2016 Summer Olympic and Paralympic Games: Chicago, Madrid, and Tokyo. On 14 September 2007, the IOC Executive Board selected the three candidate cities. On 13 May 2008, the IOC confirmed that the three final candidate cities were Chicago, Tokyo, and Madrid. The three official candidate cities for the 2016 Summer Olympic and Paralympic Games were Chicago, Madrid, and Tokyo.

The typical hunting strategy of the diamond stingray is to cruise just above the sea floor , landing atop any prey encountered

- they can easily lift themselves by fanning their fins and propelling themselves with their tails . They feed on a variety of invertebrates, such as worms, shrimp, clams, crabs, and sea urchins.
Apart from humans, the diamond stingray's only predator is the saltwater crocodile .
The diamond stingray is a species of stingray in the family Dasyatidae .
The diamond stingray may look like a smooth, rounded lump of sand, but in fact has a venomous tail spine that can inflict a painful wound.
The diamond stingray is a species of stingray in the family Dasyatidae . They are widely distributed in the Indo-West Pacific, from Pakistan in the west to Papua New Guinea in the east. They are occasionally found in the Persian Gulf.
The diamond stingray has a broadly diamond-shaped head, with large eyes and a small mouth. The body is oblong in shape, tapering off to a flat tail. Its color is typically dark brown, gray, or black. There is a white, diamond-shaped patch on the front of the head, but it is sometimes the dorsal fin that is diamond-shaped. The diamond stingray has a pair of pectoral fins, a pair of pelvic fins, and a single caudal fin.
The diamond stingray is a carnivore , eating mostly benthic bivalves , such as clams and oysters . They have also been known to eat fish and other invertebrates .
The diamond stingray is a solitary fish, hiding in caves and rock crevices during the day. It is a nocturnal feeder, emerging to the surface to hunt at dusk.
The diamond stingray is ovoviviparous, with the young developing inside eggs inside the mother's body.

After the conclusion of the Champions League tournament , Justin Langer retired from professional cricket . Trescothick replace

the captain and soon after he was injured and ruled out of the game for several months . England's next Test match was against Pakistan in Lahore . The Test started well with Trescothick scoring 113 on the first day . He went on to make a century on the second day and 116 on the third . He was 33 not out when Pakistan's bowler Saqlain Mushtaq took a catch off a ball by Matthew Hoggard .
"I was exhausted and hungry and I was enjoying the moment when I decided to go for a big hit to the cover boundary . I had never seen Saqlain Mushtaq bowl before . I was on 33 when I hit the ball and I was very surprised when he took the catch . It was a bit of a shock to me ."
"I will always remember it because it was the first time I had been dismissed since I was 15 . I was actually able to see the ball go through the hands of Mushtaq . It was an unbelievable situation ."
"I went to the hospital and I was lying on the bed with a drip in my arm . I was talking to my wife and she was trying to encourage me . The thing I will remember about the whole thing is that I was talking to her on the phone and I was going through the whole experience ."
"The doctor came in and said I had lost a litre of blood . It was scary but I had to stay calm and I wasn't panicking . I had to stay in the hospital for a while longer and I was in a lot of pain ."
Trescothick was released from the hospital on 22 April 2006 . He was later diagnosed with a rare form of blood disorder called idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) , which is a bleeding disorder that occurs when your immune system destroys the cells that help your blood to clot . He has been hospitalized several times .
Trescothick has scored more than 8 000 Test runs . He has also scored more than 8 000 one-day international runs . As a batsman he has a highest score of 294 . He has also scored a century in each innings of a Test match . He has played for the Somerset County Cricket Club since 1993 .

The Oliviers returned to London in the spring of 1963 with the revised version of _Camelot_. For the rest of the year they spent in their house at Kenwood. In the summer they went to Paris, where the Oliviers stayed at the Ritz and the Lelouches at the George V.
During the summer of 1963 Olivier and Vivien had been immersed in the French language. They were also learning the rudiments of French cooking. They had been to a number of French restaurants, where they had discovered a new culinary delight. This was the roast chicken ( _poularde_ ). The chicken would come to them whole, and the waiter would bring the joint to the table, with a knife and a fork. He would then cut off the breast with the knife, and carve it with the fork – placing it on a plate on the table, where it was no longer warm. He would then do the same with the other breast, and the legs, and the thighs. At the end of this performance, the waiter would remove the carcass. He would not be required again until the time came to clear the table. The Oliviers found that they could do no better than their French friends at this game of slicing and carving.
Olivier had at first thought that the French would not approve of him. But they discovered that their approach to the arts was very similar to his own. They were thrilled by the work of the French film director François Truffaut and the French playwright Jean Genet. They adored Jean Cocteau, and his friend the film director Jean Marais.
Olivier found that he was enjoying his comeback as an actor, and he was about to begin another film, _The Victors_ , directed by Carl Foreman. But he was unhappy. He felt that the film was a failure, and he did not like the people with whom he was working. Vivien was ill, and he was having to care for her. He had been asked to replace the film's director, but he was unable to do so. He had to return to London, where the film would be finished. He was also unhappy because he was having to be in charge of the film studio. He was still a director, but after the success of his first film, he was finding that he was not as good as he had thought.
