In contrast with this plural use of the word , in a 1954 article written by Arnold Field , a reporter for the Daily Dispatch ,

Field used the term "Ku-Klux Klan" to refer to the KKK's radical phase, from 1915 to 1944. The article stated that the term "Ku-Klux Klan" was used exclusively by Northern journalists, not Southerners.
Klan members refer to themselves simply as "Klansmen" or "Klanswomen", not as "Ku Kluxes" (the plural form of "Ku Klux" is "Ku Kluxes", not "Kluxes"). The name "Ku Klux" was never an official name of the Klan, and appears only in the title of the Reconstruction-era Klan, which was nicknamed the "Invisible Empire of the Ku Klux Klan".  The term "Ku Klux" is used as an adjective for Klan-related events and activities, rather than as a noun.
The pronunciation of "Klan" as "klan" is a modern-day mispronunciation that originated with the 1960s and 1970s, commonly used by the news media. In 1954, when the film The Birth of a Nation was re-released, the movie's publicity touted the film's "new and modern" Klan pronunciation, which had been changed from "klan" to "can".
Reports of the Klan's membership have varied greatly, depending on the organization studied and the definition of membership. In 1921, the Klan claimed 4,000,000 members,  with other estimates ranging from 2,000,000 to 4,000,000.  In 1927, the Klan claimed 4,000,000 members, and an estimate published by the Chicago Tribune that year stated that the Klan had between 4 and 8 million members. The Klan had between 15,000 and 30,000 members in the mid-1930s, and the Klan claimed 40,000 members in 1960.
The KKK is a hierarchical organization, with a national office staffed by full-time employees.  Full-time paid officers, including a national director, have been at the national level since 1915.
In the 1920s, the KKK had over 150,000 members in 500 chapters in 27 states.  By 1924, the Klan had 100,000 members in 44 states.  In 1925, the Klan had 15,000 members in 34 states.

The Adams River is a tributary of the Nicola River in the Central Interior of British Columbia , Canada . It is a popular destination for salmon fisheries , with salmon returning to spawn each year . Every four years , the Adams River is a very popular destination for sockeye salmon runs . The 2010 Adams River sockeye salmon run was declared a " run of a lifetime " by the Pacific Salmon Commission .

## Background

The Adams River is a major tributary of the Nicola River in the Central Interior of British Columbia , Canada . The river drains the east side of the Cascade Mountains and flows generally east into the Nicola River . Its mouth is located near the community of Lillooet , British Columbia . The Adams River is approximately 160 kilometers (99 mi) long and drains an area of 3,700 square kilometers (1,400 sq mi). The river is named for John Adams.

## Salmon runs

Salmon return to the Adams River and spawn every year, and the Adams River is the fourth largest spawning salmon run in the world. The salmon migration is a very visible event that attracts large numbers of tourists and photographers. Every four years, nearly 100 million sockeye salmon return to the river to spawn. These are known as "dominant years," and they are very popular among tourists. The sockeye salmon return every year. However, the numbers are much higher every fourth year. 2010 was a dominant year.

The salmon return to the Adams River to spawn from mid-August to early November. In 2010, a record 101.5 million sockeye salmon returned to the Adams River. In 2010, the salmon run was declared a "run of a lifetime" by the Pacific Salmon Commission. The sockeye salmon are the most significant salmon spawning run in North America . The 2010 Adams River sockeye salmon run was declared a "run of a lifetime" by the Pacific Salmon Commission.

## Sockeye salmon

Sockeye salmon are bright red when they return to the Adams River to spawn. An adult sockeye salmon can measure up to 90 centimetres (35 in) in length and weigh up to 15 kilograms (33 lb) .

## Sockeye salmon life cycle

The sockeye salmon spawn on the Adams River between mid-August and early November. The salmon die shortly after spawning. Their eggs hatch and the young salmon, known as "alewife", swim to the ocean. The salmon spend up to three years in the ocean. When they return, they are known as "jack salmon." The jack salmon are bright red and measure up to 50 centimetres (20 in) in length. In 2010, the salmon run was declared a "run of a lifetime" by the Pacific Salmon Commission.

## Adams River salmon fishery

Main article: Adams River salmon fishing

This was the first of many chapters in the saga of the Columbia Star, a weekly newspaper in Columbia County, New York that would go on to become one of the most successful small town papers in the United States.
But what makes a town paper successful?
Is it the content?
Is it the advertising?
Is it the community it serves?
Or is it the way the paper is run?

Professional ratings

Amanita muscaria is a cosmopolitan mushroom , native to conifer and deciduous woodlands throughout the temperate and boreal regions of the Northern Hemisphere, and has been introduced to North America and South America. It is a basidiomycete fungus, and is one of the most recognizable and widely consumed psychoactive mushrooms.
The fruiting body of Amanita muscaria consists of a cap and stipe, or stem, and is usually a dull red-brown to white in color, although other color variations are possible. The cap is flat with white gills, a white to cream-colored spore print, and a smell that is similar to the smell of a new sweater.
The name "fly agaric" is popularly applied to the red-capped Amanita muscaria (also known as the "toadstool" or "fly amanita") and Amanita pantherina . The name comes from the use of the mushroom in fly fishing, but it was not a particularly effective bait, because flies do not appear to find the smell of the Amanita species attractive.
Amanita muscaria is considered poisonous, with the principal toxin being muscarine. Ingesting large quantities of the fungus can cause paralysis and death. However, a variety of traditional uses have been documented: as a fly-repellent, as an intoxicant, and as a medicine.
The remains of Amanita muscaria have been found in Neolithic settlements in Russia, indicating that the species has been used by humans for a long time. The mushroom has been consumed for its psychoactive effects by peoples across Eurasia. The mushroom has been used in Siberian shamanism and by the peoples of the Arctic Circle. It is traditionally brewed into a tea (called 'samogon' in Russia) that is used for its intoxicating properties; it is also chewed as a way to clear the sinuses.
The mushroom has also been used as a fly-repellent. It is easily crushed and soaked in water, and the liquid can be used to coat animal fur, or plants that attract flies. In Russia, the mushroom has been used to dye Easter eggs, and the caps have been used to decorate homes.
Amanita muscaria also has a long history of use as an intoxicant.
The mushroom contains the toxins ibotenic acid and muscimol. Ibotenic acid inhibits the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, resulting in stimulation, followed by depression, and eventually, sedation. Muscimol selectively stimulates the 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A (5-HT2A) receptor in the brain, which is associated with the perception of reality and the experience of hallucinations. Amanita muscaria can also cause a sensation of heaviness in the head, which may be associated with the blockade of the cerebral blood vessels.
The Native Americans of the Pacific Northwest used Amanita muscaria to treat arthritis, and as a pain-killer and sedative. Krak des Chevaliers ( French pronunciation : ​ [ kʁak de ʃəvaˈlje ] ; Arabic : حصن الفرسان ) , also Crac des Chevaliers , Ḥoṣn

Ḥalab ( Arabic : حصن حلب , lit. 'Castle of Aleppo ' ) or Krakus ( Polish : Kracz ) , is a mediaeval castle located in the Syrian village of al-Athraya . It is one of the largest and best-preserved examples of Crusader architecture in the Middle East .
The castle was first built in 1031 by the emir of Aleppo, who was under the authority of the Byzantine Empire . It was subsequently expanded by the Seljuk Turks and then by the Crusaders. It was captured by the forces of Saladin in 1188 and remained in Muslim control until 1271, when it was returned to the Kingdom of Jerusalem in the Treaty of Acre . The castle was then expanded by the Crusaders, and remained under their control until 1291, when the last Crusader stronghold in the Levant, Acre , was conquered by the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt .
During the 1930s a large archaeological excavation was undertaken by the French, who discovered a large Roman necropolis underneath the castle, as well as the foundations of a Byzantine church. The site was listed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2006.
Krak des Chevaliers is located in the Qalamoun mountain range, 15 kilometres ( 9.3 mi ) west of Hama , 55 kilometres ( 34 mi ) east of Homs , and 100 kilometres ( 62 mi ) south-east of Tripoli , Lebanon . The castle is about 800 metres ( 0.5 mi ) above mean sea level.
The castle is situated on a ridge, 326 metres ( 1,072 ft ) above sea level, overlooking a deep valley.
The site of the castle originally covered 30 hectares ( 74 acres ) and was divided into three main parts: the bailey, the curtain wall and the upper enclosure. The outer walls were enhanced by towers, which were connected by a system of fortified gates. The northern gate opened onto an avenue that continued to the main entrance of the castle, north-west of the inner bailey.
The castle is rectangular in plan and has a total length of about 200 m (660 ft). It is 160 m (520 ft) long, 125 m (410 ft) wide (excluding the towers), and 18 m (59 ft) high. The outer walls were originally 4 metres (13 ft) thick and 12 metres (39 ft) high. The inner walls were 2.5 metres (8 ft) thick and 9 metres (30 ft) high, and the towers 5 metres (16 ft) thick and about 12 metres (39 ft) high.
The castle has four main towers that flank the entrance gate and are linked with a curtain wall. The main entrance, located at the western side of the castle, is flanked by two towers. The castle has a total of 21 towers.
The site has two main entrance gates. The main entrance is flanked by two towers and is guarded by a drawbridge. The gate is 20 metres (66 ft) wide, 5 metres (16 ft) high and 9 metres (30 ft) thick. The gates were originally protected by a portcullis and a series of barbicans. The inner entrance is protected by two smaller towers and a drawbridge. The gate is 10 metres (33 ft) wide, 3.8 metres (12 ft) high and 6 metres (20 ft) thick.
The round tower is 18 metres (59 ft) high and 16 m (52 ft) in diameter. It is situated on a 12 metres (39 ft) high rock in the middle of a small hill. It is the oldest structure in the castle and dates from the original construction of the castle. The tower is connected to the curtain wall by a ladder. It served as a watchtower and a prison.
The Romanesque chapel was built in the 13th century and is located in the centre of the upper enclosure. The chapel has a rectangular floor plan and is flanked by two towers. The outer walls are 2.68 metres (8.8 ft) thick and 12 metres (39 ft) high.

arnesio, the alliance was concluded in August 1217. They were betrothed in Paris on 10 September 1217.
 Maria had been betrothed to Conrad of Montferrat .  The children of Maria and Conrad of Montferrat , including Theodore and John II of Courtenay , were under the guardianship of the pope and the Emperor Frederick II. By the terms of the treaty, Maria was released from her betrothal to Conrad, who was married to Isabella II of Jerusalem .  The marriage treaty between Maria and John was confirmed by the papal bulls of Pope Honorius III on 24 October 1217 and of Pope Innocent III on 16 July 1218. 
The marriage was celebrated in Paris on 13 January 1218,  and the couple departed for Acre in the Kingdom of Jerusalem in September.  Maria was crowned Queen of Jerusalem in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem in June 1218.  The couple was inducted into the Templars in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre on 13 August 1218. 
Maria and John's son, Baldwin II of Courtenay , was born in Acre in 1219. 
Maria died on 20 April 1221 in the Convent of Saint Lazarus in Jerusalem.  Maria was buried in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

Syria has a total area of 185,180 square kilometres (71,498 sq mi). Of this, 184,875 square kilometres (71,378 sq mi) is land. The state borders the Mediterranean Sea to the west, Lebanon and the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights to the southwest, Jordan to the south, and Iraq to the east.
The highest point in Syria is Mount Hermon , located on the border with Lebanon, at 2, 814 metres (9, 232 ft). It is not a part of the Anti-Lebanon Mountains (which are mostly lower than 2,000 metres (6,600 ft)) nor is it a part of the Al-Jawzayyah Mountains (which are 2,000–2,400 metres (6,600–7,900 ft) high).
The Anti-Lebanon mountains are the southernmost range of the Alawite Mountains, a range of the great mountain system that stretches across Syria from the Lebanese border to the Iraqi border. The Syrian Desert lies in the center of the country. The largest river is the Euphrates , which flows through Raqqa and Deir ez-Zor. Other important rivers are the Orontes , the Balikh River and the Euphrates' tributary the Koban.
It is the only country in the world that has the four seasons (spring, summer, autumn and winter). The climate of Syria is characterized as a semi-arid climate. The area of the country is 1,851,800 km2 (715,000 sq mi), of which 1,770,560 km2 (683,430 sq mi) is land (95%).
The northern coastal areas in the west of the country are hot and humid, with cooler winters than the rest of the country. Damascus has a hot-summer Mediterranean climate (Köppen climate classification: Csa), with warm, dry summers and cool wet winters. The annual rainfall is 13.1 cm (5.1 in) and the average temperature is 17.7 °C (64 °F).
The northern mountains (the Alawite Mountains in the west and the series of mountains in the east from the Beshama Mountains to the Jindires Mountains and Koban) are cooler than the rest of the country, with heavy snowfall in winter. In the south, the climate is subtropical, with very seasonal rainfall, high temperatures and low humidity in the summer and moderate temperatures and high humidity in the winter.
The hot, humid climate in the north is somewhat moderated by the cool sea breeze (as well as by altitude) in most of the coastal cities, although the northern mountains are also home to the coldest cities in Syria. The city of Latakia is among the coolest coastal cities in summer, with an average maximum temperature of 26.5 °C (79.7 °F) in July.

In 1849 James Goodhue began publication of the Minnesota Pioneer newspaper in Saint Paul ( the paper would later be renamed the

Minnesota Pioneer and Democrat ). Its first issue in March 1849 was the first in the state. It would have no competition until 1851. Goodhue was born in Vermont in 1819 and served in the Mexican-American War. He came to Minnesota in 1848 and published the Minnesota Pioneer from 1849 to 1857. He used his newspaper to promote his political views, which were generally Whig and pro-slavery. The paper supported the Union in the Civil War. It also covered news of the Dakota War of 1862, which took place in the state. Goodhue died in 1878.
In 1851 the first rivals to Goodhue's paper began publication. The Minneapolis Daily Journal began publishing in April 1851, and the Minnesota Daily Tribune started in May of the same year. In 1852 the Minneapolis Journal merged with the St. Paul Daily Press to form the Missouri Republican, which would publish until 1854. The St. Paul Pioneer, which began publishing in 1852, was the first Minnesota newspaper to be run by women. In 1854 the Minnesota Daily Tribune merged with the Minnesota Pioneer and Democrat to form the Minnesota Daily Tribune and Pioneer Democrat.

The Land of Mist (1927) is the second novel in Edgar Rice Burroughs' The Lost World series. It was published in the United Kingdom in 1927 by Hutchinson & Co. Ltd., and in the United States in 1928 by G. P. Putnam's Sons.
The Land of Mist, like its prequel The Lost World, is a novel of adventure set on a remote plateau in the Amazon. The novel concerns an expedition to the plateau by Lord John Roxton, his nephew David Innes, and a third party, Dr. Davidson. They travel in a cylindrical iron tube powered by a powerful electrical field. When the tube is descending, it travels at phenomenal speeds. When it is ascending, it moves at a slower speed, and to compensate for this, it is occasionally stopped to allow the party to take advantage of the oxygen-rich air.
The party arrives on the plateau, and finds that it is inhabited by saurians, including the savage, man-like Pterodactyls which they refer to as "Pterrors". They find a lost city, and within it another civilisation, the inhabitants of which are referred to as "Subterraneans". The Subterraneans are a peaceful, if strange, race. They are dark-skinned, and live in underground caverns. They have advanced medical and scientific knowledge, and are able to perform surgery and provide a range of remedies. They have invented a type of "time machine" which allows them to travel forward and backward through time, enabling them to visit the surface world and observe the surface dwellers. They also use these machines for other purposes, such as travelling to other planets.
The party discovers that the plateau is the focus of a strange force which has been shaping the evolution of the life on the plateau. It is gradually turning the surface dwellers into savage, uncivilised beings, and it is responsible for the death of the Subterraneans. The party is able to reverse this process, and to restore the Subterraneans to health.
The novel ends with the party returning to the surface world, and with the Subterraneans returning to their underground home.

Zhou Tong 's fictional life story can be pieced together from two sources : The Story of Yue Fei and Iron Arm , Golden Sabre .

Iron Arm , Golden Sabre is an epic poem extolling the virtues of Yue Fei, the Song Dynasty general and Confucian scholar. The poem was written by the Ming Dynasty official and writer Zhu Shunshui (1558–1633), who was a descendant of General Yue.   While there are no explicit references to Zhou Tong in the poem, the narrative is full of characters who were in Yue Fei's camp and served under his command.  Iron Arm , Golden Sabre is a didactic poem written for young men and women, and its narrative depicts the virtues of Yue Fei as a model for the audience.
Judging from its length and the number of characters who served under Yue Fei, Iron Arm , Golden Sabre is a composite of several sources. It is noteworthy that the poem is not in the first-person, but written as a third-person narrative with General Yue as the main character. This is in contrast to the Story of Yue Fei , which is in the first person. In The Story of Yue Fei, Zhou Tong is depicted as General Yue's faithful disciple, and he is the only character who is granted a dialogue. Zhou Tong's character is further developed in Iron Arm , Golden Sabre, in which Zhou Tong is General Yue's most talented tactician. In the poem, Zhou Tong is called "the general's wise man" and "the general's guardian angel" (Figure 1).
Yue Fei was an accomplished general under the Song Dynasty, and Zhou Tong was his closest disciple and trusted advisor. However, Zhou Tong's achievements were overshadowed by Yue Fei's, and he has been criticized as a "merchant's son" in Chinese Confucian history. In The Story of Yue Fei, the last sentence of the poem, written by the Song Dynasty scholar Su Shi (1037–1101), states that "Zhou Tong is not a wise man, but the general's wise man." In this sentence, Su Shi was emphasizing the point that Yue Fei was the true "wise man." Zhou Tong was the general's "wise man" because he served under Yue Fei's command, and his loyalty to Yue Fei is unquestionable.
In The Story of Yue Fei , there is a sense that Zhou Tong is Yue Fei's equal; their relationship is one of equals. Because there is a sense of equality between the two, Zhou Tong's character is less developed and he is simply referred to as "the general's disciple" (Figure 2).
One of Zhou Tong's first duties was to guard General Yue's armoury. According to The Story of Yue Fei, General Yue was wearing his armour when Zhou Tong noticed that "the lead plate on the general's armour was loose" (Figure 3). Zhou Tong took off his own armour and removed the lead plate from the general's armour before returning it to its original position. Zhou Tong's quickness in removing the lead plate from the armour and his dedication to General Yue's welfare are praised in the poem.
In Iron Arm , Golden Sabre, Zhou Tong's quickness in removing the lead plate from the general's armour is not mentioned. But in the poem, Zhou Tong is credited with saving General Yue's life. As General Yue was preparing to lead his troops to battle, he noticed that his armour was weighing him down. Therefore, he ordered Zhou Tong to remove the lead plate from his armour. Zhou Tong's quickness in removing the lead plate from the armour was praised by General Yue. In the poem, the general's wife, Wang Yuyan, is also praising Zhou Tong for his quickness in removing the lead plate from the armour.
In The Story of Yue Fei, General Yue rewards Zhou Tong for his service by naming him the "General of the Left." This is an important position for Zhou Tong because he is the general's most trusted advisor. Interstate 45 has a southern terminus in Galveston and serves as a main artery to Galveston from mainland Galveston County and

Harris County. It is the primary east–west highway in Harris County, and it is the main highway from Houston to Galveston and the Texas Gulf Coast region. The highway is a four- to six-lane freeway from its junction with Texas State Highway 146 (SH 146) to the Port of Houston and the Port of Houston Turnaround. From SH 146 to Interstate 10 (I-10), the highway is six lanes wide with a center left-turn lane. From I-10 to the freeway's southern terminus, the highway is four lanes wide with a center left-turn lane.

## History

The route from Houston to Galveston has been in use since the late 1800s. In 1913, Galveston County, Houston County, and Harris County began lobbying for the first federal highway to Galveston, named the Galveston Road (U.S. Route 90 Alternate (US 90 Alt.) from Houston to Galveston). The highway was under the jurisdiction of Harris County. In 1925, the state of Texas assumed control of the highway. By 1936, the highway was re-designated as Farm to Market Road 105 (FM 105). The highway was re-designated as State Highway 146 in 1939, and all states had bypassed Houston by 1940. In the early 1940s, the highway was bypassed by the current route of I-45. In 1945, the highway was realigned, and the old alignment became State Highway 146 Spur (SH 146 Spur). SH 146 Spur was bypassed in 1953 and re-signed as Farm to Market Road 99 (FM 99). In 1954, the highway was re-designated as SH 146.

In the late 1950s, the Texas State Highway Commission and Galveston officials began looking into the replacement of the two-lane highway with a freeway. The commission approved construction of the freeway in 1961, and construction began in 1963. On October 3, 1963, the highway was re-designated as Interstate 45. The freeway was completed in 1964, and the highway was opened to traffic on October 6, 1964.

### Mid-1990s expansion

In the early 1990s, the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) began planning to widen the freeway between I-10 and the Port of Houston to six lanes. The project was completed with a grand opening on October 19, 1995.

### Northwest Houston

In 1991, TxDOT began studying plans to extend I-45 to the Northwest Freeway (I-45 in Dallas County) in Montgomery County as part of a plan to expand the freeway to a continuous 16-lane freeway from I-10 to the Texas-Louisiana state line. The plan was dropped in 1998 due to opposition from the Galveston City Council.

## Future

### I-45 widening

In 1998, TxDOT began studying plans to widen the freeway between I-10 and the Northwest Freeway. In 2003, TxDOT completed the study and began planning to widen the freeway to six lanes in each direction. In 2008, TxDOT added the freeway to the Texas State Highway Plan for the widening of the freeway. In 2010, TxDOT completed the environmental impact study of the freeway. By 2019, the freeway was widened to six lanes in each direction. On January 17, 2019, the Texas Transportation Commission approved the project and allocated $750 million for the freeway. The invisible rail , Wallace 's rail , or drummer rail ( Habroptila wallacii ) is a large flightless rail that is endemic to th

e island of Mauritius in th e Indian Ocean .
It is unlike any other rail , and classified as a close relative of the quail , pheasants , partridges , and grouse , in the family Phasianidae.
Distribution and habitat The invisible rail is only found on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean.
It is found in dry woodland areas with areas of dense undergrowth, and inhabits dry open woodland mainly in the south of the island.
Behaviour and ecology Invisible rails are ground-foraging birds in habitats with dense undergrowth, feeding on seeds , insects and snails.
During the breeding season, the male's plumage changes to a brownish grey with a black belly.
The female is brownish grey above, and white below.
There are no other species of rail on the island of Mauritius; therefore, it is the only rail present on the island.
The invisible rail is solitary during the non-breeding season, but it may form small groups during the breeding season.
Reproduction and threats The invisible rail is found year round in the breeding season.
It breeds between August and December, with one or two eggs being laid (usually two).
The eggs are incubated for 24 days.
Its major threats are the introduced mongoose , and the destruction of its habitat.
The invisible rail is listed as threatened by the IUCN and is protected under the Wildlife Protection Act of 1937.
The island of Mauritius was originally a volcano and is now home to many endemic species.
The island has a rich and diverse avifauna , and the invisible rail is one of four endemic rails (the other three are the Mascarene, Comoros, and Réunion rails).

The morning after the November 2015 Paris attacks , German pianist Davide Martello brought a grand piano to the street out in f

amed Père Lachaise Cemetery, where he sat down and played French composer Maurice Ravel's _Jeux d'eau._ As he played, Martello looked out over the cemetery and its rolling hills. Martello had been in Paris two days earlier. He was in the 10th arrondissement, just across the river from the Bataclan theater, where 89 people were killed by Islamic State terrorists on November 13.

By the end of the thirteenth century , several offences against either one 's lord , or one 's king , were treasonable . High t

ides of political discontent , or of religious fervour , or of military ambition , had brought many to the scaffold and the stake .

For the first time in English history, felonies without accompanying treason were made punishable by death. The _Magna Carta_ had provided that "no free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or deprived of his standing in any other way, nor will we proceed with force against him, or send others to do so, except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land". This clause was reaffirmed by the _Statute of Westminster_ , _I_ in 1275 and by the _Statute of Westminster_ , _II_ in 1285. The _Statute of Marlborough_ , _I_ in 1267 and the _Statute of Westminster_ , _II_ in 1285 required that one or more justices should be present in the trial of any felony, and that the verdict should be given upon the oath of twelve jurors.

In 1275 the _Statute of Westminster_ established the doctrine of presumption of death for felons who had been convicted and sentenced and had not been heard of within a year after the sentence.

In 1352 the _Statute of Gloucester_ provided that jurisdiction over felonies should be in the courts of the sheriff , rather than in those of the hundred and the county. Thus the sheriff , who then held the post of justice of the peace , became the chief judge of the county in the trial of felonies.

In 1363 the _Statute of Treasons_ established a flourishing trade in the executions of traitors.

The _Statute of Treasons_ (1350) was one of the most important of the statutes enacted during the reign of Edward III. It established the doctrine that English subjects could never be guilty of treason against the English king, and it provided a short list of seven offences which were to be regarded as treasonable. The offences were:

* levying war against the king
* adhering to the king's enemies in his realm
* compassing, imagining, devising, or intending to deprive the king of the throne
* conspiring with another to overthrow the king, or to take the crown from him
* abetting or advising anyone else to do these things
* denying the king's right to the crown
* denying the king's title to the crown

These offences were to be regarded as treasonable even when they were committed outside England, as when the king of Scots was slain near Edinburgh after an assembly of his barons.

The second section of the _Statute of Treasons_ established the doctrine that the king could pardon treasons and that the king's pardon could be revoked in consequence of the pardoner's death.

The _Statute of Treasons_ made treason a capital offence. It also provided that the traitor's goods could be forfeited to the king.

The _Statute of Treasons_ also provided that the traitor's body should be exposed on the gallows or gibbet and his head should be cut off and set up on a pole.

The _Statute of Treasons_ was a statute of enormous importance. It established the basic principle that an English subject might not be guilty of treason against the English crown, and it established the doctrine that treason was a capital offence.

The _Statute of Treasons_ was chiefly an English statute. It was not, however, entirely unimportant in the legislation of Great Britain. The _Statute of Treasons_ was reenacted in 1695, and the reenactment of the statute was continued by the _Indemnity and Oblivion_ Act in 1718, by the _Indemnity and Oblivion_ Act in 1746, and by the _Indemnity and Oblivion_ Act in 1814. The reenactment of the _Statute of Treasons_ in 1718 and in 1746 was also important in the legislation of the United States of America.

In the Roman empire 's hierarchical system , a vassal king usage of the King of Kings title did not indicate that he is a peer

or equal to the Roman emperor. The emperor's title was used to indicate that he was a king who was a vassal to the Roman empire . A vassal king who claimed to be the King of Kings would be considered a pretender  to the throne of the Roman empire.
 The title was first used by the Roman emperor Justin II in a letter to the East Roman emperor Heraclius  in 692. The term was used by the Eastern emperor Heraclius in 695, and again by the Roman emperor Constantine V  in 754. The title was used after this time by the Eastern emperor Basil I  and the Roman emperor Leo IV , along with Leo V in the case of the latter two.

The most recent military conflict in the region, the Bosnian Genocide, was a four-year-long war waged by the Bosnian Serbs against the mainly Muslim Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats. The conflict began with the Serb-led Republic of Srpska's secession from Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was followed by the ethnic cleansing of Muslim Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats from the areas that the Serbs wanted to join with the Republic of Serbia. Although the war officially ended in 1995, the conflict continued with smaller incidents occurring throughout the 2000s and 2010s, including the Srebrenica massacre, the 2014 Bosnia and Herzegovina floods and the 2014 Bosnia and Herzegovina earthquake .
The conflict resulted in the deaths of approximately 100,000 people and the displacement of more than two million others, with a significant amount of this forced migration being the result of the Srebrenica massacre . The massacre was the worst atrocity in Europe since the Holocaust, and was perpetrated by the Bosnian Serb Army. Over the course of three days, Serb troops killed more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys, while women and girls were taken as a part of the first wave of the ethnic cleansing campaign. Since the Bosnian Genocide, the International Community has begun to work with Bosnian Serbs to ensure that a repeat of the conflict will not occur.

It was a remarkable turnaround . In 1991, the US had withdrawn all its troops from Somalia. Its administration had been led by a US-backed warlord whose soldiers had massacred up to 7000 Somali civilians in the town of Beledweyne. The US had imposed an arms embargo which was flouted by the warlords. The United Nations had failed to bring the warring factions to the negotiating table. Now, these same warlords were being treated by the US as if they were part of the solution, not the problem.
One of the most important differences between the US and Russia in their approaches to Somalia was that, while the US introduced its own doctrine of state-building and nation-building , Russia stuck to the traditional Soviet model of military and intelligence operations. The introduction of foreign forces into Somalia was a highly controversial decision. The Pentagon had been pushing for a "peace-through-strength" approach. But the Clinton administration relented because of the threat to the US posed by Somalia. It was a very different situation from the one that had prevailed in the 1980s, when the Soviet Union had sent thousands of military advisers and instructors to Afghanistan.
The Pentagon's first step was to build up a military command based in Nairobi. In January 1994 , a small but highly specialized four-man team from the Defence Intelligence Agency arrived in Somalia. They were given the task of helping to recruit, train and equip the Somali forces, and to provide intelligence analysis and target identification. The US had no wish to be perceived as a "big-brother" but it agreed with the British and French governments that it needed to be involved to prevent Somalia from slipping back into a failed state.
During the ensuing twelve months, the DIA team played an important role in the establishment of the Somali National Army (SNA). It was instrumental in vetting potential recruits, in training the officers and in equipping the soldiers. Its work was taken to the next level in January 1995 , when the United States sent 1500 troops to Somalia. The DIA team was given the task of integrating the SNA with the US forces to form a joint task force. To facilitate this, the DIA provided an intelligence "bridge" between the US forces and the SNA. This meant that it was responsible for gathering the intelligence for the joint task force and for vetting the SNA soldiers.

We wanted to show contemporary art to the people of Split and to Croatia, and this was the first time that the city would be able to see contemporary art. It was a very difficult thing to achieve. The Museum was opened in 1994 and this was a very important event for Split and for Croatia. They had never heard of contemporary art. Some people in the audience didn't want to go in. They were shocked and didn't understand the concept. At that time I was the only person in Croatia who was engaged in contemporary art, and I was the only person who had a concept of how to present contemporary art to the general public.

On the 26th , the steamer arrived with 100 refugees . It was either too late or the Army refused to let the passengers disembark . In any event , the steamer and its passengers were allowed to stay at the port . The steamer set sail again on the 27th with 220 refugees and a few passengers . The steamer was never seen again . The storm passed by Ensenada without incident .
It's interesting to note that the refugee ship was the only vessel to go missing in the storm.
All the other ships made it to their destinations and survived .

Angelou's "On The Pulse of Morning" is her attempt to re-establish "a sense of the common good." She proclaims that "What is morally right is politically wise," and that the "Civil rights of all [are] the responsibility of all." She does not aim to persuade the reader into believing her rather than her critics, but instead she attempts to change her readers to the point where they agree with her. She does this in two ways: first, by using the imagery of the blood of the earth, and second, by using the imagery of the universe.
The blood of the earth in "On The Pulse of Morning" seems to be the spiritual soundness of one's heart. Angelou says of the blood, "I call it the blood of the earth." This is a metaphor for the soundness of a person's heart, their ability to love, to care and to be fair. She says, "It's the blood of the earth which courses through the veins of the just." She then continues, "It's the blood of the earth which courses through the veins of the free." The blood of the earth is the blood of the people, and this is the way to life.
The universe, as depicted in Angelou's poem, is a wondrous place where we can find peace. Angelou says, "A new wind is blowing and the stars are wheeling / And the universe is unfolding." Everglades and the nearby Florida Keys were first explored by the Spanish in the 1500s. The area was settled by the British in the 1700s and the Spanish again in the 1800s. For much of the 1800s, the Everglades was home to Seminoles and Miccosukee Indians.

However, it was not until the 1880s that real estate developers started buying land and creating development "canals," which drained the Everglades, making possible the development of the South Florida economy.
The Everglades was much more than just a home to the Seminoles and the Miccosukee Indians for centuries. The Everglades was a world unto itself, a unique ecosystem which supported a vast number of plants and animals. As a result of the canals, many of those animals were lost. The wading birds, the fish, the alligators were all forced to leave the Everglades. The Everglades is no longer a world unto itself, but rather a part of the world. Some 2000 miles of slow-moving water flowed through the Everglades, its width ranging from 300 feet to 100 miles. Originally the Everglades covered 4000 square miles. In 1885, the Army Corps of Engineers of the United States began the process of draining the Everglades. This drainage process was basically completed by the 1920s. As a result, the Everglades was reduced from 4000 square miles to 3000 square miles.
The Everglades are now a part of the world. They are a drainage system that is part of the nation's interstate highway system. While the Everglades are no longer a separate world unto itself, the Everglades remain a unique ecosystem.

In the Everglades, it is possible to see manatees, snakes, panthers, and dolphins. The Everglades is home to more than 30 mammal species and 300 bird species. The Everglades is also home to the endangered Cape Sable seaside sparrow.

The Environmental Protection Agency has designated the Corpus Christi Bay system as an estuary of national significance . More

than 440 species of fish, birds, mammals, invertebrates, and plants use the Corpus Christi Bay system  as a place to live, feed, and reproduce. The bay system is also very important to the people who live in or visit this area.
The Corpus Christi Bay system is unique. It is the only bay system in Texas that is a part of the Gulf of Mexico. It is, therefore, exposed to the same forces that affect the Gulf. The Corpus Christi Bay system is also unique in the diversity of its ecosystems. The 263 square miles of water are divided into four parts: bay, lagoon, ship channel, and open Gulf. These ecosystems are connected by marshes, sandbars, and mud flats. The bay ecosystem has the largest tidal range of any bay system in Texas, 16 - 18 feet, and is also the shallowest, with an average depth of just 15 feet. The lagoon is the system's largest and deepest, with an average depth of 20-25 feet. The ship channel is the shallowest part of the system, averaging only 6 feet deep. The open Gulf is the most dynamic, with tides that vary by only 2 feet.
The Corpus Christi Bay system has also been unique in its history. The bay has been a sheltered place for thousands of years, providing food, water, and protection for the people of the area. During the Spanish and Mexican eras, the bay was called "El Puerto de Santander," or "The Port of San Andres." When Texas became independent in 1836, the bay was named Corpus Christi Bay, after the city of Corpus Christi was established on the bay's northeastern shore. In 1845, when Texas joined the United States, the city's name was changed to Corpus Christi. The bay continues to play an important role in the economy of the city and the state of Texas.
The Corpus Christi Bay system has changed during the past 100 years. The Texas legislature has designated the bay as "the most environmentally-degraded bay system in the State." During the past century, rapid population growth, agricultural and industrial expansion, and the channelization of the bay have continued to change the system. The bay system has also been affected by natural processes. Storms, hurricanes, and tidal flow have shaped the bay in ways that are both predictable and unpredictable.
The purpose of this guidebook is to help students understand and appreciate the Corpus Christi Bay system. By understanding the bay system, students can become better informed and active stewards of the environment. When students know and understand the bay ecosystem, they can make better decisions about the environment and the actions they take in the bay.

The Middle Colonies comprised the middle region of the Thirteen Colonies of the British Empire in North America . Much of the a

rable land was used for extensive farms. The Middle Colonies bordered the southern colonies to the south, New England to the northeast, and the Canadian provinces to the north. The border between New England and the Middle colonies is disputed.
The Middle Colonies were the most ethnically diverse of the Thirteen Colonies. The population consisted of a large number of English, Ulster Scots and Scotch-Irish, Germans, Dutch, Swedes, Finns, Poles, Native Americans, Africans and small numbers of French and Spanish. The Middle Colonies were the most religiously diverse of the colonies, with a relatively high degree of religious tolerance. The colonies were also the most urbanized of the Thirteen Colonies, and had the most commercial ties with the British and other colonies.
The Middle Colonies were the wealthiest of the Thirteen Colonies. Their economy was diverse, and they produced a wide range of products. The colonies provided a large proportion of the food consumed by the British Army during the French and Indian War.
The Middle Colonies were also the most politically active of the colonies. The colonies were the first to be represented in the Continental Congress.

Because the nuclear membrane is impermeable to large molecules , nuclear pores are required that regulate nuclear transport of

ions, proteins, and nucleic acids into and out of the nucleus, the process of nucleocytoplasmic shuttling.
 Because the DNA of eukaryotes is packaged into chromosomes, a separate mechanism for the regulation of transcription and translation is required.
 Thus the nucleus has a dual role in gene expression: it functions as a repository for DNA in the chromosome and as a site of transcription and translation.
#  **Nuclear Structure**
The nucleus is a spherical organelle that occupies the center of the cell, with its surface surrounding the cell nucleolus (Figure 4.1). The nuclear membrane is made of a double layer of phospholipids with embedded proteins. The nucleus can be divided into three regions: the nucleolus, the nuclear periphery (peripheral region), and the central region.
**Figure 4.1** The nuclear membrane and the peripheral and central regions of the nucleus. The nucleolus is a dense region in the nucleus where ribosomal RNA is synthesized. Ribosomes are formed at the periphery of the nucleus and are composed of ribosomal RNA and proteins. The central region is called the nuclear matrix, which is a network of protein filaments that can bind to DNA.
 The nuclear periphery is the region where ribosomal RNA and ribosomes are formed. Ribosomes are composed of ribosomal RNA and proteins. The ribosomal RNAs are synthesized in the nucleolus, a dense region in the nucleus, and are transported to the periphery. The nucleolus is the site of ribosome assembly and is the site of ribosomal RNA processing.
 The central region of the nucleus is called the nuclear matrix, which is a network of protein filaments that can bind to DNA. The matrix is important in the organization of chromatin.
 Nuclear pores are located in the nuclear membrane. They are cones made of proteins that allow passage of molecules into and out of the nucleus.
 Nuclear pores are the entrance to the nucleus. They are made of nuclear pore complexes, which are large protein assemblies embedded in the nuclear membrane. The nuclear pores allow passage of ions, small molecules, and nucleic acids from the cytoplasm into the nucleus and from the nucleus into the cytoplasm.
 Nucleoporins are proteins that link the nucleus to the cytoplasm; they are found in the nuclear pores. Nucleoporins are involved in nucleocytoplasmic transport of molecules, signal transduction, cell cycle progression, and DNA replication.
 Proteins that are involved in cell cycle progression are located in the nuclear pores. The proteins are responsible for the rapid transport of the cyclin-dependent kinase complex from the cytoplasm to the nucleus in response to a signal that induces the cell to enter mitosis and for the transport of cyclin to the cytoplasm in response to a signal that inhibits mitotic progression.
 The nuclear matrix is a network of protein filaments that bind to DNA. It is located in the central region of the nucleus.
 Nuclear matrix proteins are important in the organization of chromatin and in the regulation of cell growth. The nuclear matrix is critical in maintaining the integrity of chromatin and in the regulation of gene expression.
#  **Gene Expression in the Nucleus**
The nucleus has a dual role in gene expression: it functions as a repository for DNA in the chromosome and as a site of transcription and translation.
 The nucleus is the site of replication of the DNA in the chromatin and is the site of transcription of the DNA into messenger RNA. The ribosomes are formed in the nucleus and are transported to the cytoplasm for translation. The proteins that are synthesized are transported back into the nucleus for future use.
 The DNA in the nucleus is wrapped around histone proteins to form chromatin. Chromatin undergoes remodeling and changes in its structure in response to changes in gene expression, which are events that take place in the nucleus.
 Chromatin is the primary structure of the chromosome, which is the form that DNA takes in the nucleus. It is the DNA that is wrapped around histone proteins and is the major structure of the chromosome.
 The structure of the chromosome changes in response to changes in gene expression.
As the ninth season progressed and the show 's ratings began to plummet , Fox became more and more actively involved in the sho

w's creative direction, and the writers began to have a hard time dealing with the network's interference. The show's ratings continued to drop, and, on May 15, 2003, Fox canceled the show.
 In the wake of the cancellation, speculation arose throughout the Internet and the media about the possible reasons for the cancellation. Initially, it was reported that several of the show's writers would be fired for the show's overall declining quality, and that Fox would replace them with staff from "The Simpsons" and "Malcolm in the Middle". Fox responded to the speculation by denying that any "X-Files" staff members would be fired.
 After the cancellation was announced, many of the show's cast members issued public statements in which they expressed their disappointment in the cancellation. Gillian Anderson and David Duchovny were the most vocal about their displeasure, and Duchovny publicly expressed his belief that the show could have been saved if he, as Mulder, had been given a more substantial role.
 Gillian Anderson expressed her disappointment at the cancellation of the show, saying, "I was devastated to hear the news that 'The X-Files' was not going to be continued. I have had such a fun time making these films and I am very proud of them... I thought that the way that we ended the series, with a cliffhanger, would give people something to discuss and would leave the door open. I guess that was not the case. I really wanted to finish our work on 'The X-Files' as a series and not have it end in such a disappointing way."
 Carter expressed his disappointment at the cancellation in a statement to the press, saying, "It is with great sadness that I have to make this announcement. The truth is out there...but it's not in my hands anymore. I know that the show's fans are like a family, and I've always tried to treat that family as well as I would my own. It's the reason that I have to be here today. I want to thank Fox and Chris for the opportunity to have been part of the show's journey. I wouldn't be here today if not for them. I want to thank the creators, David and Gillian, for their guidance, and the rest of the cast for their professionalism and friendship. I also want to thank the writers, producers, directors, crew, and our excellent and loyal fans who have supported us through this incredible journey...a journey that I will always be proud to have been a part of."
 An Entertainment Weekly article titled " How I Killed the X-Files " was published in the June 20, 2003, issue of the magazine. In it, Carter explained that the cancellation of the show came about in a chain of events that began when Carter pitched the idea of a nine-episode miniseries to Fox. The miniseries was originally conceived as a way to resolve the cliffhanger that the previous season had left off on, and to allow Mulder and Scully to work together without being hampered by the Mulder and Scully relationship. The miniseries was tentatively titled "The Truth" and was to be the final chapter of the X-Files saga.
 The miniseries was a success, and Fox agreed to continue the series. In the course of the next few months, Carter and the show's writers developed a story line that revolved around the existence of a government project known as "Colony" and the Cigarette Smoking Man leading Mulder and Scully to a place known as "the black oil". The story line was to be resolved in a two-part episode. Fox approved the story line, and the episodes were shot. However, in the middle of filming the episodes, Fox executives became concerned that the story line would alienate fans of the show who enjoyed the Mulder and Scully relationship and the monster-of-the-week stories. They also became concerned that the story line would be too complicated to understand, and that it might make the show difficult to follow from week to week. Fox demanded that the show be returned to the status quo, which would involve Scully and Mulder working together, but as partners rather than lovers. Carter refused to do this, and the show was canceled.

At its peak in 1954 , DuMont was affiliated with around 200 television stations . In those days , television stations were free

to choose whether they wanted to carry another network's programming , and most of the DuMont affiliates were in small markets where the network was the only option . In addition , a number of the DuMont affiliates were owned by the network ( though the DuMont network was also affiliated with a number of independent stations ) .
 consistent with its low-cost programming and "do-it-yourself" philosophy , the DuMont network was also one of the first to experiment with live television . Beginning in 1950 , DuMont affiliates began carrying a newscast called " The Walter Compton News " , which was carried live from the network's headquarters in New York City . The network was also one of the first to experiment with programming aimed at a general audience , such as live sports and quiz shows .
 The DuMont network canceled its prime-time programming in early 1956 , and its remaining affiliates began carrying the ABC network's prime-time lineup . However, the DuMont network continued to air some of its own affiliate-only programs , such as " Al Hurtz's Follies " and " The Walter Compton News " , through 1957 . The network continued to operate as a daytime network until 1958 , when it sold its remaining affiliates to the Metromedia Broadcasting Group .
 Main article : History of DuMont Television Network , Inc.
DuMont was formed in 1944 by the DuMont Laboratories , a company founded by Dr. Allen B. DuMont , a pioneer in television development and an early proponent of electronic television . DuMont had been working on a " picture tube " television set since the late 1920s , and in the early 1930s he began experimenting with a television transmitter .
In 1939 , DuMont formed the DuMont Television Corporation to develop a television network . The network, which was named the DuMont Television Network , began operations on August 15, 1944 with three stations : New York City station WABD ( channel 5 ) , Chicago station WDON ( channel 3 ) , and Pittsburgh station WDTV ( channel 2 ). DuMont's first broadcast was a one-hour program featuring the Rockettes and a speech by Mayor LaGuardia .
DuMont's New York and Chicago affiliates were the first television stations in the country . In addition , the network was one of the first to broadcast in color ( beginning in 1945 , and later becoming the first network to broadcast in color on a regular basis ). The network was also one of the first to air a soap opera ( " Secret Storm " , which began airing on October 3, 1954 ) .
While the network was initially successful , DuMont's lack of capital , as well as ownership and control issues ( DuMont was required by the Federal Communications Commission to divest WDTV ) , led to a decline in the network's fortunes . In addition , the FCC's elimination of the UHF band in the early 1950s led to the cancellation of DuMont's largest affiliates .
By the middle of the 1950s , DuMont's affiliate list had shrunk to around 20 stations , and DuMont became the first ( and only ) network to cease operations during prime time . In 1955 , DuMont affiliates began carrying ABC's prime-time lineup .
On January 11, 1956 , DuMont announced that it would stop producing its own programming and become a daytime network . The network continued to operate as a daytime network until 1958 , when it sold its remaining affiliates to the Metromedia Broadcasting Group .

Born and raised in Hilo , Hawaiʻi , he was the eldest son of Kinoʻoleoliliha , a Hawaiian high chiefess , and Benjamin Pitman ,

a Hawaiian planter.
His father was descended from a chiefly family , while his mother was of mixed Hawaiian and English ancestry.

 Kaiwi was the father of Prince Jonah Kuhio Kalanianaʻole , who was the father of the last Queen of Hawaiʻi, Liliʻuokalani.
 The Hawaiian government granted Pitman a lease on land in the Kohala district in 1874, which he named "Pitman's Plantation" and which later became a model of successful agricultural plantation.
 He died in 1891 and was survived by his wife, whom he married in 1875, and their three children: Princess Abigail Kawānanakoa, Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop and Prince David Kawānanakoa.
 He was buried in the Kalanianaeleole Church cemetery in Waimea.
The Pukui-Elbert Hawaiian Dictionary recognizes him as the source of the name of the Pukui-Elbert Hawaiian Dictionary.

In the 1920s and 1930s , as mechanization became more prevalent , both wild and domesticated breeding stock diminished to almos

t vanishing levels. The decades that followed saw a gradual rise in the numbers of bison , elk and moose . In the early 1960s , the Yellowstone ecosystem had only a tiny fraction of its original wildlife populations.
For the first time in 120 years , the bison herds in the park were moved to a wintering ground in Montana in 1963 , due to repeated conflicts with livestock. As the animal's numbers increased, they were allowed to return to the valley in 1965 , and in 1975 they were allowed to roam freely across the entire park. The elk were reduced to around 500 in the 1960s, but their numbers have risen to more than 5,000 animals. The moose population also grew, but was reduced to around 50 animals in the 1960s, and now numbers around 200.
The preservation of the Yellowstone ecosystem has led to a re-creation of the natural environment. As plants and animals have come back, they have become dependent upon the river and the lake. The beaver , for example, returned to the park in the 1930s, and by the 1960s the animal's population had reached 10,000 animals. Beavers dam rivers , and their dams help to maintain the water level in the lake and the river, as well as providing habitat for other animals. In the 1970s, the beaver population was reduced to around 5,000 animals.
Protection of the Yellowstone ecosystem has also resulted in the restoration of the wolves . In the 1920s, there were no wolves in the park. The animal returned in the 1960s and in 1975 the first breeding pair was sighted in the park. In 1995, there were 32 breeding pairs of wolves in the park.
Overfishing of the Yellowstone river was seen as a threat to the bison population, and in 1972 the river was closed to commercial fishing. In 1996, the river was closed to all fishing, and in 2002 the river was closed to all anglers and tourists. A balance between the bison , elk and grizzly bear populations was seen as necessary, and in 1997, a quota was introduced to the numbers of animals permitted to remain in the park .

Hurricane Diana struck eastern Mexico and managed to hold together , remaining a tropical depression as it entered the eastern

Gulf of Mexico. On June 9, Diana rapidly intensified to a Category 3 hurricane, but weakened again to a Category 2 as it approached the Florida Panhandle. The hurricane struck Panama City, Florida on June 12, as a Category 2 hurricane. After the storm moved inland, it weakened to a tropical storm as it moved over Alabama. The storm then caused severe damage in the Southeastern United States before dissipating over Tennessee on June 13. It was the first major hurricane in the Atlantic since Hurricane Celia in 1970 and the second major hurricane to strike the United States in 1990 behind Hurricane Hugo.
 Hurricane Diana was the second named storm of the 1990 Atlantic hurricane season. Tropical Storm Diana originated from a tropical wave that moved off the coast of Africa on May 29. The system organized into a tropical depression on June 3 while situated off the coast of Nicaragua. While the depression moved northward, it gradually developed further organization, and was upgraded to Tropical Storm Diana on June 5, while located over the extreme southern Gulf of Mexico. Later that day, it made landfall near Punta de Agua, Nicaragua, and slowly weakened while continuing to the west-northwest. As the system moved northward, it strengthened further into a Category 2 hurricane on June 7. At about the same time, Diana began to turn to the northwest, and on June 8 it had become a Category 3 hurricane. After the storm turned to the west-northwest, its intensity decreased rapidly, and by June 10 it was only a Category 1 hurricane. On June 11, Diana made landfall near Panama City, Florida, as a Category 2 hurricane with winds of 105 mph (165 km/h). After making landfall, Diana quickly weakened to a tropical storm, and by June 12 it had lost tropical cyclone characteristics completely over the Southeastern United States. On June 13, the remnants of Diana entered Tennessee.
Diana caused 21 deaths and $3.5 billion (1990 USD) in damage. In addition to the injuries and fatalities caused by Diana, 46 deaths occurred from a subsequent outbreak of Legionnaires' disease in Panama City. Most of the deaths from Diana occurred in Florida, where 20 people were killed.
Diana was the first major hurricane to strike the United States since Hurricane Andrew in 1992.
The name Diana was retired after the 1990 season and was replaced with Dennis in the 1996 season.
The name Diana was first used for the 1954 hurricane season, and was last retired after the 1990 season.

Live & Kicking was a BBC Saturday morning children 's magazine programme , running from 1993 to 2001 . The fourth in a succession of Saturday morning children's television programmes to carry the name Live & Kicking, it featured live pop music and comedy sketches aimed at children aged 8-14 .The show was broadcast from the BBC Television Centre in London .
Live & Kicking was originally presented by Tim Vincent and Tracy Harrison . Vincent left the show in 1995 and was replaced by Dani Harmer .
Over the years, Live & Kicking featured a range of regular features, including the "Bubblegum Club", "The Gig", "The Really Big Show", "What's New?", "Cool!" and "Buzz".
The show also contained a sketch show called "Gakked". It was presented by a group of characters who were either a parody of 1980s TV show "The Goonies" or 1980s TV show "The A-Team", or a mixture of the two. The cast included:
Dave - played by Mike Wozniak
Sean - played by Matt Hunt
Jonny - played by Freddie Wise
Greg - played by Nick Hutchinson
Mark - played by Ed Mitchell
Darren - played by Lance Ward
Kim - played by Jennifer Marsden
Another sketch show called "The Live Adventure Game Show" was presented by Joey Essex and James Buckley . This was a parody of the 1990s children's game show "The Crystal Maze".
The programme also featured a number of live pop acts, including Boyzone , Backstreet Boys , Sugababes , Atomic Kitten , Steps , S Club 7 , Five , A1 , Sugababes , McFly , Busted , Girls Aloud , JLS , The Wanted , One Direction , Little Mix , Olly Murs , Neon Jungle , Fifth Harmony , Union J , The Vamps , R5 , Tate Stevens , and Ella Henderson .
In 2000, Live & Kicking won two BAFTAs .
The show was axed by the BBC in 2001, following low viewer figures in the new millennium. The final episode aired on 25 August 2001, with a special "Best of Live & Kicking" episode airing the following week on 1 September 2001.
"Live & Kicking" was the name of a similarly themed show which began in 1973 and ended in 1975.
The show also had a spin-off called "Going Live!" which began in 1993, which was presented by Chris Evans and ran until 1998.

Facilitators and the people who work at the Information and Assistance and Help Desk offices are your best resource when you need to find an address. They will check their local calls, calls from other facilities, and the many computerized databases they use.
Many libraries, police stations, and government offices have local information services or information desks where you can get help in locating people. The local government or civil service office can often be helpful in locating an address.
#  **Where Can I Find a Telephone Directory?**
There are two types of telephone directories: white pages and yellow pages. The white pages are the phone book, which lists residential and business numbers. The yellow pages are the reverse telephone directory, which lists businesses by name, address, and telephone number.
The yellow pages are located at most libraries. In some libraries, both the white pages and the yellow pages are available. If you are looking for a specific name or number, the best way to locate it is to call the library and ask the librarian if the yellow pages and/or the white pages are available. If you are successful in locating the information you need, request that it be held for you. Usually, you can expect to receive the information in a few days.
Sometimes the information you need is not available at the library. In that case, you can try to locate the information by calling information. To call information, you must first dial your area code. Your area code is usually found on your calling card or telephone bill. The phone number for information is 411. The call is free.
You must first dial your area code. If you live in the Atlanta area, for example, you would dial 404-555-1212. The information operator will ask you where you are calling from. (You can avoid this step by dialing 1 for the operator.) The operator will then ask you for the number you are calling, and you will be connected with the person or business you are trying to reach.

One way to find an address in a telephone directory is to look it up by name. Start by turning to the first part of the directory, which is usually the white pages. The white pages generally list names and addresses by street address.

Gerard was born in Yorkshire, the son of a man called "Bernard". He was a Norman who was born in Yorkshire and was educated in Normandy. 

He was a chaplain to King William Rufus, who made him Archbishop of York in 1080. 

He was succeeded by William de St-Calais in 1108.

In 1912 , the family moved to Berlin , where Eva attended school.
At the age of 14 , she began helping in her father's shop and later worked in a factory .

With her father's help , Eva enrolled at a teachers' training college in 1919 , which she attended until 1921 .
During this time , she began sketching , which led to her decision to study art .

## Early career

After early art studies in Berlin , Eva went to the Art Academy in Breslau in 1921 . She studied there until 1925 , and worked as an assistant to the sculptor Carl Seffner .

From 1925 to 1930 , Eva studied at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf , where she worked with Wilhelm Morgner and HAP Grieshaber .
After graduating , she opened a studio in Düsseldorf .

## Later life and work

In 1930 , Eva moved to Berlin , where she worked as an illustrator for the journal Die Dame .
She also worked for the Jewish newspaper Selbstwehr .

In 1936 , Eva returned to Düsseldorf , where she became involved with the Düsseldorf Secession .
When the Nazis assumed power in 1933 , Eva was living with the painter Paul Baumgarten .

In 1937 , she made her first trip to Paris , where she met Max Ernst and the director of the Musée d'Art Moderne Fernand Leger .
Although she was in Paris during the German invasion of France , Eva returned to Düsseldorf in 1940 .

In 1943 , Eva moved to Paris to work as an illustrator for the newspaper Le Parisien .

She later worked in the United States , where she became close to the artists Mark Rothko and Robert Motherwell .

In 1960 , Eva's 1939 painting "Mutter" was included in the exhibition "Surrealism and the Unexpected" at the Museum of Modern Art in New York .

In 1960 , Eva moved to Santa Monica , California , where she became a member of the Art Students League of Los Angeles .
She died in 1966 , aged 69.

I was a teenager when I first visited a psychiatric hospital.
At the time, I was living in New York City and had no idea how to get to the hospital, so I struck up a conversation with a woman in the subway who told me she had been there once, too. But it was too late: the train had left.
"Just get on the next one," she said. "It'll take us right there."
It did.
The hospital was located in a wooded part of the city, and when I got off the train I could see it was surrounded by a high fence. I walked along the tracks and crossed the street, where I saw another fence, this one topped with barbed wire. And then I was inside, looking up at a building, with the fence continuing on to a gate.
I was about to walk through the gate when a guard, who was sitting in a booth, waved me away. He kept waving until I went back to the street and crossed over to the other side. At the other side of the fence was a paved walkway that led directly to the gate. I walked to the gate, looked through the bars, and saw a group of patients talking outside a building.
I found one of the patients and asked if I could talk to her.
"Sure," she said. "I'm an old friend of your mother's."
I smiled, but I didn't know her from anybody.
"Why don't you come in?" she said. "You'll like it here."
She led me through two doors and into a room filled with people, most of them sitting on a long couch. I sat down next to a man with a long, white beard and asked him who was in charge.
"I was," he said, "until she came along."
I turned and looked at the woman.
"I'm the director," she said. "My name is Elizabeth. I'm the one who sent for you."
"I'm fifteen," I said, "and I'm here to see my mother."
"Why don't you come with me?" she said.
I followed her down a long hallway and into a small room, where I found my mother sitting at a table. She was writing in a notebook.
"I'm sorry, I can't talk to you right now," she said.
"I'm sorry, too," I said. "I can't stay long. I just wanted to say hello and tell you I'm fine. I've been in school."
"I know," she said. "I've been reading your letters."
"I've been writing letters, too," I said, "but you haven't answered them."
"I'm sorry," she said. "I've been busy."
"I hope to see you soon," I said, and then I turned and walked out of the room.
The woman at the front desk was already waiting for me.
"Come with me," she said, and led me down another hallway and into a small room.
"This is your room," she said. "It's all yours."
"I can't do that," I said. "I don't want to stay here."
"But you have to," she said. "It's the law. You have to stay here until you're eighteen or you'll be put in a hospital for the rest of your life. You're lucky I found you."
I didn't know what to say.
"I'm sorry," she said. "I know this is hard. But you'll be fine. I promise you."
I looked at her and then at the door.
"I'm going to bed," I said. "I'll see you in the morning."
I walked out of the room and down the hallway and into the room where I had been sitting with the man with the long beard.
"I have to go," I said. "I'll see you tomorrow."

The Goat Puzzle , also known as The Infamous Goat Puzzle , The Infamous Goat , The Wretched Goat , The Goat of Lochmarne , or s

eldomly just The Goat , is a puzzle that is related to the large number of goats in the world. It is estimated that at least ten billion goats are alive and walking around on the planet right now, but how many are there really? More importantly, how many do we need?
The Goat Puzzle starts with the statement that there is one goat. From this you can then deduce that there are two goats, because you know that each goat has one goat. This leads to the fact that there are three goats because each goat has one goat, which means that there are two goats, which means that there are three goats. In this way you can keep going on and on, and conclude that there are an infinite number of goats.
This is of course a rather silly example of the Goat Puzzle, but it does show that the number of goats is very large. It's also an illustration of why the Goat Puzzle is so difficult to understand.
That's why this book is here. The goal is to help you understand the concept of The Goat Puzzle, and to start thinking about it in a new way.

The song was written and produced by Madonna and Stephen Bray , and served as the lead single from True Blue, preceding the " Live to Tell " single. It was also the lead single from Madonna's first greatest hits album, The Immaculate Collection (1990) . " True Blue " is a dance-pop and new wave song, and the lyrics are about the singer's dedication to her partner. It includes a brief instrumental section, with a prominent bass guitar and drum-driven beat, and a synthesizer melody that is loosely based on the bassline of the 1984 song " Cuica " by Brazilian musician Tom Ze.
The song was positively received by critics, who complimented its production and Madonna's vocals. " True Blue " is considered to be one of Madonna's signature songs, and has been cited as one of her best singles. It was a commercial success, peaking at number three on the Billboard Hot 100 , and topping the charts in Argentina, Canada, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Madonna performed the song during her Blond Ambition World Tour (1990) . The song's music video was directed by James Orlandi and Michael Haussman . It features Madonna in a sailor suit. The video was the first Madonna video to feature a male lead, piano player Stephen Bray, who was Madonna's boyfriend at the time. Madonna later recorded two Spanish language versions of the song, although neither version was released as a single.

On my third day in Princeton I was invited to give a short report on my thesis work . There were usually two or three speakers

who each had ten minutes to present their research, and then a discussion period. This was an unusual opportunity for me as a graduate student to share my work with senior faculty and graduate students, and it was good publicity for my thesis. I had spent the previous week in the department's photographic darkroom printing some of the mud-stained slides that I had collected, and I had put together a simple PowerPoint presentation with the title "Artifacts and a Shipwreck."
I led off with a slide of a small, square, grayish-black object that I had discovered a world away from the _Mary Celeste_ , in the Aegean Sea. In the course of my fieldwork in Greece, I had been looking for the remains of ancient shipwrecks. In the summer of 2000 I had been diving off the coast of Turkey, in the Gulf of Gökova, not far from the ancient port city of Miletus. I had gone diving to search for artifacts in 11,000-year-old seabed settlements off the coast of Turkey and Greece. There had been no particular reason to expect to find shipwrecks; I was only seeking colorful marine fossils that would make a good display in an aquarium. I was not looking for the remains of ancient ships.
But one day during a dive, I saw a small object on the seabed near the site of an ancient settlement. It was small, about the size of a dinner plate, and made of a dark, stony substance. I picked it up and placed it in my diving weight belt. When I got back to the surface, I realized that it was a finely carved, intricately decorated tile. It was a tile that had probably been part of the floor in a house or temple. I took it to the surface and to the shore along with many other artifacts I had collected during my dive. I took it to a hotel in Miletus and showed it to a marine archaeologist who had been acting as my guide in the underwater sites. I quickly learned that the tile was an ancient artifact that was almost unknown in the literature of Turkish and Greek archaeology. It was a difficult tile to date but probably came from the fifth or sixth century BC.
I had been collecting artifacts from ancient shipwrecks for several years, and I had been to several museums and archaeological sites in Greece to view their collections. I knew that the region I had dived in was a strategic point on the trade route between Asia Minor (modern Turkey) and Greece. In classical times there were many flourishing Greek cities along the coast, and the region was also a maritime center for the Ionians, a people who were important in the emergence of democracy and the formation of the Athenian state.
The tiles, which I later identified as _opus sectile_ , were embedded in the floor mosaic of a house or a temple in the ancient city of Miletus, and they have been dated to the fifth or sixth century BC. The _opus sectile_ tile is a type of tile that contains small pieces of colored stone, glass, or even shell in a black, stony matrix. The tiles were popular in the Roman Empire, and I had seen several examples in the museums of Rome.
I later discovered that the tile was not a typical Greek artifact, and it had never before been found in the Aegean. The type of tile was typically found only in the eastern Mediterranean, in the area known as Asia Minor. When I learned that the tile had never been reported from this region of Greece, I thought that perhaps it had come from the sea. I wondered if it could have been from one of the many shipwrecks in the Gulf of Gökova. I had been diving at this site for several weeks, and I had collected more than 100 artifacts from the seabed.
I carried the tile back to the United States with me in 2000. When I returned to Princeton, I presented the tile to the archaeology department. I had no idea what it might be worth, but I knew it was a precious piece of ancient history. I went to the office of a curator at the university's Princeton University Art Museum, and he took a look at it. He said, "Oh, I've seen this type of tile before.
