A few years ago I was discussing the delimitation of the genus Rheum with the celebrated B. E. Wildman-Thompson, who told me he had never had any doubt as to the correctness of his opinion that the British R. officinale and R. exaltatum are distinct species. 'But', I said, 'Hill thought that R. officinale was a hybrid, and he was a good botanist.' 'Ah', replied Wildman-Thompson, 'but that is Hill's mistake; he was a bad botanist.' Now it is true that Wildman-Thompson was not likely to have an unduly high opinion of himself, but one may doubt whether he was any less prejudiced against Hill than Hill was prejudiced against R. officinale.
The fallacy that Hill was wrong about R. officinale and that Wildman-Thompson was right must be regarded as one of the most characteristic of all botanical fallacies, and this is another instance of it. How could it happen that two men, apparently both of good judgement, should have held such opposite views? Hill was a skilful botanist who made a special study of the genus Rheum and was one of the first to recognize the importance of the genus in the classification of plants, and he had, besides, the advantage of an excellent herbarium. Wildman-Thompson was not a botanist in the sense that Hill was, and he had no herbarium, and he was, moreover, a botanical crank. Yet, in spite of all this, he was right and Hill was wrong, and those who come after us will be equally certain that Wildman-Thompson was right and that Hill was wrong.
The same holds good in many other cases. Many taxonomists have been convinced that the species they have described are distinct species on the sole authority of the so-called pure species, and have never troubled to examine the hybrids and the hybrids of hybrids.
The treatment of this species by certain taxonomists well illustrates the pitfalls that lie in wait for those who worship at the shrine of the pure species.

"The people of Darwin are not over-enthusiastic about the idea," he reported. A week later, Eaton was sent to the Northern Territory's capital, Alice Springs, to organise the proposed second base. Eaton had the aircraft's cockpit and a bunk bed installed in the old Darwin Post Office building, while most of the crew lived in a tent near the fuel dump.  It was a long way from Sydney.  At home, Eaton's wife, Beth, had been diagnosed with cancer.  On 21 June, he passed his word test and proceeded to Sydney to spend time with his family, while his RAAF colleagues moved to Alice Springs.
In the first week of July 1938, Eaton was sent back to Darwin.  He had received an urgent telegram from the Chief of the Air Staff.  "It is essential that RAAF personnel proceed as soon as possible to Darwin," it said.
The single-engined monoplane that Eaton had been ferrying to the Northern Territory had crashed during a test flight.  He had been lucky to survive the crash, but the aircraft was a total wreck.  He had failed to secure a replacement.
On 14 July 1938, the RAAF officially established Darwin as a station.  Two days later, Eaton was back in the skies of the Northern Territory.  With a group of training pilots, he flew a Wirraway to Alice Springs in 2 hours and 23 minutes.  The flight was a huge success.  "The Darwin Station is now assured," the Chief of the Air Staff wrote.  "The maintenance and operational problems are great but they are now being tackled and the air field is a very good one."
Eaton's Wirraway was returned to Sydney for repairs.  Then he was sent to Port Moresby, in New Guinea, to command a flight of Wirraways.  His first task was to fly to New Britain and establish a base for a flight of Wirraway aircraft.  New Britain was a tiny island, just 10 kilometres across in places.  Eaton knew the island well.  In the previous decade, he had flown to New Britain several times to establish new airstrips on its tiny coral islands.  Now there was a new threat in the region.  Japan had invaded China in 1937, and its interest in New Britain was growing.
Eaton's Wirraway was the first aircraft to land on the island since the Japanese had taken it over.  On the first day, he flew the Wirraway over the coral airstrip.  "I had no sooner landed in a cloud of dust than a couple of the Japs came out to see me," he wrote.

Eaton was looking for a site for his own airstrip.  He found a site on a tiny island off New Britain, called Onbak Island.  It was only a few minutes flying time from Rabaul. Ardvreck Castle is a ruined castle near Loch Assynt in the Scottish Highlands . It is a category A listed building .
The castle is situated on a small headland on the north side of Loch Assynt and is marked by a 30-metre (98 ft) high rocky island known as Eilean an t-Srath . It was built in the 16th century but was never completed.
The castle was built on the site of an earlier fortified house to provide a base for Clan Mackenzie in their feud with the MacDonalds of Dunvegan .
The earliest part of the castle is the main block, which was built in 1586. This has a courtyard on its south side, where the dungeon and prison were located. The walls of the courtyard are over two metres thick. The curtain wall is built on a bastion and was intended to provide a bastioned defence.
The main block was extended in 1598 when the east block and the three storey round tower were built. The tower was intended as a state room. The kitchen was also built at this time, along with a guard room and a vaulted passageway.

The earliest known written version of the Laws of Cricket , dating from 1744 , does not include an lbw rule . At the time , bat

ters and bowlers were considered equally responsible for a dead ball . In 1774 , the Marylebone Cricket Club ( MCC ) , the then-governing body of cricket in England and Wales , first introduced a 'Dead Ball' rule , which stated that a bowler was permitted to let the ball lie until the fielding side had recovered from the no-ball . This rule remained in force until 1857 , when the MCC introduced the lbw rule .

 In 1870 , the MCC decided that the delivery would be called a no-ball if it was bowled wider than the stumps , rather than just a no-ball if it was bowled wide of the stumps . This was with a view to reducing the rate of bowlers' no-balls , which had become a problem in some matches.
 The lbw rule first came into force in matches governed by the Laws of Cricket on 4 August 1899 , in a match between Kent County Cricket Club and Nottinghamshire County Cricket Club .
The lbw rule was introduced in 1899 by the MCC.
 The MCC also introduced a new method of adjudication for lbw appeals , which was introduced into first-class cricket in 1901 and into club cricket in 1903. Under this method , the umpire makes the decision on whether a delivery is a legal delivery (or not) without consulting the fielding team. If the decision is in favour of the batter, the batter is not given out, and he may continue his innings. If the decision is in favour of the fielding team, the batter is given out , and the fielding team can choose whether to continue with the wicket or not.
 A 1990 recommendation by the Marylebone Cricket Club ( MCC ) to the ICC that the lbw appeal should be umpire's decision alone was accepted by the ICC in 2005. The change came into force for Test matches and first-class matches in 2008, and for other types of matches in 2010.
The lbw rule was introduced in 1899.
 The lbw rule was modified in 2000 by the addition of the 'stumped' method of dismissal , which states that a batter is out if he is hit by a delivery that has hit the stumps before hitting the ground.
 In 2009, the MCC recommended a modification of the lbw rule to allow the umpire to query a decision made by the bowler . The umpire has the option to decide that the ball is not a no-ball , and therefore not to give the batter out lbw. This modification was accepted by the ICC in 2012.

## Game recap

### First half

The Hurricanes started the game with the ball, scoring on their opening drive. The drive was highlighted by a 25-yard run by Travis Homer and finished off with a 1-yard touchdown run by Malik Rosier, giving the Hurricanes a 7–0 lead. The Huskers responded with a 12-play drive that was capped off with a 2-yard TD run by Devine Ozigbo. The Huskers would miss the extra-point attempt, leaving the score 7–6 in favor of the Hurricanes. The Hurricanes would respond with a 6-play drive that was capped by a 26-yard field goal by Bubba Baxa. The Huskers responded with a 3-play drive that ended in a 1-yard TD run by Ozigbo, which gave the Huskers a 13–10 lead. With 26 seconds left in the first quarter, Rosier connected with Jeff Thomas on a 47-yard pass to the Huskers 7 yard line. Five plays later, Rosier found Darrell Langham in the back of the end zone with 3 seconds left in the first quarter, giving the Hurricanes a 17–13 lead.

The Hurricanes would score again in the second quarter on a 32-yard field goal by Baxa and a 6-yard TD pass from Rosier to Braxton Berrios. At the end of the first half, the Hurricanes led 27–13.

### Second half

The Hurricanes scored again on their opening drive of the second half on a 33-yard TD pass from Rosier to Jeff Thomas. The Hurricanes would score again on their next drive on a 4-yard TD pass from Rosier to Darrell Langham. The Hurricanes would score again to end the third quarter on a 3-yard TD run by Travis Homer. At the end of the third quarter, the Hurricanes led 41–13.

The Huskers would score on their opening drive of the fourth quarter on a 1-yard TD run by Devine Ozigbo. The Hurricanes would respond with a 5-play drive that was capped off with a 28-yard TD pass from Rosier to Darrell Langham. The Hurricanes would score again on their next drive on a 7-yard TD pass from Rosier to Jeff Thomas. The Hurricanes added another touchdown on a 1-yard TD run by Malik Rosier to end the game.

The epoccipital is a distinctive bones found lining the frills of ceratopsians . The name is a misnomer , as they are not assoc

ited with the ossified epicranial bones. In fact , the bones are entirely bone free, and the epoccipital is a deep cutaneous fold from the premaxillae to the nasal bone. The epoccipital is a flattened , seperable flap of skin with a deep notch in the center of the flap which was used for ventilation. The notch is located in the center of the flap of skin and is bordered with soft tissues and bone . The epoccipitals of ceratopsian dinosaurs are very large , and are thought to have been gas exchange organs.
In May 1936 Olivier and Richardson jointly directed and starred in a new piece by J. B. Priestley , Bees on the Boatdeck . Both

plays were designed by Edward Catich. Priestley was a novelist and playwright who was widely admired by the Left for his socialist views and his sympathetic portrayal of working-class characters. He was also a Poet Laureate and his plays, though popular, were not regarded as great art.
Both plays were produced by Venables and had long runs. Priestley's work, though not considered theatrically important, had an influence on the later work of John Osborne and Arnold Wesker. On television, the plays were staged by the BBC in 1948 and 1951, and then, by Granada, in 1964, with Richardson in the lead.
Olivier's performance was thought to be one of his best, and he was pleased with Richardson's too. He described it as 'a very good part', and as a 'damned good part' in his autobiography. It was the last piece of theatre he worked on with Richardson.
The play was a love story set on a ship bound for New York. In the first act a young couple, George and Kitty, are sitting on the deck, looking out at the sea. They have been married for a year, but George is a little bored with his proper wife. He is painting a watercolour of the ship's wake, and Kitty is reading a book. A man, Joe, comes and joins them. He is a soldier on leave. He begins to flirt with Kitty, and she responds. The second act shows Kitty, George and Joe on deck again, with Joe and Kitty strolling together, and George painting. In the third act George is in his cabin, reading a book. Kitty, who has been with Joe, enters. She has read the book and tells George that the two of them cannot be together. He gets up and tries to kiss her. She fights him off. He goes back to his book. Kitty goes out. Joe then enters, and the two men talk, with Joe telling George that Kitty is wrong, and that George should go after her. Joe goes. George goes out on deck. The passenger ship sinks. He jumps overboard and is drowned. Kitty is left on the deck looking out to sea.
The play was successful, and Olivier was pleased with the part. 'I like it very much,' he said. 'It's an interesting part, it's very good, it's a very good part.' He was also pleased with Richardson's performance. In his autobiography he wrote, 'It was one of those lucky combinations that do not happen often. We were both in our element and it was an excellent performance.'
The play was based on a short story by Priestley, who was also the author of a number of successful novels, and like Olivier, Richardson and Houseman, he was a socialist. The play was successful, but not considered a great artistic achievement. In his autobiography, Olivier said that the play was 'not the greatest play ever written', but that it was 'a very good play'.
The play was staged by the BBC in 1948 and 1951, and then, by Granada, in 1964, with Richardson in the lead.

Prior to the Dawn mission , only a few surface features had been unambiguously detected on Ceres . High @-@ resolution ultravio

let images from the Hubble Space Telescope  and near-infrared images from the Spitzer Space Telescope  had revealed the presence of bright and dark regions, but it was not known whether these surface features were due to differences in the composition of the rocks (and/ or ice) that make up Ceres or the result of processes acting on the surface. Because these observations had only been made from a distance, it was not known whether these features were located on a very small area of Ceres's surface or extended over most of the surface.
Images from the Dawn spacecraft have shown that Ceres is a very different world from Vesta . Vesta is a dry, cratered object with a relatively smooth surface, although it does have a few small hills and other cratered features. Ceres, however, has a multitude of craters, some with mountains and/or hills of impact ejecta up to 15 km high. Ceres's surface is littered with impact craters from space debris and meteorites, and has a complex geological history that includes a cryovolcano (a volcano that erupts ice, water and/ or other volatiles), an impact crater with a central pit, and evidence of landslides and other geological processes.
 Ceres has a very tenuous atmosphere (2 × 10−13 bar), mainly composed of carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO2) and water vapor (H2O). The abundances of these gases are not well constrained, but have been estimated from observations of its thermal emissions. Its density is 1,150 kg/m3 and it has a mean density of 2,062 kg/m3, very close to its density of 2,050 kg/m3 at the bottom of the ocean. The thermal inertia in the upper layers of its near-surface crust is 2.5 × 10−4 J/m2-K2, which is low enough for the temperature at its surface to vary by 40 K from Earth's average temperature of 288 K.
 Ceres's density and thermal inertia are low enough to allow a fluid (either water or brine) to exist up to the top of the near-surface crust. This fluid may lubricate the movement of material within Ceres's interior, allowing Ceres's rotation to be maintained. The thermal inertia of Ceres's near-surface crust is lower than that of Vesta, and therefore the temperature of Ceres's surface may be more sensitive to changes in the Sun's output than Vesta's.
 Ceres has the lowest density of any object in the Solar System, which suggests that it may contain a large amount of ice. Because its density is only half that of the densest known asteroids, Ceres may contain large amounts of hydrogen or hydroxyl in the form of water. In contrast, Vesta has a density much closer to that of other asteroids. Ceres's density is very close to that of Saturn's moon Enceladus, which indicates that the two objects may have a common origin.
 As of 2012, Ceres's mass is estimated to be 9.42 × 1020 kg. This makes Ceres the second-largest object in the Solar System, with only Jupiter greater in mass. Ceres has more than twice the mass of the Moon, and nearly half the mass of Pluto. It is the largest object in the asteroid belt, and the largest of the minor planets. Ceres has a mean radius of about 500 km, making it approximately 93% of the size of Earth's Moon.
 Ceres is a relatively old object, with a surface age approximately equivalent to that of the other inner planets. Ceres is approximately 4.57 billion years old, and it is estimated to have formed 3.97 billion years ago. It may be the oldest and second-largest of the protoplanets that formed in the Solar System's early history.

It is believed that Ceres has a small, primitive core, which is probably free of ice and has a density of approximately 3,000 kg/m3. The Battle of Romani was the last ground attack of the Central Powers on the Suez Canal at the beginning of the Sinai and Pales

inian campaign of World War I. The battle took place between 3 and 5 August 1916, when the Anglo-Indian Expeditionary Force under the command of the British Lieutenant-General Sir Archibald Murray attacked the Ottoman Army, which was led by the Ottoman Army commandant, Yusuf Izzet Pasha. The Ottoman Army had occupied Romani on 3 August, having advanced from the direction of El Arish.
The British and Indian forces and reinforcements were transported in 250 buses, 60 motorcars and 200 trucks. The fighting was intense. The Ottoman forces were defeated, and the British assumed control of Romani.

The nurse shark (Ginglymostoma cirratum) is a species of requiem shark. It is a bottom-dwelling shark found in shallow coastal waters in tropical and subtropical oceans around the world. It is further known as the horned shark, carpet shark, shovelnose shark, and Zambian shark.
The nurse shark is a large shark, with a minimum length of 1.2 m (4 ft) and a maximum length of 3.5 m (12 ft). It has a stocky, rounded body with a short, rounded snout that is distinctly broad. The eyes are large and dark. There are no visible fins on the back, although the dorsal fin is located on the top of the shark's body, followed by a pair of large pectoral fins, a pair of large pelvic fins, and a large anal fin. The first dorsal fin is very large and triangular in shape, and the second dorsal fin is located much further back on the body. The caudal fin is rounded.
The head is brown to gray in color, with a white belly. The back is a darker gray to brown, often with white or off-white spots. The shark is often confused with the similar nurse shark , with which it shares the same common and scientific names. It can be distinguished by the presence of small, sharp, spines on the rear margin of the dorsal fin of the nurse shark. The nurse shark is a plankton feeding species with a varied diet, including shrimp, crab, squid, and small fish.

This layer is the place where weather begins and changes, and it is where most of the air of the atmosphere is found. This layer is the region of the atmosphere where the ozone layer resides and which displays the most dramatic seasonal variation. The highest layer of the atmosphere is the mesosphere and thermosphere, extending from about 50 km to the top of the atmosphere, about 100 km above the Earth's surface. In early 1914 James wrote an article for The Times Literary Supplement surveying the younger generation of British novelists an

article that in many respects anticipates the aims of the present book. We have already seen how James had come to pay particular attention to the relations between the generations, and here he writes: 'The action of the novel may be confined to any period, but the best of it will only be what has happened in a young man's time; and if he is not young himself he had better not write at all.' James makes clear that he is thinking of novels that are 'representative', by which he means novels that display particular, characteristic types and attitudes. This is a crucial claim, for it indicates that James is not interested in the novel as a transcript of a particular period in history, or even in the novel as an attempt to represent the world as it is, but rather as a representation of 'reality' as the novelist sees it. The younger generation, James writes, 'represents the vigour and the spirit of the present age. It will be in the very air and life of the books.' This is a bold claim, which James immediately qualifies: 'The young novelist will be a writer to be reckoned with. He will go on writing. In the course of time he will be judged.' James is here anticipating the literary historians who would come to judge these novels, but he is also anticipating the younger novelists themselves, who would write the history of their own generation.
The articles that James wrote for The Times Literary Supplement in 1914 and 1915 often display the same concern for the relations between the generations, and are a useful starting point for our investigation of the relations between two generations of British novelists in 1900 – the generation of Edwardian novelists and the generation that followed them. James's articles are a useful starting point in at least two senses: first, James was clearly aware of the debate about the new novelists that was to follow in the wake of the publication of The English Novel: An Introduction in 1913, and in these articles he is quite deliberately intervening in that debate; second, the articles were written in the years before the First World War, and were published in the years immediately after the outbreak of the war, so they are a useful point of reference for any study of the relations between the generations in British fiction at the beginning of the twentieth century.
In James's article on the 'New School of Novelists' published in the issue of The Times Literary Supplement dated 24 January 1914, he describes the generation of novelists who were, in his view, typical of the new generation of writers who were to be judged by their successors: 'The notable thing is that the first manifestation shows that the young men have the courage to face the future and will not be satisfied with the past'. ½ – 35 inches) of rain per year, to forest clearings and mountainous areas with 75 – 300 centimetres (30 – 120 inches) of rain per year. It likes dense vegetation close to permanent sources of water, and can adapt to more open habitats.
In the Kruger National Park in South Africa, females with young do not hold territories, but rather move through the habitat, moving on when the grass becomes too high. The lack of a territorial system may make the oribi more vulnerable to predation.
 The oribi is a small antelope with a white belly and chest. There are two small black spots on the chest, and one on the lower back. The rest of the body is sandy brown. Males have short, stiff horns that are twisted and turned inwards. The tail is short, and the hind legs are slightly longer than the front. The oribi is similar to the waterbuck, but is smaller and has shorter horns.
 The oribi is about 71 – 82 centimetres (28 – 32 inches) high at the shoulder and about 104 – 127 centimetres (41 – 50 inches) long, not including the tail. Males weigh about 26 – 28 kilograms (57 – 62 pounds), and females weigh 22 – 24 kilograms (49 – 53 pounds).
 The oribi feeds on a variety of plants including grass, shrubs, herbs, bulbs and trees. When available, it prefers to eat succulent plants. It also eats some leaves and flowers.
 The oribi eats small animals such as rodents, frogs, snakes, lizards and insects. It can also eat large insects.
 The oribi is a solitary animal. It is active during the night, and is most active about an hour or two after sunset. It is most active in the warm daytime. It can run up to 58 kilometres (36 miles) per hour. It can jump about 1.8 metres (6 feet) in a single bound.
 The oribi can be found near permanent water sources. These include floodplains and rivers. It also inhabits rocky outcrops, open forests and dense forests. It is found in savannahs, grasslands, woodlands, and swamps.
 The oribi lives in many different habitats in East Africa. It can be found in woodland and savannah habitat in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda. It lives in swamp forests in Tanzania. It also inhabits dense forests and bush country in Kenya. In southern Africa, it is found in dry savannah habitat in Botswana, the Limpopo Province of South Africa and Zimbabwe. It lives in woodland, swamp and forest habitat in Namibia. In West Africa, it inhabits woodland and bush country in Benin, Cameroon, the Republic of Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal and Togo.
 There are about 750,000 oribis in the wild.
 Populations have decreased because of hunting and habitat loss. In some places, it is hunted for its meat, but in other places it is protected by law and is not hunted.
Although oribis live in forests, they are often shot by poachers who mistake them for bushpigs.

Winter had arrived in London. Mr Ransome was at his desk, as usual, when the telephone rang.
'I think I'd better see you,' said the voice on the other end.
'See me about what?'
'About all sorts of things. Would you come to my office?'
'When?'
'Now.'
The voice belonged to Mr Montague Dart, the editor of the _Literary World_. The newspapers were Mr Ransome's bread and butter. They were his lifeline, and he was not at all certain that he was ready to part with them.
'I'm writing a review of _Jack and Algy_ ,' said Mr Dart. 'I can't think of it in any other way. It was the most charming piece of writing I've read for years. It's the sort of thing you ought to publish in the _National Observer_.'
'I don't think I'd make a good editor,' said Mr Ransome. 'I'm not sure I have the time.'
'I suppose,' said Mr Dart, 'it's necessary to go in for the whole show: not just the newspapers but the magazines, the novels and the poetry.'
'It's a lot to take on,' said Mr Ransome, 'but you must do what you think best. I'll come and see you now.'
Mr Dart was in his office at the _Literary World_ , which was just another one of those great beehives of publishing and printing that exist in London nowadays. In the days when the old _Literary World_ was founded, there were not so many of them.
Mr Dart was a man of fifty, just a little younger than Mr Ransome. He had been born in the East End of London and had started in journalism as a reporter in the _Daily Press_. This was a small newspaper published in the neighbourhood of the City and he wrote vigorous articles about the social conditions of the poor. Later he became the editor of a weekly paper called the _Modern World_ , which was a radical journal, strongly opposed to most of the things that the government of the day did.
Mr Dart had a small office at the _Literary World_ , where he wrote occasional articles for it and kept in touch with radical causes. Now he was pursuing Mr Ransome, who was a man of sixty, much older than himself, a man of infinite charm and courtesy, who had written a paper for the _Literary World_ about the 'discontented middle classes'. It had been published in the week before Christmas. Mr Dart had read it and he liked it. He was now after the author, hoping that he would become the editor of the _Literary World_. He was sitting at his desk, a small man with a small moustache and a small pointed beard, which made him look like a ferret.
Mr Ransome was a tall man, with a long, angular body and a head and face that were almost bald. He had a narrow, intelligent nose and a pair of wide, almost circular, eyes, which looked at you with an expression of great kindliness. He began to think about the _Literary World_ as he was walking down the stairs to Mr Dart's office.
'I like the tone of your article,' said Mr Dart. 'It's just what the _Literary World_ needs. You ought to be its editor. It only has a limited circulation, but it's a very influential journal. It can do a lot of good.'
Mr Ransome was not sure that he wanted to do a lot of good. He thought that he had better put up with the _Literary World_ for a little while. There were too many other things that he wanted to do.
'I'm not sure I'd be any good at editing,' he said.
'You'd do it very well,' said Mr Dart. 'You ought to try it. There are all sorts of things you could do with it. You could write your own articles for it, and you could get other people to write them as well. You could take a hand in the theatrical criticism.'
'I don't see that that would be any more useful than writing for the _National Observer_ ,' said Mr Ransome. 'I don't think I'd do anything except write books and articles for the magazines. The newspapers are rather different, you know, and I don't think I'm the man for them.'

#  AFRICA—A CHANGING CONTINENT
It is 1986. Africa, a continent rich in mineral resources, is now very much a continent of people. Life is changing as the continent's population grows from 300 million in 1960 to 550 million in 1986 and to 650 million in 1990. Africa is becoming more urban as the urban population grows from 15 percent in 1960 to 25 percent in 1986 and to 30 percent in 1990. Africa is a continent of increasing education as the literacy rate rises from 20 percent to 32 percent in 1986 and to 39 percent in 1990.
Africa is a continent of great diversity. The languages of Africa are as rich and varied as the people. More than 1,200 of the world's 1,500 languages are spoken in Africa, and they all belong to a family of about 100 languages.
The continent is also divided into five geographical regions, or zones, each with its own special characteristics.
The west coast zone is made up of 17 countries.
The north-east zone is made up of 11 countries.
The central zone is made up of 14 countries.
The south-east zone is made up of 21 countries.
The south-west zone is made up of 13 countries.
These 62 countries are made up of 36 states and 26 colonies.
#  SOUTH AFRICA
South Africa is a rich, beautiful country. It has a splendid climate, picturesque mountains and a glorious coastline. It has abundant mineral resources and a rich and varied culture. It has a great diversity of people, including the black majority. It has a long history of white domination and apartheid, a policy of racial discrimination.
Since 1948 racial discrimination has been the policy of the National Party government. Under apartheid, black people have been denied their rights. The right to vote, to use public facilities, to live where they want, to work where they want, to travel freely and to meet with friends and relatives have all been denied to black people.
The National Party government has been involved in a brutal war of suppression against the black majority. It has tried to drive them off their land to live in areas reserves. It has tried to destroy their culture. It has tried to make them into a cheap labor force. It has used the army, the police, the security forces and the courts to try to keep the black majority under its control.

The main attack across the Sangro by V Corps ( Lieutenant @-@ General Charles Allfrey ) , comprising the British 78th Infantry

Division , the 2nd New Zealand Division  and the Polish 2nd Corps , was one of the most daring of the entire Italian campaign. It was planned in great secrecy, with the intention of capturing the town of San Vittore, which would enable the Allied forces to cross the Sangro and take the vital agelements in the area.
The operation began on 3 December, with a series of night assaults by the British 231st Infantry Brigade and the Polish 5th Division . The attack was aimed at the villages of Rocca and Castelchiodo , and resulted in a victory for the British and Polish forces, who took 200 prisoners and destroyed several machine-gun positions.
The main part of the attack, however, was to be carried out by the 78th Infantry Division , which had to cross the Sangro River. The operation was to be conducted in three stages: the first stage, beginning on 5 December, was to be a "feint" attack on the River Sangro itself, with the objective of diverting German attention from the main thrust, which was to take place on the night of 6/7 December. The second stage, beginning on 8 December, was to be the main attack, with the objective of taking the village of San Vittore. The third stage, which was to begin on 9 December, was to be the consolidation of the bridgehead, which would enable the Allied forces to advance to the River Gari.
The plan was for the 1st South Lancashire  Regiment, supported by tanks of the 48th Royal Tank Regiment, to enter the village of San Vittore, while the 1st/48th  Royal Highlanders  (the Black Watch ) were to cross the river and take the hill that dominated the village. The remainder of the 2nd New Zealand Division was to follow up and advance on the River Gari, to occupy the bridgeheads of the 78th and 5th Divisions.
On the night of 6/7 December, the 1st South Lancashire  Regiment crossed the Sangro, and advanced to San Vittore, which they captured at 8.30 am on 7 December. The 1st/48th Royal Highlanders, however, had been unable to cross the Sangro, and the advance on the River Gari was delayed.
It was not until the 9th that the main part of the 2nd New Zealand Division was able to enter the battle. The origins of Hurricane Tanya were from a tropical wave that moved off the western coast of Africa in the middle of October .

On the 23rd of the month, the wave entered the eastern Caribbean Sea. The wave produced showers and thunderstorms as it moved across the region.  The wave moved into the western Caribbean Sea on October 26th.  Early the next day, the wave became the focus for tropical cyclone formation as the disturbance began to interact with an upper-level trough.
 A reconnaissance aircraft was dispatched to investigate the system on October 28th, while it was still southwest of Cuba.  The aircraft found a well-organized system with warm sea surface temperatures.  It had also moved into an environment favorable for tropical cyclone development.  A tropical depression formed late on October 28th shortly to the west of Jamaica.
 The depression moved to the northwest and then north during the early stages of its life cycle.  It was the first tropical cyclone of the 1990 Atlantic hurricane season.  By the next day, the system organized into a tropical storm and was named Tanya.  Tanya's track then turned to the northeast.  The storm reached hurricane strength on October 31st and reached peak winds of 75 mph (120 km/h).  Tanya slowly weakened during November 1st and 2nd, before being absorbed into a frontal system.
 Around the time when Tanya became a tropical storm, a cold front moved south from the Great Lakes region into the southeastern United States.  This front caused Tanya to turn to the northeast.  The frontal system then became the dominant force in determining the track of Tanya.  The storm's track to the northeast was what made it a threat to Bermuda.  Tanya did not pass close to Bermuda, making it the first hurricane of record to miss the island.  Tanya was the second tropical cyclone to miss Bermuda after Hurricane Floyd of 1995.
 Tanya caused damage to the fishing and tourism industries of Jamaica and the Cayman Islands.  The storm left $20.6 million (1990 USD) in damages and killed three people.  In the Cayman Islands, a woman and a child were killed by falling trees, and a boy drowned in a flooded river.  In Jamaica, a man was killed by a falling tree.  Tanya caused $3 million (1990 USD) in damages in Cuba.  One person was killed in Cuba and another in Jamaica.
In the United States, Tanya produced heavy rainfall in the Southeast United States.  The rainfall in Alabama to Florida was heavy enough to cause flooding, which caused nearly $2 million (1990 USD) in damages.  Tanya also caused minor damage in the Florida Keys.  The storm's rainfall caused two deaths in the region.  Tanya was responsible for two deaths in total.  In the United States, Tanya caused about $10 million (1990 USD) in damages.

On 2 February 1926 , Parliament voted to nationalise the Trunk Railway . During the debate , the organisation of Spisevognselsk

apet (the Norwegian Food Supply Organisation) was raised . The Food Supply Organisation was intended to provide food for 120,000 people , i.e . 20% of the population , for a period of two years . During the debate , the issue of who should be responsible for the organisation of this organisation was raised .
 The Minister of Labour and Social Affairs, Jens Hundseid, was responsible for Labour and Social Welfare , and had already announced that the Labour and Social Welfare Department would be responsible for the organisation . Labour and Social Welfare was not, however, under the auspices of the Government . It was not part of the Government structure , and was created by the Labour market law of 1919 .
 Hundseid was not present during the debate , so the Prime Minister, Trygve Bratteli , who had responsibility for Labour and Social Welfare , replied on his behalf . Bratteli explained that the Labour and Social Welfare Department was responsible for the organisation of the Labour and Social Welfare system , which included the Food Supply Organisation . The Labour and Social Welfare Department was therefore responsible for the organisation of this organisation .
 The debate on the Food Supply Organisation was a part of the debate on the Trunk Railway ( Parliamentary Debates , 18 February 1926 , p . 18 ) .
 Bratteli's explanation was reported in Parliamentary Debates , 18 February 1926 , pp. 18–24 .
 The Labour and Social Welfare Department was established by the Labour market law of 1919 . The Government's Labour and Social Welfare Department was responsible for the Labour market boards ( Arbeidstilsynet ) and was also responsible for other institutions , such as the Labour and Social Welfare Department ( Arbeids- og velferdsdepartementet ) and the Central Labour and Social Welfare Office ( Sentralarbeids- og velferdsavdelingen ) . The Labour and Social Welfare Department was in charge of the Labour market boards and the Central Labour and Social Welfare Office, which as such had responsibility for the organisation of the Labour and Social Welfare system .
 The Labour and Social Welfare Department was under the auspices of the Government . The Labour and Social Welfare Department was therefore responsible for Labour and Social Welfare , and thus also for the Food Supply Organisation .
 The Minister of Labour and Social Affairs, Jens Hundseid , was responsible for Labour and Social Welfare , and was therefore also responsible for the Food Supply Organisation .
 The National Food Supply Organisation ( Spisevognselskapet ) was established by royal resolution on 2 February 1926 . The organisation was responsible for seeing to it that the population got the rations that were necessary to maintain them in a healthy condition .
 The Labour and Social Welfare Department was established by the Labour market law of 1919 . The Labour and Social Welfare Department was responsible for, among other things, the Labour market boards and the Labour and Social Welfare Department . The Labour and Social Welfare Department was under the auspices of the Government , and was therefore responsible for Labour and Social Welfare , and thus also for the Food Supply Organisation .

Using a joystick or keyboard , the player moves his or her character through Barbarian II 's world . Each of the four stages —

the Forest ,  the Dungeon ,  the Crypt and the Mountains —  is populated with various types of monsters, which must be defeated before the player can progress to the next stage. The player can move left or right, jump, attack and pick up various items, such as swords , shields and armor .
The game is divided into four distinct stages, with each stage containing a series of levels. The Forest is the first stage in which the player must find the Warrior's Sword. The Dungeon contains three levels, and the Crypt houses four levels. The Mountains holds five levels. Each level is populated with many different types of monsters, which must be defeated before the player can progress to the next level. The game ends when the player reaches the end of the Mountains, and the player is awarded points based on the number of monsters he or she killed and the amount of treasure collected.
Barbarian II was developed by Palace Software and published by Palace Software and MicroProse for MS-DOS in September 1988. The game was later ported to the Acorn Archimedes and Commodore Amiga by Palace Software. It was also ported to the Commodore 64 by Rainbow Arts, and to the Nintendo Entertainment System by Data East. The Amiga and Commodore 64 versions were developed by Graphic State and released by Palace Software in 1990. The Amiga version was ported to the Atari ST and ZX Spectrum by Rainbow Arts, and to the Game Boy and Game Gear by Sega. The Game Boy version was developed and published by Sega in 1991, while the Game Gear version was developed by Software Creations and published by Sega in 1992. The game was re-released for the iOS operating system on November 11, 2009 and for Google Play on September 24, 2010.
